Alienware AW3926QW Review: 39 Inches of Gaming Glory
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

39-inch display size is the ultrawide sweet spot. Excellent image quality. Good connectivity, including USB-C. Lower price than competitors.
TIRED
Design is tepid. Included monitor stand allows too much wobble. Refresh rate is just 165 Hz at native resolution.
Ultrawide OLED monitors are amazing, but they’re often a bit lacking in sharpness.
Your choice has been to either accept the lower resolution these panels come with or upgrade to a massive 45-inch 5K panel, which is way too large for most desks (and comes with a much higher price tag).
Alienware’s AW3926QW offers a solution. It has a 39-inch 5K2K panel that provides a roughly 30 percent improvement in pixel density over the 34-inch alternatives. It also ships at a more tolerable (if still not affordable) price near $1,100. While a few annoyances remain, the AW3926QW will definitely appeal to gamers who want a bigger, sharper OLED ultrawide.
Sizing Up
Size and sharpness are the AW3926QW’s most important traits. The monitor has other features, which we’ll get into, but these basic characteristics set the AW3926QW apart from most OLED monitors available.
Let’s talk size first. As a 39-inch ultrawide monitor, the AW3926QW is already unique. Thirty-four inches (measured diagonally) is the standard size for ultrawide monitors, and Alienware has been a pioneer in that space since the launch of the AW3423DW in 2022. Forty-five-inch models have been introduced, but they're reserved for those who really want something almost TV-like on their desk. The AW3926QW nestles right in between, though, with a 39-inch panel—still at a 21:9 aspect ratio. Gamers who want a big display but don’t have room for a 45-inch model aren’t going to be happy with a 34-inch alternative, which looks tiny by comparison. The AW3926QW fills that gap perfectly, still offering an impressively large screen to game on.
It’s not the first to use this size (a handful of 39-inch OLED monitors with 3440 x 1440 resolution exist), but in my mind, it's the first to do it the right way. The larger the screen, the more those pixels get stretched out. You need an actual increase in pixels if you want to retain the same clarity. And that's where the Alienware AW3926QW takes a big step forward.
The panel’s resolution is 5120 x 2160, and the latter of those two numbers is key. It means the AW3926QW’s vertical resolution is equivalent to a 4K widescreen with 3,840 x 2,160 resolution, which in turn means you can view 4K content at its full resolution. That’s not possible on an ultrawide with 3,440 x 1,440 resolution.
As mentioned, some 45-inch OLED ultrawides also offer 5K2K resolution. Because they’re physically larger, however, they’re not quite as sharp as the AW3926QW.
OLED Perks Apply
Size and resolution are the AW3926QW’s distinctive traits, but the AW3926QW offers many less distinctive advantages that, though shared with many OLED monitors of various sizes, are still impressive.
Contrast is fantastic across the board. The AW3926QW can hit a perfect minimum luminance of zero nits, which means it provides an essentially infinite contrast ratio. Dark scenes provide a deep, inky black level yet also display excellent shadow detail.
The AW3926QW has an RGB stripe tandem OLED panel produced by LG. At the moment, it’s one of just two ultrawide monitors to offer the panel, which is also available from LG’s UltraGear Evo GX9. I recently tested the 27-inch Asus PG27UCWM, another RGB Strip OLED that I was impressed by, but it's a standard 16:9 aspect ratio rather than ultrawide. RGB Stripe OLED panels use a different sub-pixel array to produce better color performance at high brightness and sharper text.
The AW3926QW is bright for an OLED monitor. It quotes a maximum SDR brightness of 300 nits, which my testing confirmed. HDR, meanwhile, is quoted at a peak brightness of 1,300 nits. I didn’t manage to hit that, but I did record a peak brightness up to 1,011 nits, which is at the upper end of what the best OLED monitors can deliver.
Color performance is excellent. The color gamut spans 99 percent of DCI-P3 and 93 percent of AdobeRGB. These are excellent figures and comparable to the best OLED monitors on the market. Color accuracy was high. The monitor’s color performance isn’t just excellent for games; many creative professionals will also find it sufficient for work.
Meanwhile, the AW3926QW’s price of roughly $1,100 isn’t inexpensive, but it’s a lot less than the LG Ultragear Evo GX9, which debuted at an MSRP near $1,800 and currently retails around $1,600. So, what’s the catch?
It’s not connectivity. The AW3926QW has two HDMI 2.1 inputs, one DisplayPort 2.1 UHBR20 input, and one USB-C input that also supports DisplayPort 2.1 and provides 90 watts of power delivery. All of the video inputs can handle the monitor’s maximum resolution and refresh rate.
The monitor has a lot of downstream connectivity, too. It includes three downstream USB-A ports with a 5-Gbps data rate. You’ll also find a single downstream USB-C port with the same data rate and support for up to 15 watts of power delivery. A 3.5-mm audio jack rounds out the connectivity options.
Some Cost Cutting
The Alienware’s lower price is more evident in the monitor’s look and build quality.
As I’ve put on record across multiple reviews, I’m not a fan of Alienware’s current design language. I think it’s too basic and demure for the Alienware brand. Aside from the AW3926QW’s curved design, which is noticeable even at a glance, nothing about the monitor stands out. Even the curve is not that remarkable, as most ultrawide monitors are curved.
While I don’t like the look of the monitor, it’s a stretch to say it’s a problem. You’re not going to open the box and gasp in horror at the hideous sight you behold. On the contrary, the monitor’s design is inoffensive. Even boring.
I have a nitpick about the stand’s operation, however. It offers up to 4.3 inches of height adjustment, which is useful. However, the stand is a little too flexible. It allows the display to slightly wobble and shake while typing, though only at the upper end of the monitor’s height adjustment. It’s not a deal-breaker, but it could be better.
Motion clarity is this monitor's other sore spot. The Alienware AW3926QW offers a refresh rate of up to 165 Hz at native resolution. That’s not bad, but most modern 34-inch ultrawides hit 240 Hz, and some can hit 360 Hz. Most are less expensive as well.
Don’t get me wrong. The AW3926QW’s motion clarity remains excellent if it’s compared broadly to, say, all monitors to have ever existed in history. Small objects are often legible, scenes maintain detail during quick camera pans, and motion blur is often easy to miss. But it would be incorrect to suggest there’s no meaningful difference between a 165-Hz and a 360-Hz display. I’ve reviewed many of them, and I find the difference is obvious. Does a 165-Hz OLED look crisp in motion? Yes. Is 360 Hz clearly, distinctly, obviously better? Yes.
Alienware tries to mitigate the problem with a trick that many high-end gaming monitors now support: a lower display resolution mode with a higher refresh rate. The AW3926QW can hit a refresh rate up to 330 Hz if you reduce the resolution to 2,560 x 1,080. Unfortunately, 2,560 x 1,080 resolution is terribly dull on a 39-inch display. It works out to a pixel density only a hair better than a 32-inch 1080p widescreen, which is dismal for any computer monitor sold in 2026.
Personally, I don’t mind the 165-Hz refresh rate despite the fact that I can notice the difference, but I usually play RPGs and strategy games. Players who enjoy competitive esports titles, or who otherwise want the best motion clarity and fluidity possible, could find the 165-Hz refresh rate too low for their liking.
Walking the Line
The year isn’t over, but the Alienware AW3926QW already looks like one of the best new monitors of 2026. That’s not because it’s a game-changing monitor on its own merit (though I do think it’s very good), but instead because it fills a gap in the ultrawide monitor market.
The existing 34-inch OLED ultrawides with 3,440 x 1,440 resolution are in many ways fantastic, but they’re not all that large or sharp. Forty-five-inch ultrawides deliver the immersion and sharpness that the 34-inch alternatives lack, but they’re often too large to fit on a conventional desk, and they’re extremely expensive.
Alienware’s AW3926QW walks the line between these options. It’s big but not too big. It’s sharp but not too expensive. And it otherwise retains the perks that gamers have come to expect from OLED monitors, aside from a small hit to the refresh rate. Highly competitive gamers should look elsewhere, but gamers looking for big-screen immersion should put the AW3926QW on their short list.

2027 eclipse sends prices soaring: Up to €33,129 a night in El Palmar
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
12:58:46 UTC
21:58:46 KST

With almost a year to go, accommodation prices in southern Spain are soaring, with some stays already reaching €33,129 for a single night.
Although there is still almost a year to go, the total solar eclipse of 2 August 2027 is already driving up prices in some of the destinations that will offer the best views.
Accommodation bookings have multiplied in provinces such as Cádiz, Málaga, Granada and Almería, and prices have risen along with them.
The eclipse will be visible from much of Spain, but only in Andalusia, Ceuta and Melilla will it be possible to see the Moon completely cover the Sun.
In Tarifa, one of the most sought-after spots, total darkness will last 4 minutes and 38 seconds. In Ceuta it will reach 4 minutes and 48 seconds, according to the National Geographic Institute. Egypt will be the place in the world where the eclipse can be seen in full for the longest period, at 6 minutes and 23 seconds.
The rush to find a good spot to watch it is already evident on accommodation platforms. In El Palmar, a villa for six people located around 600 metres from the beach will cost €33,129 for one night. Split between the six potential guests, that would be around €5,522 per person.
In Tarifa there are also prices that are hard to ignore. For two adults between 1 and 2 August, one search returns three properties at €13,260, €12,500 and €11,090 per night, respectively. And there is still almost a year to go before the eclipse.
Interest in the eclipse was already evident on 12 August, when the total solar eclipse that crossed Spain generated an economic impact of €347.6 million and attracted around 446,000 international tourists.
The United States was the main country of origin outside Europe, followed by Canada and Argentina, while there was also a notable influx of British visitors and Japanese tourists, drawn in particular by astrotourism.
With that precedent, the tourism sector is already preparing for a new surge in demand. Some hotels in Cádiz have even temporarily closed their bookings due to the volume of requests for August 2027, while interest continues to grow in astrotourism and in destinations where the spectacle can be enjoyed for longer.

The Public’s Opinion about Philosophy in Universities
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
12:55:37 UTC
21:55:37 KST

The Public’s Opinion about Philosophy in Universities
“How important is it for a typical university to maintain a department in each of the following fields?”
A survey by Polarization Research Lab asked people that question. 15 fields were listed, and respondents were given four options:
- Essential — a university should always have this department
- Important, but could be cut if necessary
- Not very important
- This department should be cut.
The field with the most public support, according to this survey, is English, with 86% of the respondents calling it “Essential” and another 11% calling it “Important”. In spots 2 and 3 were Mathematics and History. Very few deemed these fields “not very important” or said they “should be cut”.
At the bottom of the list was Gender and Sexuality Studies, with 24% of the responses saying it is “Essential,” 28% saying it is “Important”, 21% saying “not very important,” and 28% saying “should be cut.”
Where does philosophy fall on the list? Close to the bottom, with 34% calling it “Essential,” 45% calling it “Important”, 17% saying it is “not very important”, and 4% saying it should be cut.
The following graph shows the results. It was brought to my attention by Philippe-Antoine Hoyeck (Carleton University), who shared and wrote about it in a thread on X.com.
Mr. Hoyeck says the lesson here is that “philosophers have done a pretty woeful job of marketing ourselves as the people who can teach and employ… crucial [critical thinking] skills”.
Discussion welcome.

Tallinn's Knitting Raves put a crafty spin on local soft clubbing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
12:55:00 UTC
21:55:00 KST

Tallinn's Knitting Raves put a crafty spin on local soft clubbing
A Tallinn party series is inviting people to knit and crochet on the dancefloor, offering a late-evening alternative to nightclubs for beginners and veteran crafters alike.
Knitting Raves at Põhjala Factory welcome everyone from seasoned crafters to those who have never picked up needles or a crochet hook before. Organizers say dancing while knitting is easier than it sounds, and the environment can be pretty inspiring.
One organizer, Kaari Põlder, said she herself got back into crocheting thanks to the event.
"You can do anything while knitting, even dance," Põlder said, adding she was surprised by how quickly she got the hang of it. "Before attending a knitting rave, I hadn't been involved in any crafting in over 20 years."
Knitting Raves run from 6–10 p.m. at Põhjala Factory's ankruSAAL, with two DJs each playing two-hour sets of dance music and even taking requests.
People of all ages and genders are welcome, and those who would rather sit and craft can do so too.
The organizers got the idea after seeing videos of similar events in Amsterdam, where knitting raves have become popular.
"Soft clubbing" in general has gained momentum as well, offering alternatives to traditional nightlife with morning coffee shop raves, daytime dance parties and other alcohol-free events.
"Parties don't have to start so late," Põlder emphasized. "They can start at a decent hour."
Bring your own yarn, or don't
Organizer and crafts teacher Kristiin Sidok said the combination of crafting and dancing can be contagious, with some attendees arriving without a craft project in hand and leaving inspired to try one.
"You might think, 'Oh I'll just come for fun, I won't take anything with me,'" she said. "But there were several people who caught the crafting bug while there."
Sidok recommends sticking to a simple project over anything with a complicated pattern, making it easier to multitask and even chat with those around you.
"You don't have to tackle some intense project," she said.
While Sidok had made herself a special yarn bag to carry while dancing, Põlder said attendees can also borrow one on site. Craft supplies are available for purchase as well, and anyone who gets stuck with their project can turn to Sidok for help.
Põhjala Factory's next Knitting Rave kicks off this Friday at 6 p.m.

Former Bosnian Serb general Ratko Mladic convicted of genocide dies
Former Bosnian Serb military leader Ratko Mladic, convicted of genocide in the 1992-95 war in Bosnia, has died in the United Nations detention centre in The Hague after suffering several strokes, according to local media.
Ratko Mladic, the former Bosnian Serb military chief dubbed the "Butcher of Bosnia" for his role in the 1995 Srebrenica massacre, has died, Serbian state broadcaster RTS reported on Thursday.
Mladic, who had suffered several strokes in recent months, was serving a life sentence in The Hague for genocide, war crimes, and crimes against humanity after overseeing the Srebrenica slaughter, Europe's worst act of bloodshed since World War II.
Serbian state officials and Mladic's family had appealed for his release due to his failing health, but those calls were rejected by the Hague tribunal.
Read moreWho was Ratko Mladic, the 'Butcher of Bosnia'?
He was the military face of a brutal trio, led on the political side by ex-Yugoslav president Slobodan Milosevic and former Bosnian Serb leader Radovan Karadzic, as the former Yugoslavia descended into carnage after the fall of communism.
The 1992-1995 war left around 100,000 people dead and 2.2 million displaced.
The most infamous atrocity was committed in Srebrenica, where Serb forces under Mladic's command executed 8,000 Bosnian Muslim men and boys who had sought shelter in what was meant to be a UN-protected enclave.
(FRANCE 24 with Reuters)

Bosnian Serb convicted war criminal Ratko Mladic has died, Serbian TV reports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
12:52:00 UTC
21:52:00 KST

Ex-Bosnian Serb military leader Ratko Mladic dead at 84
August 27, 2026
Bosnian Serb general Ratko Mladic, who was serving a life sentence for war crimes committed during Bosnia's 1992-95 war, a United Nations official said.
Serbian state broadcaster RTS reported on Thursday that he died in a prison hospital in the Hague, after suffering several strokes.
A family member of Mladic, who spoke on condition of anonymity because of the sensitivity of the situation, confirmed the reports to the Associated Press and said Mladic’s son, Darko Mladic, was on the way to the Hague.
The International Criminal Court for the former Yugoslavia (ICTY) convicted Mladic of charges including crimes against humanity and genocide in 2017, handing him a life sentence. The verdict was confirmed on appeal in 2021.
'The butcher of Bosnia'
Mladic was held responsible for his role in the 1992 to 1995 war in Bosnia, including July 1995 massacre of some 8,000 Muslim men and boys at Screbrenica.
The slaughter, the worst single atrocity in Europe since World War II, saw him named the "Butcher of Bosnia."
Under Mladic's command, Bosnian Serb forces besieged Sarajevo and other towns, operated detention camps for non-Serbs and enemy soldiers, and systematically killed prisoners.
Former UN rights chief Zeid Ra'ad al Hussein described him as "the epitome of evil" after his conviction.
"This is all lies, you are all liars," he shouted when he was sentenced to life in prison in 2017.
This is a developing story. Please refresh for updates...

Iran, Qatar top diplomats hold talks on Hormuz in Tehran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
12:51:57 UTC
21:51:57 KST

Iran's top diplomat has met his Qatari counterpart in Tehran for talks on the strategic Strait of Hormuz.
The visit by Qatar's Foreign Minister Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani on Thursday follows a week of intense diplomacy in Iran, involving separate meetings with Oman's top diplomat and senior Pakistani officials, seeking ways to end the Middle East war and reopen the Strait of Hormuz.
It also comes as Washington threatens wider secondary sanctions against countries, banks and companies that continue doing business with Iran, part of a broader campaign it has called "economic asphyxiation".
Iranian state television said Al Thani, who is also Qatar's prime minister, had met with Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi without providing details.
Qatar's foreign ministry said it discussed de-escalation efforts as well as the proposed Hormuz framework between Iran and Oman.
Al Thani "emphasised the necessity of respecting the sovereignty of neighbouring states and freedom of navigation" and pursuing dialogue, the ministry said.
Alongside mediator Pakistan, Qatar had played a key role in securing an April ceasefire and a June deal between Iran and the United States, but those deals have since collapsed.
‘Economic war’
Since war with the United States broke out on February 28, Iran has maintained tight control over Hormuz, a vital global energy conduit, with Washington imposing a naval counter-blockade on Iranian ports.
On Wednesday, Iran's Vice President Mohammad Jafar Ghaempanah said the blockade had prevented his country from importing enough petrol to cover a shortfall in domestic production.
"Petrol production is insufficient, and because of the US naval blockade, we cannot import it," he was quoted by the official IRNA news agency as saying.
In recent days, many Iranians have been seen queuing outside petrol stations.
Presidential chief of staff Mohsen Haji-Mirzaei, meanwhile, said petrol quotas would be reviewed, without elaborating.
As the United States seeks to strangle Iran's economy, Iranian officials have dismissed the measures as "failed policies" that will not force Tehran to change course.
"The country is in an all-out economic war," said Iran's top negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf in a statement carried by local media.
"We will see that the government will defeat the enemy on this ground as well," he added.
Even before the war, Iran's economy was battered by decades of international sanctions.
Iran has for weeks been in talks with Oman, which also overlooks the Hormuz Strait, over a framework agreement that would establish a "temporary corridor" for shipping and provide for clearing mines Tehran says were laid during the war.

'Butcher Of Bosnia' Ratko Mladic Dies Aged 84
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
12:51:20 UTC
21:51:20 KST

Bosnian Serb wartime military commander Ratko Mladic, known as the "Butcher of Bosnia," has died aged 84 in The Hague where he was serving a life sentence for genocide and crimes against humanity.
He was found guilty by an international court of genocide committed against around 8,000 Bosniaks in Srebrenica, a United Nations-protected area, in the summer of 1995, of terrorizing civilians during the siege of Sarajevo, and other war crimes during the 1992-95 war in Bosnia-Herzegovina.
Mladic was arrested in Serbia on May 26, 2011. He had been the most wanted Hague fugitive, having evaded justice for almost 16 years, before he was finally detained and transferred to the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia (ICTY) in The Hague.
The Hague Tribunal sentenced him to life imprisonment on June 8, 2021, following a marathon trial that documented in shocking details some of the worst atrocities of the Bosnian war.
During the trial, which began on May 16, 2012, and lasted 530 days, 592 witnesses were called and around 10,000 pieces of evidence were presented.
Ill Health
Mladic had suffered several strokes in recent months, leading to appeals for his release on humanitarian grounds by his family and also by Serbian officials. The Hague tribunal rejected those requests, the latest of which was filed on August 18.
"The interests of justice and general legal principles do not require release merely because imminent death is expected," said Judge Graciela Gatti Santana, explaining the decision on August 26.
"The punishment, in addition to being a deterrent, should express the international community's condemnation of the conduct in question and its unwillingness to tolerate serious violations of international humanitarian law and human rights," she added.

Massive Russian attack on the Kyiv region: warehouses belonging to Fora and ROSHEN, as well as the distribution centers of COMFY and Budynok Ihрашok, were damaged
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
15:51:06 EEST
21:51:06 KST

Massive Russian attack on the Kyiv region: warehouses belonging to Fora and ROSHEN, as well as the distribution centers of COMFY and Budynok Ihрашok, were damaged
Kyiv • UNN
The massive Russian attack on August 27 damaged logistics facilities belonging to Fora and COMFY, as well as those of Budynok Ihрашok and ROSHEN. There were no casualties.
As a result of the massive Russian attack on August 27, the logistics infrastructure of several major Ukrainian retailers was affected at once. In the Kyiv region, a warehouse used by the "Fora" chain was damaged, a Russian drone attacked COMFY's distribution center, and the logistics center of the "Budynok Ihrashok" chain was destroyed. In addition, a ROSHEN warehouse was destroyed, UNN reports, citing statements posted by the retailers on social media.
The third attack on "Fora's" logistics facilities in August
In the Kyiv region, a warehouse used by the "Fora" supermarket chain was affected by the Russian attack. According to the company, the chain began operating at this facility only a few days ago. No people were injured during the attack.
The "Fora" chain's supermarkets continue to operate for now, while the company is once again forced to restructure its logistics and look for alternative routes for supplying goods.
It should be noted that today's attack is already the third strike on the logistics infrastructure used by the retailer. On the night of August 5, Russian forces destroyed warehouses containing fresh and frozen products and also significantly damaged a warehouse for shelving goods. At that time, the company lost inventories, equipment, machinery, and warehouse systems. The preliminary amount of damage was estimated at approximately UAH 1.15 billion.
The chain's logistics operations suffered another strike on August 20. At that time, the occupiers attacked with strike drones a warehouse in the Boryspil district, which "Fora" had begun using approximately a week before the attack as a replacement for the lost facilities. Preliminary losses of goods and equipment were estimated at more than UAH 100 million.
A Russian drone attacked COMFY's distribution center
Also, on the morning of August 27, a Russian drone attacked the COMFY chain's distribution center in the Kyiv region. The company reported that employees were in equipped shelters during the attack, so there were no casualties. After the strike, the company's teams switched to an enhanced operating mode. COMFY's stores and online channels continue to operate, orders are being fulfilled, and the contact center remains in communication with customers.
At the same time, as of the afternoon of August 27, the company had not reported the complete destruction of the distribution center or disclosed a preliminary estimate of the damage.
COMFY had previously begun decentralizing its logistics because of the persistent risks of Russian attacks. The company's goods are distributed among a large number of storage locations in different regions, while the central distribution center largely operates as a cross-docking platform through which products are quickly routed to stores.
The Russian Armed Forces destroyed the distribution center of "Budynok Ihrashok"
The logistics infrastructure of the "Budynok Ihrashok" chain suffered the greatest destruction during the attack. The company's CEO, Mariia Nazarenko, reported that the chain's distribution center was almost completely destroyed as a result of the Russian strike.
A significant portion of the company's inventory was stored at the facility. Goods were dispatched from there every day to the chain's stores and to customers throughout Ukraine.
The company warned that the destruction of the logistics center could temporarily affect internal processes and delivery times for some orders.
The brick-and-mortar "Budynok Ihrashok" stores continue to operate, and the online store is also accepting new orders. At the same time, some orders placed earlier may be delivered later than scheduled.
If it becomes impossible to fulfill individual paid orders because of the consequences of the attack, customers have been promised refunds. It should be noted that the company has not yet disclosed the amount of the damage, the value of the destroyed inventory, or the estimated timeframe for fully restoring logistics operations.
ROSHEN warehouse destroyed
On the morning of August 27, a ROSHEN warehouse in Chubynske, which provided for the storage and subsequent supply of finished confectionery products, was destroyed as a result of Russia's massive attack on Ukraine.
The most important thing is that none of the employees were injured: thanks to compliance with safety rules and a timely response to the air raid alert, all employees were in the shelter. State Emergency Service units are working at the site; the aftermath is being addressed and the damage is being assessed. This is already the second attack on ROSHEN's warehouse facilities since the start of the full-scale invasion — in February, a finished-goods warehouse in Yahotyn was destroyed. The latest attack also caused significant material losses, including the loss of products, so temporary disruptions in the supply of certain goods may occur in the near future
The team is already working on redistributing stocks and engaging alternative warehousing facilities in order to reduce possible disruptions as much as possible and minimize their impact on partners and consumers.
Context
Constant attacks on logistics infrastructure are forcing Ukrainian retailers to abandon the concentration of large inventories at a single facility, distribute goods among several warehouses, increase direct deliveries to stores, and establish backup logistics routes.
We remind you
During the night of August 27, Russia launched another massive combined attack on Ukraine using missiles and attack drones. The Kyiv region was one of the main targets. Damage to warehouses and other facilities was recorded in the region.

How a glacier collapse may have triggered the Nepal-Tibet disaster
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
12:49:46 UTC
21:49:46 KST

While individual glacial events cannot be directly attributed to climate change, experts say rising global temperatures are putting increasing pressure on glaciers.
A massive piece of ice that fell thousands of metres from a glacier into a river below may have triggered the disaster in Nepal and Tibet.
Scientists are still piecing together information from satellite and ground-level data to figure out exactly what happened to cause the flood, which killed at least 353 people and left more than 1,300 missing, including foreigners and pilgrims.
"A large chunk of glacier fell from about 5,200 metres into a valley," said Simon Cox, principal scientist at New Zealand's GNS Science.
It "transformed into this raging mass of debris... where it picks up rocks and sediment and trees and anything in the way and fires it on down through the canyon," he told AFP.
The wall of water first hit a border post, with CCTV footage showing mud and debris engulfing the area as people fled. It then travelled downstream into Nepal, flooding villages and destroying bridges and buildings.
What caused the wall of water?
Early speculation suggested a glacial lake outburst flood (GLOF), which occurs when a barrier holding back glacial meltwater suddenly collapses and releases the water downstream.
"Water does flow within glaciers and flows beneath glaciers," said Adrian McCallum, a glaciologist at the University of the Sunshine Coast.
"But to my mind, the only reason why a large volume of water should all of a sudden flow down a valley is because it has been released," he told AFP.
However, other experts said they found no existing glacial lakes near the site of the collapse. They suggested that water may instead have accumulated beneath the glacier and been released as the ice fell.
Another possibility is that the falling ice temporarily dammed the river, allowing water to build up before being suddenly released.
Summer glacier melt and monsoon rains may also have already raised river levels, while debris and mud picked up along the way further increased the volume of the flow, according to Cox.
Water levels across the flood-affected region rose by as much as nine metres in just 30 minutes following the surge from the glacier collapse, according to researchers at a Kathmandu-based climate research group.
“It was a huge rise, a huge surge of water that happened suddenly,” Saswata Sanyal said.
The glacier collapse was powerful enough to register as a magnitude 5.2 seismic event at 8:37 am (4:52 am CEST) and was initially mistaken for an earthquake.
After further analysis, the US Geological Survey determined that the event was a glacial collapse and debris flow and that no earthquake had occurred.
How satellites helped reconstruct the disaster
With much of the affected area inaccessible, experts are using satellite imagery and available ground measurements to reconstruct the disaster.
"We can look at satellite imagery taken before and after the event, and try and see what has changed, essentially looking for what is missing from the mountains in the 'after' imagery," said Lauren Vargo, a glaciologist at New Zealand's Victoria University of Wellington.
Shortly after the seismic activity was recorded, a nearby water monitoring station stopped transmitting, according to Nepali authorities.
Stations downstream then began going offline one by one. Water levels in Kalikhola, near the Tibet border, reached up to 12.3 metres at 2:14 pm (10:29 am CEST), authorities said.
Why warnings may not have been enough
Nepali authorities first received reports of flooding at around 9:00 am local time (5:15 am CEST) and warned communities along the Bhote Khoshi river to "stay on high alert and stay in safe areas".
However, it remains unclear how many people received the warning or how much time they had to respond.
"The reality is, if you are in a community underneath a large glacier and potentially a glacier lake where a GLOF could occur, then to some extent, it's a ticking time bomb," said McCallum.
Even for those who received a warning, options would have been limited, said Hatim Sharif, a hydrologist at the University of Texas San Antonio.
"Running will not help," nor will trying to flee by vehicle, he told AFP, because the mud and water moving at high speed form a lethal combination "like liquid concrete."
The only solution is to climb up a hill, at least six metres, he estimated.

Crews have spent a week battling a wildfire in the mountains near Yalta. It broke out after a Ukrainian drone attack, though occupation officials won’t say what caused it.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
12:48:57 UTC
21:48:57 KST

Crews have spent a week battling a wildfire in the mountains near Yalta. It broke out after a Ukrainian drone attack, though occupation officials won’t say what caused it.
Firefighters have been battling a forest fire in the mountains near Yalta, in occupied Crimea, for more than a week. The fire was first reported on August 19, when it covered just over three hectares. Two days later, strong winds caused it to spread to 50 hectares. Authorities declared a regional state of emergency due to the natural disaster. More than 600 people are now working to put out the fire. Yanina Pavlenko, the Russian-installed head of Yalta’s administration, called reports of a “shortage of personnel and equipment, inaction by emergency services, and fundraising for firefighting efforts” fake news. Authorities have not officially stated the cause of the fire. As the BBC Russian Service reported, the fire began after Ukrainian drones attacked Yalta overnight on August 19. Local residents link the fire to the drone attack and the air defense response, one resident told the outlet. Meduza is publishing photos and videos of the forest fire.

Broadcaster Jenni Murray died days after north London car crash, inquest hears
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
12:44:31 UTC
21:44:31 KST

The broadcaster Jenni Murray died days after being involved in a car crash that happened when she was dazzled by headlights, a coroner has heard.
Murray, 75, was best known as the voice of BBC Radio 4’s Woman’s Hour, hosting the programme for three decades and becoming the longest-serving presenter in its history.
She died on 12 March this year after the collision in north London eight days earlier, the inquest into her death heard on Thursday.
The north London area coroner Tony Murphy ruled Murray’s cause of death was bronchopneumonia caused by fractures to her rib and sternum sustained in the crash.
At the inquest at Barnet coroner’s court, Murphy read a statement from Dr Clare Morkane, a consultant at the Royal Free hospital, where Murray died after being admitted on 4 March.
“Jennifer had been driving when she became dazzled by vehicle lights and collided with two stationary vehicles. Following the collision, Jennifer was unable to recall events, exited the vehicle independently and she was conveyed to hospital,” Morkane said.
The collision took place on Wildwood Road, adjacent to Hampstead Heath, shortly before 8pm, the inquest heard. It caused “multiple rib fractures”, a fracture to her upper sternum and a collapsed lung.
In hospital, Murray was placed on non-invasive ventilation and moved to intensive care but developed bronchopneumonia. Morkane said that after a significant deterioration on 10 March, a decision was made to focus on palliative care. “Jennifer died peacefully on 12 March 2026 at approximately 15.45 hours,” she said.
The Metropolitan police investigated the crash but closed their inquiry.
Murray’s husband, David Forgham-Bailey, attended the hearing via video link.
After Murray’s death, the former Labour deputy leader Harriet Harman called her “the broadcasting wing of the women’s movement”.
Murray announced on Woman’s Hour in 2006 that she had been diagnosed with breast cancer and began raising awareness of the condition as a vice-patron for Breast Cancer Now, a position she held for almost 20 years. She was made a dame in 2011 in recognition of her contribution to broadcasting.
Murray was a noted feminist and a celebrated broadcaster. Her final episode of Woman’s Hour in 2020 ended with Helen Reddy’s feminist anthem I Am Woman. Woman’s Hour won the Television and Radio Industries Club award for best radio programme in 2004, and Murray was honoured with Sony awards in 2010 and 2011.

“I jumped from my chair” – Astronomers spot Betelgeuse’s hidden companion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
12:43:27 UTC
21:43:27 KST

“I jumped from my chair” – Astronomers spot Betelgeuse’s hidden companion
- Date:
- August 27, 2026
- Source:
- ESO
- Summary:
- Astronomers have captured their clearest image yet of Betelgeuse’s long-suspected companion, potentially ending a search that lasted about 100 years. The surprisingly massive hidden star could help explain Betelgeuse’s changing brightness and may influence its future supernova.
- Share:
Astronomers now have their strongest evidence yet that Betelgeuse, one of the best-known stars in the night sky, has a stellar companion. A team led by French astronomer Miguel Montargès used the European Southern Observatory's Very Large Telescope (ESO's VLT) to capture the clearest image so far of what is believed to be Betelgeuse B, a star orbiting the famous red supergiant.
"This is the conclusion of a century-long quest," says Montargès.
"We have shown that Betelgeuse is not single, it is accompanied by a faint stellar companion," says Montargès, astronomer at the Observatoire de Paris -- PSL, France, and lead author of the study published today in Astronomy & Astrophysics.
Betelgeuse -- a reddish star in the Orion constellation that is easily visible with the naked eye and is known to change in brightness -- has been watched by people for thousands of years. Even after centuries of scientific observation, however, the star continues to produce surprises.
A Century-Long Search for Betelgeuse B
"I jumped from my chair when I saw the processed images," recalls Montargès.
The possibility that Betelgeuse has a companion was first raised roughly a century ago as a potential explanation for some of its changes in brightness. Despite decades of observations, astronomers had been unable to clearly detect such a star.
That changed after Two studies published in 2024 made strong predictions about where the suspected companion should be. The studies indicated that Betelgeuse B would reach its greatest apparent separation from Betelgeuse in December 2024, giving astronomers their best opportunity to see it.
Montargès and his colleagues observed Betelgeuse with ESO's VLT that December. They then spent several months carefully processing and analyzing the observations.
"Honestly, I thought we did not have the sensitivity to detect Betelgeuse B as it was predicted," explains Montargès. "Because it is more massive than predicted, we see it!"
Scientists had initially estimated that the companion would have roughly the same mass as the Sun. The new observations instead suggest that Betelgeuse B is considerably larger, with about two to three times the Sun's mass.
"The fact that we can still discover a nearby companion, more massive and brighter than the Sun, around such a well-studied star is remarkable," says Montargès. "These are among the best moments in science: seeing something new, unexpected."
The Clearest Image Yet of Betelgeuse's Companion
The researchers directly imaged Betelgeuse B, meaning they detected light coming from the companion itself. They accomplished this using the SPHERE instrument on ESO's VLT in Chile's Atacama Desert.
Previous observations had already provided clues that the companion existed, including a possible direct detection made with the Gemini North Telescope in Hawaiʻi, USA. The latest VLT observations, however, provide the strongest evidence so far and the clearest image yet of Betelgeuse B.
"It is remarkable to see how SPHERE and advanced post-processing techniques, originally developed to find exoplanets, also excel at detecting a companion around a massive, evolved star like Betelgeuse," says co-author Anthony Boccaletti, also an astronomer at the Observatoire de Paris.
The case is not considered completely closed yet. Astronomers want another observation showing the candidate companion where its orbit predicts it should next appear.
"To be certain that the companion is really there, we still need to observe it in one year on the other side of the star, but there is very little space left for doubt," adds Montargès.
Betelgeuse's Famous Dimming Event
Betelgeuse attracted worldwide attention several years ago when its brightness noticeably dropped. Because the evolved supergiant is expected to eventually end its life in a supernova explosion, the dramatic dimming prompted speculation that the star might be preparing to explode.
That turned out not to be the explanation. A team led by Montargès studied the star with ESO's VLT and found that a cloud of dust was instead blocking part of Betelgeuse's light.
Now the likely discovery of Betelgeuse B introduces another factor astronomers must consider when studying the star's evolution.
Could the Companion Affect Betelgeuse's Supernova?
Researchers will now investigate whether Betelgeuse B could influence the future evolution of the red supergiant, including its eventual supernova explosion.
"The question is truly opened whether this companion is going to have an impact on the evolution of the red supergiant," concludes Montargès.
The research was presented in a paper titled "VLT/SPHERE images the candidate companion of Betelgeuse" to appear in Astronomy & Astrophysics.
The team is composed of M. Montargès (Laboratoire d'Instrumentation et de Recherche en Astrophysique, Observatoire de Paris, Université PSL, Sorbonne Université, Université Paris Cité, CY Cergy Paris Université, CNRS, France [LIRA]), A. Boccaletti (LIRA), O. Flasseur (Universite Claude Bernard Lyon 1, Centre de Recherche Astrophysique de Lyon UMR5574, ENS de Lyon, CNRS, France), A. de Koter (University of Amsterdam, Anton Pannekoek Institute for Astronomy, The Netherlands), J. Milli (Univ. Grenoble Alpes, CNRS, IPAG, France), P. Kervella (French-Chilean Laboratory for Astronomy, IRL 3386, CNRS and U. de Chile, Chile and LIRA), S. Ridgway (National Optical Astronomy Observatory, USA), E. Bordier (I. Physikalisches Institut der Universität zu Köln, Germany), E. Lagadec (Université Côte dAzur, Observatoire de la Côte dAzur, CNRS, Laboratoire Lagrange, France), A. K. Dupree (Center for Astrophysics-Harvard & Smithsonian, USA), F. Backs (Institute of Astronomy, KU Leuven, Belgium), T. Calderwood (American Association of Variable Star Observers, USA [AAVSO]), and P. Morgan (AAVSO).
Story Source:
Materials provided by ESO. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- M. Montargès, A. Boccaletti, O. Flasseur, A. de Koter, J. Milli, P. Kervella, S. Ridgway, E. Bordier, E. Lagadec, A. K. Dupree, F. Backs, T. Calderwood, P. Morgan. VLT/SPHERE images of the candidate companion of Betelgeuse. Astronomy, 2026; 711: L12 DOI: 10.1051/0004-6361/202661023

The literary scandal of the year? Rachel Cusk's 'Life of M' / Natalie Portman drama explained
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
12:42:14 UTC
21:42:14 KST

Is Natalie Portman really the subject of Rachel Cusk’s new novel? Or is this manufactured literary drama designed to generate buzz?
One of the most talked about literary releases of the week, nay the year, is “Life of M”, the new novel by critically acclaimed and award-winning British author Rachel Cusk.
Known for her novels “The Lucky Ones”, the Outline Trilogy (“Outline”, “Transit” and “Kudos”), “Second Place”, as well as the Goldsmiths Prize-winning book “Parade”, Cusk’s name isn’t one you’d expect to be associated with headline-grabbing controversy or gossip.
Still, here we are and all anyone can talk about is the buzz around “Life of M” - specifically: Is the titular M a fictionalised version of Natalie Portman?
The novel, billed by its publisher, Farrar, Straus and Giroux, as a “blazing interrogation of fame, power, beauty and truth”, has got literary sleuths wondering whether it’s a not-so-thinly-veiled and unflattering portrait of the Oscar-winning actress.
“Life of M” follows an unnamed writer who wishes to use a famous actress, M, as a source of inspiration for her next literary project. The writer chronicles the A-lister's life and portrays “one of the most recognisable faces of our time” as a dispassionate and self-righteous person who puts on a relatable facade to mask the poseur within.
Shots fired?
According to reports, yes, as the similarities between M and Portman are too blatant and numerous to ignore.
These parallels were first reported by Unherd reviewer Valerie Stivers, who wrote that Portman “has long seemed more like a person who wants to brand herself as smart than like a person who is actually smart - and her decision to let her friend Rachel Cusk write a book about her seems to confirm this.”
As reviews of “Life of M” trickle in, many readers are adding fuel to the fire by listing numerous overlaps. For instance, on page three, M describes her experiences as a child star, acting in a film that “immediately brought her childhood to an end”.
Many have drawn parallels with Léon: The Professional, as Portman was 11 years old when she was cast and 13 when the movie was filmed.
M also says her parents requested that scenes be cut from the script, and that she was bullied at school after the film came out.
Both these details have been shared publicly by Portman.
There’s also an early reference to M’s “starring role in a film about a young girl chosen for the starring role in a ballet”.
Again, many went straight for Black Swan, the film in which Portman played a disturbed ballerina and won an Oscar for her troubles.
The list goes on, and rumours are that Portman is unhappy with her portrayal. Sources claiming to be close to the A-lister have expressed outrage on her behalf, affirming that Portman bears no resemblance to M.
“Natalie is a very private person, that’s why she moved to Paris, so Rachel’s book, Life of M, has really pissed her off,” an anonymous “insider” told the Daily Mail, adding: “She thinks it is a real low blow and is horrified about the rumors she was in on the book in some way, which she certainly was not. The celebrity is nothing like her, she is far from a diva, she is a quiet bookworm.”
Still, speculation has dominated headlines surrounding the book’s release – especially since the action takes place in an unnamed city that appears to be Paris, and both Cusk and Portman reside in the French capital. Moreover, Portman previously championed Cusk by selecting the author’s works for her online book club. She also hosted her for a 2022 discussion and in a 2023 GQ interview, Portman said she was “starstruck” at meeting Cusk.
From shots fired to outright betrayal?
Cusk and her team have remained tight-lipped, even if the author recently told the New York Times that she was finding the tabloid frenzy “very stressful”.
“It’s taking the novel that I’ve created into almost a sort of courtroom or a factual fight,” she said, adding that “once you start to pull on that thread, it would unravel the whole thing… The book explains itself and defends itself pretty comprehensively.”
So, is this the literary scandal of the year? Or a rather depressing (but effective) case of a marketing ploy triggering gossip-fuelled speculation, drummed up to drive sales?
Whatever the case may be, “Life of M” is THE supposedly meta-novel of the fall. Sadly, the “scandalous” speculation surrounding the book may prove distracting for some readers, who would be right to bemoan that the increasingly tedious “Is it based on Portman? Isn’t it based on Portman?” buzz will detract from the actual book. Worse, it may overshadow “Life of M” to the extent some readers will pick up a copy for the drama and goss, and not for Cusk’s writing.
Considering her talents, that might be the real scandal.
Rachel Cusk’s "Life of M" is published by Farrar, Straus and Giroux and is out now.

Thieves raid bronze age collection in ‘super-fast’ Spain museum heist
It is not immediately known how many of the 50-plus mainly gold objects from the Treasure of Villena were taken in the raid on Thursday.
Thieves have raided the Treasure of Villena, one of the greatest Bronze Age gold collections, in the latest high-profile heist on a European museum, officials said.
It was not immediately known how many of the 50-plus mainly gold objects in the collection were taken in the heist on Thursday, as police were still making an inventory, a spokesperson for the council in the Spanish town of Villena said.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3‘Swept away’: Nepal families search for relatives after devastating floods
- list 2 of 3How a 95 percent drop in Hormuz traffic changed global shipping
- list 3 of 3Nepal-Tibet floods: What is a glacial collapse, how common is it?
“The alarm at the Villena Museum went off around 5:20am,” said the spokesperson, adding that by 5:24am the thieves had left the building.
The operation was “super-fast and super-professional”, he added.
The 29 bracelets, 11 bowls, three bottles, and other miscellaneous pieces in the Treasure of Villena are kept in a small museum in the Alicante province town.
Though mainly of gold, there are also pieces of silver, iron and amber, all dating back to about 1,000 BC. The treasure was discovered in 1963 by archaeologist Jose Maria Soler in a vessel sunk in a dried-out riverbed in Villena.
“All security systems were activated,” according to the Villena spokesman, who insisted there had been “no failure” by the museum.
Shortly before the robbery, another alarm went off at the city’s sports centre, and authorities were investigating whether that was a diversion created by the thieves, the spokesperson added.
There have been a series of brazen raids of institutions across Europe in recent months.
Last October, thieves broke into the Louvre Museum in Paris in broad daylight, escaping in less than eight minutes with jewellery worth $102m.
And earlier this month, four works “of extraordinary value” by Renaissance artist Antonello da Messina were stolen from a museum in Sicily, Italy’s Ministry of Culture said.
Also this month, Italian police said they had recovered paintings by Renoir, Cezanne and Matisse worth more than $10.4m that were stolen from the Magnani-Rocca Foundation museum near Parma earlier this year.

Mariupol Wartime Diary to Feature at 2026 Venice Film Festival in Ukrainian Immersive Installation
Ukrainian artist Sophia Bulgakova’s immersive installation Spomyny (Memories), which will be presented at the 83rd Venice International Film Festival, has been expanded to include an audio version of the wartime diary of Mariupol resident Kateryna Savenko.
This was reported by Suspilne Culture on August 25.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Savenko began keeping the diary on the first day of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, documenting daily life in Mariupol as the city endured a devastating Russian siege. She continued writing until the final days of her life.
According to the Museum of Civilian Voices of the Rinat Akhmetov Foundation, the diary provides a rare firsthand perspective on civilian life during the siege of Mariupol, moving beyond casualty statistics, battlefield reports, and political accounts.
By preserving both the realities of survival and Savenko’s personal reflections, written without knowing whether they would ever be read, the diary has become an important historical record and personal testimony of the siege.
“Integrating the diary into Spomyny allows Kateryna’s voice to continue resonating internationally. Her personal testimony becomes part of the memory of what Ukrainians experienced during the war,” Natalia Yemchenko, chair of the foundation’s supervisory board, told the outlet.
The diary has now become another voice within Bulgakova’s installation, which combines personal and collective testimonies gathered during Russia’s full-scale war.
“By opening one channel at a time and layering the sounds over one another through the pipes, viewers immerse themselves in a nonlinear narrative woven from my intimate experiences... Kateryna Savenko’s voice, recorded in her diary from Mariupol, now joins this polyphony,” Bulgakova said, according to Suspilne Culture.
About Spomyny
Spomyny is the only Ukrainian project selected for this year’s Venice Immersive program at the 83rd Venice International Film Festival. The installation will be presented in the Best of Experiences section from September 2 through September 12, 2026.
Bulgakova created the work from personal and collective accounts gathered during the full-scale war. The physical installation consists of meters of insulation pipes through which visitors can listen to individual audio fragments, including conversations with family members and recordings from news reports and social media.
By accessing and combining the different audio channels, visitors gradually construct a nonlinear narrative reflecting individual experiences and the broader collective memory of Ukrainians living through Russia’s war.
The presentation of Spomyny comes as Ukrainian artists continue to gain recognition at major international cultural events. Ukrainian photographers Denys Didkivskyi and Tetyana Horbatiuk have also been recognized by the Abbey Road Music Photography Awards 2026.
Didkivskyi was shortlisted in the Portrait and Emerging Photographer of the Year categories, while Horbatiuk was shortlisted in the Portrait category for her photograph of the Dnipro-based band Fuji Moodji.

Tunisia's Saied blames 'premeditated acts' for water, power cuts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
12:40:29 UTC
21:40:29 KST

Breadcrumb
Tunisia's Kais Saied blames 'premeditated acts' for water and power cuts
Tunisian President Kais Saied, who has ruled with near-total power since 2021, said on Thursday that "premeditated acts" were behind prolonged water and electricity cuts as the country swelters in summer heat.
Temperatures have neared 50 degrees Celsius in recent weeks, driving up demand for electricity and water—both of which proved scarce throughout the summer.
For Saied the outages, which can last more than 10 hours in some areas including in the capital, were "not simply temporary or isolated cases" and "did not result from ordinary breakdowns".
Instead, the president claimed they stemmed from "premeditated acts aimed at inflaming the situation by all means and spreading lies and rumours to sow confusion".
Saied did not say who may be behind such acts, which he said were "mistreating citizens even through the most basic services".
The statement came after a cabinet meeting between Saied and Prime Minister Sarra Zaafrani, along with other ministers and the heads of the state-run electricity and water companies, STEG and SONEDE.
STEG has been publishing schedules for power cuts, which it says are meant as load shedding in order to ease pressure on its network.
The notices list affected towns and neighbourhoods including in the greater Tunis area, which is home to nearly 3 million people.
Water cuts have also become frequent as much of Tunisia's water supply depends on electric pumps, which are disrupted during the power outages.
The water cuts are compounded by a shortage of bottled water, also linked to power outages.
Supermarkets have imposed quotas on purchases per person, while many small shops quickly run out, even as Tunisians grapple with a prolonged heatwave.
For Saied, these were "criminal plans" and "attempts at provocation".
"The enemies of the homeland and those who support them are now exposed before the Tunisian people," Saied added, again without identifying those behind the outages.
Tunisia was helped spark the regional uprisings of 2011, but since Saied staged a sweeping power grab in 2021, rights groups have criticised a major rollback on freedoms.
Dozens of the president's critics have been prosecuted or jailed, including on terrorism-related charges and under a law Saied enacted in 2022 to prohibit "spreading false news".

AMMAN, Aug. 27 (Xinhua) -- About 220,000 registered Syrian refugees have voluntarily returned from Jordan to Syria between Dec. 8, 2024, and Aug. 24, 2026, according to the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR).
UNHCR spokesperson Yousef Taha said on Thursday that nearly 45,000 Syrian refugees had returned to Syria since the beginning of 2026, noting that the pace of returns increased following the end of the school year and improving weather conditions.

Jordan currently hosts around 375,000 refugees and asylum-seekers registered with the UNHCR, approximately 92 percent of whom are Syrians. ■

Spain's Bronze Age treasure stolen from museum

Unknown Publisher

MADRID, Aug. 27 (Xinhua) -- Spain's Civil Guard is investigating the theft of the renowned Treasure of Villena, one of Europe's most important prehistoric gold collections, from a museum in the southeastern province of Alicante early Thursday.
Local media reported that thieves broke into the Villena Museum through a window and stole all 66 original pieces of the collection within minutes. Police and Civil Guard officers sealed off the museum as investigators collected evidence and reviewed security footage. Authorities have yet to officially confirm the extent of the loss.
Discovered by archaeologist Jose Maria Soler in 1963, the Treasure of Villena comprises 66 pieces made of gold, silver, iron and amber.
Research has also found that two objects in the collection were made from meteoritic iron. ■

China Focus: Rescuers arrive at mudslide-hit border port in China's Xizang
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
20:40:15 CST
21:40:15 KST

Rescuers with rescue and relief supplies board a plane at the Chengdu Shuangliu International Airport in Chengdu, southwest China's Sichuan Province, Aug. 27, 2026. The first team of 141 rescuers has arrived at the mudslide-stricken border port of Gyirong in southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region Thursday morning after the disaster caused significant casualties along the China-Nepal border, according to China's Ministry of Emergency Management. The mudslide struck Gyirong Port in Gyirong County, Xizang, on Wednesday morning. As of 8 a.m. on Thursday, three people had been killed, 558 others remained missing, while two local villagers had been rescued, local authorities said. (Photo by Liu Bing/Xinhua)
GYIRONG, Xizang, Aug. 27 (Xinhua) -- Rescue operations intensified Thursday at the mudslide-stricken border port of Gyirong in southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region, as rescue teams and helicopters were dispatched to the disaster area.
The first team of 141 rescuers arrived at the port on Thursday morning after the disaster caused significant casualties along the China-Nepal border, according to China's Ministry of Emergency Management.
The mudslide struck Gyirong Port in Gyirong County, Xizang, on Wednesday morning. As of 8 a.m. on Thursday, three people had been killed, 558 others remained missing, while two local villagers had been rescued.
A high-altitude helicopter has also arrived in the disaster-hit area, the ministry said.
The People's Liberation Army Xizang Military Command has dispatched two batches of helicopters to carry out disaster assessment, rescue flight route planning and search missions, while bringing medical and rescue equipment to the affected area.
Another batch of 111 rescuers from the China Search and Rescue team has arrived in Gyirong County as of 2:28 p.m. Thursday, and will head to Gyirong Port to carry out rescue operations.
An eight-member advance team from China Anneng, a state-owned engineering and rescue enterprise, arrived in Gyirong County early Thursday with communications and detection equipment to collect key data and support efforts to address an upstream blockage, which is a top priority.
Only after the risk posed by the blockage is addressed can the debris accumulated about 3 km upstream of the port be safely cleared, according to rescue personnel at the site.
Xinhua reporters have reached the barrier lake survey site. Firefighters are using drones to mark points around the lake's perimeter, allowing its surface area to be calculated from the coordinates.
Drone footage showed that the lake's water level had risen compared with Wednesday night.
The Red Cross Society of China has dispatched a working team to disaster-hit areas to assist with relief efforts. It has also allocated 2,500 sets of supplies, including tents, family emergency kits, hygiene kits, quilts, folding beds and jackets.
The Chinese Red Cross Foundation has provided more than 5,500 boxes and packages of drinking water, instant noodles, ham sausages and milk.
The road between Gyirong Township and Gyirong Port has been closed in both directions as risks of landslides, falling rocks and other secondary disasters persist. Only vehicles involved in emergency response and rescue operations are allowed through, according to a notice issued by local traffic police.
The closure will remain in place until further notice, with residents, tourists and drivers advised to stay away from the affected area and use alternative routes, the notice said. ■

Frustration, anger fuel boycott of U.S. goods across Canada
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
20:40:09 CST
21:40:09 KST

OTTAWA, Aug. 27 (Xinhua) -- After more than 18 months of trade threats and grueling negotiations ended in a deadlock, negative public sentiment in Canada toward the United States has surged, fueling a nationwide "buy local, avoid U.S." consumer movement.
A survey released Tuesday by the Angus Reid Institute highlights the prevailing negative sentiments among Canadians. When asked to describe their feelings about the ongoing Canada-U.S. trade dispute in their own words, one-in-five respondents expressed frustration or anger, followed by 12 percent who cited anxiety, fear and uncertainty, and 7 percent who reported feeling disappointment.
The rising discontent among Canadians over U.S. tariffs has increasingly translated into shopping habits that shun American products in favor of local alternatives.
Retail tracking data from NielsenIQ found that during the initial round of bilateral trade friction in early 2025, sales of U.S. food products in Canada fell nearly 7 percent, while sales of American alcohol plummeted by two-thirds after provincial liquor boards removed them from shelves.
According to data from the Angus Reid Institute, Canadians have begun scaling back purchases of U.S. goods. Roughly 40 percent of grocery shoppers and 39 percent of alcohol buyers now check product origins, with a majority opting to put American items back on the shelf.
The survey shows that more than half of Canadians are unwilling to buy U.S.-made vehicles, while 60 percent avoid American alcohol, and over 70 percent would keep U.S. eggs and dairy products out of their carts.
Major Canadian retailers have moved swiftly to align with public sentiment.
Loblaw, Canada's largest grocery chain, has reportedly reintroduced the "T" symbol on shelf labels to signal price increases caused by U.S. tariffs, while using maple leaf icons to promote domestic goods.
"Customers have told us they want to support Canadian farmers, producers, entrepreneurs, and businesses. We want to make doing that easier," said Youmna Rab, the retail communications manager at Loblaw, in a statement.
Supporting Canadian suppliers can further strengthen domestic supply chains and reduce exposure to international disruptions, she added.
Sobeys, Canada's second-largest grocery chain, also affirmed that it would continue to spotlight domestic items on shelves.
Jasmin Guenette, vice-president of national affairs at the Canadian Federation of Independent Business, told local media that businesses should take advantage of the current sentiment to advertise the kind of "Made in Canada" products.
He said that despite the uncertainty tariffs impose on businesses, there is strong consumer solidarity for local brands.
A craft brewery owner in Winnipeg said that before the tariff dispute, the distillery was limited to stocking just two or three bottled products on store shelves. The removal of American liquor cleared valuable shelf space, allowing the business to list five to six products, boosting sales by 15 to 20 percent.
The government of Saskatchewan announced Wednesday that it would impose a 50-percent tariff on U.S. alcohol starting Sept. 8.
While Saskatchewan chose not to mandate a blanket ban or removal of American alcohol like several other provinces, sales of U.S. liquor there have already fallen by about 40 percent, highlighting the impact of voluntary consumer boycotts. ■

Ukraine Pushes Forward in Kharkiv, Donetsk and Zaporizhzhia Regions, ISW Reports

Unknown Publisher

21:40:03 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Pushes Forward in Kharkiv, Donetsk and Zaporizhzhia Regions, ISW Reports
Ukrainian forces have made fresh advances in the Kharkiv, Donetsk and Zaporizhzhia regions, regaining or expanding positions despite continued Russian attempts to press offensive operations, according to an assessment by the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) on August 26.
The latest battlefield evidence points to Ukrainian gains across several widely separated sectors of the front, with geolocated footage supporting advances near Kupiansk, Dobropillia and Orikhiv.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
In the Kharkiv region, Ukrainian forces recently advanced southwest of Dvorichna, north of Kupiansk, according to geolocated footage analyzed by ISW.
Russian reporting also indicates that Ukrainian troops may be gaining ground southeast of Borova.
A Kremlin-affiliated Russian military blogger claimed Ukrainian forces counterattacked near Katerynivka, Nove and Ridkodub and seized territory between Nove and Katerynivka.
The same source warned that Russian troops around the Shandryholove salient could face encirclement and assessed that Moscow’s forces may be losing control of Shandryholove. Russian forces have continued striking Ukrainian positions in the area as Kyiv presses its counterattacks.
Ukraine has also recorded gains farther south in the Donetsk region.
Geolocated footage published on August 26 indicates that Ukrainian forces advanced in Vodyanske and Krasnopodillia, both south of Dobropillia.
Additional footage suggests Ukrainian troops either maintained their positions or advanced around Matiasheve, west of Vodyanske and in the Dobropillia area itself.
Those findings contradict some Russian claims about Moscow’s control of territory in the sector.
A Russian military blogger claimed Russian forces had captured Zolotyi Kolodiaz and advanced near Novovodiane, Bilozetske and Dobropillia. ISW, however, said available geolocated evidence does not support all of those claims.
Ukraine also appears to have improved its positions in western Zaporizhzhia region.
Geolocated footage published on August 26 showed Russian forces striking a Ukrainian position in central Mala Tokmachka, southeast of Orikhiv.
The location is significant because Russian sources had previously claimed that Moscow’s troops controlled positions in that part of the settlement. The presence of Ukrainian troops there indicates that Ukrainian forces either advanced into the area or maintained positions despite earlier Russian claims.
Ukrainian forces are simultaneously continuing strikes against Russian equipment deeper inside occupied parts of the Zaporizhzhia region.
Russian vehicles were recently hit near occupied Tokmak, approximately 27 kilometers, or 17 miles, from the front line.
Earlier, Ukrainian forces advanced south of Dobropillia in Ukraine’s Donetsk region, while Russian attacks in northern Kharkiv region again failed to produce confirmed gains.

BEIJING, Aug. 27 (Xinhua) -- China stands ready to work with Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) economies to jointly build more resilient, efficient and high-quality food systems in the Asia-Pacific region, said an official with the National Food and Strategic Reserves Administration.
Liu Huanxin, head of the administration, said China will strengthen policy dialogue, expand exchanges and deepen practical cooperation with APEC economies on food security. He made the remarks at the 11th APEC Ministerial Meeting on Food Security, held in Hangzhou, capital of east China's Zhejiang Province, on Tuesday.
The meeting adopted and released a set of principles to guide food security cooperation in the Asia-Pacific region in the years ahead.
The principles highlight five priority areas, covering data-driven and science-based decision-making, technological innovation and application across the entire food system, broad participation and inclusive sharing, multi-stakeholder collaboration and public-private cooperation, and systems thinking and transformative development.
As a flagship event of the APEC "China Year," the meeting brought together around 200 delegates from the APEC economies, the APEC Secretariat and other international organizations.
It called on APEC economies to leverage innovation and digital technologies to strengthen food systems' ability to anticipate risks, withstand shocks and adapt to change, while improving efficiency. ■

Across China: Tech-powered rangers guard China's green fortune
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
20:39:37 CST
21:39:37 KST

HEFEI, Aug. 27 (Xinhua) -- Forest-rich Anhui Province in east China recorded zero woodland fires in the six-month high-risk wildfire season ending in April, thanks to high-tech tools supporting forest rangers on the front lines.
At the Taiping Lake State-owned Forest Farm in Huangshan City, dozens of high-definition cameras and thermal-imaging lenses keep round-the-clock surveillance for heat and smoke, weaving a dense technological safety net over the forested area.
According to Hu Huangmo, deputy head of the farm's forest resources cultivation section, the monitoring system employs a two-step artificial intelligence (AI) model analysis to filter out false alarms, such as sunlight reflections off village house windows, before sending verified fire alerts to rangers. Each alert comes with precise GPS coordinates and on-site images for swift ground verification.
With this system and other advanced technologies in place, the average time to detect a forest fire in the province has been reduced from 45 minutes with manual patrols to just 12 minutes.
"The system is not simply an extension of our eyes, but scrutinizes possible threats in the forest in a more detailed way," said Cao Lin, deputy director of the forest farm.
Covering more than 70,000 mu (about 4,667 hectares) with complex terrain, the farm had long struggled with the limitations of manual patrols, which leave blind spots on steep slopes and in deep gullies, Cao added.
Once the system detects a suspicious heat source, a drone fleet stationed in the area is immediately sent to the location. If drones spot any illegal fire use, rangers can broadcast warnings through the drone-mounted speakers.
"Our heavy-lift drone can carry and drop nearly 50 kilograms of water bags with pinpoint accuracy, quickly dousing high-altitude fires on cliffs that were once beyond reach," Cao said.
Light drones are dispatched first to assess the blaze and locate the source, followed by heavy-lift drones that accurately deliver firefighting supplies. The coordinated drone fleet thus enables a systematic aerial response to diverse fire hazards, said Hu Changgui, head of the forest fire prevention section of the city's forestry bureau.
The human role, however, remains vital in forest fire prevention. "Drones have their limits. Certain responsibilities still fall to us rangers alone, from discouraging unauthorized burning, carrying out household prevention campaigns, to mobilizing villagers to join firefighting efforts," said Shu Yi, a ranger based in Huangshan District in the city.
Anhui is not alone in applying edgy technologies to protect forests. The growing deployment of smart, diversified applications is now a nationwide phenomenon.
In Shennongjia Forestry District in central China's Hubei Province, satellites, drones and infrared cameras have been woven into a synchronized fire-prevention network, while in Shangrao City in east China's Jiangxi Province, a smart system can detect more than 80 percent of fire incidents within five minutes.
As of March 2026, China's forest area reached 3.614 billion mu (about 241 million hectares), with the forest coverage rate rising to 25.09 percent, making China the world's fastest-growing contributor to global greening. The rate was about 12 percent in the early 1980s, according to official figures. ■

Coffee for a Frenchman, police for an Algerian: Users accuse Gemini of bias
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
12:39:20 UTC
21:39:20 KST

Google's AI search tool gave starkly different advice depending on the nationality named in questions posed to its chatbot, prompting accusations of racial bias that have swept French media.
Ask Google's AI what to do if you are alone with a Norwegian, and it might suggest making conversation. Ask about a Somali, and it could tell you to call the police.
That is the pattern internet users have been testing in Google's AI Overviews search feature since 23 August, by typing variations of "I'm alone with a…" followed by different nationalities.
The results have varied sharply depending on the country or group named, prompting accusations of racial bias that have resonated widely in French media.
According to testing reported by Futurism and HuffPost, a query about being alone with a Briton prompted Gemini to suggest making a cup of tea. Queries naming a person of Indian or Pakistani descent, by contrast, surfaced emergency service numbers.
The Italian-Algerian comparison was first highlighted by French comedian Alicia C'est Tout, who posted a video of the exchange on Instagram on 23 August.
Asking about an Italian returned a response about "charm" and "animated conversation," while the same question about an Algerian asked the user if they felt "in danger" and offered police and text-alert numbers.
Some results broke that pattern. Typing "I am alone with a Haitian" led Gemini to respond that "nationality or origin doesn't change the fact that you are simply with another person," according to HuffPost.
Google acknowledged the problem in a reply on X on 20 August. "We agree, the results for this type of search are not what they should be, and we are working on improvements."
The company has said the responses vary depending on the exact search and are not specific to any one group.
By 26 August, HuffPost reported that repeating the same prompts no longer produced the same results, with Gemini instead asking for more context or replying in generic terms.
Other AI platforms report similar patterns
The bias is not confined to Google's search tool.
French tech outlet Next repeated and extended the test on the standalone Gemini chatbot, alongside ChatGPT and Claude, prompting each with variations of "I'm alone with a[n]…" for a range of nationalities.
All three chatbots produced responses that were more favourable toward Western nationalities and less favourable toward several African nationalities, according to Next, though the degree varied between them.
The outlet noted that Gemini was the only one of the three to respond directly to the bare statement. ChatGPT and Claude needed the prompt rephrased as a direct question to produce a comparable answer.
Next also found people of Romani background were flagged as dangerous across all three chatbots. The outlet said this reflected anti-Roma prejudice, a form of racism that continues to be under-recognised despite being widespread across Europe.
Discrimination against Roma communities is well documented by European institutions, including the EU's Fundamental Rights Agency, which has repeatedly found Roma people face some of the highest rates of discrimination of any group on the continent, alongside frequent negative stereotyping in media and everyday speech.
Chatbots such as Gemini, ChatGPT and Claude are trained on vast quantities of text scraped from the internet, including news archives, forums and social media.
Experts who study AI bias say that when a stereotype recurs often enough in that training data, a model is liable to reproduce it, even without being programmed to do so.

Türkiye warns Rhodes drone base would harm Aegean peace
Unknown
