The report says the additional mobilization wave is a response by Russia’s political leadership to the loss of initiative in the war, steadily rising personnel losses on the front and a significant slowdown in contract recruitment across the regions.
“Russia’s personnel losses from January through July 2026 amounted to around 240,000 people, of whom at least 140,000 were irrecoverable. At the same time, fewer people – 232,000 – were recruited under contract into the Russian occupation contingent during this period,” the presidential office said.
How many people and whom Russia plans to mobilize
Ukraine says the Russian General Staff has already prepared a plan for the additional mobilization of 600,000 people over specified periods this year and next.
“As part of preparations for the additional mobilization wave and the recruitment of criminal elements under contract, the process of amending Russian legislation and regulations has begun. Control over military registration is being significantly tightened, mechanisms are being created to recruit people serving sentences in Russia’s prisons and penal colonies, and additional coercive measures are being developed,” Ukraine’s military intelligence agency said.
CIA Chief Warned Putin Against NATO Attack During Surprise Moscow Visit – Reports
The categories of convicted people eligible for military service have been expanded to include people with outstanding or unexpunged convictions under 11 articles of Russia’s Criminal Code.
These include crimes involving the smuggling of poisonous, radioactive and explosive substances, weapons and narcotics; banditry and organizing or participating in criminal groups; organizing illegal migration; violations of safety requirements at fuel and energy facilities; and the illegal handling, theft or extortion of nuclear materials or radioactive substances, among other offenses.
The Russian leadership has also approved extending mobilization and/or contract recruitment to significant categories of women serving sentences in prisons and penal colonies.
Work is also underway to establish recruitment quotas for law enforcement agencies, including the Interior Ministry, Federal Bailiffs Service, Federal Penitentiary Service and Investigative Committee, to send employees for military service under mobilization.
How long will mobilized troops be trained?
Depending on their level of training and the anticipated “survival” period of those mobilized by Russia, training could last between 15 and 60 days.
Some mobilized personnel could also be trained at military ranges in Belarus, according to Ukrainian intelligence.
The Russian leadership is preparing a package of measures to respond to potential negative social and economic consequences of placing cities and regions under a stricter wartime regime.
Internal Russian documents reportedly justify the need for an additional mobilization wave by pointing to a significant increase in regional dissatisfaction with the war, with dissatisfaction levels reaching as high as 69%, and a corresponding decline in the number of people willing to voluntarily sign military contracts.
Where is Russia struggling most to recruit?
Recruitment problems are reportedly most pronounced in the Oryol and Vladimir regions, as well as in Dagestan.
In the Kurgan region, monthly recruitment targets have been only 57–69% fulfilled since the beginning of the year. In the Volgograd region, the number of potential contract recruits has fallen by 40% compared with 2025.
Similar declines are being recorded in many other Russian regions.
Compared with 2025, some regions have seen a 30–40% drop in the number of debtors, convicted prisoners and other criminal elements, migrants and other groups that had long served as a key pool of contract recruits for the Russian military and its war against Ukraine.
A campaign to recruit students has also failed, despite involving the overwhelming majority of Russian universities.
How the Kremlin plans to enforce mobilization
The Russian leadership also plans to increase the personal responsibility of regional authorities and expand the powers of law enforcement agencies.
Russia has already introduced a system for issuing electronic mobilization notices. Authorities are developing additional coercive measures, including bans on leaving Russia, taking out loans, buying or selling real estate, revoking driving licenses and blocking funds in bank accounts.
Businesses are also expanding their military registration and mobilization departments. As of the end of July 2026, more than 2,500 new vacancies had been posted on Russian employment platforms for positions in these mobilization units, according to Ukrainian intelligence.
The most likely scenario is that Russian President Vladimir Putin will make a decision on mobilization after Russia’s State Duma “elections,” scheduled for Sept. 18–20 this year.

Why we’re all hooked on tinned fish
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
12:10:13 UTC
21:10:13 KST

I can’t find it, despite having spent the past 35 minutes looking, but somewhere in the house is The Crisis Cook Book. It’s a standard paperback, postbox-red with white writing on the cover, and full of recipes from chefs including Rowley Leigh, Heston Blumenthal and Jeremy Lee. Not having found it, I needed Amazon to tell me it was published in 2007 and compiled by Nick Lander, at the time the Financial Times’ restaurant correspondent. He asked 28 chefs to donate three recipes – their favourite starter, main course and dessert – and proceeds from the book went to the national homelessness charity Crisis.
The reason I needed (and still need – it is now a mission) to find the book is because inside it is Rowley’s recipe for pasta with tinned sardines, fennel, chilli and lemon zest. It’s a recipe that I have made so many times, and for so many years, that I don’t need to look at the book; but, equally, because I’ve made it so many times and so much time has passed, I have no idea how far I have drifted from the original, and want to check. I’ve even written about this recipe in my weekly Guardian column, without referring to the book or even mentioning Rowley! Not that a store-cupboard version of the Sicilian pasta con le sarde (pasta with sardines and wild fennel) is owned by anyone, although Rowley did teach me.
So here I am, setting the record straight, Rowley taught me to – and this is approximate – soften thinly sliced red onion, fennel and red chilli in lots of olive oil, add a tin of sardines (mashed), then toss the lot with al dente pasta, minced parsley and enough lemon zest to scent the pasta and the kitchen. It’s a meal that is not only deeply delicious but also thrifty, because a small amount of fish goes a long way.
In short, tinned fish rules. It gives a product with a notoriously short life an extremely long one, thus drastically reducing the risk of food waste. Sardines, mackerel, herring, pilchards, sprats and anchovies are my tinned fish of choice – tasty, rich in essential omega 3 fatty acids and, if watchfully sourced, sustainable. That sourcing is very important, though (sardine stocks in some parts of the world are struggling), so I’d recommend keeping an eye on the Marine Conservation Society’s Good Fish Guide. The other thing about tinned fish is the deep umami flavour that can develop during the curing and canning process, especially when the fish is preserved in a good-tasting brine or oil.
And now, more than ever, it’s easier to find fish preserved in these delicious brines and oils thanks to enterprises such as Mitch Tonks’s Rockfish in the West Country and Sea Sisters in Dorset, both of which take great care with their canning, and to exceptional producers such as Giribizzi and La Belle-Iloise. Not to mention The Tinned Fish Market, which has stalls in Old Spitalfields and Borough markets in London (and an online shop) dedicated to excellent tinned fish. All of which is encouraging supermarkets to keep up.
Back to recipes. Yotam Ottolenghi also has a play on the classic Sicilian sardine pasta, using mackerel fillets, za’atar and lime, served with linguine; another Yotam recipe for conchiglie with tinned smoked oysters is a template that can be adapted to just about any tinned fish you happen to have in the cupboard. Anna Berrill, meanwhile, uses tinned sardines instead of anchovies for her tomato, caper and olive puttanesca, which she serves with polenta, as well as in a great-sounding sardine, caper, chive and celery salad.
I generally use sardines in my recipe for potato and tinned fishcakes, but mackerel, herring, pilchards and sprats all work. Hugh Fearnley-Whittingstall’s tinned mackerel paté is equally flexible, and yes to his quick-pickled onions, too! Hugh, a tinned fish champion, also suggests a sardine omelette (his daughter’s recipe) and mixing sardines with canned white beans and thinly sliced red onion for a store-cupboard salad, as well as reminding us they’re tasty just piled on toast. I agree – it is always a good idea to have a tin or two of sardines in the cupboard. Now where is that bloody book?
My week in food
Can do | In keeping with the tinned fish theme, Marcus Ansell – known to his millions of Instagram, YouTube and TikTok followers as Tinned Fish Reviews and usually found wearing a fez – opens, decants and taste tests cans of fish. Calm to the extreme, even when appalled or ecstatic about the contents of the tin, he is a joy to watch and learn from. As is his dog, King Arthur.
Dear diaries | This week, I have been cooking from Thom Eagle’s Allotment Diaries, which isn’t a cookbook, nor does it contain recipes. Rather, it is a record of a year on an allotment and his thoughts on growing, which are inseparable from those about family, grief, the seasons, and how he might slice, cook and flavour whatever he has picked. In turn, he has sent me into the kitchen with a reminder that a short phrase about courgette “stewed as filling for an omelette” can often be more helpful and inspiring than a long recipe. A stunning book.
Wrap up warm | My son this week reminded me how great chickpea flour pancakes are. I’d recommend a batter made from 250g chickpea flour, 450ml cold water and a big pinch of salt, so it’s the consistency of smooth single cream. Leave it to rest, then fried as you would pancakes, they should be firm but floppy, and frilly at the edges. The flavour is like a pancake crossed with hummus and they’re fantastic with some stir-fried greens and a big blob of ricotta.

After six months of Iran war, US shifts goals, tactics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

21:08:42 KST

Six months after U.S. President Donald Trump launched a war with Iran forecasting a quick four-to-five-week victory, the conflict has morphed into an open-ended struggle with shifting objectives, diminished U.S. weapon stockpiles and a strategic pivot toward economic pressure.
While the U.S. achieved tactical successes, establishing air dominance and severely degrading Iran’s navy, air force and defense manufacturing, key strategic goals remain unmet.
Tehran retains proxy influence, missile strike capabilities and a 970-pound stockpile of enriched uranium buried under bombed sites.
Meanwhile, early promises to protect regional allies have frayed, highlighted by Trump’s recent threat to bomb Oman over diplomatic disagreements.
The war’s central focus has now pivoted to an objective absent from Trump’s original plan: Reopening the Strait of Hormuz.
By blocking the vital waterway, which previously carried 20 percent of global oil, Iran created a massive chokepoint that spiked global fuel and fertilizer prices.
Despite Trump’s claims that the strait is functioning and assertions that a resolution is near, the June memorandum of understanding has stalled, leaving the U.S. adapted to a drawn-out economic standoff with no clear off-ramp in sight.
In the meantime, Qatari Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani will visit the Iranian capital on Aug. 27 to discuss de-escalation efforts.
The discussions will cover freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz and the need to restore the waterway to the status quo that existed before Feb. 28, he wrote.
It would mark the first visit by the Qatari premier to Iran since the war between Washington and Tehran began with U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran in late February.

====================================================================================================

A Britain of wildfires and flood risks: be sure, the climate crisis is real, and we will deal with it | Angela Eagle
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
12:05:25 UTC
21:05:25 KST

This long, hot summer has brought our third drought in five years and the driest July in almost two centuries. We’ve seen wildfires burn down homes and now face the risk of flash floods as we move into autumn. It should be a wake-up call for those saying that concerns about the climate crisis are overblown; that we should simply sit back and do nothing; or row back on attempts to restore our natural environment. As the new environment secretary, I won’t let that happen.
No one who has experienced this summer in the UK should be in any doubt that our climate is already changing. We know the future holds warmer, wetter winters, hotter, drier summers, and more extreme weather.
Honesty about what is required to deal with this changing reality is the least we should expect from our politicians. But last week we saw an astonishing response from Reform UK’s deputy leader, who told people to “enjoy” the scorching heatwaves and described this government’s efforts to combat the climate crisis as “arrogant”.
This response isn’t just ignorant; it is insulting.
Insulting to the firefighters risking their lives to fight blazes up and down the country. Insulting to the public whose lives are disrupted by scorching temperatures that were once a rare occurrence. And insulting to our farmers struggling to turn a profit as drought damages their crops.
This government’s response is not to throw in the towel and accept the chaos caused by extreme weather. It is to work to build and manage landscapes so they are resilient enough to withstand it and recover.
We know that healthy ecosystems retain more water and can help act as natural firebreaks. That resilience does not just protect us from the impacts of wildfire. It guards against flooding and pollution, too.
But some, including the Conservatives, have made the argument that rewilding lowers resilience to fire and that we should reverse restrictions on burning heather on our moors and peatlands. The exact opposite is true.
The evidence clearly shows that wetter, healthy peatlands hold more water and are less likely to develop species that are vulnerable to fires. The damage that has been done to these vital habitats by decades of burning has made them more vulnerable to wildfires in the long term, not less.
The solution to raging wildfires is not more burning of our countryside. It is to restore and better manage our environment.
Where rewilding has been prioritised, as at the National Trust’s Holnicote estate, you can clearly see the stark difference that it makes to the ability to withstand extreme weather. In areas where rivers and wetlands have been restored, the plants are green and blooming. Elsewhere, the ground is brown and dry.
As environment secretary, most of what comes across my desk is underpinned by the need to adapt to our changing climate – and this government is taking these challenges head on.
That’s why the prime minister this month convened an emergency Cobra meeting, bringing together senior ministers, firefighters, weather forecasters and other experts to make sure we’re doing all we can to keep the country safe from wildfires. That includes a temporary ban on the sale of disposable barbecues.
We are spending almost £100m to strengthen the country’s capacity to respond to wildfires and extreme weather.
And we are backing our farmers during the drought with a £65m funding boost, rule changes to make building on-site reservoirs easier and the largest nature-friendly budget in history to make our farms more resilient to extreme weather and to protect our food security.
Adapting to our changing climate demands sustained attention, effort and investment. Others may simply deny the problem or stick their heads in the sand, but this government will rise to the challenge.
- 
  Angela Eagle is the secretary of state for environment, food and rural affairs

Philip Colligan Is One of TIME's 100 Most Influential People in AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
12:02:39 UTC
21:02:39 KST

Philip Colligan’s greatest fear is that parents and educators will treat the AI revolution the way they treated the advent of the Internet—which is to say, they won’t engage in teaching children how to responsibly use it until it’s too late.
“We are in the middle of those systems being introduced into healthcare, finance, criminal justice decisions, education decisions,” the CEO of the Cambridge, U.K-based tech-literacy educational nonprofit Raspberry Pi Foundation says. “Kids need to learn these skills for economic opportunity, but also for power and agency in a world where AI is affecting everything.”
That’s the motivation for Experience AI, one of the world’s most widely-used AI literacy curricula; the educational program has been localized in 40 countries and has been used by some 50,000 teachers to explain the new technology to about 5 million kids. Developed in partnership with Google DeepMind and launched two months before ChatGPT debuted, it provides lessons on how AI systems are built, data privacy, misinformation, deepfakes, and more.
Beyond Experience AI, which is intended for teachers and students in the 11-to-14 age range, the nonprofit—funded in part by an $1 billion endowment from the low-cost computer company Raspberry Pi’s London Stock Exchange IPO in 2024—will pilot a new qualification for A-level students in England on data science and AI this fall.
“What we got wrong in the nineties and aughts is we didn't talk enough about ethics and the societal implications of technology,” says Colligan, who last year was awarded the Commander of the Order of the British Empire for his leadership. “We've got a generation of people who built social media without really thinking about the negative effects it's going to have on society. We are all living with the consequences of that.”

Andrea Bartz Is One of TIME's 100 Most Influential People in AI

21:02:38 KST

New York Times-bestselling thriller author Andrea Bartz struggled for years to hone her writing style and gain success in the literary world. So when she found out in 2023 that pirated versions of her books were being fed into AI systems, allowing them to spit out dozens of pages in her prose style in a matter of seconds, “it was like a gut punch,” she says.
The New York-based writer fought back by becoming one of the three main plaintiffs (alongside Charles Graeber and Kirk Wallace Johnson) in a class-action lawsuit against Anthropic that accused the company of using stolen works to train its chatbot Claude. Bartz being alphabetically first of the trio, she “got the privilege and the tax of having my name become shorthand” for the legal precedent. After a judge ruled that Anthropic's downloading of pirated books was not protected as fair use, the company agreed to pay $1.5 billion, the largest known copyright settlement in history. Authors whose work was stolen would receive $3,000 for each book.
Critics charge that the case didn’t settle larger questions about AI and copyright—only that Anthropic violated the law because the company trained its models on pirated books. Bartz hopes other lawsuits set stronger precedents, but nonetheless views her case as “a crucial victory.”
The author—whose next novel, which she calls a “tech thriller,” is due to be released in May 2027—also hopes the settlement serves as a morale boost for writers and a symbol of defiance. “This makes it clear that it is illegal for big tech companies to download troves of pirated e-books to use however they see fit,” she says. “It is theft, and it sounds pretty obvious, but that had not been established before.”

Since the release of the 2000 Oscar-winning movie about her, the name Erin Brockovich has been synonymous with grassroots activism against powerful institutions. When she founded the nonprofit Tech Justice Law in 2023, Meetali Jain did not plan to become the go-to attorney for people suing companies over harm from AI chatbots—but she’s also unsurprised it happened. “It was a matter of time, I knew, before some kind of generative AI product was going to harm children,” she says. “I just didn’t realize how many other vulnerable people it would hurt.”
Her first case was that of Sewell Setzer III, a teenager who died by suicide in 2024 after being allegedly encouraged by a Character.AI chatbot based on Game of Thrones character Daenerys Targaryen. Other lawyers had passed, Jain believes, because they assumed the company would get the matter dismissed. She persuaded a judge to allow it to move forward to discovery on product-safety liability grounds. Character.AI and its technology licensor Google settled for an undisclosed sum in January.
After the Sewell case was filed, Tech Justice Law was flooded with calls about other ways AI chatbots had harmed would-be plaintiffs, including the parents of Adam Raine, who sued OpenAI and CEO Sam Altman, accusing the company of wrongful death after the 16-year-old California boy died by suicide using a method they say ChatGPT advised him on. OpenAI has extended its sympathies to the family and said that protections for minors are a priority, but has denied liability for his death. On Aug. 18, the company released ChatGPT for Teens, which has content restrictions around topics including suicide, self-harm, and romantic conversations.
Jain sees part of her role as giving families a voice. “We’re able to focus lawmakers or attorneys general or courts on how these harms actually manifest,” Jain says. “I really see us as storytellers. We are telling stories of what has happened to people.”
If you or someone you know may be experiencing a mental-health crisis or contemplating suicide, call or text 988. In emergencies, call 911, or seek care from a local hospital or mental health provider.

Max Spero Is One of TIME's 100 Most Influential People in AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
12:02:38 UTC
21:02:38 KST

AI-generated writing has distinct patterns—and Pangram Labs says it can detect them. The company says its AI-powered models can discern with over 99.5% accuracy whether a piece of writing was produced entirely by humans or AIs, according to its internal tests. Those tests also show its tools are able to differentiate between human- and AI-written segments within a given text, estimating the degree of AI involvement. As co-founder and CEO Max Spero explains, because most AI writing comes from just a handful of model families—ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and the like—identifying it is easier than many believed just a few years ago. “Ultimately, what we’re doing is an authorship detection problem,” he says.
Spero says his company, founded in late 2023, was “close to shutting down” before Pangram spiked in popularity last fall as AI slop proliferated across platforms. By July of this year, it had a $9 million fundraising round, a tool for detecting AI-generated images, and a partnership with Substack to integrate its technology into the blogging platform.
Some AI text detectors also offer “humanizers”—tools intended to reshape AI writing so it can slip past detection. Spero says Pangram Labs will never release one. It’s not just a matter of principle—Pangram’s long-term aspiration is for every layer of online communication to use its tools to verify authorship, a function for which he expects there to be a far larger market in the age of slop and AI impersonation.
The deeper challenge of tracing the extent to which ideas themselves are influenced by AI may be intractable. And frontier AI models are getting better all the time, while some people may be writing more like AIs. But Spero believes Pangram’s is deterring people from passing off AI writing as their own. “The LLMs aren’t static,” he says, “but neither is Pangram.”

Max Tegmark still believes the AI industry isn’t doing enough to protect us from the potential harms of its increasingly powerful models. The MIT professor is the founder of the Future of Life Institute (FLI), a nonprofit aimed at reducing the global catastrophic risks posed by AI.
In 2023, FLI’s open letter urging AI companies to temporarily halt the development of systems more powerful than OpenAI’s GPT-4 garnered support from a number of high-profile signatories. And last October, it issued another letter, calling for the prohibition of the development of superintelligent AI.
To the Swedish-American physicist, lagging regulation on the AI industry has built a “race to the bottom,” where firms overlook safety concerns in favor of fast shipments. But a rapid shift in public sentiment towards AI in recent years may change things. An American public increasingly wary about job security, data center construction, and AI use by minors could make AI safety a hot-button issue in the upcoming midterms—and lawmakers are responding with legislation. “I haven’t seen as much shift in U.S. policymaking in the past decade, as I have in the past three months. It’s been amazing,” Tegmark says.
The organization also issues grades on safety and security to the world’s biggest AI companies, hoping to incentivize the relatively unregulated industry to establish some guardrails. And its scores have been unflinching: top scoring Anthropic earned a C+ on the nonprofit’s AI Safety Index released this summer.
Tegmark, who has met with lawmakers and advisers from both sides of the aisle, says, “From left to right, there’s this vast support for AI that cures cancer and complements and helps humans by providing useful tools we’re still in charge of.” At the same time, he says, “There’s this massive opposition to building AI that we don’t know how to control, that’s romancing our kids, that’s teaching terrorists to make bioweapons.”

Senator Bernie Sanders believes AI and robotics are the most transformative technologies in humanity’s history—and that we’re not ready for them.

Though neither proposed legislation has a clear path to passage, Sanders is undeterred. “Making sure the public enjoys their fair share of the profits of the companies is one thing,” he says, “but essentially protecting the people from the damage that AI and robotics may do is even more important to me.”

David Autor Is One of TIME's 100 Most Influential People in AI
Unknown

21:02:36 KST

In February 2024, the MIT economist David Autor first published his most contrarian notion about generative AI—that, “if used well,” it would create jobs and increase pay. It was something of an about turn for Autor, who had written for decades about why technological advances had hollowed out the middle class.
The intervening years have only reinforced the theory of Autor, one of the nation’s most vocal and prominent economists aiming to ascertain AI’s potential impacts on labor. “All this talk of everyone being replaced has been debunked,” he says. “It hasn’t happened yet. The U.S. labor market is actually in pretty good shape.”
Autor calls AI “a crappy automation technology” because it’s “just not a replacement for a sentient worker with judgment and domain knowledge. It’s a supplement to them. It can be useful to them.” While it might reduce headcount in some roles or areas, “it’s just not a wholesale replacement of people,” he says. He insists he’s not a Pollyanna, acknowledging that some kinds of expertise may be replaced by the tech and affect corresponding workers.
And yet he sees AI as a potential expertise-leveler. “It could enable more people to do legal work, more people to write software, more people to do a higher level of healthcare, more people who are doing kitchen contracting to do more design, more people who are doing skilled repair to expand the set of things they can fix do it more efficiently,” he says.

Sanmi Koyejo Is One of TIME's 100 Most Influential People in AI
Unknown

2026-08-27
12:02:36 UTC
21:02:36 KST

Sanmi Koyejo, co-founder of AI security startup Virtue AI, has devoted his career to finding out what AI models can and cannot do. The aim is to push companies towards building AI systems that are more reliable, accurate, and secure, and less vulnerable to misuse by bad actors. It’s an effort that’s drawn the attention of Meta, which in June announced it had hired Koyejo and co-founders Dawn Song and Bo Li to join its Superintelligence Labs in its security efforts. Koyejo in particular will play a crucial role in shaping Meta’s fundamental AI research division, FAIR, whose workforce was substantially reduced by the company last fall.
Koyejo, who has served as president of Black in AI for five years, is also the director of Stanford University’s Trustworthy AI Research Lab (STAIR), where he oversees work in AI measurement science—a field devoted to pressure-testing how AI models perform in the wild. As Koyejo explains, AI models are evaluated before they are deployed to the public. But once they are shipped, there’s no telling how well the systems will fare with daily use. And the gulf between how well an AI model performs on a coding benchmark and how it performs in various settings can be considerable.
“That gap is what would let a hospital, a school district, or a regulator ask whether a given evaluation means anything in their setting and get an answer with an error bar. Every other field that certifies anything [has] this,” says Koyejo. “Clinical trials have biomarkers with known predictive validity, and auditing has standards that survive being tested against real failures.” In his work, models should have to measure up to the same performance standards, he says.

Veronyka Gimenes Is One of TIME's 100 Most Influential People in AI
Unknown

2026-08-27
12:02:36 UTC
21:02:36 KST

Veronyka Gimenes wants you to know AI can be used to fight back. In 2025, Gimenes and Amanda Claro, co-founders of the Brazilian advocacy group Código Não Binário, created TybyrIA, an open-source AI model for detecting anti-LGBTQIA+ hate speech. The model allowed them to categorize evidence at scale for a lawsuit against social media companies.
The motivation for TybyrIA traces back to 2024, when a clip of Entre Amigues—a queer podcast produced by Código Não Binário—went viral. The clip, which discussed the Brazilian transmasculine identity “boyceta,” triggered an anti-trans hate campaign. Far-right figures mockingly shared the clip with their audiences. Gimenes says the resulting round-the-clock bombardment of comments and messages took a severe toll on the team’s mental health.
Gimenes realized the scale of hate could provide the data for a “counter-attack.” But after manually sorting malicious comments proved too psychologically taxing, she turned to AI. Fine-tuning an open-source model allowed her to catalogue hate speech at a previously unimaginable scale—evidence Gimenes later used to file a public civil action lawsuit against Meta, Google, X, and ByteDance. The suit seeks roughly $20 million in damages and demands platforms take more proactive measures to curb anti-LGBTQIA+ hate on the platforms. According to court filings viewed by TIME, the companies argue that their policies already prohibit discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity, and that there are mechanisms to remove content that violates those policies in place. (Meta declined to comment. Google, X and ByteDance did not respond to requests for comment.)
Gimenes now works to help others understand how they can use AI critically, rather than altogether rejecting the technology. Her online course with Código Não Binário, which has already seen more than 1,700 enrollments, teaches people how they can leverage and adapt open-source technologies.

Yann LeCun Is One of TIME's 100 Most Influential People in AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
12:02:36 UTC
21:02:36 KST

Mark Zuckerberg called Yann LeCun one Sunday last November. Word had gotten out that LeCun, who built Meta’s Fundamental AI Research (FAIR) lab, was leaving to start his own venture. Zuckerberg urged him to stay. Good luck raising the money and good luck building a product the market would believe, LeCun recalls him saying. The following month, LeCun unveiled Advanced Machine Intelligence Labs. By March, it had raised $1.03 billion in seed funding—one of the largest rounds in history.
Much of the tech industry has converged on the idea that scaling large language models will eventually produce human-level intelligence. But LeCun, one of the field’s pioneers, believes they are chasing a dead end. Advanced Machine Intelligence is pursuing a fundamentally different approach to training, aiming instead to give AI an intuitive understanding of physical reality. So-called “world models,” he believes, will eventually make AI far more capable in areas like robotics, self-driving cars, and medicine.
LeCun was never one to follow the crowd. When he championed neural networks in the 1980s, the research community dismissed the idea for decades before it eventually became the foundation of the current AI boom, earning him a Turing Award in 2018. Being a contrarian takes a pinch of “confidence,” he says, and an ability to step back. “You just need to lift your nose from the trench you're digging, and look around.”

Mira Murati Is One of TIME's 100 Most Influential People in AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
12:02:35 UTC
21:02:35 KST

Mira Murati says she wants you to have a choice.
Major AI companies have cohered around proprietary, one-size-fits-all intelligence rented by the token. They are also racing to automate more of what humans do, she says. In 2025, she founded Thinking Machines Lab to build an alternative: models you customize with your data, then steer through more humanlike interaction. The result, she says, will be to extend human agency, rather than handing it off to machines.
To pursue this alternate vision, Thinking Machines has raised $2 billion—the largest seed-funding round in history—and in March inked a deal for Nvidia to provide the next-generation chips needed to support its models. “If humans want to delegate everything in their lives to AIs ... there will be options. But if they don’t want that, they shouldn’t feel like [they] have no choice,” Murati says.
But most may not get to decide. In a competitive market, if autonomous systems outperform human-AI teams, people might have no choice about whether they’re replaced. Murati expects that might happen in math and coding, but counters that many domains rely on “human participation, on the messiness of the real world.”
The founder and former OpenAI executive has witnessed that messiness up close. During Sam Altman’s brief ouster in 2023, Murati served as OpenAI’s interim CEO, caught between the board that removed him, employees demanding his return, and Microsoft, the company’s key partner.
Thinking Machines Lab has hit the ground running. Tinker, the startup’s first product, which came out in October, lets users customize open-weight AI models more deeply than they could through prompting alone.
Meanwhile, the battle for talent has challenged the company. Several prominent researchers, including many on the founding team, have departed for rivals. Murati says success isn’t measured by how much of the original team remains, but by what the company delivers.
In July, the startup released its first model, Inkling. While the company does not claim it is the strongest model overall, it describes Inkling as a broad, balanced generalist designed for customization.
To Murati, tailoring models around people’s knowledge will expand their agency rather than replace them. But the more completely those systems absorb people’s expertise, the more capable they may become at automating them. Her answer is to keep people continuously involved in shaping what the systems do. Thinking Machines previewed “interaction models” in May that, rather than alternating between listening and speaking, can continue processing while a person talks, much like a human does. Murati says this is a first step toward increasing the richness between people and machines, which she believes is key to keeping us involved in shaping what AI does.
“We have machines that can think; they already exist today,” she says. “But what they think about should still be up to us.”

Andy Konwinski Is One of TIME's 100 Most Influential People in AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
12:02:35 UTC
21:02:35 KST

In June, Andy Konwinski assembled around 100 influential AI researchers and engineers at San Francisco’s Exploratorium to discuss how to keep the frontier of AI research from closing. In Konwinski’s view, leaving the development of leading AI models to a handful of private companies centralizes power, posing unprecedented risks. “The frontier will not close on its own,” he told attendees. “It closes through a series of decisions.”
Konwinski grew up as a Jehovah’s Witness in rural Wisconsin. “I sold Bibles for free until I was 17,” he says. In 2013 he co-founded Databricks, a $190 billion analytics and AI company built on an open-source framework for working with large volumes of data, which Konwinski helped create as a Ph.D. student at Berkeley. He later became a co-founder of AI search company Perplexity.
Now Konwinski says he is focused on the future of open science. In 2024, he launched Laude Ventures, a $150 million fund backing technical founders that counts more than 50 leading computer scientists among its investors. By 2025, he committed $100 million of his own money to launch a nonprofit, the Laude Institute, to offer computer science researchers grant funding and direct support. Collectively, they seek to produce scientific breakthroughs others can build on and breakout companies to steward them. “The open science community needs a heavyweight contender in the ring with OpenAI and Anthropic,” says Konwinski.
One Laude-backed project, an AI benchmark called Terminal-Bench, has been used by almost every major lab to evaluate its agents. In October, the institute will announce which among the eight “moonshot” projects it backs—targeting areas from health care to civic discourse—will receive $10 million in additional funding. Though he has long since left his former faith, Konwinski is still motivated by drawing people into something bigger. “It’s more exciting to me, when the magic happens, that I feel small,” he says.
Disclosure: TIME has a licensing agreement with Perplexity. Investors in Databricks include Salesforce, where TIME co-chair and owner Marc Benioff is CEO.

The extent to which the pioneering venture capitalist Sarah Guo believes in the promise of AI can be summed up in a stunning sentence: “Yes, I think we can solve disease.” That is to say, the 37-year-old isn’t simply one of her generation’s savviest and most forward-thinking investors—she’s a true believer.
There is a reason, after all, that Guo’s four-year-old AI investment firm is called Conviction. I would not invest in all of these companies if I didn’t believe the outcomes were good.”
And there’s still plenty more to fund. “I think we’re in maybe the third inning of this revolution,” she says. “We’re at the beginning.”

The AI race has increasingly become an electricity race, as companies sprint to build the power infrastructure necessary to power data centers. Joe Dominguez, president and CEO of Constellation Energy, is betting that nuclear energy will be one of the most important sources of that power.
To do that, Constellation has signed a series of agreements with hyperscalers to provide long-term nuclear power to their data centers. No such deal has received more attention than Constellation’s partnership with Microsoft to restart a reactor at Three-Mile Island nuclear facility. (The facility, renamed the Crane Clean Energy Center, is best known for the infamous 1979 meltdown, though it occurred at a different reactor).
The project is part and parcel of a broader transformation Dominguez has helped drive. For decades, nuclear plants struggled to compete with cheap natural gas and renewable energy. Now the relentless, around-the-clock electricity needs of AI have made existing reactors enormously valuable assets.

Alessandra Sala Is One of TIME's 100 Most Influential People in AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
12:02:34 UTC
21:02:34 KST

How do we cope when we can no longer trust what we see and hear to tell us what is real? That’s a challenge that Alessandra Sala, senior director of AI and data science at Shutterstock, grapples with every day. One inciting incident: when her father received an AI-generated voicemail that sounded exactly like her sister, nearly fooling her family.
“Our senses were never designed to cope with this digital world where what’s synthetically generated seems so real that we cannot differentiate anymore,” says Sala. As the AI industry remains fixated on releasing more powerful and autonomous models, the Italian-born computer engineer is one of the leading voices pushing for safer and more inclusive AI systems.
One of those is in disinformation: Sala represents Shutterstock in the AI and Multimedia Authenticity Standards Collaboration, a group focused on developing authenticity standards for AI-generated multimedia and tackling the growing problem of deepfakes.
The other is in representation: Sala also serves as co-chair of UNESCO Women in Ethical AI and is the global president of Women in AI, which are both addressing the gender gap in the AI industry. In a world where algorithms can shape our reality and govern everything from hiring to healthcare, underrepresenting women or other minorities in training models could hold serious consequences for society. Many of the latest AI models don’t just automate the discrimination and institutional biases that already exist, she says—they amplify it.
“Those models converge to an average of the things that they see, and if they receive very [few] examples of women or any other minority, this information gets forgotten very early,” says Sala. “We see an amplification of the discrimination and the gap.”

Beth Barnes Is One of TIME's 100 Most Influential People in AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
12:02:34 UTC
21:02:34 KST

One chart has become a kind of Moore’s Law for the AI’s rise. Published by METR, a Berkeley-based AI evaluator, the graph tracks the growing complexity of tasks AI models can complete, measured by how long they would take a human to perform. Since 2023, that “time horizon” has doubled every four to seven months. Project the trend forward, and by 2030 AI systems could complete tasks that take humans a month.
METR’s graph has been cited by AI executives, investors, and those who fear the technology’s rapid ascent could imperil humanity’s future. Skeptics point to its limitations: it covers only software-engineering tasks and measures whether an AI can succeed 50% of the time, even though many real-world domains demand far greater reliability. They also cite a 2025 study finding that AI coding assistants actually slowed experienced engineers down; the research was itself published by METR.
“Being happy to publish evidence that points in very different directions is something I’ve been most proud of,” says Beth Barnes, who left OpenAI in 2022 to found METR as an independent means to track AI’s rise. Barnes says the two findings are less contradictory than they appear. To her, AI in its current form can be overhyped even as many people “under-anticipate the longer-term trend.”
AI companies have given METR access to unreleased models, even as the group has shown itself willing to publicly critique them. In March, METR sought nonpublic information from top AI firms and even embedded a staff member at Anthropic to assess whether an AI agent could establish a “rogue deployment,” or a set of agents running without human knowledge of permission; the group concluded that contemporary models might already be capable of small or temporary breakouts. Two months later, an OpenAI model escaped its constraints and hacked another company. OpenAI is now working with METR to investigate the incident.
Until recently, Barnes says, many AI risks remained theoretical because “the models just weren’t that capable.” Now, as METR sees it, they are “getting increasingly close to being able to do some amount of damage.”

Emil Michael led the Pentagon’s negotiations with Anthropic over military AI safety guardrails, attempting to strongarm one of the world’s fastest-growing companies into accepting terms it deemed unacceptable. When Anthropic refused in February, Michael helped trigger an unprecedented reaction: designating it a supply chain risk—the first time the label has been applied to an American outfit.
Michael, a former Uber executive, was no stranger to dealmaking. A decade ago, he led the negotiations behind the ride-hailing business’s $3.5 billion Saudi investment and helped close its historic deal with Didi in China. After taking charge of the Pentagon’s AI portfolio last August, Michael said he inherited Biden-era contracts burdened by “25 pages of restrictions” that prevented basic military activities. He pushed providers to permit “all lawful uses” of their models.
Anthropic has said the dispute came down to two exceptions: keeping Claude from conducting mass surveillance of Americans and from independently controlling lethal autonomous weapons. Michael rejects that account, saying Anthropic instead wanted the Pentagon to seek its approval for particular uses of Claude, effectively inserting the company into the military chain of command. Anthropic has called that characterization “patently false.”
After negotiations failed, the Pentagon imposed the supply chain risk designation. “They turned it into a PR thing,” Michael told TIME in March. “When you do that, you are a supply chain risk.” Though Michael did not persuade Anthropic, he won the broader fight. OpenAI, xAI, and Google subsequently reached agreements allowing the Pentagon to deploy their models under terms closer to those he had laid out.

Archaeologists discover medieval cemetery beneath Ghent Vlasmarkt
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27

During a trial excavation, archaeology firm BAAC uncovered a medieval cemetery beneath the Vlasmarkt or Flax Market in Ghent. The city authorities in the capital of East Flanders had planned to plant a tree on this location following roadworks. BAAC estimates that there may be up to 240 skeletons buried here. The tree will now not be planted for the time being. Ghent has also decided not to carry out any further excavations at the minute.
Archaeologists found four skeletons during a trial excavation on the Vlasmarkt. A small section of the market was examined at the spot where a tree was to be planted. The excavation took place whilst roadworks were underway. Ghent is removing the traditional cobblestones and resurfacing the market with tarmac.
It was known that the current Vlasmarkt was a cemetery from the 11th to the 18th century. The square is situated next to St James’s Church. Until now, it had been unclear how many people were buried here.
The archaeologists found the skeletons at a depth of just over 1 metre. A deeper borehole indicates that there are a further four burial levels underneath. This means that there are probably only 20 skeletons buried at that specific location. Based on this, the archaeologists have made an estimate for the entire site, which covers 23 square metres. Beneath the Vlasmarkt, there is thought to be a cemetery containing more than 240 skeletons.
Ghent has decided that the tree will now not be planted and that no further excavations will take place. The finds will therefore be preserved for the time being. The city authorities have, however, promised to take the remains into account during any future, larger-scale redevelopment.
Today the Vlasmarkt is one of the places where Ghent residents and visitors enjoy a night out. During the Ghent Festival, the square is the place to party until the early hours of the morning.

Iran, Qatar hold Hormuz talks as US blockade chokes Iran oil imports
Iran's top diplomat met his Qatari counterpart on Thursday in Tehran for talks on the strategic Strait of Hormuz, as a US naval blockade squeezes oil supplies to Iran amid a domestic shortfall.
The visit by Qatar's Foreign Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani follows a week of intense diplomacy in Iran involving separate meetings with Oman's top diplomat and senior Pakistani officials seeking ways to end the Middle East war and reopen Hormuz.
It also comes as Washington threatens wider secondary sanctions against countries, banks and companies that continue doing business with Iran, part of a broader campaign it has called "economic asphyxiation".
Read moreNavigation, jurisdiction, costs: Iran, Oman attempt to hammer out Hormuz deal
Iranian state television said Al Thani, who is also Qatar's prime minister, had met with Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, without providing details.
Qatar's foreign ministry said they discussed de-escalation efforts as well as the proposed framework for Hormuz between Iran and Oman.
Al Thani "emphasised the necessity of respecting the sovereignty of neighbouring states and freedom of navigation", and pursuing dialogue, the ministry said.
Alongside mediator Pakistan, Qatar had played a key role in securing an April ceasefire and June deal between Iran and the United States, but those deals have since collapsed.
Fuel shortage
Since war with the United States broke out on February 28, Iran has maintained tight control over Hormuz, a vital global energy conduit, with Washington imposing a naval counter-blockade on Iranian ports.
Read moreUS unveils expanded sanctions aimed at Iran's 'economic asphyxiation'
On Wednesday, Iran's Vice President Mohammad Jafar Ghaempanah said the blockade had prevented his country from importing enough petrol to cover a shortfall in domestic production.
"Petrol production is insufficient, and because of the US naval blockade, we cannot import it," he was quoted by the official IRNA news agency as saying.
In recent days, many Iranians have been seen queueing outside petrol stations. Presidential chief of staff Mohsen Haji-Mirzaei meanwhile said petrol quotas would be reviewed, without elaborating.
Iran, a major oil producer with some of the world's cheapest fuel, has for years heavily subsidised petrol, making changes to pricing politically sensitive.
As the United States seeks to strangle Iran's economy, Iranian officials have dismissed the measures as "failed policies" that will not force Tehran to change course.
"The country is in an all-out economic war," said Iran's top negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf in a statement carried by local media.
"We will see that the government... will defeat the enemy on this ground as well," he added.
Even before the war, Iran's economy was battered by decades of international sanctions, and has long suffered from chronic inflation and a weakening currency.
- Talks on Hormuz -
Iran has for weeks been in talks with Oman, which also overlooks the Hormuz strait, over a framework agreement that would establish a "temporary corridor" for shipping and provide for clearing mines Tehran says were laid during the war.
Iran's Revolutionary Guards on Wednesday said the two countries had agreed on each country's share of the waters and any revenues collected from managing the waterway.
Tehran has nonetheless insisted that the strait will not be reopened unless Washington meets its demands, including lifting its naval blockade, unfreezing Iranian assets abroad and removing oil sanctions.
Since the war broke out, Iranian forces have required vessels to obtain permission to transit the waterway and struck ships that failed to comply.
Tehran has also sought to impose service fees on ships using the strait -- a move strongly opposed by Washington and regional countries.
On Thursday, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations said an "unknown projectile" had struck a tanker in Hormuz this week, causing a fire that was later extinguished.

Persistent financial hardship is linked to later-life brain shrinkage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
12:00:52 UTC
21:00:52 KST

Money worries can keep us up at night, but could decades of financial stress leave a lasting mark on the brain itself? That’s the question my colleagues and I set out to answer in a new study – and the answer, it turns out, is yes.
Most research on money and brain health looks at people’s financial circumstances at just one point in time. This makes it hard to know whether a few difficult years have the same effect as decades of enduring struggle. For our study, published in the journal Innovation in Aging, we tracked the same people throughout their adult lives to find out.
We used data from the MRC National Survey of Health and Development, also known as the 1946 British birth cohort study. A cohort study follows a group of people born in the same period throughout their lives. This is the world’s longest continuously running study of its kind, tracking thousands of people born in one week in March 1946 – participants who celebrated their 80th birthdays earlier this year.
The study’s origins go back to the economic anxieties of the 1930s, when the Great Depression left many families worrying about money and the cost of raising children – making it a fitting dataset to revisit those same questions decades later. Using this rich resource, we examined the financial circumstances of 2,759 participants at multiple points across adulthood.
Participants reported their household income at ages 26, 43 and 53. We classed those in the bottom 20% of the group on at least two of these occasions as having persistent low income – about one in six people. Separately, we measured financial hardship by asking whether people struggled to manage on their income or had trouble paying bills, at least twice between ages 36 and 53. This applied to about one in eight.
At age 53, participants took tests of verbal memory and processing speed. A smaller group also had brain scans between ages 69 and 71, which let us measure brain atrophy (shrinkage) and ventricular expansion – the widening of fluid-filled cavities within the brain, a recognised marker of poor brain health.
We found that people who had experienced more financial hardship and low income scored lower on the cognitive tests at age 53. These links held even after we accounted for their childhood thinking skills, education and childhood disadvantage. Among those who had brain scans, persistent low income was linked to greater brain shrinkage in later life.
When we looked at how memory changed from age 53 to 69, those who had faced persistent hardship actually showed slower decline over that period. We believe this is because they had already lost more ground by age 53 – they started from a lower point, so there was less left to lose.
We also found that the link between financial adversity and brain shrinkage was stronger for men, for those who grew up in disadvantaged homes, and for carriers of a gene that raises the risk of developing Alzheimer’s disease.
For men of this generation – born in 1946, when the male breadwinner model was the norm – the pressure of being the main earner may have made financial stress more acute. Disadvantaged men also had higher rates of smoking and drinking than disadvantaged women.
The finding on genetic risk suggests that people who are already biologically vulnerable may be more susceptible to the effects of financial strain. These subgroup findings are based on smaller numbers within our sample, so we are treating them as suggestive rather than conclusive.
Why would money worries harm the brain?
How might financial hardship affect the brain over time? Chronic stress is known to increase inflammation, which accelerates brain ageing. There is also the simple fact that constantly worrying about money uses up mental energy, leaving less capacity for other thinking tasks – a cognitive load that competes with everything else the brain is trying to do.
We acknowledge that our study cannot prove cause and effect, and the results, drawn from a single generation of British adults, may not apply directly to other populations or countries. But following the same people over many years gives us a clearer picture than studies that only look at a single moment in time.
Financial hardship is increasingly recognised as one of several factors – alongside things such as hearing loss, smoking and physical inactivity – that may shape our risk of cognitive decline in later life. Our findings suggest that reducing chronic financial hardship among working-age adults, wherever they live, could help protect brain health and potentially reduce dementia cases in the future.

Russia sentences former ‘king of state contracts’ to 12 years in prison in absentia for bribing a colonel
Moscow’s Basmanny District Court sentenced Boris Usherovich, a former co-owner of the “1520” group of companies, to 12 years in prison in absentia for bribing former Interior Ministry colonel Dmitry Zakharchenko, the Russian business news outlet RBC reported.
Usherovich, who has been placed on an international wanted list, was arrested in absentia in 2019. The court, which began hearing the bribery case in October 2025, also fined him 500 million rubles.
Investigators said that from 2007 to 2016, Usherovich, his “1520” partner Valery Markelov, and former Inkredbank vice presidents Dmitry Motorin and Ivan Stankevich paid Zakharchenko bribes totaling more than 1.4 billion rubles.
Investigators believe the payments were meant to secure protection for a platform the men had set up to run shadow banking operations, including cash withdrawals and currency conversion. Zakharchenko initially received 150,000 euros a month; those payments stopped in 2009–2011, after which his cut rose to 20% of the platform’s monthly income in each currency.
Motorin, Stankevich, and Usherovich left Russia after the case was opened. Zakharchenko has denied protecting the bankers and businessmen. Valery Markelov was sentenced in 2019 to eight years in prison and fined 500 million rubles. He was diagnosed with cancer during the trial and died several months after the sentence was handed down.
The “1520” group of companies designs and builds railroads. In 2018, its owners — Alexei Krapivin, Valery Markelov, and Boris Usherovich — topped Forbes Russia’s ranking of “kings of government contracts,” after receiving government contracts worth 218 billion rubles that year, according to Forbes Russia’s calculations.

Nepal floods leave hundreds dead, thousands missing
A catastrophic flash flood on Wednesday morning wreaked massive destruction upon Nepal’s northern mountainous region, bordering China. The torrent of water, rock, and mud wiped out entire villages, washed away roads and destroyed power infrastructure and dams.
Thousands of people are missing, Nepalese Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal has said, among them pilgrims to Mansarovar in Tibet, a sacred site for Hindus. “Town after town has been wiped out within hours,” he said. Nearly 400 of the 579 tourists missing are Indians.
Nepal’s army has pressed in helicopters to rescue people trapped in mud and in buildings that survived the deluge, and deliver emergency supplies. More than 100 people have been rescued so far, including foreigners.
In China, where the border customs post at Gyirong Port was wiped out by the rushing water and rocks, 558 people are missing – 260 of them foreigners. However, rescue efforts are hindered because of the lack of road connectivity and the thick mud covering the area.

11:59:11 UTC
20:59:11 KST

The French Chief of the Defense Staff, General Fabien Mandon, warned on the 26th of August that the country is not yet ready to confront relatively cheap and mass-produced threats such as drones, writes Politico.
Since Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine, financially sustainable defense against relatively cheap, mass-produced weapons, including the Iranian-made Shahed drones, has become one of the main challenges for Western militaries.
Mandon, at an event organized by France’s main business lobby, Medef, warned that there are enemies who have developed a large number of cheap solutions that can drain French defense resources. He said that this is not happening yet, there is no catastrophe, and the country is peaceful, but action must be taken.
NATO’s arsenal consists of sophisticated, high-tech missiles, each worth millions, that the army, navy and air force use to shoot down remotely piloted aircraft worth tens of thousands of dollars.
The main goal now is to reduce the so-called cost per kill — that is, to reduce the price of neutralizing a threat.
Recently, the French Air Force has used expensive missiles to shoot down cheap Iranian drones that it has been targeting in the Persian Gulf.
French arms manufacturers such as MBDA and start-ups including Alta Ares and Harmattan AI are working on cheaper, mass-produced weapons to counter the threat. Mandon said defensive weapons are not yet being produced in the quantities needed to stop intense waves of attacks. He added that he is working to accelerate the use of drones in the French armed forces. The general also noted that defense industry companies must be able to adapt to a rapidly changing world where competitors are adapting very quickly.

Is it safe to buy airBaltic tickets? Tallinn Airport representative gives his assessment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
11:56:18 UTC
20:56:18 KST

Latvia’s national airline airBaltic needs to make changes in order to survive, but there is no reason to fear that flights will be suspended in the coming months, Eero Pärgmäe, a member of the management board of Tallinn Airport operator Tallinna Lennujaam, said in an interview with Estonian public television on Thursday.
He said there are two possible scenarios for airBaltic’s future.
“The first is that they will manage to complete the restructuring, continue operating with a smaller fleet and make the company profitable. The second scenario is that, at some point, it will be concluded that there is no place in the market for this kind of business model, that the major airlines have taken over the European market and that this smaller model no longer works. In that case, the company will be shut down,” Pärgmäe said.
In his assessment, the measures airBaltic is taking to reduce its fleet are a step in the right direction.
“Reducing the fleet is entirely reasonable. Here in the Baltic States, there is simply no use for a fleet of more than 35 aircraft — there is nowhere to deploy that many planes. So these measures are moving in the right direction. The question is whether they were taken in time,” Pärgmäe said.
airBaltic is the largest carrier at Tallinn Airport, with a market share of 29%.
Asked about the impact of the airline’s restructuring on Tallinn Airport, Pärgmäe said airBaltic aircraft are still operating according to schedule and tickets remain on sale.
However, the advance booking window for airBaltic has shortened — passengers are now booking tickets one or two months in advance, which is the period for which customers are currently willing to purchase tickets. Regarding January, the airline needs to provide additional explanations in order to strengthen market confidence, Pärgmäe said.
“If you ask me whether I would buy airBaltic tickets, then yes, I would — for the end of September. According to today’s flight schedule [from Tallinn], they are selling tickets on 12 routes. I think they will also continue flying during the winter. However, to make it through the winter, they will need both additional financial resources and positive signals to the market,” the Tallinn Airport management board member said.
He suggested that
airBaltic aircraft would likely operate somewhat less frequently from Tallinn during the winter season.
“airBaltic will most likely continue serving the so-called core routes that it has operated until now. If airBaltic reduces the number of flights, it will undoubtedly affect the market for some time. However, demand for air travel is currently strong. We can see that people want to fly, and I am completely confident that we will be able to introduce new routes to the market and attract new carriers,” Pärgmäe said.
He stressed that Tallinn Airport has deliberately sought to maintain as broad a portfolio of airlines as possible.
“For a small country like ours, having 15 scheduled carriers is a very good figure. If we look at our customer profile, 50% of our passengers travel through major hubs — Frankfurt, Helsinki, Copenhagen, Warsaw and Riga. This means that Estonia will by no means be left without air connections; such a problem will not arise,” Pärgmäe said.
The Tallinn Airport management board member predicted that low-cost airlines would see the strongest growth in the coming years.
He also noted that aviation fuel prices are having the greatest impact on airlines this year.
“If we look at last year, aviation fuel was 70–80% cheaper then. Because of the situation surrounding the Strait of Hormuz, aviation fuel remains very expensive. We can already see the consequences in the winter flight schedules — airlines are cutting longer and less heavily used routes that were operated last winter, simply because they are not profitable. Fuel is currently that expensive,” Pärgmäe concluded.
Pärgmäe is one of four members of the Tallinna Lennujaam management board and is responsible for commercial matters.
As previously reported, airBaltic’s Supervisory Board has approved a business plan that, among other measures aimed at improving liquidity, provides for raising 225 million euros in interim financing using the existing collateral pool securing the 2029 senior bonds.
In the longer term, the plan provides for the company’s recapitalisation through up to 225 million euros in new debt and 100 million euros in new equity. Part of the existing 2029 bonds will be converted into equity in the company, while
the remainder will be replaced with new, reduced debt of up to 125 million euros.
The business plan also provides for the airline to operate 36 Airbus A220-300 aircraft by the end of 2026, compared with 54 aircraft currently, with the fleet gradually increasing to approximately 40 aircraft by 2031.
The airBaltic Group’s revenue increased by 4.2% last year compared with 2024, reaching 779.344 million euros. Meanwhile, the Group recorded a loss of 44.337 million euros, 2.7 times lower than in 2024. In 2025, the airline carried a total of 5.2 million passengers, an increase of 1% compared with 2024.
Last summer, German flag carrier Lufthansa became a shareholder in airBaltic. The Latvian state currently owns 88.37% of airBaltic’s shares, Lufthansa holds 10%, Aircraft Leasing 1, a company owned by Danish businessman Lars Thuesen, holds 1.62%, while other shareholders own the remaining 0.01%. The company’s share capital amounts to EUR 41.819 million.
Taking into account the 2025 financial results and current market conditions, airBaltic has suspended its potential initial public offering (IPO) and does not currently consider it a potential source of capital in 2026, according to airBaltic’s annual report.

Three Italians still untraceable in Nepal says Farnesina (3)
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
13:55:39 CEST
20:55:39 KST

Three Italians are missing and still
untraceable in Nepal after the deadly floods there, the
Farnesina reported Thursday.
                                    
                                       
				The foreign ministry said that of the dozen Italians still
untraceable this morning, three cases remain.
                                    
                                       
				The first is a 50-year-old goldsmith from Rapallo near Genoa,
Marco Ratto, who was leaving Nepal for Tibet.
                                    
                                       
				The Chinese travel agency that was supposed to take care of the
group confirmed that it had lost contact at the crossing.
                                    
                                       
				This information was also confirmed by the Nepalese agency
directly to the family.
                                    
                                       
				Then there is an Italian-Swiss couple traveling from Tibet to
Nepal.
                                    
                                       
				The Farnesina explains that the agency's contact information is
missing and there is still no confirmation that they crossed the
crossing.
                                    
                                       
				The data released by the Nepalese side, the Ministry of Foreign
Affairs informs, is based on information shared by tour
operators and may be inaccurate and may not take into account
those who did not cross.

Farmers to recieve €26.4 million to offset rising prices and bad weather

Farmers to recieve €26.4 million to offset rising prices and bad weather
Agricultural producers will recieve an additional €26.4 million next year to help alleviate the rise in prices following the Middle East crisis and losses resulting from adverse weather conditions.
The amendments to Estonia's strategic plan for the European Union's Common Agricultural Policy (CAP), approved by the government on Thursday, will increase next year's direct payments budget by the maximum possible amount, a statement said.
"The additional funds come from the European Union's long-term budget and their use does not require additional funding from the state budget," Minister of Regional Affairs and Agriculture Hendrik Johannes Terras (Eesti 200) was quoted as saying.
The money will reach producers mainly in December next year, helping to improve companies' financial position and cover sharply increased operating costs.
The distribution of the funding was agreed following proposals from the Chamber of Agriculture and Commerce, the Central Union of Farmers and organic farming organisations.
Cow and sheep and goat farmers, as well as cultivators of fruit and vegetables, berries, cereals, pulses, and seed potatoes will all recieve extra support.

Satellite images show destruction from Nepal-Tibet floods
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
11:54:59 UTC
20:54:59 KST

Satellite images show destruction from Nepal-Tibet floods
A glacier collapse high in the Himalayas on Wednesday triggered catastrophic flooding along the Nepal-Tibet border.
At least 359 people have been confirmed dead and more than 1,300 remain missing across Nepal and China’s Tibet region after a Himalayan glacier collapse sent a wall of water, mud and rock through border towns and valleys.
Rescue teams are searching for survivors in terrain that is hard to access at the best of times. At least 19 bridges and about 40km (25 miles) of road have been destroyed, further hampering the search.
Nepal Police spokesperson Abi Narayan Kafle said the death toll is expected to rise further.
Satellite imagery captured by Planet Labs before and after the flood shows how buildings and roads have been washed away.
The imagery also shows large parts of Syapru Besi village submerged in mud.
What happened?
At about 8:40am local time (02:55 GMT) on Wednesday, a large section of glacier broke away high above the Lhende river in Tibet. The falling ice and rock dammed the river and, shortly afterwards, when the blockage gave way, the surge tore through settlements in Nepal’s Rasuwa district, destroying homes, hydropower plants and border infrastructure.
The resulting ice and rock avalanche struck the river about 20km (12 miles) northeast of the Rasuwagadhi border crossing.
Early reports attributed the collapse to a magnitude 4.4 earthquake. But the United States Geological Survey later said the seismic signal was caused by the landslide itself, not an earthquake. The landslide packed enough force to register as a magnitude 5.2 seismic event.
Where did the floods hit?
Some of the worst damage was in Rasuwa district, on Nepal’s northern border with China. The surge travelled down the Lhende Khola (river) into the Bhotekoshi and then the Trishuli river, which rose by as much as 9 metres (30 feet) in 30 minutes, according to Nepali officials.
Timure and Syapru Besi were among the settlements hit in Rasuwa. Further downstream, the flooding reached parts of Nuwakot and Dhading. Bodies have since been recovered much further south, in Gorkha, Tanahun, Chitwan and the two Nawalparasi districts.
In Tibet, mud and debris struck Gyirong Port in Shigatse.
The Trishuli eventually joins the Narayani, which flows into India’s Bihar state, where it is known as the Gandak.
