Hajooj, I'd like to start with you.
Hajooj Kuka
Hi, and thanks for having me. So, yeah, I'm a member of the emergency response room, and the emergency response rooms are decentralised mutual aid groups that span Sudan. So there's over 800 of these small little mutual aid groups that are based on the neighborhoods and on then from the district level and then the state level. And I belong to one small one in Khartoum called [Al] Giref Gharb, so that's my base ERR. It's in a group, in a place that has over 30,000 people living in our neighborhood. When the war was in Khartoum, we had like eight community kitchens with 24 pots that were cooking, and then two clinics, and about 19 women co-ops. So this is the kind of stuff that we were doing. And what we do is mutual aid. So, basically, we're all volunteers. I'm a volunteer. I've been volunteering since the war started, and we have all these different members that are volunteers. We do a lot of different activities. It depends on what the community we sit together with, the community, and the community can come to the communal kitchens, or whatever, and then we decide what we want to do with the resources we have. The resources is, first, our time, what the community owns – so the spaces, pots to cook in, whatever the skills we'd have, be it medical, be it teaching awareness. So we had places where we would get the kids training and whatnot, and then this expands to be for the 800 different rooms and over 28,000 members from the ERRs that work throughout Sudan. And we coordinate and work together, and we base our ideas on mutual aid, on the idea of solidarity economy, on the ideas of good governance, transparency, accountability, quality, participation. Over time, we had all these different systems, and bureaucracies, and whatnot that we created, the structures that want to make sure that we're democratic enough, we're grassroots enough, or whatnot. And what is actually more important than all that is the spirit of volunteerism, the spirit of what we call the spirit of mutual aid. And when we translate it, we translate it into solidarity aid. So that's the core of it. What got me personally into it: when the war broke out, I happened to be traveling and wanting to travel back into Sudan, and it happened. And in the beginning we were trying to find ways to do, stand against the war, be anti-war, and whatnot, but really, really quickly, the bombs were really louder than what we can do. The methodologies that we used before of social media doing whatnot were just overwhelmed with images of war, and fighters, and the youth were following the destructions and bombing and whatnot. So the images were too.. it was too loud for us. And to find a way to keep the civic space open, we started like looking at other ways. And when, when the needs came about, we switched to mutual aid. And for me personally, being a filmmaker, it was like: what was my role? Like I'm away from Sudan or whatnot. And for me personally, it was finding the narrative, listening for hours to these emergency response rooms on the ground, talking about what they're doing, and trying to put that into a narrative that then unites all the different rooms. And they're very different, every ERR is different, but what brings us together is the spirit of volunteerism and the spirit of mutual aid.
Christina Bennett
Would you say that the impetus for the ERRs, did it start as a social media movement and then turn into an action movement? Or was one already happening and one just amplified the other?
Hajooj Kuka
It happened on the ground. It started by people finding things to do. So the first group of people were transporting medical staff and people on the ground to the hospitals and whatnot, and people were getting together and cooking together, and people were getting on bicycles, going, buying medicine from pharmacies to folks who can't move. So it started on the ground. And actually it was exactly the opposite, where in the beginning we wanted not to even have a presence anywhere. We didn't want people to know about us. We're just like working, working really a lot, and different things, and we got a lot of funding from the diaspora. So it was really started really Sudanese, really close-knit, really about your neighborhood, people from the diaspora sending you money, getting things from the people who left would leave their stuff behind and go, "You can go to my house and grab whatever you want.” So it really started that very local and very, during the beginning was more about organising together and talking to each other. And it wasn't until later that we needed attention and whatnot, when we needed more solidarity from bigger groups, and from different places, and UN agencies, and stuff. So it was later on that we started doing that. And up to today, the social media is really distributed, so we have over 1,000 different Facebook pages that represent the ERR, so we don't really have a united thing.
Christina Bennett
Bashair, what's your story? Tell us about Shabaka and how you got involved.
Bashair Ahmed
Thank you. It's a long story. It's... I've been in the sector for now 20 plus years, and I guess Shabaka kind of came from a time, you know, having worked in the UN with the INGO world, that the diaspora voices just were not heard. Diaspora communities who are responding to crises, I could see it, whilst the accolade and everything is going “Oh, the INGOs is stepping up.” And if you kind of talk about figures, you know, diaspora remittances are massive, and this is just through official channels. I think last year something about $685 billion were sent to lower, lower-income countries, so that's bigger than foreign investment and international aid combined. So that tells you a little bit what, the aid sector is about what, $41 billion? So it's really small in comparison. So that's why Shabaka, kind of, was born essentially. Shabaka is a research, a small research organisation and practice. We're very much focused on amplifying those voices, documenting these experiences and these stories about what diaspora, and increasingly mutual aid groups, are doing in their communities in terms of responding to crises. And my heritage as well, you know, with Sudan, I, we have covered several countries, but come April 2023, we had project covering several countries, like Haiti, Syria, Sudan, and such, and we had to step up. So one of the things we ended up having to do is essentially facilitate some of this coordination and connecting the dots. The work that Hajooj kind of talked about was so critical, and still is, in Sudan, is still being led by the communities themselves. So, how do you do that? And Sudan is always a blueprint, it's always the test case for the humanitarian sector, and I feel that is, at the moment, we need to do much more – not just the learning, but also how do we amplify this blueprint? Not just talk about yes, the accolade, the emergency response room. How many prizes have they got? We all kind of admire what, not just emergency response room, but generally mutual aid, but that is not translating to how we fund and how we support in reality. So we're using the language of localisation and support, but it's not coming with the practice either. But yeah, so I guess Shabaka is really problem-solving and addressing some of the nitty gritty kind of challenges of almost translation between the different groups and organisations.
Christina Bennett
You mentioned you’re, you've got Sudanese heritage. What drove you personally? Was there an actual personal frustration or something that really motivated you to start Shabaka? And research, why a research organisation? Why did you think that research was going to be so important in this world of mutual aid, of grassroots aid, of diaspora prominence?
Bashair Ahmed
In terms of research, I always say, if you want to do advocacy, you want to engage in policy, you need to have the evidence, and it needs to come from the communities and hearing their voices. So, we've done really interesting projects looking at, you know, different diaspora communities. You know, we did projects with African Union, with the European Union, Global Diaspora Facility, where we looked at concrete example of how it's done, because it's learning for the sector from how these communities are doing it, potential for collaboration. So it's to facilitate that. So if we don't know what we've done before, what we're doing now, how can that inform our future? It's not just to have a nice report sitting on some shelf. The other part, my Sudanese heritage, I guess, is kind of one of the drivers to why I engage in this sector for so long as well. So it wasn't just Sudan, it's kind of looking at communities affected by crises. So this is maybe something personally I've been working on for many years and decades, but when you kind of see clearly the discrepancy between this is our roles, regulations, the approach, and paper, but then you see the practice, and it just feels sadly that divide between rhetoric and practice widening even further now. You know, I can see myself in many ways as part of this sector, this world – it’is just retreating into what's easier. So when we're talking about reset, I don't think it's reset. We’re actually just reworking to come back to this, so we're not changing the mechanics. And the reflex is usually to, when money tightens, like, we’re having a lot of cuts here, so the behaviour is very much, it's not a reset, it's a retreat. It's consolidating the center and not sharing. So you're seeing that pattern much more prominently. So, in many ways, it’s: What skills can we bring to the table and highlight it to at least start problem-solving. Yes, the big organisations have a role, but what does that look like in future?
Christina Bennett
Thank you so much for that. So much to unpack there, and we'll get to some of this in a minute, but before that, Fanta, tell us your story. What is the Resilio Fund, and how did you get involved, and what has your journey been through the sector til now?
Fanta Toure
Thanks, Christina. It's a pleasure to be here alongside Bashair and Hajooj. I have so much respect for their work. Resilio was launched recently in November of 2025 building on a pilot work that's been done for about four years to support community-led response to crisis. And that's the idea. The idea is to recognise that there's an ecosystem for grassroots humanitarian aid that exists and plug into it and help that ecosystem thrive, as opposed to the way the things have been traditionally designed. And to me, it's fascinating to see how we as humans have turned solidarity into an industry. And so this idea of supporting mutual aid and supporting community-led effort, for me, goes with going back to the way things were or are supposed to be. We know that in a crisis the first person to respond is a neighbour, and if my house is on fire, that my neighbour comes, it's not because they're trying to save me or to help me, it’s because our lives are interconnected and they know this intrinsically. I'm personally very curious intellectually about: What does a global solidarity system that is based on this premise looks like? Some of the things that Hajooj was describing sound a lot like the culture and values in which I grew up. So actually, I was trying to respond to your question of “How did you come to this?” and I thought: I don't know. Like, I think if you grew up in a collective culture, and certainly things that I've seen in many parts of the U.S., it's people showing up for each other, and doing things for each other, and doing it collectively. And my first, when I was cutting my teeth in this field, I worked in Somalia for the organisation that later evolved into Adeso with Fatima Jibrell – a phenomenal environmental activist and someone from the community. And I remember seeing how, as an individual, she was treated by the international aid system. I remember witnessing the knowledge, and the expertise, and the wisdom that was being dismissed. And this was my wake-up moment of thinking that my contribution to our communities could be trying to be a little bit of a translator between the aid system and what people are trying to do and achieve with and for their communities.
Christina Bennett
Great, thank you. So I'm wondering a little bit about how you think that your efforts are driving change in the way the whole humanitarian endeavor works. Not the humanitarian system, so to speak. As you say: solidarity, humans helping humans, coming together around crises. How is what you are doing fundamentally shifting the way that we do, that we've been doing things as a sector, I suppose, for a century? Maybe I'll start with you, Bashair. From where you sit, how are grassroots efforts, grassroots aid efforts driving change in the way that we act in crises?
Bashair Ahmed
No, that's such an important question, and an important dialogue to have, because the reality is, as the sector, there's different pressure points happening to it, which is: legitimacy is a challenge, funding for the sector specifically is getting tighter, and it's just change isn't on the table. So what's happening is we have a shortage of courage, capacity to just being able to kind of evolve. Somebody referred to it as a permafrost, which is a system that we just refused to change. And this is where we're at at the moment. We could see the pressure from the top, the decision being made. The communities are kind of like, this is not happening – you know, Sudan is a prime example, you know, leading and all of that – and you have this kind of like the middle just refusing to shift, using the language, adjusting it, the comms, and all of this, but the reality is nothing is really changing. You still have only about 1% of funding going directly, through the pooled fund, directly to frontline responders in Sudan, for example. The same in Ukraine, and just numerous other examples. So essentially, if you, the sector, is not able to evolve, it will die. It's like a dinosaur. So, we really need to have a change of mindset kind of going forward.
Christina Bennett
So, I love this idea of permafrost, and you're not the first person I've heard to call it that, this kind of, yeah, middle layer of just a brick wall, like an inability to get over it, around it, through it. An obstinance of the sector. What's the permafrost that you see? Where does it sit? You say it sits in the middle somewhere, somewhere between the top – whatever the top is – and communities. Describe that to me. And how are you, or how are we, how is this group going to shift it, or break through it somehow?
Bashair Ahmed
The permafrost is coming in mechanisms. For example, you might have a donor or funder want to support a mutual aid group, or a group of network. Firstly, the challenge for them is the red tape at their end. You have to pass certain due diligence, you have to have a bank account, you have to have this kind of particular structures. That's one. You design it, and the community is kind of like we have money to spend on AB, like really specific, and you have to kind of jump the hoops with that. So yeah, the red tape, the due diligence, that passporting, “Oh, we can't do this,” that concept of professional. I still remember back in 2023 that because, as I said, Shabaka is a research organisation, but we got approached by different diaspora groups who wanted to respond, like medical doctors who wanted to go to the border to facilitate that, And this is in the NHS, at the National Health Service here in the UK – doctors, consultant, and such. And one of our partners on the ground is like, “Oh, this is great; however, they'll need to have basic humanitarian training on the humanitarian principles before we can even consider that,” and I was like, these are the people who are doing the surgeries, who are looking after a whole massive population here, and you want them to spend time on doing your hoops of all these trainings, safeguarding, the different things that you have to do to be onboarded? So that kind of lack of capacity to evolve with the realities on the ground, you really want to save lives? Do it. Yes, we do need to have the rules and regulations around it, but, yeah, it needs, it's not fit for purpose.
Christina Bennett
Hajooj, do you buy this concept of permafrost? Do you see it, nd how do you experience it where you sit in the ERRs? and what do you feel the emergency response rooms in Sudan is doing to break through, or to shift, to shift the mindset, as Bashair was talking about, of this highly structural, highly rules-driven humanitarian sector.
Hajooj Kuka
We’re, in the end, grassroots. We don't know about the humanitarian world. We didn't know it existed. We didn't know any about that. When Sudan, the war broke out, what was happening in the NGO world, they were getting the NGOs and the UN people out of the country. so when they were supposed to be the ones who were supposed to be sit there and help us, when we went to them for help, they were like, they didn't have time for us. they were like, the first few weeks was all about evacuation and getting them out, and there's all these hero stories that were covered internationally, and we were like, “Okay, what do we do?” And then we learn from them. Hopefully, a few of them had enough time to teach us about how do we work, what do we need to do, and whatnot. And one of the most important things was figuring out this word called mutual aid. And the difference between mutual aid and our cultural way of doing things, nafeer, and helping, having the ideas of us helping each other – and I think this comes back to the whole thing – is that nafeer and neighbours helping each other happens at one time, and we can do it in the beginning, but there's a moment where we need to do it for a long time. How do we survive for three years still doing this? And that's when you need the structures, and you needed organising, and you needed whatnot. But having ideas about neutrality, about transparency, accountability, quality, participation – all these things helped us set up a system, and we call it the F-system. And the system is growing, volunteers really know it, and we have peer-to-peer teaching, and whatnot. And we got that from talking and translating that, in what we hope is a decolonised way, because the structures are structures that we came up with. The charters, and whatnot, are things that we came up with. It's important for us to have had people in the middle, like Bashair and whatnot, who were on our side, who understood the system, but we were not in the mindset to understand what the problem was. So, at that moment, when they were telling us problems, we're like, we just wanted solutions. What do we do? How do we work? And we need to survive. We need life saving. And I think it's only until the point where the war slowly started reaching a stalemate in a way, in a lot of different states, and we were in a state where different states are going into recovery and into trying to think about what does thriving look like for them, that we started actually facing this issue. And only when we became bigger and more known, and people started working against us. Some NGOs had issues with us, where now they think we should just disappear. WFP is like, “Now we can take it over.” Other NGOs, being like local NGOs, “Localisation is about us, not about you guys. So, you guys, we will do this stuff, and you guys, it's not good for the communities to have their own money and deal with it.” So now we're noticing these issues are starting in areas where the NGOs can be on the ground and thinking that we should take over. You know they started hiring some of the volunteers and talking about “No, people need to have salaries, they need to work, you cannot just have volunteers,” and this whole idea of the community doing it, here's better, more efficient ways of doing it. So now we're noticing we're in this conversation. What makes it really hard for the ERRs is because, from the beginning we're like, we are only going to be happening, and then we're going to dismantle, and we're not going to be around. What happened is: the crisis is long. It's been three years. None of us think it's going to end up anytime soon. So now they have to deal with us, and it's becoming like, “Okay, everybody needs to deal with us staying, and we're going to be here for a while,” and we're not this “Ah, it's great to have grassroots anymore.” It's more like, “Okay, now what do we do?” And there is a clash, and we're calling it like the all-civil society – and I think this is what Bashair is a little bit talking about it – and then there's us, which is a lot of people, different ideas. There's people on the left, right, there's everything going on, there's communities from the different groups, like people who think their government is the militia of the RSF, or people who think their government is the Islamic SAF army people, or people who think they're— so it's like different people are so different, and we're all in this group trying to figure things out and talk to each other and whatnot. And in the middle we have to deal with this humanitarian sector, and what's happening, and USAID disappearing, and what this government thinks, and what that people think, and what this NGO think that we should work, and they have an opinion on us, and they don't like the way we do stuff, and they want to control it, and they want to change it. So suddenly, we have to deal with, and they're aligning with groups, and people finding, like, “Ah, if you break away from this, then you can get money this way.” And now there's all these things we're noticing, and we have to deal with. And in the middle of all that, right now, the crisis, the frontline crisis, is in North Kordofan in El-Obeid. So it's this one city that's being surrounded. And I just want to say this story. Like, we have this member who's super active, and he's like working with us, and suddenly he's like, "Guys, my wife is about to give birth, so I have to evacuate because the hospital that she was supposed to give birth, and just got hit by a drone, and I don't know what to do. So I'm just trying to run away and going to Kosti to try to give birth because she needs a C-section and nobody here can give a C-section.” So we're in the middle of this where the whole ERR sit together and everybody's in solidarity, and all the states are like, okay, all our money goes to North Kordofan. So all what we have, this flexible funding that we can decide on, just goes there. And then everybody else has to fundraise again for everybody else. And that was a decision that was just suddenly made. Now we have to wait for the, you know, the UN, everybody else. They need time, they need to have the old methodology of they need data to decide on things, and people need to get together. While in the ERRs, it just happened, and we're all like, “Okay.” So I feel like we hear about the humanitarian sector, we are part of it, but, like Bashair said, we're a tiny part. Like, we're fighting to get 5% of the funding, to raise it to maybe, hopefully, 10% of the funding. We're like, we're not even.. I think our highest level is we're talking about maybe we'll reach 20% of the funding goes to grassroots groups, one of them is mutual aid, but also other methodologies.
Christina Bennett
And I'm not surprised at the fact that you, that the ERRs are still operating, you know, three years after the war began, basically, because this is the way crises grow. Crises are never emergencies, they're never short term. They're never that first response and then done. I was reading a statistic the other day that 94% of funding in the humanitarian system goes to protracted crises or crises that are five years or more. You're probably going to be bumping up with this system for quite a long time. It's not surprising that you're already finding that.
—
Like Hajooj Fanta, you speak about solidarity and mutual aid as things that have already existed in communities and that are that are just coming to prominence now, because the rest of the system hass kind of collapsed in these last few years, or is, is on the back foot. You've also talked a little bit about what the humanitarian system can learn from, for example, feminist and Indigenous movements. So I wanted to hear a little bit more about that. What can those movements tell us about how aid should be organised differently? Not only around delivery, but also things that your colleagues are just talking about now, around solidarity. What does solidarity look like? What does volunteerism look like? What does dismantling power, or shifting power look like in practice from the practice of feminist aid and Indigenous movements?
Fanta Toure
First, I want to say mutual aid, I believe, existed most times and comes under stress when it's running all the time. It's not a permanent way of living, to relying and over relying on each other like this. And because we are in this world of polycrisis now, where you're seeing emergencies everywhere, it is becoming more visible. And I think that's the opportunity that we're looking at now. And I'm going to ramble a bit, but I'll come back to your question. I have three kids, they're young, and they sometimes compete for my attention, and every now and then I have to tell one of them, “Baby this is not your moment.” And I feel a little bit that way about the moment that we're in. I feel that it is the moment of community-led work. My dream is that five years from now, nobody can say we don't know how to resource locally-led movements. And the last rambling thing that I'll say before I go back to your question is – and I think it's NEAR that was one of the most recent ones or first ones to point that out – it's important to start shifting from localisation to locally-led, because localisation keeps centering the traditional aid system, and that's not, that's, that's not what we're trying to do anymore. There's a few things that surprised me, returning back to the humanitarian aid sector, quote unquote, from the feminist space, and one of them was the silos. I feel like the conversation on silos, and on flexible core long-term funding has moved far ahead in the feminist movement place. Right now in the humanitarian sector, we're still looking at conversations about: is this resource going to be for the life-saving part of the emergency, is it going to be for recovery, is it going to be for…? So that's one of the pieces that I think we have lessons to learn, that the young lady in Eastern DRC, right now, who's dealing with Ebola is also dealing with issues of protracted crisis, access to water, wants to go to school, wants to play with her friends, doesn't want to be married early, safety, ll of this together, and this is going to last for a long time. So, flexibility and less silos is one lesson that stays with me. The other one that stays with me is – I feel like it's the muscle that the feminist space had to build – is this capacity to dream and to imagine, and to say that this different world that we are fighting for is happening. It's there, and we can drive towards it. And perhaps because I, this is something that made me uncomfortable coming back to the humanitarian space, like I felt nervous talking about joy and talking about dreaming, because people's lives are at stake. And I think now, the sense of guilt is starting to go away, because as I visit communities, I see, and I, this is not the romantic “Oh look at people, they're suffering, and they're still clapping” —this is not what we're talking about. This is really like people getting married in Gaza, people going on with their life, that ability to dream and to persevere is another one tthat is staying with me when I think about the feminist movement. Solidarity is another one. Wellness, resourcing oneself is another one. Being creative in finding solutions, thinking beyond strategies. I'm still meeting many actors in the humanitarian field who say “My strategy allows me to do this and not that,” and I feel that in the feminist space we have started reversing this and say: A strategy is a guiding map, you have to move with what's happening in the moment and make that happen. 
Christina Bennett
Oh they're great, and I wanted to maybe now turn back to Hajooj for a second. What Fanta’s just described is a system based on joy, based on dreaming and daring to dream in a time of crisis. Does that resonate with what the ERRs are doing? I mean, you've described to us a very intricate system of governance and radical transparency and accountability, and that's all really important. Is there room to dream in the emergency response rooms? Is that one of the elements that drives them?
Hajooj Kuka
When we get together, the difference between getting food and distributing it, where you get to eat at home, and when it has to be like, there's these boxes, and the box is enough nutrition, and you get it, and you go home, and this will fit you, but we only have 1,000 boxes, so we're going to give it to 1,000 families, and we have to register them, and whatnot, and there's individual cash transfers that we give to these individual families, it'll be great, and when the community gets the money, and they cook food, and whoever comes gets to eat, whoever comes gets to have some coffee, sit together, have discussions, whoever the kids come in and they get to play, and they get to share the toys… So there's this idea that: together we will survive this. And I think, together we still dance and play music, and we still, yeah, dream, because we think we're going to be okay. Together we're going to create a better place, and we're going to do it, and whatnot. So, hope and creativity and joy are always there. It's only when you put the camera on us and you ask us, “Okay, so what's the situation?” w have to tell you, “Yeah, we're hungry, we need food, there's rapes and stuff.” I mean, because you want to hear that to get funding. So this idea is like that's the only story you want to hear, this, the single story you want to hear. But like, I was living in a war situation where throughout a whole year I didn't see a piece of soap, I didn't have a full meal until I was full, I was never full for a whole year, my water was always dirty, but if you ask me about stuff, I was happy. I was creating films, and we were doing theater games, and we were playing, and we were like super thin. All of us were super thin, but we were happy. We were dancing, we're doing things, and we're doing– and I didn't reflect on the fact that I was never full through a whole year until later. But if you asked me, I was like, I was fine. And it was all looking at pictures, it's like, wow, I was super, super thin, and it's because I didn't have enough food. But that doesn't negate the fact that we're all together on it. When we were bombed, and we’re all sitting together and running into shelter and whatnot, we were, by the time we're out, we're laughing, we're like checking on everybody, making sure everybody was okay. So the idea that joy and dreaming and hope is weird is like, no, that is humanity. We're humans, so we always look for those things. And like I just said, like this guy in El-Obeid, I mean, when hopefully they get their child, we will all be like celebrating the child and saying, like, how amazing that is, and whatnot. And yes, we have members who get married and have weddings, and the wedding is normally in the communal kitchen, and we get all the food together and make a little cake. So we still do those things within our communities, and celebrate the Eid. And we know that when Eid comes, we hide our funding because the diaspora sends enough money to cover us, and we know that when it comes, we don't need to spend any money, because there will be like slaughtering, people will send money, people stuff. So Eid is a time where, like, the money is totally spent by the diaspora. So Eid is covered, and everybody expects somehow there's going to be new clothes for the kids, and whatnot. And it happens every year. We know it's going to be last minute. Sudanese people are so last minute. But in the end it happens, and there's going to be joy, and there's going to be bakhoor, and maybe things. And one last thing I want to say, in my neighborhood, there was a time during when the war was in that area, there was a famine. We lost a lot of kids. There's a moment where we're losing kids, like two kids every day. But now we're seeing some of the kids who are now going into the ERRs, the women response rooms part of the ERRs, that are doing kindergartens. And the idea of the kindergartens, of course, is for the kids, but also for the mothers to go back to work. And we're seeing the kids are now like, you know, they're fluffy, they're big, they're a little bit fat, and they're running around, and it's great to see that, and there's a lot of joy in it. Still, the situation is really bad, but, but there's a lot of joy, and going through this and still being together, there's a lot of joy. So I feel like, definitely, there's a lot of joy. One thing I want to talk about feminism: So the majority of our members are women, and the amazing work that's being done by the women’s response room. And they get to do the kindergartens, they get to do soap-making, and leather stuff. They do all these like projects that are very different than just feeding and whatnot, and it's really empowering. Fanta Toure

And for an organisation to even have access to a source of funding that will say, take that funding and do what you need with it, or take that funding and continue to do more of what you're already doing – not subcontracted, not something that I've established is your need based on a needs assessment – I think, can be transformative for an organisation, as we've seen it done. It also helps with the response time. Some of our partners in India are able to move micro programs to the communities within 10 minutes of a crisis occurring if the money has been pre-positioned ahead of time. We've seen how community agency is activated when these microgrants are provided to a community group who can then continue to do what they're doing with it. Provide more food, for example, if that's what they were doing.
Christina Bennett
Some really good examples, I think, of where Resilio is putting money in the hands of communities in that flexible way, and I guess, as you say, without the audits, without the requirements to demonstrate value for money alongside it. Is that the key to this? Is it the flexibility on the funding side? What is the key?
Fanta Toure
I think the flexibility is part of it, but also understanding your place in the ecosystem. Our place is not to deliver anything, really. It’s to move resources to those who understand their reality, and then can put this capital to good use. I've seen some of the conversations that our partners had with communities on community contributions lead to end results that were fully owned by the community. There's a community in Ethiopia that said, “We have gotten to a point where we would wait for an aid agency to come and distribute goats in the case of a drought.” Now, if you're goats got sick, you would go to the whoever distributed the goat and ask them to replace the goat. But now this is not happening because we have decided that we didn't need goats, we needed this instead, and this is how we've organised for it, and this is what we've contributed to it. So, this power of agency and ownership, and also that sense of contribution, I think, goes a long way to – I don't want to say restoring dignity, because I think dignity is always there – but making space for it to flourish and set the path for a recovery that is a lot healthier. I've seen in places where, in the Philippines, for example, one of our partners, ECOWEB, has brought in the district-level government into some of the work that communities were doing, mutual aid type of work that the communities were doing, and to organise, and the national government now is interested and wants to provide a little bit of a budget. We're seeing similar conversations in Sri Lanka, where after the Cyclone Ditwah, the government was also interested in supporting more of this community-led effort, because they were impressed at how the communities was activated. I think that one of the key challenges is definitely, if you're going to play the role of a translator, to arbitrate between who you are accountable to, especially if there's going to be conflict between what the community will define as success, and what an external actor will define as success. I want to be able to say a classroom or an ECD center with children who are plump a couple of years or a year after a famine and who are running and playing is an indicator of success. How do I reconcile that or try to explain that you shouldn't need to have an audit for this to happen? And so what we're trying to do at Resilio is really to make more space for this type of interventions to occur, and then go back to the donors and say, “See, you didn't need an audit, and this is what happened.” And hopefully that can shift culture.

Hajooj Kuka
I want to first say something. What Fanta was saying about: we have to behave a certain way. It's important to realise that when we're talking— because we do life saving, we do recovery, and then we do what capacity building, but internal. When Bashair was talking about capacity building, the real capacity building that works for us was peer-to-peer, and it's continuous. It's not one workshop for two weeks. I mean, I do agree, that's BS. But when we're in a situation of saving lives, we cannot say no, because our biggest risk – although we had over 100 volunteers who lost their lives during the war – but our biggest risk is not having the resources to evacuate whoever wants to get evacuated, feed people, and fight famine. And we're really talking about this quote unquote partnership that happened between the mutual aid of the ERRs and the different partners – be it WFP, UNICEF, IOM, the foundations, FCDO, USAID, GFFO, the donations – it actually did stop a famine that was supposed to break crazy. So the idea is like, we have to take that money, we're not going to say no, no to the money. We will bend over because that money will save people's lives. And is it going to destroy us? It is going to destroy us. The ERRs will not survive this. The ERRs is not going to stay alive, and we know that as a fact. Like, we will be destroyed in the end. But the idea of us is not to stay forever, the idea of us is to save people's lives. The idea of us is to get enough trainings and thinking that once we're destroyed, something better will come out of us. So, I think one of our powers is knowing that we're not gonna survive this. If it's going to be saving one life, but it’s gonna destroy us, we will go that route of saving the one life. It's more important than us surviving. Is it possible? I don't think it's possible. I don't think we can survive… So, when we started, we started with our own resources, and then there's the diaspora, and as I said, the diaspora never stopped. It's always there. There’s fluctuation, we cannot survive only on it. Other than diaspora, we had foundation money in the beginning, we had donations, that is amazing, like people reading articles about Sudan then sending money to us. That money is flexible money, and it's an amazing form of solidarity. And then we had institutions like I said, WFP, UNICEF IOM, FCDO, USA, GFFO, like we had all that happening. And to deal with them, we had to meet them not in the middle, very close to where they’re at. So we came up with a system. The amazing thing is, we came up with our own system, and a lot of them were okay with our system, which is the F-system. One thing about when it comes to reporting and everything, we notice really early: we need reporting internally, because when we're so open and we're such a big group, and the Sudanese civil society is a really harsh space to be in that's very critical of each other, and it's very easy now online, somebody will call somebody corrupt, and somebody's like— so you really needed a system that where I'm external comes, I know that none of the money comes through me, and if somebody wants to claim, “Where's this money?”, the money goes through the finance folks. And then there's a different reporting folks, and there's a different programming folks of how was the money spent. Like, there is this system that people can follow that we need it. One time a funder came in and they're like, "Oh, we don't need any reporting,” and we're like, "It's still going to go through our F-system, we still going to use our forms, we're still going to do this because you might not need it, but we're accountable to a community, and our community is really harsh.” With that said, I actually like that. I like the ownership of the ERRs. This is not charity. They know that this money comes in, I have right to it. Why did you make that decision? Why did you guys decide to take it to North Kordofan? I'm here also dying. So this questioning, that's why we need to have all these systems. Our guys are using all these different methodologies to make the system transparent, as transparent as possible. It's really hard with so much data, because there is, the data is there, but to actually be transparent, you have to know how to communicate it, and we're struggling to do that. So with all that said, I want to end with one thing. One of our inspiration was the breakfast program of the Black Panther Party, and what happened was, you know, the country fought them, and when they were fought, they destroyed them. But one form of being able to destroy them is to actually give a breakfast program that the state had to give to the community. One thing about mutual aid, it is a form of resistance. So I feel like if we end up dying, but the system changes because they have to cover what we're doing, then that would be great. Because you cannot kill the ERRS without actually providing these services. Which almost happened when the, when SAF took over Khartoum, for example. They tried to kill us off and stop us, but the community after a few weeks, community came back to us, and they're like, “Hey, we need help, what's happening?” And they came to us, and they asked us to come back and work, because the services were not provided by SAF. In the beginning, they were happy, like, “Oh, yeah, go away, we don't want your lentils and rice, and we're so happy to now have a different variety of food,” but then, after a while, it was like, “Hey, we want your services.” So I feel like one part of mutual aid – and this is just me thinking out loud – mutual aid is here to disturb the system. The system needs to change. I don't want to be, like, volunteering for three years. It's really hard on me. Like, I'm working for a lot of hours, and whatnot, and I have to. I'm not making any money, and I have to survive, and I have to find different ways of dealing with things. So, with all that said, I don't know, I don't think there is a way for systems like the ERRs to survive unless the system changes and wants us to stay. WFP is a great example. We did amazing work with WFP. We saved a lot of lives with WFP. The partnership was great – and now they don't want us to exist, and literally they just want to go and do their own work. Like, we disturbed their systems in a way that we shouldn't exist. The same thing with a lot of local NGOs that worked amazing work with us. They were almost shut down when we appeared, and we got them to work, but now they notice that, hey, they have to share money with us. They have to go through endless talking with the community. They can't just program. So they don't want us to exist. We are problematic to them, and the whole idea that we're not registered, and now they come up with all these ideas us now, we don't work. So, the biggest thing with the ERRs is that they had to work with us, because the normal model is the UN wants access, and they want the warring parties to give them access. For us, it's like, you don't need access. We can work in this situation, and the people are there, so you just need to stand in solidarity with them. This whole idea of access doesn't matter. And when they have access, then suddenly it’s like, “Okay, now we don't need your idea anymore, we don't need the solidarity, we don't need the people anymore. We will just provide things in our own method,” and as a fact, the best way to give money is through this, what is called multi-cash system transfer, individual funding, and this whole giving money to a group is really not good. So they come up with their studied reports, and they want to do things their methods, and they want us to go away. So, with that said, I think one of our power is: we're okay with going away. We're just going to keep doing it, and we are going to save lives until we're destroyed. And I think for us not to be destroyed, the system has to change. But I think we will be destroyed, but hopefully, we would have changed the system enough that the next time a crisis happens – even in Europe or the US or somewhere – mutual aid is something that's not a side thing, but it's, at least they get 10% of the funding, like put aside in a methodology that works for people.

Hajooj Kuka
Romanticising… why not? It's amazing. The spirit of mutual aid is amazing. The idea that we can, we can be there for each other when we're stuck. The idea of that happened in COVID, and people were like organising, and if the system collapses, we'll be okay. Actually, we might even be better, we'll be more human. You get the resources, you give it to them. They'll figure it out, they're not just going to become corrupt, they're not just going to steal it, and they're not— all that talk is not real. They also saved my life. So it's just like this feeling that you can't just explain, and I think romanticising it: this is the reason why we're together, these are the reason why we're volunteers. The system only works because we have 28,000 volunteers. It's not going to work if you're trying to pay them and give them money, because you can't – there's not enough money to give them. Hajooj Kuka

And having that as a percentage. Like, I really think if people can be like, "Hey, in any crisis, there's going to be a small percentage – 5%, 10% – like a small amount that just this 5% will always going to go to the community directly.” And I know that the idea of community is a difficult thing to wrap your head around, like, what is a community? Who's going to get the money? But just to be like, this is just going to happen, and we're just going to empower that, and we know that that's going to change – the community itself is a flexible thing that's going to change – and we're just going to be really flexible, and really step aside, and look and just keep supporting, and the support is not going to stop. So, I feel like if, if a number, a percentage is put in place, things can change.
Christina Bennett
What’s that number?
Hajooj Kuka
I mean, we started with 5%. If 5% of the aid that goes to Sudan goes, then the mutual aid will stay alive. If you raise the number to 20% then mutual aid would reach its potential. And when I say that, in Sudan, for example, it's not just humanitarian aid, it's also like keeping our stories for the future of transitional justice, allowing media and journalism to happen, allowing all these other things that we need as a society to happen. And allow that money to be mutual aid money, so journalists could have stayed working, human right activists could have become like professionals and work. So all this stuff that, if it was allowed, it would have continued, then if you give them 20% of the money and allow them to do all that, to do the reporting, to do the stories, mental health, to do all these different activities, the community would do a lot. So I'm almost think if you reach that number to 30%, then you almost only then need professional expertise to come in to help us, not actual money. It’s enough. In the end, let's just face it, the system that exists is so expensive. In the end, they need to live in high-end places in Nairobi, and travel in these expensive airplanes, and get food that is super expensive that comes flying from I don’t know where, and they don't trust the local markets, and they don't trust people getting food on camels and donkeys for some weird reason. So I feel like, in the end, the system, it will be cheaper. But for now, stay as a partnership, give us 5 to 20%. Five [per cent] means we’re gonna survive and mutual aid will exist, 20 [per cent], It will reach its potential.
Christina Bennett
Fanta, same question: What are grassroots movements teaching us about the future of aid, and what will it take for the system to change for the better?
Fanta Toure
The word that's coming to my mind is “keep going,” honestly. They're proving the extent to which you can rely on external aid and have various different forms of aid. I'm trying not to use the word ‘reliance’ and ‘resilience’. I have a lot of feelings about resilience, but there is something about keeping moving towards the direction of where you need to go that is coming back to me now. I’m honestly sitting with the idea of bringing back humanitarian humanity in the systems. Like, I think there's the people, as Hajooj mentioned, within traditional systems – we have allies everywhere – but I think the need to change the system is necessary if we're going to continue uplifting each other. And so that spirit of moving forward towards a future that uplift us all is the one that's really in mind for me. That's what the communities are doing. I hope we can bring back dignity in giving as much as we give back dignity in receiving, because I think part of the elements of controls that we see now in the traditional aid system is also coming from lack of dignity and guilt in the giving.That's where I am with this.
Christina Bennett
Bashair?
Bashair Ahmed
It's what we can learn from the grassroots, is: Be humble, and you know, seeking equitable partnerships, and also that the social contract is our accountability. Hajooj kind of mentioned it, the accountability is to the communities themselves, also what makes that work kind of legitimacy. I think what the system can do is to move from leading by default to actually supporting by design – so they can do the convening, they can do the amplifying, the accompaniment, the brokering the access, but not lead it. We’re gonna be seeing less and less funding, so, you know, with a scarcity of resources, the reality is we have to do these changes now rather than wait for it until your organisation withers, closes, whatever it may be. So this is the time to do it – not have further discussions, but act. And I think that's what's missing.
Christina Bennett
Thanks so much to our guests, to Bashair, to Fanta, to Hajooj.Thank you for the fantastic discussion. It's been really special for me to hear what has been motivating and mobilising you and all of your work, and to hear a little bit about how we as the humanitarian formal system can do better to enable it or just to simply get out of the way.
—
Christina Bennett
To our listeners, we would love to hear from you. Is mutual aid the future of humanitarian action?
Tammam Aloudat
Thank you for joining us on this special edition of Rethinking Humanitarianism in collaboration with Start Network.
Christina Bennett

Court rejects family’s bid in Narin Güran murder case
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
11:21:00 UTC
20:21:00 KST

(AA Photo)
Turkish courts have rejected a request by the family of Narin Güran, an 8-year-old girl found dead in southeastern Türkiye, to reclassify her death as an unsolved murder two years after the incident.
Authorities said the case had already been reviewed publicly by trial and appellate courts and that no new, concrete evidence had emerged to warrant reopening it under the “unknown perpetrator” category.
Meanwhile, prosecutors in Diyarbakır have launched a judicial investigation into “Şeytantepe,” a documentary about the case, over allegations that it sought to discredit the investigation and court proceedings.
The probe covers its filming, production and financing, including financial transfers and possible links to efforts challenging the finalized ruling.
Narin disappeared on Aug. 21, 2024, and was found 19 days later in a streambed. An autopsy found she had been strangled. Her uncle Salim Güran, mother Yüksel Güran and brother Enes Güran were sentenced to aggravated life imprisonment, while neighbor Nevzat Bahtiyar received 17 years for aiding the murder.

Iranians ‘shopping with a smile’ despite US sanctions – RT reports from Tehran (VIDEO)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
11:20:43 UTC
20:20:43 KST

Iranians ‘shopping with a smile’ despite US sanctions – RT reports from Tehran (VIDEO)
Iranian businesses are increasingly turning to discounts and installment payments to keep customers shopping, as sanctions and the economic fallout from the US-Israeli war squeeze household budgets, RT’s Salman Khujuri reports.
The trend comes nearly six months after the US and Israel launched the war against Iran in late February. Large-scale fighting has subsided under a series of temporary agreements, but efforts to reach a lasting settlement have stalled as Washington ramps up economic pressure on Tehran.
Businesses in the Iranian capital are adapting to soaring prices and falling purchasing power, with some allowing customers to spread purchases over several payments.
Bobak Shirpour, who runs a large clothing retail business in Tehran, told RT on Thursday that worsening economic conditions after the war and years of sanctions prompted his company to seek suppliers offering better prices and quality. With many larger families unable to pay in cash, the retailer also introduced discounts and installment plans.
“People have welcomed it, they come in with a smile and leave with a smile,” Shirpour said, adding that despite the narrower profit margins, business remains steady.
Shoppers interviewed by RT said installment plans have become increasingly useful as household budgets come under pressure. “They allow people to buy things they can’t afford to pay for in cash and pay in four installments instead. It gives people some peace of mind and helps them meet some of their basic needs despite these difficult circumstances,” one customer said.
Iranian households have been cutting spending on food and other essentials as inflation and the falling rial erode purchasing power, according to recent media reports. Installment shopping has also expanded to Iranian companies offering deferred-payment services as consumers struggle with the rising cost of living, the Financial Times reported earlier this month.

Türkiye unveils Emissions Trading System regulation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
11:15:35 UTC
20:15:35 KST

Türkiye aims to accelerate the green transformation.
Türkiye’s Emissions Trading System (TR ETS) Regulation, prepared by the Climate Change Directorate under the Environment, Urbanization and Climate Change Ministry, has been published in the Official Gazette.
According to a statement from the ministry, the regulation sets out the rules governing the implementation of the Turkish Emissions Trading System.
Under the framework, the TR ETS is expected to play a key role in advancing climate-friendly transformation and green development goals at both the national and international levels.
The establishment and implementation of the system will also provide one of the mechanisms envisaged for achieving the greenhouse gas emission reduction targets outlined in Türkiye’s Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) submitted under the Paris Agreement.
The regulation consolidates existing greenhouse gas emissions monitoring rules under a single framework and aligns monitoring, reporting, verification and market operation requirements with the European Union Emissions Trading System.
Through the TR ETS, Türkiye aims to encourage reductions in greenhouse gas emissions, accelerate the transition to low-carbon production technologies and support the country’s green transformation process.
Environment, Urbanization and Climate Change Minister Murat Kurum said in a social media post that the emissions trading system represents an important milestone in Türkiye’s green development objectives.

Молодежь в возрасте 16-17 лет составляет 15% сотрудников McDonald's в Украине
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
14:15:24 EEST
20:15:24 KST

Молодежь в возрасте 16-17 лет в настоящее время составляет 15% сотрудников McDonald’s в Украине, в некоторых ресторанах доля несовершеннолетних достигает 40%, сообщил директор по корпоративному влиянию "МакДоналдс" в Украине Назар Бедий.
"В первые три месяца после введения возможности приема на работу с 16 лет (летом 2025 года – ИФ-У) мы получили более 12 тыс. заявок, и сегодня 16-17-летние составляют около 15% сотрудников. В отдельных ресторанах их доля достигает даже 40%. Давая работу с раннего возраста, мы показываем, как в Украине можно развиваться. У нас есть директора ресторанов в возрасте 22-25 лет, которые начинали с базовых должностей и стремительно прошли по карьерной лестнице. Это вдохновляет и демонстрирует реальную траекторию роста", – рассказал он в эксклюзивном интервью агентству "Интерфакс-Украина".
Программу официального трудоустройства с 16 лет "МакДоналдс" в Украине запустил 23 июня 2025 года. Как сообщил Бедий, в настоящее время компания работает с государством над совершенствованием трудового законодательства, в том числе в части трудоустройства несовершеннолетних.
"Мы полностью поддерживаем необходимость защиты несовершеннолетних и в то же время ищем более современные и гибкие механизмы, которые дают молодым людям возможность быстрее приобретать компетенции и развиваться. В европейском законодательстве разрешено привлекать детей в возрасте от 14 лет к работе в рамках программ профессиональной подготовки, стажировки или дуального образования, а также к легкому труду при определенных условиях", – рассказал он.
В связи с этим эксперты компании выступают, например, за пересмотр ограничений на рабочее время и за то, чтобы молодежь до 18 лет, получающая профессионально-техническое образование, могла работать без чрезмерных регуляторных ограничений при сохранении гарантий защиты труда.
"Если у них будет доступ к более широкому кругу задач в ресторане, то они быстрее будут приобретать опыт и смогут раньше переходить на руководящие должности", – уверен Бедий.
Всего в компании сейчас более 12,5 тыс. сотрудников.
"Людей в возрасте 50+ у нас примерно 540. Несовершеннолетних, как уже говорилось, 15% – это более 1800 сотрудников. Остальные – в основном люди 18-25 лет, которые составляют 51% сотрудников ресторанов. Но есть и значительная доля сотрудников в возрасте 26-50 лет – почти 3750 человек, то есть 30% команды. Также в компании работает около 500 людей с инвалидностью, которые имеют равные возможности для развития", – рассказал Бедий.
По его словам, 450 сотрудников компании мобилизованы, им продолжают выплачивать зарплату (в общей сложности около 132 млн грн только за 2025 год). Также в компании работают 27 ветеранов, большинство из них – сотрудники компании, вернувшиеся после службы, но есть и те, кто пришел в компанию уже после возвращения из армии.
"Мы работаем над программами поддержки ветеранов и ищем индивидуальные решения. Например, если после возвращения человек физически уже не может выполнять ту же работу на определенном посту в ресторане, мы ищем другие возможности: административные функции в ресторане или вакансии в других отделах. Конечно, это зависит и от желания самого человека. Но мы стараемся найти решение", – говорит Бедий.

EU countries urging European Commission to revive efforts to use Russian assets for Ukraine – FT
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
11:15:00 UTC
20:15:00 KST

EU countries urging European Commission to revive efforts to use Russian assets for Ukraine – FT
According to Ukrinform, the Financial Times reports this, citing people familiar with the matter.
Plans to finance Ukraine using more than €200 billion in Russian central bank assets frozen under EU sanctions collapsed last winter after Belgium, where most of the assets are held, blocked the initiative.
According to the sources, a coalition of EU member states, including Sweden, the Netherlands, Spain and Poland, will send a letter to the European Commission on Thursday, August 27, urging the EU executive to resume work on the proposal and clarify whether any progress has been made in developing alternative legal and technical frameworks that could circumvent Belgium’s veto.
“Now is the time to start a new discussion about how we can make further use of Russia’s frozen assets for Ukraine’s, and our, benefit. This is the fair and smart way to make sure that Ukraine can defend itself and all of Europe,” said Swedish Foreign Minister Maria Malmer Stenergard.
One source said the letter would be “a call to the Commission to do the technical work” to use the assets and alleviate Kyiv’s budget needs.
Ukraine has long urged the EU to use the frozen Russian assets to finance its defense against Russia.
As reported by Ukrinform, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said at a joint press conference in Kyiv with Belgium’s Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs, European Affairs and Development Cooperation Maxime Prévot that Ukraine believes it is time to step up work on a legal mechanism for using frozen Russian assets to support Ukraine.

Russians destroy remaining equipment at Kherson Combined Heat and Power Plant
Russian forces attacked the Kherson Combined Heat and Power (CHP) plant yet again, using guided aerial bombs to completely destroy and disable all the remaining heat- and power-generating equipment at the plant.
Source: Naftogaz Group, Ukraine's national oil and gas company, on Facebook
Details: The company reported that Russian forces attacked the Naftogaz Group's Kherson CHP again on the night of 26-27 August, striking the site with four guided aerial bombs at once.
The plant sustained critical damage. The strike completely destroyed and disabled all the heat- and power-generating equipment that remained at the plant.
"The Russians struck an exclusively civilian facility that supplies heat to a significant part of Kherson's residential buildings," said Serhii Fedorenko, acting CEO of Naftogaz.
More details: Fedorenko pointed out that this attack serves no military purpose whatsoever and that its sole aim is to terrorise the civilian population and attempt to deprive tens of thousands of Kherson residents of their source of heat ahead of the heating season.
Background:
- Earlier, Russian forces attacked the Kherson CHP – the city's main source of heating – with a guided aerial bomb, causing serious damage.
- Russia's constant attacks on energy infrastructure in Kherson Oblast have officially been classified as threatening an emergency situation, meaning any worsening of the current state could endanger human welfare. The same status has also been applied to the state of the heating supply in Kherson due to the risk of disruptions during the heating season.
- On 28 December, Russian forces again shelled the Kherson Combined Heat and Power (CHP) plant with artillery, causing significant damage. Russian forces attack the plant almost daily. The strikes have left between 10,000 and 12,000 people without heating.

'Issue of enormous significance': Kharge writes to PM Modi, demands 25-year delimitation freeze
Edited by: Rohitashwa Ranjan / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Aug 27, 2026, 16:43 IST
Comments

NEW DELHI: Leader of opposition in Rajya Sabha Mallikarjun Kharge on Thursday wrote to Prime Minister Narendra Modi, reiterating the Congress' demand to maintain the existing strength of the Lok Sabha at 543 for another 25 years.Kharge's letter came after Union parliamentary affairs minister hinted at a possible special session of Parliament for the passage of the Delimitation Bill.In his letter, Kharge urged the government to convene an all-party meeting to discuss its proposed delimitation exercise before any such session.
"I have written to PM Modi on delimitation, the delay in prorogation of the Monsoon Session of Parliament, and the likely special session mentioned by the Union minister of parliamentary affairs in a television interview last evening," Kharge said."I had last written to you on July 16, 2026 requesting you to convene an All-Party meeting for discussing the Government's proposals for delimitation. I had also requested you to give all political parties adequate time to study such proposals in detail before they are introduced in any special session of Parliament that you may be contemplating," he added.
Kharge also urged PM Modi to maintain the state-wise strength in Lok Sabha for another 25 years and introduce one-third reservation for women from the 2029 Lok Sabha elections.
"Maintain the existing strength of the Lok Sabha at 543 for another 25 years; Maintain the existing state-wise strength in the Lok Sabha for another 25 years; "Introduce one-third reservation for women from the 2029 Lok Sabha elections.Kharge reiterated his demand that the government convene an all-party meeting and give political parties and state governments adequate time to examine the proposals."This is an issue that has enormous significance for the country. Please do not again try and bulldoze as you attempted on April 16 and 17, 2026," Kharge said.

Emilia-Romagna mussel farms are
issuing an SOS due to a major die-off caused by high
temperatures and the resulting critical conditions of marine
habitats, which has already decimated the local clam industry.
                                    
                                       
				The cooperative associations—AGCI Emilia-Romagna,
Confcooperative Agroalimentare e Pesca Emilia-Romagna, and
Legacoop Emilia-Romagna—have reported the situation to the
Region, which has launched an assessment of the extent of the
damage and production losses and is reviewing the available
support tools.
                                    
                                       
				The Region is paying close attention, given the already complex
situation.
                                    
                                       
				"We're talking about businesses that have already faced a series
of environmental emergencies and critical issues in recent
years, from the proliferation of blue crabs, which severely
impacted regional shellfish farming, to the mucilage and anoxia
phenomena that have affected our seas," explains Alessio Mammi,
Regional Councilor for Agriculture and Fisheries.
                                    
                                       
				"To these challenges, we are now adding the effects of
exceptionally high temperatures, which are once again
jeopardizing production, business profitability, and their
ability to plan investments and ensure job continuity.
                                    
                                       
				Therefore, based on the findings of the survey, we will evaluate
all available intervention options."
Scientists say the climate crisis caused by human greenhouse gas
emissions is making extreme weather events such as heatwaves,
droughts, supercharged storms and flooding more frequent and
more intense.
                                    
                                       
				Although there are many sources of the greenhouse gases that are
causing global heating, the main driver is the burning of fossil
fuels such as oil, gas and coal, sales of which generate huge
profits for the world's energy giants.

habitats, which has already decimated the local clam industry.
                                    
                                       
				The cooperative associations—AGCI Emilia-Romagna,
Confcooperative Agroalimentare e Pesca Emilia-Romagna, and
Legacoop Emilia-Romagna—have reported the situation to the
Region, which has launched an assessment of the extent of the
damage and production losses and is reviewing the available
support tools.
                                    
                                       
				The Region is paying close attention, given the already complex
situation.
                                    
                                       
				"We're talking about businesses that have already faced a series
of environmental emergencies and critical issues in recent
years, from the proliferation of blue crabs, which severely
impacted regional shellfish farming, to the mucilage and anoxia
phenomena that have affected our seas," explains Alessio Mammi,
Regional Councilor for Agriculture and Fisheries.
                                    
                                       
				"To these challenges, we are now adding the effects of
exceptionally high temperatures, which are once again
jeopardizing production, business profitability, and their
ability to plan investments and ensure job continuity.
                                    
                                       
				Therefore, based on the findings of the survey, we will evaluate
all available intervention options."
Scientists say the climate crisis caused by human greenhouse gas
emissions is making extreme weather events such as heatwaves,
droughts, supercharged storms and flooding more frequent and
more intense.
                                    
                                       
				Although there are many sources of the greenhouse gases that are
causing global heating, the main driver is the burning of fossil
fuels such as oil, gas and coal, sales of which generate huge
profits for the world's energy giants.

Allies asked in writing for views on US bases in Europe
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
12:10:57 BST
20:10:57 KST

NATO members have been sent a written questionnaire seeking their views ahead of the American review of United States force posture in Europe, the Pentagon’s senior policy official has confirmed in Brussels.
Elbridge Colby, the Under Secretary of War for Policy, disclosed the mechanism in remarks alongside NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte on Thursday, having been asked about it by reporters.
He said: “We want to hear from our allies. That’s the questionnaire that some of you asked about. We wanted to hear from them directly in writing, in the spirit of NATO 3.0.”
Colby also named the areas where he expects difficulty, singling out the arrangements that govern where American forces can be stationed and how they move.
He said: “Let’s look at some of things like access, basing and overflight, where there is a lot of good, but there’s some things that we need to work out to make sense going forward.”
Access, basing and overflight are the legal and diplomatic arrangements that determine which airfields and ports American units can use, what they can store there, and whose airspace they can transit without seeking permission each time. They are agreed bilaterally with host nations rather than through NATO, they vary considerably between countries, and they are what any redistribution of American forces across the continent would have to be built on.
Colby said the review would “look at the strategic posture at a high level of the US forces in Europe, obviously Europe remaining a critical interest of the United States, even as we prioritize the Western Hemisphere and the First Island Chain”, and that the aim was to make it “fit for purpose, not only for today but going forward”.
He said: “Let’s make it adaptive. Let’s make it make sense.”
The United States keeps around 80,000 personnel in Europe, a figure that rose after the 2022 invasion of Ukraine, with the largest concentrations in Germany, Italy, Poland and the United Kingdom. Successive American officials have signalled that the total will fall as Washington weights its forces towards the Pacific, and the question allies have been pressing is not whether that happens but which capabilities go and how much warning they get.
Colby set out the division of labour he expects, describing “a world in which Europe, which is obviously a very wealthy continent, can and is taking primary responsibility for its own conventional defence, obviously the United States remaining committed to NATO, remaining linked to this alliance, and also Europe taking the lead in support to Ukraine.”
He named Poland, Germany and the Netherlands as examples of what he called extraordinary investment, and said he hoped others would follow.
Rutte used the visit to press the case that European and Canadian spending is already moving. He said: “When you look at the moment in 2025, 139 billion dollars extra spent on defence by the Canadians and the Europeans compared to the years before, and it is still continuing. Still much more to be done. We will get there.”
The Secretary General credited Colby with coining the phrase NATO 3.0, which he defined as “a stronger Europe and a stronger Canada in a stronger NATO”, and pointed back to a June visit by Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, who said Washington would consult allies before changing its footprint.
The sequence of Colby’s visit indicates the review remains at the consultation stage. He said he met US European Command on Tuesday for a working session with General Grynkewich, heard from the staff at Supreme Headquarters Allied Powers Europe on Wednesday, and joined the North Atlantic Council with allied ambassadors on Thursday.

McDonald's to launch annual sustainable stores in Ukraine

Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
14:09:40 EEST
20:09:40 KST

McDonald’s Ukraine Ltd., which operates the McDonald’s fast-food restaurant chain in Ukraine, plans to open restaurants with sustainable (environmentally friendly) design every year, which will be 35% more expensive than standard restaurants, McDonald’s Ukraine Director of Corporate Impact Nazar Bediy said.
"There are currently two such restaurants in Ukraine: one in Lviv and one in Kyiv. We are proud that we have started moving in this direction. We definitely plan to continue investing in restaurants with sustainable design, but in the short and medium term we do not plan to convert the entire chain to this design because it is significantly more expensive – by approximately 35%. We view such restaurants as a promising project with potential for future development. On average, we plan to invest in approximately one such restaurant per year," he said in an exclusive interview with Interfax-Ukraine.
At the same time, the main focus will be on expanding the adoption of environmental practices across all new restaurants.
"We make them energy-efficient, work on thermal insulation, introduce heat-recovery systems and other solutions that help use energy resources more efficiently. Energy consumption is directly linked to environmental impact, so this is an important area," he stressed.
The first McDonald’s restaurant in Ukraine opened on May 24, 1997, in Kyiv. McDonald’s currently employs nearly 11,000 Ukrainians. There are currently 130 restaurants operating in 43 localities.
According to the OpenDataBot analytical system, McDonald’s in Ukraine generated UAH 21.3 billion in revenue in 2025, 26.6% more than in the same period a year earlier. Net profit increased by 21.3% to UAH 1.567 billion. Last year, the company paid UAH 3.5 billion in taxes to the budget.
McDonald’s in Ukraine is a founding partner and the largest corporate partner of the Ronald McDonald House Charities Ukraine.
MCD Europe Limited (100%, London, United Kingdom) is listed as the owner of McDonald’s Ukraine Ltd.
