New funding for long Covid research centre raised
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
10:18:53 UTC
19:18:53 KST

New funding for long Covid research centre raised
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
The Long COVID Foundation (SLC) has launched a National Research & Innovation Center to investigate long covid in the Netherlands as government money has dried up.
With some €40 million the government provided for research having been spent and no new budget yet allocated, the foundation awarded €500,000 to seven researchers to keep their research going and to “translate scientific discoveries more quickly into diagnostics and targeted treatments for adults and children.”
“SLC wants to prevent years of investment, knowledge and research power from being lost.”
The money is being given to researchers from the hospitals Amsterdam UMC, the Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam, UMC Utrecht and Erasmus MC. The foundation’s goal is that the centre, operating as an independent foundation and an open national research network, will be a central hub for stimulating and linking research under one national program.
Still no treatment
Calling long covid “one of the great unresolved medical challenges of our time”, the foundation estimates 400,000 people have been affected by it – 100,000 of them seriously. “Yet there are no proven healing treatment, effective diagnostics and targeted therapies yet.”
Long covid sufferers struggle with fatigue, brain fog, loss of concentration, and memory and immune system problems that have severely limited their ability to work and lead normal lives.
Targeted treatments
The foundation says it’s becoming increasingly clear that long covid suffers can be distinguished by groups. “An important task for the centre will be to better distinguish these groups and to investigate which treatments can work in which patients.”
The foundation is also looking into other the post-acute infection syndromes, such as ME/CFS, a chronic illness characterised by an inability to function.
In the future, says SLC, “long-term public and private financing is also needed”.
“The stronger and more structural the research is organized, the more likely it is that scientific discoveries will lead to the diagnostics and targeted treatments that patients have been waiting for so long.”

Syria's post-Assad prisons: Detainee death reignites fear
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
10:17:13 UTC
19:17:13 KST

Breadcrumb
Syrians fear the return of Assad's prisons as death of young detainee sparks anger
The mountain town of Al-Haffah in northwestern Syria's Lattakia governorate was engulfed in grief and anger last week amid the funeral of 29-year-old Mohammad Ghamira, a man who died in hospital after security officers allegedly beat him while in detention, an incident that has stirred traumatic memories of the former regime’s worst abuses.
Immediately upon his arrest over a financial dispute, Ghamira's family informed the police that he suffered from haemophilia, requiring special care and the strict avoidance of any physical trauma, as his blood lacked the ability to clot.
The family's warnings were ignored. After three days in detention, the young man's health deteriorated rapidly. Despite being rushed to hospital after his release, he died a week later.
As news of Ghamira's deteriorating condition spread, the Internal Security Command in Lattakia initiated an investigation.
Following the announcement of his death, authorities detained seven individuals who were present at the Al-Haffah police station holding cell during his detention.
On the evening of Sunday, August 16, the Minister of Interior issued an administrative order forming a committee to investigate the circumstances surrounding his death, mandating a report within 72 hours.
On Thursday, August 20, the committee announced its findings, confirming that an interrogator had slapped Ghamira on the neck.
Consequently, interrogator Ahmad Jawad was referred to the public prosecution in Lattakia, while the Ministry of Interior's disciplinary department was tasked with expanding its investigation into Captain Ahmad Shaker Al-Masri and interrogator Omar Youssef.
The incident has triggered widespread outrage among Syrians, many of whom see it as reminiscent of the Assad era, when police stations and detention centres were sites of unchecked violence and murder.
Bashar al-Assad was overthrown in December 2024, ending 54 years of the Assad family's rule that was marked by absolute control over politics and civic life and widespread human rights violations.
Questions remain over whether the new administration, led by former militant leader Ahmed al-Sharaa, will usher in genuine reform.
Syria's memories of torture
"For Syrians, prison is not merely a penal institution; it is tied to a deeply painful national memory of arbitrary detention, torture, forced disappearance, and death," said Almoutassim Al Kilani, a prominent Syrian human rights lawyer and legal expert specialising in international criminal law and transitional justice.
"Hearing news of a detainee being tortured or dying in a security facility after being released is not seen as an ordinary criminal incident, but as an alarm that touches the very meaning of liberation," Al Kilani added.
Ezzedine Ezzedine, a lawyer who has worked for years on detainee files documenting the abuses and crimes committed in Bashar al-Assad's prisons, called it "a massive shock" for him or any human rights lawyer who monitored the violations of the previous regime.
"We considered that the absolute minimum achievement of the regime's fall was the eradication of forced disappearance and torture," he said.
Ezzedine notes that his frustration, and that of other Syrians, stems from the persistence of violence in prisons and the fear that it could evolve from isolated incidents caused by inexperience into a general policy.
"We hope we are wrong," he adds. His fears are compounded by the lack of concrete legal measures to prevent such violations.
Forming investigative committees is insufficient, he said, because they lack judicial authority and are merely internal bodies formed by the Ministry of Interior.
"The idea of a committee is good, but the issue cannot be resolved by committees alone. Is it reasonable to form a committee every time a violation occurs? The solution lies in implementing radical procedures, applying the Code of Criminal Procedure, and empowering the law to take its true, independent role."
A legacy of fear
In the Syrian consciousness, prisons evoke deep fears and tragic stories. The mere thought of entering a police station is terrifying, let alone a political detention centre.
While mass detention and mistreatment in prison were not common during the period of national rule following the French mandate, from 1946 to 1963, torture emerged as a systemic tool of control when the Baath Party seized power.
The rise of Hafez al-Assad, who took over in 1970, marked a brutal turning point. In the 1980s, the regime filled prisons with thousands of political opponents, using torture as the primary means of subjugating detainees and quashing the opposition base.
From this point, and continuing under his son, Bashar al-Assad, Syria was ruled by an authoritarian security apparatus that infiltrated every aspect of the state and society.
It spread fear and silenced dissent, creating a profound lack of trust, where everyone felt monitored and suspected their neighbours might be informants, said civil and political activist Youssef Al-Banni.
"After the Syrian people suffered for 40 years under the father and 14 years under the son, sacrificing blood, enduring oppression and displacement, every Syrian has the right to react to any act of violence by security forces," said Al-Banni.
"This requires a courageous and clear stance on the necessity of investigation, follow-up, and holding those involved accountable, regardless of their rank or justification. Silence on such violations undermines the very goals for which the nation revolted."
Al Kilani agrees that the Assad legacy is heavy and changing it takes time. "Liberation does not mean violations will automatically disappear, because changing the authorities is much faster than changing institutional culture and power dynamics," he says.
"But the hallmark of the new phase must be how the state handles a violation. Under the previous regime, torture was part of a vast system that protected perpetrators and hid victims. After liberation, any assault must be treated as a criminal and exceptional act, to be exposed, investigated, and penalised."
Civil society is now stepping in to fulfil this monitoring role.
Following Ghamira's death, activists organised a protest in Aleppo, while another group planned a similar demonstration in Damascus, which was later postponed.
Journalist and activist Fadi Zeidan, one of the organisers of the postponed Damascus protest, explains that the organisers include independent activists and former detainees, collaborating with civil society and human rights representatives.
While the public was deeply shocked by the incident, Zeidan noted intense societal polarisation.
Some voices called for boycotting the protest, fearing it would be exploited by remnants of the former regime to attack the new government.
"Despite this, we are the children of the 2011 revolution, and we believe that safeguarding the path of freedom and dignity requires us not to remain silent about any violation, regardless of who committed it," Zeidan says.
The Damascus protest was postponed after political figures, parliamentarians, and Ministry of Information officials reached out to request time to address the protesters' demands.
The government was also concerned that the issue of deaths under torture could be exploited politically or internationally to undermine stability.
Accounts of abuse
But Ghamira's story is not an isolated incident.
In July of last year, a young man named Youssef Al-Labad was arrested after a verbal altercation with public security personnel at the Umayyad Mosque. He was transferred to the Hamidiyeh prison, run by Internal Security, where he died under mysterious circumstances.
His body was returned to his family bearing clear signs of torture.
Al-Labad had been a soldier in the Syrian regime's army before defecting at the start of the 2011 revolution to join the Free Syrian Army. He later sought asylum in Germany with his family, only to be killed two days after deciding to return to Syria.
Another case is that of activist Laith Al-Zoubi, who was arrested at his home on September 14, 2025, and released a week later. Now back in Syria, Al-Zoubi explains that while his initial arrest was non-violent, he was beaten and insulted upon arriving at the Sahnaya police station in rural Damascus after asking why he was detained. He was thrown into solitary confinement for seven days.
Despite informing them that he suffered from partial epilepsy and bipolar disorder and urgently needed his medication, he was denied medical care or visits from his family or lawyer. On the seventh day, he was forced to sign a document without reading it.
"I just wanted to get out and travel, and I will never return as long as this is how things are," he told The New Arab.
"It is not just my case. There are several people like me who were arbitrarily arrested and signed pledges, and I don't think I am the only one who was tortured. To this day, I do not know why I was arrested. They never informed me of the charges or interrogated me."
Calls for justice
Human rights organisations have documented arbitrary arrests, mistreatment, torture, and deaths in custody in post-Assad prisons.
Human Rights Watch's 2026 World Report cited accounts of such abuses in facilities run by transitional authorities, and the Syrian Network for Human Rights confirmed that these practices did not completely cease after the regime's fall.
Documented abuses like these, said Al Kilani, indicate that prisons remain in a dangerous transitional phase.
Legally, Syrian legislation contains provisions protecting detainees, but the problem often lies in enforcement and in the disregard for these provisions.
Ezzedine points out that the Anti-Torture Law No. 16 of 2022 explicitly penalises violence against detainees. Furthermore, the Code of Criminal Procedure guarantees a fair trial, bans violence against detainees, and upholds the presumption of innocence.
He notes that the Constitutional Declaration nullified all previous laws that granted immunity to security personnel and that violated international human rights treaties, which should serve as safeguards for detainees.
To ensure these laws are applied, Al Kilani stressed the need for a clear political and legal message that torture, beatings, insults, and the denial of medical treatment are crimes, not minor administrative errors.
He proposes closing all secret or unregistered detention centres, creating a unified national registry of detainees, and installing cameras in detention corridors.
Crucially, he suggests that medical services in prisons should fall under the technical and administrative jurisdiction of the Ministry of Health, rather than the Ministry of Interior, thereby allowing doctors to document injuries and order hospital transfers without pressure from security.
He also calls for permanent, qualified paramedics and binding protocols for critical conditions like haemophilia, diabetes, epilepsy, and heart disease.
These recommendations align with the demands of the postponed Damascus protest.
According to Zeidan, their sit-in was delayed in the hope that their demands would be met. These demands emphasise the strict criminalisation of torture, truth and accountability, the protection of detainees' rights, security sector reform, and human rights training for security personnel to ensure these practices do not return.
"For us in civil society, our role is to monitor the authorities' performance and not allow the legitimisation or justification of any violation under any pretext," said Zeidan.
"We will continue to apply pressure through all legislative and civil means, and we are currently preparing for field and legal mobilisation coinciding with the International Day of the Victims of Enforced Disappearances on August 30 to send a message that human dignity is a red line and the Syrian people will not be humiliated."
Mawada Bahah is an independent Syrian journalist with bylines in local, regional and international outlets

Five Kyiv Regional Council deputies were served with suspicion notices over a scheme involving budget funds, says the Prosecutor General
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
13:15:09 EEST
19:15:09 KST

Five Kyiv Regional Council deputies were served with suspicion notices over a scheme involving budget funds, says the Prosecutor General
Kyiv • UNN
Five deputies and four relatives are suspected of misappropriating funds from the “Care” program. Investigators allege the use of fictitious documents and personal expenditures.
Five deputies of the Kyiv Regional Council have been notified of suspicion of fraud involving budget funds through a scheme connected with the "Care" program, Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko said on Thursday on social media, UNN reports.
"Care" for their own: five deputies of the Kyiv Regional Council notified of suspicion of fraud involving budget funds
He noted that the "Care" program was created for people who genuinely need assistance: families of persons and children with disabilities, people facing difficult life circumstances and those affected by the war, veterans, military personnel, and families of fallen defenders. During 2021–2025, approximately UAH 384 million in budget funds was allocated for its implementation.
"I remember well how much effort it took to secure funding for this program when I headed the Kyiv Regional Military Administration. Every hryvnia had to work for those who truly needed support. And indeed, many deputies conscientiously performed their duties, communicated with people, determined their needs in difficult life circumstances, and genuinely helped," Kravchenko said.
"However, there were also those who, according to the investigation, turned the assistance mechanism into a scheme for personal enrichment. It was established that some of the budget funds under the "Care" program were received not by those for whom it had been created, but by relatives and close associates of certain deputies of the Kyiv Regional Council," the Prosecutor General noted.
According to him, "the scheme was simple." "Fictitious medical documents were prepared in the names of relatives. Based on them, the deputies applied for material assistance payments. At the same time, the recipients had no real need for treatment or social support. The money received from the budget was spent on aesthetic medicine services, the purchase of expensive cars, and other personal needs. In some cases, part of the assistance was returned to the deputies – tens of thousands of hryvnias were transferred directly to their personal bank cards," the Prosecutor General reported.
"Today, under the procedural guidance of the Prosecutor General's Office, five deputies of the Kyiv Regional Council and four of their relatives have been notified of suspicion," Kravchenko said. "Depending on their roles, their actions were qualified as organizing, carrying out, and aiding fraud committed on a large and especially large scale, including by an organized group – Parts 2, 3, and 5 of Article 27 and Parts 4 and 5 of Article 190 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine."
The investigation is ongoing. Other possible participants in the scheme are being identified, he added.
"Budget programs are created to help people, not to enrich those who have access to the distribution of funds. When money intended for people in difficult circumstances is directed to "their own," and part of it is subsequently returned to deputies, this is no longer "Care." It is fraud involving budget funds," the Prosecutor General emphasized.

Russia is preparing for the possible consequences of a new mobilization – the DIU and the FIS
Kyiv • UNN
Intelligence reports that the Russian Federation is preparing for a new mobilization and strengthening coercive measures. The decision may be made after the elections on September 18–20.
The Russian leadership is preparing measures in case of the social and economic consequences of tightening the martial regime. This information from the Main Intelligence Directorate and the Foreign Intelligence Service was published on the website of the Office of the President, reports UNN.
Details
The Russian leadership is preparing a set of forceful response measures to address the possible negative social and economic consequences of transferring cities and regions to a stricter martial regime. In internal Russian documents, the need for an additional wave of mobilization is justified by a significant increase in dissatisfaction with the war in the regions (dissatisfaction rates reach 69%) and, accordingly, a decrease in the number of people willing to voluntarily sign a contract
According to intelligence information, the greatest problems with recruiting contract soldiers are being recorded in the Oryol and Vladimir regions, as well as in Dagestan. In addition, a trend toward a further decline in the figures is being recorded in many other Russian regions.
Compared with 2025, in some regions the number of debtors, special contingents among convicts and criminal elements, migrants, and other categories that for a long time formed the main pool for contract recruitment to serve in the Russian army and participate in the war has decreased by 30–40%. The campaign to recruit students, in which the absolute majority of Russian higher education institutions was involved, has failed
The Russian leadership also plans to strengthen the personal responsibility of regional authorities and expand the powers of law enforcement agencies. Thus, a system for serving electronic mobilization orders is already in operation in the russian federation, and additional coercive measures are also being developed.
A ban on leaving russia, obtaining loans, buying / selling real estate, cancellation of a driver's license, blocking funds in bank accounts, and so on. At enterprises, the staffing of mobilization work and military registration departments is being expanded. As of the end of July 2026, more than 2.5 thousand new vacancies for staffing the aforementioned mobilization units at enterprises had already been posted on electronic employment platforms
According to the Main Intelligence Directorate of the Ministry of Defense and the Foreign Intelligence Service, the Russian leadership will most likely make a decision on a new mobilization after the "elections" to the State Duma of the russian federation, scheduled for September 18–20 this year.
To remind
Russian military personnel across the country are conducting exercises to test readiness for a possible new wave of mobilization, but the Kremlin has not yet made a corresponding decision.

Wrocław councillors approve resolution condemning attacks on Ukrainians
Wrocław city councillors have approved a resolution condemning ethnically motivated violence following a heated debate and remarks about "Ukrainians' ingratitude".
Source: Polish news portal Onet, as reported by European Pravda
Details: The draft resolution, submitted by councillors from the Left Forward (Lewicy Naprzód) group, condemned the recent wave of "aggression, hatred and ethnically motivated violence". It also stressed that the councillors oppose "any violence, regardless of the ethnicity of the perpetrator or victim".
"Everyone who has chosen Wrocław as their home and place to live is welcome here, regardless of ethnicity," the resolution states.
The resolution lists a number of incidents in Wrocław, including an attack by three men on a Ukrainian couple and a violent knife attack on a Polish woman by a Ukrainian man. During the debate, councillors also mentioned a recent bottle attack on a Belarusian taxi driver.
Councillors from the right-wing Law and Justice party attempted to add an amendment registering their protest against "generalised accusations of aggression, xenophobia or hatred on ethnic grounds against Poles, Polish women and the local Wrocław community". It also called on the government and Sejm to "immediately regulate the status of Ukrainian citizens of conscription age" who are in Poland without a valid permit, "so that they can return to their homeland and begin their service".
Law and Justice representative Sławomir Śmigielski, who presented the amendment, mentioned the enormous amount of aid Poland has provided to Ukraine. "And what did we get in return? Enormous ingratitude. President Zelenskyy has named a military unit after the heroes of the UPA. We believe this is a slap in the face for Poland and the Polish people," he said.
Robert Suligowski, a councillor from the Left Forward group, said Ukrainians living in Wrocław cannot be held responsible for the actions of the Ukrainian government. "These people expect our support; they should feel at home here. We should be greeting them with smiles and flowers, not knives and bottles," he said.
The debate was closed, although not all the councillors had an opportunity to speak. The council eventually adopted the resolution. Twenty-four councillors voted in favour, and Śmigielski of the Law and Justice party voted against. Six councillors abstained.

Nepal scrambles to find 1,300 missing as floods death toll hits 273
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
10:13:00 UTC
19:13:00 KST

Nepalese rescue teams searched devastated areas Thursday for more than 1,300 people still missing a day after flash floods and landslides along the Nepal-Tibet border killed at least 353 and swept away entire villages.
Homes were engulfed and vehicles tossed around by the tsunami-like rumble of water and mud that struck villages and towns Wednesday morning on the path of two rivers, Bhote Koshi and Trishuli.
Many of the missing are foreign tourists, including scores of Hindu pilgrims to Tibet's sacred snow-capped Mount Kailash.
According to the U.S. Geological Survey, the disaster was caused by a glacial collapse that sent forth an overwhelming flow of icy debris.
Emergency teams were racing to evacuate survivors from affected zones, fearing new flash floods.
Nepali soldiers used sniffer dogs to search for bodies buried under thick grey sludge.
"Everything is finished," Omkar Joshi, 35, a Nepali customs agent rescued from a hilltop in the border town of Timure, told Agence France-Presse (AFP).
"It is a giant graveyard. All that is left are sand and pebbles, soaked red by human blood."
Nepali police said they had recovered 353 bodies.
Another 823 people, including 517 foreign tourists, were out of contact in the country. Beijing says 100 Chinese citizens are missing in Nepal.
In China, state media said the "mudslide disaster" at the Gyirong Port in Tibet killed three people, while 558 people, including 260 foreigners, are missing.
Chinese Premier Li Qiang visited the area Thursday, state media said, to oversee "emergency rescue and relief work, and to visit rescue workers and affected people."
In Nepal, rescuers waded through mud and sludge to look for survivors after floodwaters buried the lower floors of multi-story buildings.
Prime Minister Balendra Shah, who urged the Himalyan nation to "stand together" hours after the disaster, visited some of the hardest-hit areas Thursday.
Shah told local authorities to "provide immediate relief to displaced families" and to open blocked roads, his office said in a statement.
The foreigners out of contact were from 30 different countries, including Indians and others from Australia, Britain, Malaysia, the Netherlands, Portugal, South Africa, South Korea and the United States, Nepal's tourism board said.
The sudden rush of mud and debris was "like an inland tsunami," traveling nearly 170 kilometers (100 miles) south into Nepal, said environmental historian Ruth Gamble, of Australia's La Trobe University.
Rasuwa, in the north of Nepal, was the first district to be affected, but deaths have been reported as far south as Chitwan in the south, on the border with India.
Chinese government officials in Tibet mobilized nearly 800 emergency workers, as well as sniffer dogs and speed boats to help the rescue efforts, official news agency Xinhua said.
Promises of aid and assistance came in soon after reports of the scale of the disaster.
The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies said it was dispatching emergency supplies including blankets, first aid kits, stretchers and body bags.
The U.S. Geological Survey said the flood was sparked by a glacial collapse, that caused seismic activity and the "catastrophic" downstream impacts in Nepal and Tibet.
"This event was initially reported as a magnitude 4.4 earthquake," it said, but added that the seismic recordings were analyzed and found instead to be a "glacial collapse and debris flow."
Climate change is causing glaciers to melt worldwide, increasing the risks of glacial lake floods and glacial collapses.
Fears of potential further floods remain, with water trapped by the immense piles of debris blocking the valley.
"With a blockage still lodged upstream on the Nepal-China border river, authorities warn a second flood may occur," said Qianggong Zhang, head of climate and environmental risks at the Kathmandu-based International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development.
Li Qipu, a member of China's paramilitary People's Armed Police, cited "the instability of a reservoir lake upstream" and "the narrow mountain road" as elements complicating rescue efforts.
Scores of Hindu devotees from across the world are among the hundreds missing on the border, Indian spiritual leader Sadhguru said Thursday.
They had been returning from a holy pilgrimage to Mount Kailash, on the Chinese side of the frontier, when they were caught in the floods at an immigration post.
"The entire group was there in the building," Sadhguru said in a video message to his millions of followers, weeping as he spoke from Tibet, with the anguished wails of other pilgrims heard in the background.
"This is a terrible and extraordinary event."

Nepal scrambles to find 1,300 missing as floods death toll hits 353
Unknown

2026-08-27
10:13:00 UTC
19:13:00 KST

Nepalese rescue teams searched devastated areas Thursday for more than 1,300 people still missing a day after flash floods and landslides along the Nepal-Tibet border killed at least 353 and swept away entire villages.
Homes were engulfed and vehicles tossed around by the tsunami-like rumble of water and mud that struck villages and towns Wednesday morning on the path of two rivers, Bhote Koshi and Trishuli.
Many of the missing are foreign tourists, including scores of Hindu pilgrims to Tibet's sacred snow-capped Mount Kailash.
According to the U.S. Geological Survey, the disaster was caused by a glacial collapse that sent forth an overwhelming flow of icy debris.
Emergency teams were racing to evacuate survivors from affected zones, fearing new flash floods.
Nepali soldiers used sniffer dogs to search for bodies buried under thick grey sludge.
"Everything is finished," Omkar Joshi, 35, a Nepali customs agent rescued from a hilltop in the border town of Timure, told Agence France-Presse (AFP).
"It is a giant graveyard. All that is left are sand and pebbles, soaked red by human blood."
Nepali police said they had recovered 353 bodies.
Another 823 people, including 517 foreign tourists, were out of contact in the country. Beijing says 100 Chinese citizens are missing in Nepal.
In China, state media said the "mudslide disaster" at the Gyirong Port in Tibet killed three people, while 558 people, including 260 foreigners, are missing.
Chinese Premier Li Qiang visited the area Thursday, state media said, to oversee "emergency rescue and relief work, and to visit rescue workers and affected people."
In Nepal, rescuers waded through mud and sludge to look for survivors after floodwaters buried the lower floors of multi-story buildings.
Prime Minister Balendra Shah, who urged the Himalyan nation to "stand together" hours after the disaster, visited some of the hardest-hit areas Thursday.
Shah told local authorities to "provide immediate relief to displaced families" and to open blocked roads, his office said in a statement.
The foreigners out of contact were from 30 different countries, including Indians and others from Australia, Britain, Malaysia, the Netherlands, Portugal, South Africa, South Korea and the United States, Nepal's tourism board said.
The sudden rush of mud and debris was "like an inland tsunami," traveling nearly 170 kilometers (100 miles) south into Nepal, said environmental historian Ruth Gamble, of Australia's La Trobe University.
Rasuwa, in the north of Nepal, was the first district to be affected, but deaths have been reported as far south as Chitwan in the south, on the border with India.
Chinese government officials in Tibet mobilized nearly 800 emergency workers, as well as sniffer dogs and speed boats to help the rescue efforts, official news agency Xinhua said.
Promises of aid and assistance came in soon after reports of the scale of the disaster.
The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies said it was dispatching emergency supplies including blankets, first aid kits, stretchers and body bags.
The U.S. Geological Survey said the flood was sparked by a glacial collapse, that caused seismic activity and the "catastrophic" downstream impacts in Nepal and Tibet.
"This event was initially reported as a magnitude 4.4 earthquake," it said, but added that the seismic recordings were analyzed and found instead to be a "glacial collapse and debris flow."
Climate change is causing glaciers to melt worldwide, increasing the risks of glacial lake floods and glacial collapses.
Fears of potential further floods remain, with water trapped by the immense piles of debris blocking the valley.
"With a blockage still lodged upstream on the Nepal-China border river, authorities warn a second flood may occur," said Qianggong Zhang, head of climate and environmental risks at the Kathmandu-based International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development.
Li Qipu, a member of China's paramilitary People's Armed Police, cited "the instability of a reservoir lake upstream" and "the narrow mountain road" as elements complicating rescue efforts.
Scores of Hindu devotees from across the world are among the hundreds missing on the border, Indian spiritual leader Sadhguru said Thursday.
They had been returning from a holy pilgrimage to Mount Kailash, on the Chinese side of the frontier, when they were caught in the floods at an immigration post.
"The entire group was there in the building," Sadhguru said in a video message to his millions of followers, weeping as he spoke from Tibet, with the anguished wails of other pilgrims heard in the background.
"This is a terrible and extraordinary event."

Economic Watch: Dry ports deliver Chinese inland goods more efficiently to int'l market
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
18:08:58 CST
19:08:58 KST

CHANGSHA, Aug. 27 (Xinhua) -- Huaihua is a humble inland city that once saw its development hindered by geographical isolation. Despite breeding world-known hybrid rice, the city, located in deep mountains in central China's Hunan Province, long found it challenging to bring its high-quality agricultural products and manufactured goods to the global market.
However, its fortunes would take a positive turn in 2019, when the city was designated as an important node on the New International Land-Sea Trade Corridor -- a key international connectivity initiative now connecting more inland parts of China to the global market.
Local goods in Huaihua, now an international dry port, can undergo the custom clearance procedure just minutes after leaving the factory.
Then, the goods are loaded onto a freight train, sent to the coastal Qinzhou Port in Guangxi about 800 km away, and transferred to ships bound for customers overseas, said Tian Ping, a manager at Hunan Litong Hengyu Electrical Cables Tech Co., Ltd.
The company Tian worked for used to serve traditionally domestic power-grid customers. But now it is eyeing expansion into Southeast Asia, Central Asia, the Middle East and Africa.
"The dry port services and faster and cheaper transportation services are advantages of Huaihua that we value," Tian said.
Tian did the math. If companies shipped goods to Indonesia via Qingdao Port in east China, the logistics cost would be about 500 yuan (about 70 U.S. dollars) higher per tonne than using the rail-sea intermodal transport service available in Huaihua.
"In international competition, key advantages ultimately come down to production and logistics costs," said Tian.
Official figures show that the number of freight train services handled by Huaihua's dry port rose from 17 in 2021 to 1,220 in 2025. Its connectivity network now comprises seven major international logistics corridors and 200 domestic and international routes, reaching 216 ports and stations in 69 countries and regions.
More inland businesses are benefiting from such economically viable logistics option via dry port as China is encouraging inland regions to grow export-oriented economy and deeply integrate in Belt and Road cooperation.
In Ganzhou, east China's Jiangxi Province, its dry port is helping connect local furniture industry with suppliers and customers across Eurasia.
Six years ago, Jiangxi Sanyou Furniture Co., Ltd. could never have imagined making significant inroads into the European market. The furniture maker's opportunity for European expansion came when a staff member from the local dry port brought a Hungarian business delegation to visit.
One company from the Hungarian delegation placed an order worth 100,000 yuan, and Sanyou shipped the furniture by China-Europe freight train.
"It took only 20 days from loading the furniture to delivering it to Hungary, less than half the time required by sea," said Zhu Hao, Sanyou's marketing general manager. "The customer was satisfied with the furniture, and we saw the benefits."
The furniture company later established stable business relationships with customers in Hungary, Germany and Poland. Its European orders reached 7.36 million yuan in 2025.
By the end of 2025, Ganzhou International Land Port had handled more than 1,700 China-Europe freight trains. The trains have transported local products, ranging from porcelain tableware and toys to fresh farm produces and new-energy vehicles, to European customers. ■

Singapore launches liquid cooling standard for tropical data centers
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
18:08:30 CST
19:08:30 KST

SINGAPORE, Aug. 27 (Xinhua) -- Singapore has launched its standard for adopting liquid cooling technologies in tropical data centers, as the growing use of artificial intelligence (AI) drives demand for more energy-efficient digital infrastructure.
The new "Singapore Standard (SS) 726:2026 Liquid Cooling in Tropical Data Centres" is the world's first, according to a statement released Thursday.
"Tropical conditions such as high temperatures and humidity present additional challenges, including equipment corrosion, which can affect cooling efficiency and reliability," it said.
The standard equips data center operators with technical guidelines to design, deploy and operate various liquid cooling systems, manage potential risks, and integrate liquid cooling with existing air-cooled data centers.
It was jointly developed by the Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA) and Enterprise Singapore, through the Singapore Standards Council, in consultation with industry players.
"Liquid cooling is increasingly important to support the higher power densities required for AI and other advanced computing workloads, while improving cooling efficiency," said Aileen Chia, deputy chief executive at the IMDA.
As demand for digital infrastructure grows, Singapore will continue to develop industry-relevant standards that enable the safe, reliable and energy-efficient adoption of emerging technologies, said the statement. ■

He added that while governments and parliaments hold distinct constitutional responsibilities, they share a common purpose: to serve the citizens, preserve peace, and foster conditions for durable prosperity.
"When formal diplomatic channels face strain, parliamentary dialogues can help maintain communication and rebuild trust," he said.
The ISC is an intergovernmental organization dedicated to promoting inter-parliamentary diplomacy and enhancing collaboration among national legislatures to address global challenges through dialogue and partnership. The first ISC was held in Islamabad, Pakistan, last November. ■

Russia’s oil giant Lukoil has emergency-halted crude processing and petroleum product manufacturing at its Nizhegorodnefteorgsintez (NORSI) refinery following a fire caused by a drone strike on August 26, three industry sources reported to Reuters.
With NORSI offline, all major Russian refineries belonging to Lukoil have ceased raw material processing, following earlier shutdowns at Permnefteorgsintez on August 21 and the Volgograd refinery on July 31.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The governor of the Nizhny Novgorod region, Gleb Nikitin, confirmed a drone attack on Wednesday that damaged an industrial facility in the area, though he did not name the specific company.
According to Reuters sources, the strike damaged individual processing units, inter-shop communications, and general plant utility systems. The sources were unable to provide a timeline for repairing the damage or resuming refining operations at NORSI.
NORSI ranks as Russia’s fourth-largest refinery by crude processing volume and second by gasoline production, with an annual capacity exceeding 15 million metric tons of crude oil.
The facility is capable of producing roughly 5 million metric tons of gasoline, over 5 million metric tons of diesel fuel, more than 2 million metric tons of fuel oil, and around 0.5 million metric tons of road bitumen per year.
The August 26 disruption follows multiple recent shutdowns at NORSI caused by drone strikes, with previous processing halts recorded on July 2, June 24, May 20, and April 5.
Following the production shutdown, Lukoil did not put up wholesale lots of motor gasoline, diesel fuel, or other petroleum products from the NORSI refinery for sale on the St. Petersburg International Mercantile Exchange on Wednesday.
According to satellite imagery analysis from the Dnipro Osint project on August 25, 2026, Russia’s LUKOIL-Permnefteorgsintez oil refinery lost approximately 86% of its primary crude-processing capacity—totaling roughly 11.3 million tons of crude oil per year—following Ukrainian drone strikes more than 1,500 kilometers from the border.
Several key atmospheric-vacuum distillation units sustained severe damage, including the AVT-5 unit with an annual capacity of 4.53 million tons, where distillation columns and crude oil dehydration systems were critically hit.
Additional repair work and crane activity were observed at the AVT-4 unit, which processes 4.94 million tons annually, while the AVT-1 unit, capable of handling 1.83 million tons per year, previously suffered a fire during the attack.

Malaria outbreak kills two workers at Germany’s busiest airport
Two employees at Germany’s Frankfurt Airport have died in a rare malaria outbreak caused by infected mosquitoes believed to have been accidentally brought in by plane from a malaria-endemic country.
The outbreak began in early July, according to the Frankfurt Public Health Department. The first worker died shortly afterward, with the malaria diagnosis confirmed posthumously. Authorities traced the outbreak to the airport, where operator Fraport set traps and captured several mosquitoes, sending them for genetic analysis to determine their origin. Staff were advised to seek medical attention if symptoms developed.
In mid-July, the Robert Koch Institute (RKI), Germany’s federal disease-control agency, confirmed four cases among airport employees.
“The affected individuals fell ill between July 4 and 6, 2026,” the RKI wrote in its Epidemiological Bulletin. “It is assumed that the infection was transmitted by an infected Anopheles mosquito imported by plane.”
Citing medical sources, local media later reported that a total of six male workers, largely in jobs handling luggage, had been infected.
On Wednesday, Frankfurt health authorities announced that a second infected worker had died. They insisted, however, that “for the population of Frankfurt, the risk is considered very, very low.”
“The disease is not transmissible from person to person but is always transmitted by mosquitoes,” the authorities said in a statement to German media. They did not confirm the total number of cases but said those affected were receiving treatment.
Frankfurt health chief Peter Tinnemann similarly sought to reassure residents, telling DPA news agency that “the risk to the Frankfurt population is insignificant.”
Malaria is a potentially fatal disease caused by Plasmodium parasites spread by infected female Anopheles mosquitoes. It typically causes fever, chills, headaches and fatigue, while severe cases can lead to organ failure, seizures and coma. The most dangerous form, malaria tropica, can become life-threatening within 24 hours if undetected, though malaria is generally considered preventable and curable with early treatment.
The disease is concentrated mainly in tropical regions, particularly sub-Saharan Africa. The latest WHO data shows an estimated 610,000 people died from malaria worldwide in 2024 out of roughly 282 million cases – around 9 million more infections than the previous year. More than half of the deaths occurred in Nigeria, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and Niger.
Malaria cases in Germany normally involve travelers who were infected in endemic countries. In rare cases, however, infected mosquitoes can be carried into the country aboard aircraft, including in luggage, and then bite people on the plane or at the airport – a phenomenon known as “airport malaria.” Europe’s last documented airport-acquired case also occurred at Frankfurt Airport in 2023, according to the RKI.

US Democrats increasingly oppose arming Israel: poll

Breadcrumb
US Democratic voters are rapidly shifting on Israel, favour presidential candidate opposing arms
There has been a significant shift within the US Democratic Party towards Israel, according to a recent poll that found an overwhelming majority of Democratic voters in the first six states to hold presidential primaries in 2028 would support electing a presidential candidate who pledges to halt military aid to Israel and impose an arms embargo on it.
The poll by the Policy Project at the Institute for Middle East Understanding with YouGov surveyed about 4,000 likely voters in the Democratic primaries in South Carolina, Nevada, New Hampshire, New Mexico, Michigan and Virginia, with a margin of error of plus or minus two percentage points.
The significance of the poll appears to lie in the fact that it extends to some states that do not have Arab and Muslim communities capable of influencing the course of elections, compared with the 2024 presidential election, in which Arab-American voters emerged as an influential bloc in states such as Michigan.
The results showed that most of Arab-Americans did not vote for presidential candidate Kamala Harris as punishment for her position on the genocide in Gaza. It also extends to states that predominantly vote Republican, such as South Carolina.
The shift in the general mood does not mean that this issue will determine the choice of the Democratic presidential candidate in 2028. But, it shows how Democratic voters view US military aid to Israel and the US position of providing it with unconditional support at the expense of Palestinian rights.
It should be noted that the party's presidential candidate is chosen through voters casting ballots for their preferred candidate in each state. Each candidate receives many delegates based on the proportion of votes they receive in each state, who pledge to support the candidate who selected them as delegates.
At the Democratic National Convention before the election, they vote to select the candidate. If no one secures a majority in the first round, senior delegates, including former presidents, state governors and members of Congress, vote in the second round. They account for about 15% of the delegates.
There are about 4,696 delegates to the party's national convention, including 3,949 pledged delegates and 747 known as senior delegates.
Some 75% of likely voters in New Hampshire, New Mexico and Michigan preferred a candidate who would prevent weapons from being sent to Israel, as did 74% in Nevada, 66% in Virginia and 65% in South Carolina.
Between 4% and 6% preferred a candidate who would send weapons to Israel.
Asked whether reducing US support for Israel would play a role in their vote, 65% of Michigan voters, 63% in New Hampshire, 61% in Nevada, 59% in New Mexico, 55% in Virginia and 46% in South Carolina answered "yes".
Some 70% in New Hampshire and New Mexico supported imposing US sanctions on Israel, compared with 68% in Nevada and Michigan, 61% in Virginia and 49% in South Carolina.
Meanwhile, 80% of likely voters in Michigan said they believed Israel was committing genocide against Palestinians in Gaza, compared with 78% in New Hampshire and Nevada, 76% in New Mexico, 72% in Virginia and 57% in South Carolina.
Reasons behind the shift
In this context, Dr Edmund Ghareeb, a professor of political science at American University in Washington, DC, listed the reasons for the shift in Democratic voters' mood, foremost among them Israel committing genocide in Gaza, which was broadcast publicly on social media; its attacks on Lebanon; and its crackdown on the student movement on university campuses over Gaza.
"There has been a major change in the position of Democratic voters, particularly in states with Democratic majorities," Dr Ghareeb told TNA.
He noted that most Americans sympathised with Israel following 7 October 2023, when the Hamas-led "Al-Aqsa Flood operation" took place, but Israeli policies, attacks on civilians, the commission of genocide, attacks on Palestinians in the occupied West Bank, the expulsion of residents and Christians from their homes, and the destruction in southern Lebanon all contributed to changing the positions of Democrats and independents, according to Ghareeb.
He said the US administration's handling of university student protests over Gaza, the dispersal of those protests, the arrests of students, and restrictions imposed on the right to protest and freedom of expression all significantly affected how American society viewed the issue, particularly students and young people under 35.
He pointed out that the decline in support for arming Israel had extended to a proportion of American Jews, who had begun adopting positions against arming Israel that did not align with Democratic political leaders.
He cited New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani receiving 33% of the vote among New York Jews, adding that rising food and petrol prices and their impact on the middle and ordinary classes because of the US-Israeli war on Iran had also had a significant effect on both Democrats and Republicans.
Ghareeb warned that this change in public opinion may not last long if there is no effective organisation to capitalise on this shift in voters' views and if new currents within the Democratic Party, such as progressives, fail to make significant use of the change.
He said the Gaza issue and its spread on social media, as well as Israeli policies, had pushed progressives to change their positions, reject the genocide and benefit from the movement on US streets.
"We see a split within both the Democratic and Republican parties, and even if President Donald Trump has control over the Republican Party, he is losing between 20% and 25% of his overall supporters, which represents a severe blow to him," he said.
He attributed this to the presence of Republican figures who oppose wars, such as Thomas Massie, Tucker Carlson and Marjorie Taylor Greene.

Bulgaria will get seven minehunter ships from Belgium and Netherlands to protect Black Sea
SOFIA, Aug 27 - Bulgaria has approved the purchase of seven minehunter ships from Belgium and the Netherlands, as the NATO alliance seeks to bolster its capabilities to clear naval mines and secure shipping routes in the Black Sea, local media reported on Thursday.
Along with Romania and Turkey, Bulgaria agreed at a NATO summit in July to expand a joint task force that clears mines floating in the Black Sea to include missions to protect critical infrastructure.
The three NATO states, which share the Black Sea with Georgia, Russia and Ukraine, formed the de-mining task force in 2024 to counter the threat of floating mines after Moscow's invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Under a sale agreement with the Netherlands approved by the Bulgarian parliament on Wednesday, Bulgaria will receive three ships equipped to seek and destroy mines and mine-like objects, while a separate transfer agreement between Belgium, the Netherlands and Bulgaria covers another four vessels.
The Netherlands has committed to restoring the technical capabilities and increasing the operational capacity of three ships before transferring ownership, with Bulgaria paying for repair and restoration work to bring all seven vessels to NATO operational readiness standards.
"These mine hunters are particularly necessary. We have three of the same type, and with these seven we will complement and further enhance our capabilities,” Defence Minister Dimitar Stoyanov said before lawmakers approved the deal.
“Bulgaria is part of the mine countermeasures group established together with our colleagues from Turkey and Romania, and it is working in excellent coordination to clear the maritime areas of the three countries.”
A memorandum of understanding covering the acquisition also includes crew training, spare parts and additional equipment. REUTERS

Famed U.S. drone maker accused of using Ukrainian drone footage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
10:03:13 UTC
19:03:13 KST

- A Ukrainian defense expert said AeroVironment's Switchblade 600 promotional video may show footage of a Ukrainian RAM-2X drone strike instead.
- He pointed to a targeting reticle repainted green and repositioned in the video as evidence, while also crediting Switchblade drones for a separate confirmed strike.
A Ukrainian defense expert has flagged an apparent discrepancy in a promotional video from American drone maker AeroVironment, saying footage the company presented as a successful Switchblade 600 strike actually shows the Ukrainian-made RAM-2X strike drone in action.
Bohdan Miroshnychenko, military analyst and editor-in-chief of the Ukrainian defense outlet Oboronka, raised the discrepancy in a post analyzing AeroVironment’s promotional video, which showcases the Switchblade 600 loitering munition’s use in Ukraine.
Miroshnychenko compared frames from the AeroVironment video against footage released separately by Ukrainian military personnel from a command post and a report from Ukraine’s Security Service, the SBU.
“It seems that the American manufacturer of the legendary Switchblade strike drones, in its promotional video, presented a strike by Ukrainian RAM-2X drones as the work of their own product,” Miroshnychenko wrote.
He pointed to a specific visual detail as evidence: the targeting reticle shown in the footage. A red reticle, which Miroshnychenko said is characteristic of the target-lock symbology used by the RAM-2X’s guidance system, appears repainted green in the AeroVironment video and shifted closer to the center of the vehicle shown on screen.
“The red targeting reticle, characteristic of target lock by the autonomous guidance system, was repainted the branded green and shifted closer to the center of the vehicle,” Miroshnychenko wrote.
Miroshnychenko framed the apparent mix-up as a sign that some Ukrainian-made weapons have reached a level of battlefield performance that allows them to be marketed internationally alongside established American systems.
“Another symptom that some Ukrainian weapons can already be brightly advertised with classic music under a beat and sold on the global market on par with American ‘hits,'” Miroshnychenko wrote. “Of course, as soon as we saturate our own Defense Forces with them and put things in order with the regulatory framework.”
Miroshnychenko also credited the Switchblade 600 for a separate, verified result in the same SBU operation he referenced. He said Switchblade drones were used effectively in that strike, which destroyed two Buk surface-to-air missile systems, two Tor-M2 systems, a Strela system and a Tunguska air defense system.
RAM-2X is a Ukrainian-developed strike drone. Switchblade 600 is a loitering munition built by AeroVironment that has been fielded by Ukrainian forces and, separately, by the U.S. Army, which has ordered additional units under an existing contract this year.

Nepal-Tibet floods: What is a glacial collapse, how common is it?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
10:01:48 UTC
19:01:48 KST

Nepal-Tibet floods: What is a glacial collapse, how common is it?
More than 165 people are killed, with thousands missing, in floods triggered by a huge glacial collapse near Nepal-China border.
More than 1,500 people are missing across Nepal and China’s Tibet, including more than 800 foreign tourists, after rare flash glacial-lake outburst floods submerged towns and communities under a sludge of mud and water.
More than 270 people have been killed, but officials say the toll is expected to rise as rescue teams attempt to reach farther areas that have been cut off by the floods, with several key bridges and highways also devastated.
With skies still clear above the Nepal-China border, and no rain pouring, officials earlier believed that a magnitude 4.4 earthquake could have triggered the downstream floods.
However, several experts and the United States Geological Survey have confirmed that “the seismic event” was a consequence of “a glacial collapse and debris flow that caused subsequent catastrophic impacts downstream” – rather than the other way around.
So, what is a glacial collapse, and is this a catastrophic outcome of worsening climate change?
What is glacial collapse?
In simple terms, a glacial collapse is the detachment of a large mass of glacier ice from its bed – sometimes involving millions of cubic metres of ice, rock, and water – that can transform into a highly mobile ice-rich avalanche or debris flow.
This collapse is not a formally defined scientific term in glaciology, but is widely used to describe the event.
Earth System Science Data, an international open-access scientific journal, describes this as gravity-driven failures of glacier ice on mountain slopes, including ice avalanches, glacier detachments, and rock-ice avalanches.
An initial study of Planet Labs satellite imagery showed a landslide of ice and rock unleashed a flood carrying debris in the Lhende River in Tibet, about 20km (12 miles) northeast of the Nepal-China border crossing in Rasuwagadhi, Nepal’s disaster management officials said on X.
Television images showed collapsed homes, floating cars and a metal bridge being washed away, while witnesses said the waters engulfed entire villages.
What happened in Nepal and Tibet?
The disaster struck the mountainous Nepal-Tibet border region, with some of the worst damage in Nepal’s Rasuwa district, immediately south of the Chinese border.
The initial surge entered the Lhende Khola, which feeds into the Bhote Koshi and then the Trishuli river, carrying floodwaters south through Nepal. Water levels in the Trishuli reportedly rose by as much as 9 metres (27ft) in just 30 minutes.
Nepal’s National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority said the “glacier-inclusive flood” occurred in the Lhende River due to “an ice-rock avalanche on the Nepali side”, according to Prakash Pokharel, a geologist at the authority.
Vikram Gupta, who specialises in engineering geology and teaches at Sikkim University in India’s northeast state bordering Nepal, said it was “confirmed that a substantial portion of that glacier snout collapsed to initiate the event – probably including or entraining a fair amount of rock and sediment”.
Earth scientist Dan Shugar, an associate professor at the University of Calgary, said the imagery seemed to show that a large amount of snow had melted in the 24 hours before the disaster. “The lower part of a glacier broke off at about 5,200 metres and crashed onto the valley floor about 1,200 metres below,” Shugar said.
The disaster comes against a backdrop of rapid warming and glacial loss across the Himalayas.
Glaciers across the Hindu Kush Himalaya mountain range – which spans Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Bhutan, China, India, Myanmar, Nepal and Pakistan – lost ice 65 percent faster between 2011 and 2020 than during the previous decade.
Nepal’s glaciers – sandwiched between two major carbon emitters, India and China – have lost close to one-third of their ice volume in roughly three decades due to global warming, the United Nations said in 2023.
“It was a huge gush of mud coming straight towards us,” said Keshav Prasad Baral, a 68-year-old survivor being treated in a Nepali hospital.
“As it got closer, it kept rising higher and higher. When I saw it enter our home, I tried to grab my wife’s hand and take her to the terrace. But she was swept away by the mud.”
A helicopter ferried him to safety four hours later. “My wife is still somewhere beneath the mud,” he added. “She’s gone.”
Did global warming cause it?
Experts note it is too soon to tell conclusively if global warming and worsening climate change were the cause behind the devastating floods.
The so-called glacial lake outburst floods (GLOF) – the sudden and catastrophic release of vast volumes of water from melting glacier-fed lakes – are among the dangers associated with such events in the region’s extreme topography.
Dorothy Heinrich, a researcher at the United Kingdom’s University of Reading, said GLOFs were among the hazards posed by a warming planet in the region.
“We do know what climate change trends look like in the Himalayas. There is high confidence of more heatwaves, glacial retreat, permafrost reduction, these sorts of things that can drive things like landslides and glacial outburst floods,” she said.
Hatim Sharif, a hydrologist at the University of Texas San Antonio, said the one thing that struck him was the lack of rainfall beforehand. “That defeats essentially every operational flood warning system in the world,” he said.
By the time you see the mud flow coming, it’s too late. “Running will not help,” nor will trying to flee by vehicle, Sharif said, because the mud and water moving at high speed form a lethal combination “like liquid concrete”.
Are glacial collapses common?
There have been a handful of instances of glacial collapse over the last decade, where scientists and geologists see them as highly unusual and rare.
Tibet has emerged as a hotspot for some of the world’s largest documented glacier collapses, although scientists say their causes are site-specific.
In July 2016, the lower part of a valley glacier in Tibet’s Aru Range – far western Tibet, near the Pangong Tso region – detached, sending about 68 million cubic metres of ice down the mountain and killing nine herders and hundreds of animals. Two months later, a nearby glacier collapsed, releasing about 83 million cubic metres of ice. NASA called it a rare occurrence.
Two years later, this time in Tibet’s Sedongpu Basin, two ice-rock avalanches occurred, spilling large quantities of glacier ice and debris into the Yarlung Tsangpo River, the upper Brahmaputra. Here, the debris blocked the river and created a dangerous temporary lake, showing how a glacier collapse can turn into a major downstream flood hazard.
In November 2022, about 40 million cubic metres of glacier ice detached from the Bukadaban Feng glacier in the Kunlun Mountains, and an ice avalanche crashed into a lake below, creating a 13-meter (42ft) high wave, according to analysis by the European Space Agency. It initially went completely unseen due to the site’s extremely remote location.
In India’s northern state of Uttarakhand in 2018, about 27 million cubic metres of rock and glacier ice collapsed from the steep north face of Ronti Peak, killing more than 200 people. But it was seen more as a rock avalanche, coupled with ice, rather than a straight-up glacier collapse.
In May last year, in Switzerland’s Blatten, a cascade of rock, soil, and ice roared down the mountainside in a vast cloud of dust, burying much of the village of Blatten. Experts have said the collapse was linked to climate change in the Alps.

Brazilian study provides objective data on breast proportion preferences
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
10:00:50 UTC
19:00:50 KST

A recent survey of medical students reveals a strong preference for symmetrical breast proportions and centrally located, smaller areolas. The findings aim to offer plastic surgeons objective data to guide patients seeking cosmetic breast procedures. The research was published in Revista Brasileira de Cirurgia Plástica.
Plastic surgeons regularly perform procedures to alter breast size and shape. However, surgical literature contains very few objective measurements regarding what constitutes an aesthetically pleasing breast. This lack of concrete data can make it difficult for doctors to advise patients and select the most appropriate surgical techniques.
Cosmetic surgery relies heavily on defined standards of beauty and proportion. For example, facial procedures often use precise geometric angles to plan a rhinoplasty. Gluteal surgeries follow established waist-to-hip ratios to produce consistent results. Historically, breast surgery has lacked similar standardized guidelines.
Researchers have long debated the ideal aesthetic parameters for breast reconstruction and augmentation. Earlier surgical pioneers proposed various proportional rules to help doctors achieve harmonious results. For instance, the renowned Brazilian surgeon Ivo Pitanguy helped establish early aesthetic principles for breast reconstruction, focusing heavily on proportional parameters.
Other specialists emphasized the geometry of the breast and the specific distances between the breast poles, which are the upper and lower halves of the breast mound. Previous studies have often suggested that a bottom-heavy breast is the most popular ideal. In these models, the lower pole carries slightly more volume than the upper pole.
To gather more contemporary and specific data, a team of researchers from the Universidade de Passo Fundo in Brazil initiated a new survey. Lead author Luís Gustavo Ramos Raupp Pereira and colleagues sought to evaluate visual preferences among medical students. They wanted to see if variables like gender influenced these aesthetic ideals. They aimed to provide updated information that could assist surgeons in preoperative planning.
The researchers conducted an observational, cross-sectional study. This type of research analyzes data from a specific population at a single point in time. They used an online questionnaire to gather responses.
The team sent the survey via institutional email to medical students at their university between May and September 2024. The questionnaire was based on parameters from previous international research on breast aesthetics. It asked participants to review a series of images and select their preferred breast shapes.
These visual aids displayed different volumetric ratios between the upper and lower poles of the breast. The options included a 40/60 ratio, a 50/50 ratio, and a 60/40 ratio. The images also showed variations in the position and size of the nipple and areola, known as the nipple-areola complex.
Alongside the visual choices, the researchers collected basic demographic information. They asked participants for their age and gender. They also inquired about education levels and physical exercise habits.
Participants were asked whether they had ever undergone breast surgery, such as augmentation or reduction. In total, 239 medical students completed the survey. The study group included 173 women and 66 men. The vast majority of respondents had no history of breast procedures, with only about eight percent reporting previous surgeries.
The group was also highly active. Nearly 90 percent reported participating in regular physical exercise. Almost half of the respondents stated they exercised up to five times a week.
The survey revealed a strong overall preference for symmetrical breast shapes. When asked to choose the most pleasing distribution of volume, 61.1 percent of participants selected a 50/50 ratio. This indicates they preferred an equal distribution of tissue between the upper and lower halves of the breast.
About 30 percent of the respondents preferred a 40/60 ratio. In this shape, the bottom half is slightly fuller than the top half. Less than 10 percent of the students preferred a 60/40 ratio, which features a fuller upper half.
Preferences regarding the placement of the nipple and areola were also consistent across the surveyed group. Nearly 60 percent of the students preferred a centrally located nipple-areola complex. About 26 percent chose a placement angled upward by 20 degrees.
Only 14 percent of the respondents favored a laterally positioned nipple. A lateral position means the nipple sits closer to the outside of the chest. When evaluating the size of the areola and nipple, the results leaned heavily toward smaller proportions.
Nearly 84 percent of all respondents selected the image depicting a smaller areola and nipple combination. Only 16 percent of the participants preferred the larger areola option presented in the survey. The researchers also compared the responses of male and female students to see if gender played a role in aesthetic preferences.
They found that the differences between men and women were not statistically significant. Both groups predominantly favored the 50/50 volume ratio, central nipple placement, and smaller areola size. Among women, roughly 63 percent preferred the symmetrical volume ratio. By comparison, 56 percent of men chose the exact same option.
Female respondents did show a slight preference for smaller areolas compared to men. About 85 percent of women chose the smaller size, versus 79 percent of men. However, the overall trends aligned closely between both sexes, showing a unified perspective on breast aesthetics.
The study authors noted a few limitations to their research. The sample size consisted entirely of medical students from a single university in southern Brazil. This specific population may possess a technical understanding of human anatomy.
This academic background could influence their visual preferences, potentially separating their views from standard cultural trends. Additionally, the participant group was unbalanced. The survey featured substantially more women than men.
This uneven distribution could affect how well the male preferences represent the broader population. A wider group of male respondents might have yielded slightly different percentages. The researchers suggest that future studies should include a broader variety of participants from different backgrounds and regions.
The study, “Breast Esthetic Preferences from the Perspective of Medical Students: A Cross-Sectional Study,” was authored by Luís Gustavo Ramos Raupp Pereira, Laura Librelotto Rubin Rodrigues, Maria Eduarda Caldato, Mateus Eduardo Giovelli, Karoline Scussel Ruhmke, Ana Luíza Fontana, and Eduardo Madalosso Zanin.

Viral China maths genius’ new workbook sells 26,000 copies in 4 days, sparking mixed reactions
Wei’s venture into supplementary education prompts criticism that he is profiting from his fame at the expense of his academic reputation
A famous Chinese mathematician known for his dishevelled genius image recently began selling workbooks for primary and secondary school students, which were quickly sold out within days.
Wei Dongyi, 35, is an associate professor in the Mathematics Department at Peking University.
He gained instant fame in 2021 after a vox pop on the Peking University campus. In the video, he appears dressed simply, carrying a 1.5-litre plastic bottle of water and a bag of steamed buns.
In the clip, he shared that he has studied at Peking University since his bachelor’s degree and is now a teacher there. Although he comes across as introverted, he remains unfazed, a characteristic later described by his admirers as typical of genius.
Wei’s remarkable past was uncovered by curious onlookers. The mathematician from Shandong province in eastern China was a mathematics prodigy.

Why We Love Watching Robots Fail
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
10:00:03 UTC
19:00:03 KST

When Tiangong Ultra unofficially smashed Usain Bolt’s 100m world record in Beijing, China, unballetically flailing past the finish line in 8.86 seconds, he did not flash an Olympian grin down the camera lens. In fact, he has no face. He is a headless robot.
Ultra, the work of the Beijing Humanoid Robot Innovation Center, was competing in the penultimate day of the unapologetically dystopian World Humanoid Robot Games, which has been hosting 666 teams at China’s National Speed Skating Oval. At this event, more than 2,000 robots are put to the test in track and field events (like long jump and an obstacle course); sports (like table tennis and soccer); and “scenarios” (like bricklaying and firefighting).
The event produced several eye-catching moments, including when humanoids beat human records at the high jump and the 400m. Just a few days before Ultra’s race, Lightning, a robot developed by phone company Honor, ran the 100m in 9.39 seconds, again thundering home quicker than Bolt.
But these tumbling records will likely be, in the pop cultural consciousness, eclipsed by something far more entertaining: tumbling robots. Along with the epic wins, there have been some seriously old-school, epic fails. One humanoid at the weightlifting event lost its balance with a weedy 15kg barbell, started jerking and slammed into the judges’ table, its helpless arms aloft, as if to say, “Why me?” Most memorably, a robot ended his dash by careering into a safety mat, Tom and Jerry style, before cartoonishly arching backward and setting on fire. Each spark was like a beautiful firework.
These slapstick scenes are deliciously satisfying. It’s deeply reassuring to watch robots fizzle out into smithereens. I myself have fond memories of watching the fire-hazard creations on Robot Wars in the U.K. (the successor to BattleBots in the U.S.) get shredded into shrapnel. This time, it’s a reassuring reminder that we can beat robot replicants at our own games.
This robot schadenfreude is fuelled by a fear of the future. Pointing out their flaws makes humanity’s finish line feel further away, even if that’s a highly unintelligent thing to think.
In many ways, this feeling can be filed next to our twisted delight in belittling generative AI. ChatGPT’s past inability to spell “strawberry” has made it an object of ridicule online. Calling AI-generated content “slop” has become a knee-jerk reaction to artificial intelligence’s catastrophic metastasisation in the creative industries.
And our collective giddiness about technical mishaps is not reserved just for AI. For instance, we love to watch the armored glass windows of the Tesla Cybertruck break. One possible reason: it shatters the illusion that the future is here and already decided. Robots surely can’t replace us if we haven’t figured out car windows yet. This feeling is magnified when they are humanoids—ersatz versions of ourselves.
Seen through a sports lens, it mirrors how I felt with the Enhanced Games. The painfully brotastic event held in Las Vegas in May allowed athletes to take performance-enhancing drugs or wear banned gear. With social media instilling a chronic fatigue for actual human achievement, technophiles are moving the goalposts; if being pumped full of steroids or titanium plates makes you more likely to beat a world record, it’s worth it. Once again though, disappointment was on show. Just a single best-ever-time, in the men’s 50m freestyle, was (unofficially) recorded by Kristian Gkolovmeev; he wore an outlawed polyurethane skinsuit. Otherwise, the non-artificially-enhanced athletes dominated the competition.
My concern: when it comes to humanoids, at least, our schadenfreude is set to be a short-lived pastime. While advanced robots are still relatively primitive, their improvement is staggering. To put it into perspective, at last year’s World Humanoid Robot Games, Ultra won the 100 meters in 21.50 seconds, much closer to Bolt’s 200m record than his 100m time. They’re only getting stronger and faster. Dunking on “clankers,” a derogatory term for clumsy robots (like this one dancing to Billie Jean), may be the most classically human response: laughing off the impending doom.
Many futurists predict that in the near future, our factories and farms and battlefields and back gardens will be filled with humanoid helpers. In 2024, Elon Musk said that by 2040 there will probably be more humanoid robots than people. And according to research by Morgan Stanley over 1 billion humanoids may be in use by 2050 and the market could be worth $5 trillion.
Spectators from afar like me, viewing the drama on our phones, will continue to watch with a sort of futuristic gallows humour. Laughing at misfortune, however spiteful it may be, leads to social bonding—in this case, as an entire species, against robots—that humans desperately need right now.
Every time a clanker goes crash, bang, wallop, and kaput, it’s a visceral reminder that we still matter. And unlike them, when faced with their destruction, I’m able to smile.
