More than 1,300 missing in Nepal and China after deadly Himalayan flood
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
07:18:00 UTC
16:18:00 KST

More than 360 dead, 1,400 missing in Nepal and Tibet after Himalayan flood
At least 359 people confirmed dead in Nepal and three in China’s Tibet as search and rescue efforts continue.
Some 360 bodies have been recovered and more than 1,400 people are missing across Nepal and China’s Tibet region after a huge collapse of mud and rock into a Himalayan river triggered catastrophic flooding across local towns and valleys, authorities have said.
Rescue teams waded through mud on Thursday searching for the missing, as authorities in Nepal said at least 359 people have been killed there.
At least three people have died in the neighbouring Tibet region.
Nepalese police and tourism officials said that more than 500 foreigners were among 910 people missing in Nepal.
Among the missing are tourists from more than two dozen countries: 177 are from India, 63 from the United States, 34 from Australia, 33 from the United Kingdom, and 25 from Canada.
Beijing’s foreign ministry also said nearly 100 Chinese nationals were among the missing in Nepal.
Across the border in Tibet’s Gyirong county, 558 people are reported missing, including 260 foreign nationals, according to Chinese state broadcaster CCTV.
Search and rescue operations are proving to be a “massive challenge” as just simply “getting to the affected areas … to try and recover the survivors”, is proving to be extremely difficult as the roads and bridges there have suffered extensive damage, said Al Jazeera’s Minelle Fernandez, reporting from the Nepalese capital, Kathmandu.
A mix of government and private helicopters have “been drafted to fly into the areas to try to bring as many survivors as possible” to hospitals to receive treatment for injuries that doctors say include broken ribcages and skin burns, said Fernandez.
Rescuers in Nepal have deployed helicopters to search for survivors and drop emergency supplies to thousands of people cut off in a rugged mountainous area popular with trekkers and pilgrims travelling between Lhasa in Tibet and Kathmandu.
Video footage verified by news agencies showed rapid torrents of water and debris sweeping away dozens of people at a border crossing in Gyirong, while downstream in Nepal, homes, roads, and power infrastructure were destroyed.
Army spokesperson Raja Ram Basnet said helicopters were dropping tents, food, and medicine provided by neighbouring India into the hardest-hit districts. More than 5,000 army and police rescue personnel joined the rescue effort that retrieved 125 people on Thursday, including 20 foreigners, he said.
Nepal’s Prime Minister Balendra Shah left by road for Bidur in one of the worst-affected districts of Nuwakot, to assess the flood situation, his office said on social media.
Early reports from Nepalese officials suggested an earthquake in the area may have caused the lower section of a glacier to collapse, triggering the flash floods.
However, the US Geological Survey noted that the seismic event, initially recorded as a magnitude 4.4 earthquake, was actually the seismic energy generated by the sudden collapse of glacial rock and ice, followed by a huge debris flow.
Chinese authorities warned that a still-dammed lake in Gyirong, upstream from the flood-affected border crossing, poses further risks and could severely complicate rescue efforts in the area, CCTV reported.
Many of those caught in the disaster were on a pilgrimage to Mount Kailash and Lake Mansarovar, high-altitude sites in Tibet revered by Hindus, Buddhists, and followers of other faiths.
Some 77 Hindu pilgrims were at the Nepal-China border immigration office when the flood hit on Wednesday, popular Indian spiritual leader Sadhguru, whose real name is Jagdish Vasudev, said in a video message from Tibet on his social media accounts.
The pilgrims were part of several Hindu groups organised by the Isha Foundation of Sadhguru, who had been visiting Mount Kailash.
“Literally, the entire group was there in the building; this is a terrible and extraordinary event,” he said.
International response
The US State Department announced it was dispatching a disaster response adviser and providing $500,000 in emergency aid.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney described the flooding as “devastating”, adding that Canadian officials were monitoring the situation closely.
United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres confirmed that UN teams were delivering emergency supplies and support staff to affected communities in Nepal.
Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese noted that gathering clear information from the remote area remained challenging due to limited local infrastructure and resources.
Sagar Pandey, chief executive of a Himalayan tourism operator, said 15 Indian-Australian pilgrims travelling with his company were among the missing.
“There are no human-made structures, no human settlements left. Everything is just flat,” he said after conducting an aerial survey of the disaster zone. “Anyone in the hotels, restaurants, or vehicles – I believe everyone is gone.”
CCTV footage from the Chinese side of the border showed residents fleeing as a surge of mud, rocks, and floodwater submerged buildings and vehicles.
Preliminary satellite imagery analysis by Planet Labs indicated that a landslide of ice and rock triggered a debris-laden surge down the Lhende River, approximately 20km (12 miles) northeast of the Rasuwagadhi border crossing between Nepal and China.
In the affected valleys, thick mud swathed homes, trees, and vehicles, while aerial footage showed collapsed houses, submerged cars, and a metallic bridge washed away by the torrents.
“There is devastation everywhere we look,” said Tula Bahadur BK, a healthcare worker in Rasuwa. “The settlements next to the river have been completely swept away. Five of my own relatives are missing.”
The flood highlights Nepal’s growing exposure to climate hazards, Sunil Acharya, a climate and public policy specialist, told Al Jazeera.
“It is not simply an unpredictable natural hazard. It is a brutal example of what it means to be living in the front line of climate crisis,” said Acharya, speaking from Kathmandu.
Nepal can only do so much to prevent such disasters, he said, adding that the government does not have enough resources to deal with the climate crisis on its own.
“International cooperation in limiting greenhouse gases so that the global warming doesn’t cause further damage like this is very imperative.”

US tech firm drops takeover bid for DigiD operator Solvinity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
07:17:45 UTC
16:17:45 KST

US tech firm drops takeover bid for DigiD operator Solvinity
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
The American IT services company Kyndryl has abandoned its attempt to buy Solvinity, the Amsterdam-based firm that runs the hosting platform behind DigiD, ending a takeover the Dutch government blocked in May on national security grounds.
A company spokesperson told the NRC that Kyndryl no longer wants to acquire Solvinity. The company’s latest quarterly report to US regulators also noted that the €100 million deal had been prohibited and that Solvinity’s owners were weighing their response.
DigiD is the login that millions of people in the Netherlands use to file tax returns and reach health insurers, pension funds and local councils. Solvinity runs the platform it sits on, along with the Berichtenbox message service in the MijnOverheid portal, and also supplies the justice ministry.
Security concerns
 The takeover, announced last November, alarmed MPs and security experts because it would have brought the data behind DigiD within reach of the US Cloud Act, which can compel American-owned companies to hand over information even when it is held on servers in Europe.”
Junior digital economy minister Willemijn Aerdts blocked the sale in late May “to protect the public interest”, acting on advice from the BTI, the agency that vets foreign investments for security risks.
What happens next
 Solvinity, owned by the British private equity firm Vitruvian Partners, is appealing. A Rotterdam judge refused to suspend the ban in July but told Aerdts to weigh a lighter measure than an outright ban.
Aerdts is due to rule on the company’s objection by the end of September. Solvinity and its owners are “exploring remedies, including contesting the government’s decision”, according to Kyndryl’s filing, and may also pursue a claim against Kyndryl.
The current DigiD contract runs until August 2028. The government has said the successor contract will be tendered under defence and security procurement rules that let it exclude bidders from countries whose laws could force access to Dutch data – meaning the platform’s next operator will have to be European.

Japan to probe popular animal cafes amid hygiene, welfare concerns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Japan to probe popular animal cafes amid hygiene, welfare concerns
A WWF Japan survey has found that some shops keep endangered species while others have inadequate hygiene management
Japan has hundreds of the cafes where campaigners say animals are sometimes kept in cramped spaces, and that their popularity encourages the capture and illegal trade of rare wildlife.
A fact-finding survey will begin as early as next month, starting with obtaining basic information such as the number of establishments and what animals they keep, according to an environment ministry official.
The ministry would examine whether they complied with relevant laws, including whether animals had enough space and how often cleaning took place, the official said, without wishing to be named.
“We may then do on-site inspections if we find facilities that appear to be breaching rules” stipulated by the animal welfare law, he said.
The decision to launch the survey followed recommendations by members of an expert panel about animal welfare.

27-square-meter steel and timber pavilion in chiang mai is built for flood resilience
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
07:17:04 UTC
16:17:04 KST

Following the major floods that hit Chiang Mai, Thailand, in 2024, local studio ROOF RAIN designed Sala Kin Khao as a compact piece of temporary architecture addressing some very immediate needs. The 27-square-meter pavilion brings together hygiene facilities, storage, and an open kitchen, responding to the period after the waters recede, when a dry place to cook and keep basic belongings can suddenly feel rather luxurious.
Its name translates as ‘Dining Pavilion,’ and food sits quite literally at the center of the project. Inspired by the owner’s simple admission — ‘I simply love cooking for others’ — the layout allows the two residents to cook side by side while friends and visitors gather around them. Rather than treating resilience as a bunker-building exercise, ROOF RAIN gives the structure a more sociable purpose: surviving the next flood matters, but so does having somewhere pleasant to eat dinner in the meantime.
flooding in Chiang Mai in 2024 left homes and daily infrastructure severely affected | images courtesy of ROOF RAIN
A THREE-METER GRID KEEPS THINGS SIMPLE
The pavilion is organized around a 3 x 3-meter modular grid, derived from locally available six-meter steel sections cut precisely in half. This approach minimizes material waste while establishing a repeatable structural system that can accommodate future additions without forcing the building to reinvent itself each time. More than 80% of the pavilion uses dry construction methods, reducing work on site and allowing much of the assembly to rely on familiar regional building techniques.
ROOF RAIN raises the entire structure 70 centimeters above the natural ground level, creating both a buffer against future flooding and a ventilated void beneath the floor. The additional clearance gives residents time and space to relocate possessions if water begins to rise again. Off-the-shelf industrial elements are left largely unmodified, while steel-to-timber connections can be assembled by local craftspeople with standard tools — a deliberately straightforward system in which resilience depends less on specialist technology than on knowing how things go together.
Sala Kin Khao stands elevated above the ground in Chiang Mai
OLD TIMBER SOFTENS THE INDUSTRIAL SHELL
Outside, matte-black corrugated fire-resistant asphalt sheets wrap the pavilion in a sharply vertical skin. The cladding was selected for its durability, easy maintenance, and reduced glare toward neighbouring buildings, lending the small volume an almost utilitarian directness. Against this dark industrial envelope, reused antique timber frames collected by the owner bring an entirely different register, their dimensions adjusted to align with the building’s three-meter grid.
Those aged wooden elements introduce grain, irregularity, and a little history into an otherwise systematic construction. They also keep Sala Kin Khao from reading purely as emergency infrastructure. Whether another severe flood arrives or, ideally, stays away, the pavilion is designed to remain useful as an everyday living space shaped by cooking, shared meals, and visitors passing through. Disaster preparedness is built into the floor level, structure, and materials, while everything above that is allowed to get on with life.

Australia's Nepali and Tibetan communities fear for loved ones after flash flood
Tibetan and Nepali Australians are anxious about family and friends missing after disaster struck the Nepal-Tibet border.
At least 160 people were killed and hundreds more — including 34 Australians — are missing after a huge wave smashed through villages yesterday.
It is believed a glacier avalanche likely caused the flood.
Tashi, a 51-year-old from Tibet who has lived in Melbourne for 13 years and asked to only use her first name for safety reasons, said she was worried about her nephew's wife and child.
She called home to Chinese-controlled Tibet as soon as she heard about the flash flood.
Her nephew works at the border police station in Gyirong County, where CCTV footage showed floodwaters sweeping through the area.
He escaped the disaster as he had left Gyirong a week earlier to care for his mother.
But his wife and daughter were missing, Tashi said.
"They tried to ring her, but the phone was not able to connect," she said.
"They're not sure what happened to them."
Tashi said there are several villages and schools in the affected area, and popular tourism sites.
She said she has communicated with her family through WeChat, but the connection has been intermittent.
"It's very risky sending that kind of footage outside," she said, adding that the platform is closely monitored by Chinese authorities.
"I'm worried about the Tibetan people affected around my village or nearby, and also the people in the downstream as well."
Tenzin Khangsar, co-chair of the Australia Tibet Council, said many community members had seen news of the disaster on social media.
"It was devastating, and my heart goes to the families and the people who are affected by this flood outburst."
Damaged home and missing relatives
Melbourne University PhD student Tulsi Ram Gompo received a call overnight that his family was safe, but his home and family farm in Nuwakot district, north of Nepal's capital Kathmandu, have been destroyed.
"Lucky my parents escaped, but my home and all our fields are all buried in the mud," he told the ABC.
"They told me many [people] were working in the fields and ran when a mudslide came," Mr Gompo said.
"But unfortunately many women, old-aged people, and children got stuck or were at home and didn't have time to escape."
He said he was waiting to hear about locals and relatives missing in his district.
"I have had family members contact me to try and find out information about dozens missing in my home town, so I try to find information on Facebook," he added.
Sujan Tamang from the village of Goljung in the Rasuwa district, in northern Nepal, said he was worried about his family.
"My relatives, my close friend and my villagers — they are still missing," he said.
"It's very sad for me, because there's no network, no electricity and it's very hard to connect with them.
"We want more help; they're still missing."
Community in shock
Northern Territory Nepalese Association secretary Anupam Dhungana said the flash flooding event was a "black day for the Nepalese".
"Everyone is shocked because there was no pre-information that the glacier was blocked; it came all of a sudden, so everyone is shocked," he said.
"It was unpredictable."
He said many Nepali people in the NT — of which there are almost 3,000 — spent much of yesterday looking at the emerging photos and videos from the natural disaster.
"Some of them … their friend has been lost," Mr Dhungana said.
"Lots of people are missing".
Melbourne-based Nepali woman Neelima Shrestha said it was overwhelming to see the footage of the devastating floods from her home country.
"Whenever we're scrolling, it's all about the flood and the victims, and it's really, very disturbing," she said.
"I think this is the [most] massive flood that Nepal has ever faced. This is very bad destruction that we have."
Nepali grocer Sanjay Manandhar, from the Melbourne suburb of Glenroy, said people were rallying to support one another and donate.
"We're just trying to help the community, like raising funds," he said.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan should become a partner in Asia-Pacific sustainability and help advance sustainable development worldwide, President Lai Ching-te (賴清德) said Thursday.
Speaking at the fifth Asia-Pacific Sustainability Expo in Taipei, Lai said Taiwan has strengths in technology, industry, democracy, and innovation. He said these advantages can help the country respond to global challenges and share solutions with other countries, CNA reported.
Lai said resilience is increasingly important as the country faces extreme weather, geopolitical tensions, the energy transition, and changes in global supply chains. The government plans to announce a national urban forest plan by the end of the year to help cities better withstand climate risks.
Taiwan will also expand renewable energy and strengthen the power grid, Lai said. The government will improve energy storage and power dispatch capabilities to make electricity supplies more reliable, per Economic Daily News.
Innovation is another key part of the country’s sustainability strategy, Lai said. He said Taiwan should use its strengths in semiconductors, information technology, and precision manufacturing to stay competitive as industries cut emissions.
The government is also carrying out a national carbon reduction plan supported by technology, financing, and other measures, Lai said. Taiwan completed its first carbon fee declarations and payments this year, which he described as an important step in building a carbon pricing system, per Rti.
Lai said sustainable development should balance economic growth, social progress, and environmental protection. The government spends more than NT$10 billion (US$315 million) a year to support small and micro businesses and plans an NT$100 billion fund over eight years to help them adopt digital technology and reduce emissions.
The government will also work with businesses, workers, and other groups to improve industrial competitiveness while supporting people affected by the transition, Lai said. Taiwan is also willing to share its technology and experience with Pacific allies and like-minded countries facing extreme weather, per NOWnews.
Lai said the expo’s themes of resilience, innovation, and shared prosperity reflect the country’s approach to sustainable development. He said Taiwan hopes to turn its experience into practical support for regional and global sustainability efforts.

Philippines’ rising military pensions risk triggering budget ‘time bomb’
The surge in pensions may weaken the country’s push to buy modern military assets to strengthen its deterrence
The Department of National Defence has proposed spending 142.95 billion pesos (US$2.3 billion) on military and uniformed personnel (MUP) pensions in 2027, out of a total proposed defence budget of 324.6 billion pesos.
The planned pension budget is 7 per cent higher than the 133.91 billion pesos allocated in the 2026 General Appropriations Act amid increasing calls for Manila to review the pension system.
While civilian workers typically contribute a part of their salaries to state fund systems, military and uniformed personnel are not required to make pension contributions, which are drawn from the national budget.
Proposals to legislate reforms to the armed forces’ pension system have long languished in Congress, with lawmakers warning that it is unsustainable.
The debate comes as the Philippines faces growing pressure from the US to spend more on its military.

RAF and US fighters complete Combat Archer in UK
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
08:00:52 BST
16:00:52 KST

British and US combat aircraft have completed live-fire weapons evaluations during Combat Archer 2026, using more than 120,000 square kilometres of controlled training space around the Hebrides and Aberporth ranges.
RAF and US Air Force combat aircraft have completed a major air-to-air weapons evaluation exercise in the United Kingdom, with Typhoons, F-35s and F-15E Strike Eagles operating against unmanned and towed targets during Combat Archer 2026, according to the company.
The exercise was conducted across MOD Hebrides and MOD Aberporth, both operated by QinetiQ under the Long-Term Partnering Agreement with the Ministry of Defence. According to a QinetiQ news update, it was the first time the two ranges had been used together to support a single defence exercise, allowing the activity to make use of more than 120,000 square kilometres of air and surface space.
Participating aircraft included British Typhoon fighters, F-35Bs, F-35A Lightning IIs and F-15E Strike Eagles, supported by KC-135 Stratotankers from the US Air Force’s 100th Air Refuelling Wing. The evaluation itself was conducted by the Weapon System Evaluation Program team from the 83rd Fighter Weapons Squadron at Tyndall Air Force Base in Florida, where Combat Archer exercises are normally staged.
Combat Archer is designed to evaluate aircraft, weapons and crews under representative live-fire conditions rather than functioning solely as a conventional training exercise. The event allows participating units to employ weapons against realistic targets while specialists collect performance data from the aircraft, missile systems and supporting range infrastructure.
QinetiQ said its teams supported mission planning, preparation, range operation and specialist technical activity throughout the exercise. Staff at Hebrides and Aberporth were responsible for preparing and managing the large air and maritime operating areas required for live weapons activity while maintaining the safety arrangements needed to support multiple aircraft and target systems.
The exercise also involved QinetiQ teams from both the UK and Germany. A specially equipped PC-12 aircraft, registration D-FRMT, was used for maritime surveillance around the exercise area and to support flight safety before live-fire activity began.
Additional target presentation was provided by a PC-9B aircraft towing targets for participating fighter crews. QinetiQ Target Systems also supplied Banshee Jet 80+ unmanned aerial vehicles, which are designed and manufactured in Ashford, Kent. The combination of expendable unmanned targets and towed systems allowed crews to conduct weapons evaluations against different representative airborne threats.
Lee Rowe, Mission Rehearsal Lead at QinetiQ, said, as quoted in a news update: “Combat Archer 2026 highlights the unique range of capabilities that QinetiQ offers. The expertise of our teams in the United Kingdom and Germany has supported the US Air Force and the Royal Air Force in conducting realistic operational assessments, thereby strengthening interoperability between the air forces of the allies.”
He added: “We conduct complex exercises, thereby creating the necessary safety and reliability to maintain operational readiness and ensure that the armed forces are optimally prepared.”
The participation of the 83rd Fighter Weapons Squadron brought the US Air Force’s established weapons evaluation methodology to British ranges. The squadron’s Weapon System Evaluation Program assesses the effectiveness of aircraft and weapons during live employment, providing information on how crews and systems perform under more demanding conditions than can be reproduced through simulator training alone.
For the RAF, the event also provided an opportunity to train alongside US units operating different fighter types and support aircraft. The combination of Typhoon and Lightning aircraft with F-15Es, US F-35As and KC-135 tankers allowed crews to practise multinational procedures while the weapons evaluation element generated performance data from live activity.
Using Hebrides and Aberporth together was a significant range-management element of the exercise. QinetiQ said the combined area available was roughly equivalent to the size of England, giving planners sufficient space to conduct complex live-fire scenarios while coordinating aircraft, unmanned targets, surveillance assets and supporting range infrastructure.

Egypt courts Libya's rival factions in push for unity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
07:00:44 UTC
16:00:44 KST

Breadcrumb
Egypt courts Libya's rival factions in push for unity and elections
Egypt is scaling up communications with rival Libyan factions to advance a political process and end institutional divisions in their country.
Egyptian intelligence chief Hassan Rashad met Deputy Commander–in-Chief of the Libyan National Army (LNA) Saddam Haftar in the Egyptian Mediterranean city of Alamein on 22 August to discuss developments on the Libyan scene.
Talks between the two sides also focused on proposals made in the past period to unify Libya's executive authority as a basis for greater stability and elections in the restive North African country, according to media reports about the meeting.
The Egyptian intelligence chief called for capitalising on the current momentum around the same initiatives, describing it as an "opportunity" to promote stability and strengthen Libya's unity, the same reports said.
The Egyptian effort comes as a regional and an international consensus builds on the need for ending Libyan rifts and advancing the North African state towards a settlement that contributes to its stability, observers in Cairo said.
It also comes amid unanimity on the need for restoring peace in Libya, which could contribute to stability in the Eastern Mediterranean region which acquires greater importance against the background of turmoil in crucial regional maritime chokepoints, including the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, they added.
"International and regional parties, especially Senior Advisor to the US President for Arab and African Affairs Massad Boulos, the UN mission in Libya, Egypt and Turkey, make serious efforts to unify Libyan institutions," Egyptian political analyst Abdel Sattar Heteita said.
Speaking to The New Arab, he described this cooperation as a "positive development", given traditional international and regional rivalries over Libya, following the downfall of the Muammar Gaddafi regime in 2011.
Changing approach
Egypt has broadened its involvement in Libya for several months now.
Yet, this involvement shows a clear break from Egypt's traditional approach to the same topic, political analysts said.
Egypt's post-Gaddafi approach to Libya specifically started forming following the 2012 parliamentary elections in the North African country, which shaped the rise and eventual institutional power of Islamist factions in it.
The same rise has later opened the way for Libya's division into an Islamist-controlled west and a military, probably secular, east.
Egypt took sides with the eastern Libya government and army (the LNA) for ideological and security reasons, analysts said.
Nevertheless, the same approach started to witness considerable change in recent months, having coincided with a change in the map of regional alliances and the demise of the regional order created by the series of pro-democracy uprisings that swept through the region as of late 2010, they added.
"The demise of this order has had its effect on Egypt's foreign policies, in particular, mainly changing its approach to the western Libya government," Egyptian political researcher Islam Mansi told TNA.
This policy change, he added, serves Egypt's final goal of protecting its own national security by embracing all factions in the neighbouring country.
Unlike Egypt, Turkey backed the western Libya government, offering insights into regional polarization on Libya.
However, ongoing reconciliation between Cairo and Ankara is opening the door for common ground on contentious files, including Libya, analysts said.
The 22 August meeting between the head of Egyptian intelligence and the deputy commander-in-chief of the LNA came only three days after Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi met LNA Commander-in-Chief Field Marshal Khalifa Haftar in Alamein.
During the meeting, Sisi reiterated his country's support for Libya's unity, territorial integrity and stability.
The Egyptian president also called for unifying Libyan institutions and holding simultaneous elections, the Egyptian Presidency said in a statement following the meeting.
It added that President Sisi also expressed support for initiatives aiming at ending Libya's prolonged stalemate.
Egypt's bid to balance its relations with different Libyan factions was manifested almost 19 days earlier when Sisi received Abdul Hamid Dbeibeh, the prime minister of the Government of National Unity (GNU) which is based in Tripoli.
Among other things, discussions between the Egyptian president and the prime minister of the western Libya government focused on efforts to advance the political process in Libya to consolidate stability in it, unify its institutions and create conditions to end its transitional period, according to Egyptian media reports.
Challenges ahead
Libya was also at the centre of phone talks between Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty and Boulos on 22 August.
Egypt's intensifying efforts on Libya and engagement with its different factions also reflect the vast opportunities it sees in the neighbouring country as well as the growing role it plays in regional security, specialists said.
Economic cooperation, particularly on reconstruction, was present in talks between the Egyptian president and the Libyan officials he met in Alamein.
These discussions came as Egypt tries to also widen its economic leverage in Libya, with the oil-rich nation seeking to rebuild itself, following years of chaos, the same specialists added.
"Libya buzzes with chances for Egyptian companies," Mansi said, noting that Cairo's embrace of all political forces in the neighbouring country creates more potential for business.
Egyptian companies have been intensely involved in the implementation of infrastructure projects, especially in eastern Libya, in the past years.
The same companies are also probably hoping to expand the scope of their work to GNU-controlled parts of Libya, where Turkey has strong presence too, observers said.
Egypt also has plans to establish an 800-kilometer pipeline between Tobruk, in the north-eastern part of Libya on the Mediterranean, and its northern coastal city of Alexandria.
The $1 billion pipeline will transport Libyan crude oil to refineries in the Egyptian coastal city, in Egypt's bid to get dependable oil supplies amid disruptions to traffic in the Strait of Hormuz.
Clear in Egypt's current approach to the Libyan file is also the evolution of this approach from a view of the neighbouring country as a security and ideological file to a geostrategic file at the centre of an emerging regional order, analysts said.
This is particularly true with Libya's aspired stability and unity possibly contributing to tightening the screws on regional forces supporting parties to the civil war in Sudan, they added.
In the past few years, Libya has emerged as a central supply route and logistics hub for parties to the war-torn African state.
Nevertheless, international efforts aiming at unifying Libyan institutions and holding elections face challenges, analysts said.
The entrenchment of dual rival power structures, the lack of consensus on an electoral and constitutional framework, the presence of foreign mercenaries, and disputes over economic and financial resources are but a few of these challenges, they added.
The same challenges, analysts said, highlight the importance of dialogue among rival parties.
"There can be no agreement between different Libyan factions in the absence of this dialogue," Libyan political analyst Abdel Khaliq Maatouq told TNA.
Most Libyans, he noted, want to move directly straight to an end to their country's transition.
"This can be done by holding simultaneous elections that terminate this transition and divisions among the Libyans," he added.

How to properly bake in foil so that meat, vegetables, and fish remain juicy
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
09:59:40 EEST
15:59:40 KST

How to properly bake in foil so that meat, vegetables, and fish remain juicy
Kyiv • UNN
Foil retains moisture during baking, but it is important to choose the right thickness and wrap the food properly. At the end, unwrap the package to achieve a crust.
Baking in foil helps preserve moisture and flavor in food, and it does not require complicated cookware. However, the result depends on several cooking details. UNN will tell you more about which foil to choose, how to wrap the food, what to put inside, and when to open the package.
Which foil to choose for baking
For the oven, it is better to use foil 11 microns thick. If the product is cooked for a long time or the dish is going to be grilled, it is worth choosing a denser material—14 microns thick. Thinner foil, about 9 microns thick, is more suitable for storing food. At the same time, foil must not be placed in a microwave oven, as it may spark. For cooking, you should also avoid wrapping acidic or very salty foods for a long time, because aluminum can react with such foods, which may affect the taste.
Which side of the foil to place against the food
The shiny and matte surfaces of foil appear due to the specifics of its production. They do not differ in composition, so there is no fundamental difference when baking.
Therefore, when cooking, you can place either side of the foil against the food. It is more important to wrap the product properly so that moisture remains inside.
How to wrap food in foil so that the juices remain inside
For an airtight package, the sheet of foil can be folded in half. The product is placed on one half, and the other half is folded over it without pulling it too tightly. The edges along the longer side should be folded over several times, after which the sides should be sealed in the same way. The result should be a tightly sealed packet that can be gently pressed around the product while leaving enough space inside. By the way, before baking, meat can be made more aromatic by making several shallow cuts in it and adding spices. If vegetables are being cooked together with the meat, it is better to place them on the bottom and put the piece of meat on top.
Which foods are best baked in foil
You can cook meat, poultry, fish, and vegetables in foil. For meat, it is better to choose boneless cuts. River fish can be baked whole. It is advisable to choose vegetables that are approximately the same size. Then they will cook at roughly the same rate, preventing some from remaining raw while others become too soft.
Temperature and cooking method
For meat in foil, it is optimal to set the oven to about 170 °C, for poultry—to 160 °C, and for fish—to approximately 145 °C. Foil helps retain moisture, so the food dries out less. When cooking over an open fire, it is worth waiting until the heat subsides slightly. This will reduce the risk of burning. If you want to achieve a browned crust, carefully unfold the foil at the end of cooking and leave the dish in the oven for another 5-10 minutes.
How to check whether food in foil is done
Doneness depends on the product. For example, potatoes can be checked with a knife or wooden skewer, while for meat, one indication may be the darkening of the package seams and the appearance of the characteristic smell of a cooked dish. For poultry, fish, and bryndza, however, the foil puffing up may be a sign that they are done.
Top-5 ideas for a quick dinner when there's no time to cook25.04.26, 20:58 • 76366 views

Our commitment to building an organisation where everyone is safe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
06:58:04 UTC
15:58:04 KST

Over the past eight  years, Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) has published annual figures on reports of abuse and misconduct in our organisation. The latest figures tell an important but difficult story. As in previous years, the number of complaints has continued to increase. This may mean people are more aware of our reporting systems, and feel more confident coming forward, but it also makes clear the scale of the work still ahead to prevent and address abuse in our organisation.
Among the most serious cases we confronted last year were those in eastern Chad. Investigations we completed in June 2025, following alerts reported in the media, found serious abuse and misconduct involving people working for MSF, including sexual exploitation, abuse, and harassment.
Our review involved 16 investigators working over eight months to examine 59 allegations concerning employees and others, such as suppliers, who were connected to MSF. Where we were able to establish serious misconduct and identify those responsible, action was taken. Eighteen staff were dismissed and permanently barred from working with MSF. 
Most importantly, I want to acknowledge the harm caused to the patients and colleagues who were abused. As International President of MSF, I feel a profound sense of responsibility and regret that we failed to keep people safe. Sexual exploitation, abuse and harassment are completely incompatible with MSF’s principles, values and safeguarding commitments. When they occur, they represent a profound abuse of trust and can have devastating consequences for survivors, communities and our colleagues.
Most importantly, I want to acknowledge the harm caused to the patients and colleagues who were abused.
As someone of Sudanese heritage, with family members who fled the war in Sudan, what happened in eastern Chad also affects me personally. Women who had already survived horrific violence in Sudan and sought safety in Chad had every right to expect dignity, respect and safety from MSF. Female colleagues were also among those affected. This is unacceptable and should never have happened.
Our investigations identified important shortcomings in the safeguarding measures we had in place. As our teams rapidly expanded to respond to hundreds of thousands of people arriving from Sudan, we had not consistently ensured that all staff understood and upheld our behavioural commitments, nor had we systematically assessed and mitigated safeguarding risks. We should have done more to ensure that patients, community members and staff knew how to report abuse safely and confidentially.
We must also acknowledge that the support we provided to the survivors we were able to identify was limited, beyond medical and psychological support.
Considerable barriers can prevent survivors from accessing support, inside and outside MSF, and these can be even more acute in the places where we work. Survivors may face significant stigma and consequences for coming forward; appropriate survivor-centred services may be limited, difficult to access, or not widely known or trusted; and women in particular may face practical constraints, including caring responsibilities, that make it difficult to seek or receive support. This makes prevention work and actively trying to detect abuse cases before harm is caused, even more important.
Despite these challenges, greater efforts were needed to proactively engage with survivors, understand their individual needs and preferences, and identify appropriate forms of assistance, including support beyond that which MSF could directly provide.
The findings have led us to make important changes in eastern Chad. We have strengthened recruitment, induction and training processes, carried out risk assessments across our programmes, put in place measures to mitigate identified risks, and increased the safeguarding support available to our teams so they can identify and respond to risks earlier. We have also worked with patients, women’s groups and community leaders to build awareness of what constitutes abuse and ensure people know how to report concerns.
Beyond eastern Chad, over the past year, we have strengthened our global screening processes to prevent people found to have committed abuse or serious misconduct from moving between MSF projects and being rehired elsewhere in the organisation. We are also working to improve the package of support we can provide to survivors. You can read more about the events in eastern Chad and our response in our dedicated explainer on investigating abuse and strengthening prevention in eastern Chad, which you can access here.
What happened in eastern Chad also reflects broader inequalities and power imbalances that we have a responsibility to confront within MSF. Women face a higher risk of abuse, particularly sexual abuse, while conflict, displacement, deprivation and dependence on humanitarian assistance can create significant imbalances of power that can further amplify risks of abuse. These circumstances make it even more important for us to ensure the safeguards we have in place, across all our projects, are as strong as possible.
These circumstances make it even more important for us to ensure the safeguards we have in place, across all our projects, are as strong as possible.
We are not starting this work from scratch. Years of efforts by teams across MSF have strengthened how we prevent, detect, and respond to abuse. However, what happened in eastern Chad shows that significant gaps remain. We need to make faster and more substantial progress.
As a doctor, I recognise that creating safe environments for patients, communities and colleagues is fundamental to who we are as a medical humanitarian organisation and to our medical and ethical commitment to do no harm. I take that responsibility extremely seriously.
Every MSF project and office must be a place where people feel safe, respected and protected; where abuse is not tolerated; where people are always encouraged and supported to report unacceptable behaviour; and where the voices and experiences of those who are most affected help shape how we prevent and respond to abuse. Continuing to strengthen this urgent work demands attention, accountability and action from every MSF colleague, every single day.

Brussels appoints a ‘Gold Commander’ to coordinate fight against drug-related violence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
06:55:41 UTC
15:55:41 KST

A ‘Gold Commander’ is to be appointed in Brussels with immediate effect to coordinate the six police districts of the Brussels capital region, the mayors of Brussels have decided. Michel Goovaerts, Chief Constable of the Brussels-Capital Elsene police district, will take on this role. At the same time, interior minister Bernard Quintin (Francophone liberal MR) is deploying 50 additional police officers.
Brussels appoints ‘Gold Commander’ to coordinate fight against drug-related violence
In addition to the appointment of a ‘Gold Commander’, the police presence in the most troubled neighbourhoods of the capital is being stepped up, particularly in the evenings and at night. Detectives are also being given the necessary resources to investigate the violence and dismantle criminal networks.
“The violence is linked to conflicts between criminal networks involved in drug trafficking. This is unacceptable and calls for an immediate and visible response on the ground,” says Brussels Mayor Philippe Close.
Unified command
Various police services, such as the K9 units (dog teams), the special units and the rapid response units, will henceforth operate under the unified command structure. “The aim is clear: to make better use of these resources, particularly in the evenings and at night,” says Close.
By October, all dispatching activity for the Brussels police zones is to be brought under one roof, that of the regional security body Safe.brussels. In addition, the ARGOS service, which is responsible for analysing CCTV footage and number plate recognition, will also be strengthened.
‘Gold Commanders’ have earlier been deployed on New Year’s Eve and other occasions. Brussels is usually turbulent on that night, a unified command is established to ensure the festivities run smoothly.
Michel Goovaerts, Chief of Police for the Brussels-Capital Elsene police zone, took on that role during previous New Year’s Eves. He will do so again now. For the time being, he believes it is still too early to comment, he told VRT NEWS.
Interior minister Bernard Quintin has also announced additional resources to tackle drug-related violence in the capital. He is deploying 50 extra federal police officers, and the Special Units Directorate (DSU) is also being reinforced with special police support teams. The federal judicial police in Brussels are also set to receive permanent reinforcements.
Quintin has described the situation as a “national emergency” and wants the issue to be placed on the agenda of the National Security Council.
“The fact that a police station has come under fire shows just how serious the situation is. This new dimension of violence, involving military grade weapons of war, requires us to deploy all necessary resources. The fight against organised crime is a shared responsibility and must be an absolute priority,” said the minister.
“To guarantee the safety of our citizens, extra effort is required. If we do not act jointly and decisively today, we will continue to lag behind events. That is why we are significantly stepping up the federal presence on the ground, because if Anderlecht loses, Brussels loses. And if Brussels loses, the whole of Belgium loses.”
Deployment of military personnel and registration of e-scooters
In addition, the minister proposes that work continue at federal level on a number of specific measures. These include creating more places in secure centres for undocumented migrants, the compulsory registration of e-scooters, sufficient detention capacity, a firm approach to illegal residence and return, sufficient places in secure youth detention centres, and the expansion of the deployment of military personnel.
Since April this year, 45 military personnel have been patrolling alongside police officers at metro and train stations in Brussels.
However, Quintin believes that local authorities must also strengthen their approach to organised crime. He refers, for example, to administrative enforcement measures such as bans on assembly or entry to certain areas.
In this way, mayors can also take further action against rogue businesses linked to organised crime. Quintin also calls for local and regional authorities to better coordinate their efforts, with direct coordination between the various operations and services at the level of the Brussels Region.
Finally, according to the minister, a permanent command centre must be established to enable the monitoring of incidents linked to drug-related violence and organised crime 24 hours a day and to respond swiftly.

Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, accused of masterminding the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks in the US, and three alleged co-defendants will stand trial beginning June 5, 2028, according to media reports on Wednesday.
US military judge Lt. Col. Michael Schrama rejected prosecutors’ request to begin proceedings in 2027, Fox News reported.
Schrama ruled that the prosecution’s proposed Jan. 11, 2027, trial date did not allow sufficient time to resolve pending pretrial matters.
“A realistic trial date must account for the hearing and resolution of pretrial evidentiary and compliance motions,” Fox News quoted Schrama as saying.
Mohammed and the three co-defendants have been held at Guantanamo Bay since 2003 in connection with the attacks that killed nearly 3,000 people.
Under the scheduling order, jury selection will begin June 5, 2028, with opening statements set to start 30 days after the military commission members are empaneled.
The order also establishes deadlines for the presentation of evidence, defense motions, rebuttal proceedings and closing arguments.
The ruling follows years of legal disputes, including a failed effort to resolve the case through plea agreements.
In 2025, a federal appeals court ruled that then-Defense Secretary Lloyd Austin had the authority to withdraw plea agreements that would have allowed Mohammed and two co-defendants to plead guilty in exchange for life sentences without parole.
“Having properly assumed the convening authority, the Secretary determined that the families and the American public deserve the opportunity to see military commission trials carried out,” Judges Patricia Millett and Neomi Rao wrote in the majority opinion.
Mohammed, a US-educated engineer, is accused of masterminding the Sept. 11 plot in which hijacked commercial airliners struck the World Trade Center and the Pentagon, killing nearly 3,000 people.

Feature: Modern tech gives voice to Chinese wine over 2,000 years old
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
14:41:13 CST
15:41:13 KST

A researcher observes a bronze ware specimen via a microscope at the Ningxia Institute of Cultural Relics and Archaeology in Yinchuan, northwest China's Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region, Aug. 10, 2026. (Xinhua/Yang Zhisen)
YINCHUAN, Aug. 27 (Xinhua) -- What did ancient people seal in a bronze pot 2,000 years ago? Chinese archaeologists and scientists have jointly confirmed the liquid residue as grain wine of millet and barley from the Warring States Period (475 BC-221 BC), uncovering the mystery quest via cutting-edge technologies.
A well-preserved bronze garlic-head-shaped pot with liquid preserved caught archaeologists' attention. It was unearthed from a tomb at the Shanjiabu cemetery of the Qin State of the Warring States Period in the city of Guyuan, northwest China's Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region.
The cemetery is located near the Great Wall built by the Qin State during the Warring States Period, with 183 tombs excavated as of 2024.
Though it lacked a cap, the pot's interior was sealed with textile fabric, and its exterior was coated in a layer of mud blended with organic matter--an ancient double seal that somehow kept a large volume of liquid intact for more than two thousand years.
Using sterile scalpels and tweezers, archaeologists carefully peeled away these seals, collecting roughly 3,740 milliliters of clear, pale bluish-green, odorless liquid and a minor amount of sediment.
The bronze garlic-head pot is a type of representative artifact of Qin culture, normally regarded as a wine vessel. As this pot was placed as a funerary object inside the tomb chamber, archaeologists preliminarily speculated that the liquid might be Qin wine from around two thousand years ago. However, they could not draw a conclusion without scientific testing.
To reach a more accurate conclusion, the Ningxia Institute of Cultural Relics and Archaeology and the School of Cultural Heritage at Northwest University jointly conducted a multidisciplinary analysis of the ancient liquid in the bronze pot.
Wen Rui, a professor at the School of Cultural Heritage at Northwest University, led a study team to analyze the liquid using infrared spectroscopy, ultra-high-performance liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry, and other high-precision testing techniques, along with microfossil analysis.
The results showed that more than 2,000 small-molecule compounds were detected in the ancient liquid, belonging to 24 compound categories, including organic acids and their derivatives, amino acids and their derivatives, and carbohydrates.
Notably, the distribution pattern of organic acids matched artificially aged yellow rice wine, a typical beverage of east China, confirming the liquid as grain wine.
Researchers also detected large quantities of starch grains from wheat and barley in the unearthed samples, as well as large quantities of yeast and some phytoliths from the wheat tribe, indicating that the ancient wine's brewing raw materials were wheat and barley.
The discovery provides physical evidence of the sophistication of ancient Chinese grain fermentation and offers valuable clues for studying agriculture, food culture and craftsmanship during the pre-Qin period, which refers to the period before the Qin Dynasty (221 BC-207 BC) was established.
Rather than relying on general historical texts or documents, this archaeological study provides strong evidence of Qin brewing practices, revealing practical fermentation skills, varied grain use, and sealing methods.
The scientific analysis provides key evidence and new perspectives for research on brewing practices in the late Warring States period, enriching understanding of traditional Chinese brewing craftsmanship.
This multi-dimensional, collaborative archaeological analysis has clearly reconstructed the picture of brewing during the Warring States period. It not only corroborates China's long-standing grain-based brewing civilization, but also provides new, authoritative physical evidence for studying pre-Qin agricultural development, ancient dietary culture and the evolution of craft techniques, according to the study team.
In fact, the discovery is also part of new explorations in the archaeological sector, giving voice to "silent" unearthed discoveries through modern technologies.
"Ever since the founding of modern archaeology, there is a lasting principle -- to maximize extraction of buried data in archaeological sites," said Li Yulong, deputy director of the Ningxia Institute of Cultural Relics and Archaeology.
"Our tools in hand have evolved dramatically -- ranging from tape measures, steel rulers and pencils to nowadays' drone filming, RTK (real-time kinematic) surveying, total station mapping and laptops," Li added.
As for the newly confirmed grain wine of millet and barley from the Warring States Period, he noted that, before scientific testing, experts could only speculate it was wine, which could invite skepticism that it might be water or something else. Now modern technologies not only confirmed that it's wine, but what's in it and how it was made. "The data is richer and more accurate," Li said.
This transformation stems from the country's steady support for the archaeological science sector, a broad field covering chronology, environmental archaeology, human-bone archaeology, animal archaeology, isotope analysis, ceramics, metallurgy, and more.
"Today, the collaboration of archaeologists and scientific researchers is a popular practice in the sector of archaeological science, enabling 'silent' cultural relics to 'speak,' thus continuously cracking long-standing puzzles and curiosity for archaeologists and the public," said Zhang Hongying, deputy director of the Ningxia Institute of Cultural Relics and Archaeology. ■
This photo taken on Aug. 5, 2026 shows a bronze garlic-head-shaped pot in Guyuan, northwest China's Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region. (Xinhua/Yang Zhisen)
This photo taken on Aug. 10, 2026 shows a liquid sample collected from a bronze pot at the Ningxia Institute of Cultural Relics and Archaeology in Yinchuan, northwest China's Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region. (Xinhua/Yang Zhisen)

How Moscow Turned AI Into a Ghostwriting Machine for Global Influence
Unknown

- Category
- World
How Moscow Turned AI Into a Ghostwriting Machine for Global Influence
OpenAI has identified and banned a series of ChatGPT accounts linked to Russia that were secretly used to push Kremlin talking points and create the illusion of an independent research community.
Accessing the system through virtual private networks to circumvent geographic restrictions, the operators directed artificial intelligence to write posts and comments in English while explicitly instructing the models to conceal any Russian origin.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The operation centered around a fake entity registered in February 2025 called the International Policy Institute, which claimed to be an Israel-based think tank.
A review of 36 articles published on the institute site between September 2025 and May 2026 revealed that 34 were stolen from online sources.
The covert network generated tailored social media and messenger content across multiple platforms, including X, LinkedIn, Facebook, and Telegram.
Beyond promoting fake think tank materials, the operators produced German-language posts attacking Ukraine, the European Union, and the German government, while advocating for closer ties with Moscow.
The artificial intelligence tool was also deployed to craft logos for roughly a dozen Telegram channels targeting audiences in Germany, the United States, France, Poland, and Turkey, with specific channels amassing between 10,000 and 20,000 subscribers.
A key feature of the effort was a self-styled sovereignty index created to portray Russia favorably while disparaging countries opposing Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
While OpenAI assessed the immediate reach of the posts as low, researchers emphasized that the main risk lay in establishing infrastructure for future foreign influence, expanding on earlier Russian plans targeting African elections in countries like Burundi, Cameroon, and Madagascar with budgets reaching $600,000 annually.
Russian-linked influence operations targeting Western audiences have intensified in recent weeks. On the same day, it was reported about a Russian-linked network that circulated at least 20 fabricated video clips pushing narratives about a possible future war between Armenia and Russia.
The identical campaign reportedly involved fabricated covers attributed to French outlets such as Libération and Ouest-France, along with AI-generated clips featuring actors from the US television series The Office.

SAN FRANCISCO, Aug. 26 (Xinhua) -- Four people were killed after a small plane crashed into waters near the coastal town of Seldovia in the U.S. state of Alaska on Wednesday, the Alaska Department of Public Safety said.
Alaska State Troopers were notified of the crash at about 1:18 p.m. local time (2118 GMT), according to the department. The Piper PA-24 aircraft was flying from Anchorage to Seldovia when it crashed into the water and became fully submerged.
Troopers dispatched a helicopter crew from Anchorage and sent personnel by boat from Anchor Point to reach the crash site. After the tide receded, troopers recovered the bodies of four adults from the aircraft.
The bodies were transported to the State Medical Examiner's Office for autopsies. The victims' names will be released after their next of kin have been notified.
The cause of the crash remains undetermined. The National Transportation Safety Board is investigating the accident. ■

Australian spy agency gains extended power to secretly question people
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
06:40:00 UTC
15:40:00 KST

Why some of ASIO's most controversial powers have been expanded
It takes a certain kind of issue to unite the parliament's most conservative members with its most progressive members.
But that was what occurred last week, as figures like Liberal Senator Alex Antic and One Nation's Malcolm Roberts sat down with the Greens in the Senate to vote against prolonged powers for Australia's domestic spy agency.
The bill extended a contentious remit held by ASIO for more than two decades that essentially allows it, in certain circumstances, to force people to answer questions.
It was an idea introduced in the wake of the 2001 September 11 attacks, and the 2002 Bali bombing, to bolster ASIO's counter-terror tools.
They have been used sparingly since then — just 20 times in more than 20 years — but have been regularly extended, and even expanded since then.
Legislation that went before the Senate last week wound up passing with the broad support of both Labor and the Coalition.
But it was furiously opposed by some of the most progressive and conservative voices in federal parliament, including Senator Antic, a far-right figure who crossed the floor against his colleagues.
"In a free society, the state shouldn't be handed an open-ended power to compel citizens to answer questions about speech or association that falls short of actual criminality," he said.
It was a speech immediately followed by Greens Senator David Shoebridge, who had a similar message.
"If this legislation gets through, Australians will have a right to fear their own government — because whenever the government chooses to, it can pluck you off the street," he said.
A contentious power
ASIO itself describes its compulsory questioning tool as "unique and critical".
In effect, it allows the domestic spy agency to ask the attorney-general to agree to issue a warrant to require anyone over 14 years old to answer ASIO's questions.
The questioning itself is different to an ordinary police interview, and is supposed to be used as something of a last resort.
While a person is compelled to answer questions put to them by an ASIO agent, the answers cannot then be used as evidence against them.
It also has to take place with a very senior legal officer in the room, like a former judge or an experienced King's Counsel. Those being questioned can have a lawyer present, but there are limitations on when a lawyer can intervene during questioning.
Crucially, those questioned cannot tell anyone that the questioning took place.
ASIO says it has never sought a warrant for a person under 18, but has argued it needs to keep the power in place due to increasing concerns about radicalisation among minors.
It is a shift from a position the agency held a few years ago, when it argued its power to compulsorily question minors should be cancelled.
In a submission to a parliamentary inquiry into the bill, the agency said its limited use of the powers should be seen as evidence of its responsibility in using them.
"The sparing use of ASIO's compulsory questioning powers does not indicate a lack of utility, but rather that these are specific, carefully targeted powers, and that ASIO only uses them when less intrusive methods have been exhausted or would have been ineffective," a spokesperson said.
Sunset clause brought back
The legislation that passed parliament last week was actually somewhat weaker than what was originally proposed.
When the bill was first put to parliament, it included the removal of a 'sunset' clause.
The sunset clause had been included in the laws since they were first introduced — meaning they automatically expire every few years, and had to go back to parliament to be extended.
ASIO had argued that given they had been in place for more than two decades, and had been only infrequently used during that time, the parliament should feel comfortable making them permanent.
Parliament's powerful joint committee on intelligence and security, made up of Labor and Coalition MPs, agreed, but it was a step too far for some of the Coalition's most conservative and progressive MP's.
Conservative South Australian Liberal Senator Leah Blyth successfully argued in the partyroom that the sunset was an important check on the extraordinary powers and needed to stay.
Labor eventually agreed to the change, and added an amendment to the bill in the Senate that would see the powers return to parliament in three years' time.
But the changes were not enough for everyone in the Coalition.
The bill had the unusual effect of uniting the Liberal Party's most conservative senator, Alex Antic, with one of the party's most progressive figures, Andrew McLachlan.
Both voted against the bill when it came to a final vote, despite moves to accommodate them.
Many of those who opposed the bill this time supported relatively similar legislation the last time it came before the Senate in 2020 — including Malcolm Roberts, Alex Antic and Andrew McLachlan.
Broadening the scope of powers
Chris Taylor, an intelligence expert with the Australian Strategic Policy Institute, argued keeping the sunset clause was the wrong call.
"I was really disappointed. These are de facto permanent powers; they have been continually kicked down the road by the parliament since 2003," he said.
"Everyone pretends they're not permanent — they are, and the legislation should reflect that."
The bill that passed parliament last week contains more than just an extension of existing powers.
There is also a change to the grounds on which someone can be questioned, to try and reflect the evolving threats ASIO argues that Australia faces.
Before 2020, ASIO could only bring people in for questioning in relation to terrorism. That year, the powers were broadened to include espionage and foreign interference, responding to escalating concerns in those areas.
As of last week, the powers have been broadened again to reflect ASIO's broad definition of security — including politically motivated violence, sabotage and "promotion of communal violence".
Those changes do not appear to impact minors, who can only be questioned on "politically motivated violence".
In his annual threat assessment earlier this year, ASIO director-general Mike Burgess sought to outline how the ideologies motivating potential terror attacks are becoming less rigid, and harder to identify and counter.
"Instead of embracing fixed ideologies, radicalised individuals are increasingly embracing mixed ideologies," he said.
"Instead of being radicalised by associates in the real world, individuals are often being radicalised by strangers online.
"And, instead of spending time and resources planning sophisticated attacks, radicalised individuals are moving to low-capability attacks with little or no warning.
"These dynamics make the contemporary terrorism environment different — and in some ways, more difficult — than we saw with Al Qaeda and ISIL."
He pointed to real-world examples, like the Bondi terror attack and the attempted bombing of an Indigenous rally in Perth within just a few weeks, as illustrative of the varied ideologies motivating terror attacks.
Mr Taylor said changing those elements of the questioning powers makes sense.
"I think it's a reflection of the increasing level of security threat to Australian interests, including a real upsurge in phenomena like sabotage across the world," he said.
During debate in parliament, Greens senators raised concerns that the broader scope of the questioning powers could be used to target those involved in pro-Palestine rallies.
Greens Senator David Shoebridge said the expansion in ASIO's powers goes too far.
"People are deeply angered that ASIO has yet more scope to pluck you off the street, secretly detain you, question you for 24 hours, kick out your lawyer and then put a blanket of secrecy over it," he said.
"That's not how our government is meant to operate."

Ghent University has imposed a three-month mandatory remote working order on controversial American researcher Nathan Cofnas. During this period, he is not permitted to carry out any teaching activities. The university announced this on its website. Earlier today, Ghent university rector Petra De Sutter, the university's head, defended her university’s approach to the Cofnas case following international criticism.
Ghent University imposes 3-month mandatory home-working on US researcher Nathan Cofnas, removes his teaching duties
The new measure follows Nathan Cofnas’s preventive suspension on 20 August. The suspension is reportedly now over, but it appears he cannot return to the university for the time being.
Ghent University has ordered Cofnas to work from home for three months and he is not permitted to carry out any teaching activities during this period. According to the university, all research activities carried out by Cofnas as part of his appointment at Ghent University must “remain strictly limited to the research topics for which he was appointed”, a notice on the university website states.
Ghent University has been asked to clarify the measure, but VRT News has not yet received a response.
What is at issue?
The controversial Ghent University researcher Nathan Cofnas – an American who describes himself as a ‘racial realist’ – was suspended by his university as a precautionary measure on 20 August. A preliminary disciplinary investigation was also launched.
The trigger was the death of former Cambridge professor Jason Arday. In an online article Cofnas had accused the academic of plagiarism, after which the British press pounced on the story. In England, Cambridge University launched an investigation into Arday, and Arday himself resigned. Not long afterwards, he was found dead.
Cofnas takes to X
Cofnas broke the news of his suspension via X. In that post, he suggested that the decision might have been politically motivated, as it had been taken by Rector De Sutter, “a former leading figure in the Flemish green party Groen”. “They will almost certainly sack me,” he concluded.
The university explicitly refers to this as a disciplinary measure within an ongoing staff case. Meanwhile, the preliminary disciplinary investigation against Cofnas is continuing. This should determine whether there is sufficient evidence to take further disciplinary action.
Academics back Cofnas, Rector De Sutter responds
Earlier, some 800 academics signed an open letter in which they described Ghent University’s disciplinary proceedings against Cofnas as retaliation. In the letter, the signatories ask Ghent University to protect Cofnas and not to impose any sanctions. They describe his statements as an exercise of academic freedom.
Ghent University Rector Petra De Sutter says that the university does not curtail academic freedom and, in fact, considers it to be of the utmost importance. She further states that too many people with insufficient knowledge of the matter are commenting on the disciplinary case.
Ghent University does not wish to comment further on the controversy surrounding the case. According to the university, preliminary disciplinary investigations must be able to be conducted “in complete serenity, independence and with respect for the rights of all those involved”.
“It would be inconsistent to, on the one hand, guarantee the confidentiality of the proceedings and, on the other, to prejudge the arguments or the possible outcome through the media. All parties involved will be given the opportunity, within the established procedures, to set out their position and defend themselves,” says Ghent University.
Inquiry into Arday’s death
The inquest into the death of Jason Arday has also begun in London, England. Chief Coroner Julian Morris told the British media that “the various reports suggest that Professor Arday died an unnatural death.”

Tackling institutional discrimination and racism within MSF
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
06:36:13 UTC
15:36:13 KST

In July 2020, the international leadership of Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) made a public commitment to tackle discrimination and racism within our organisation. The Core Executive Committee (Core ExCom) pledged to “lead the way for the radical action sought after and demanded by our associations.” This commitment came amid powerful global movements for racial equity and health equity, spurred in part by the impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic. It also followed years of advocacy by MSF staff calling for change.
In 2020, the Core ExCom (see glossary at bottom) defined an action plan, identifying seven priority or key areas as requiring urgent and concrete action:
1: Management of abuse and inappropriate behaviour
2: Staff reward, including remuneration and benefits
3: Exposure to risk – safety and security  
4: People recruitment and development  
5: Communications and fundraising
6: Standards of care for the patients and communities with whom we work
7: Executive governance and representation
In mid-2024, we provided an update on progress for the previous 18 months, up until December 2023. Six years on from the Core ExCom’s initial commitment, and two years since the last update, we are outlining our progress on these seven areas over 2024 and 2025.
We are publicly publishing our progress, as we want staff, patients, communities, donors, stakeholders, and the public at large to see where we stand on each of these areas, including areas where we are struggling to move forward. Doing so is the best way to be transparent and demonstrate accountability for our actions. We have taken stock of what we managed to achieve in the two years to the end of 2025, and acknowledge that there is work ahead of us to continue addressing inequities in our organisation.
We recognise that the progress we have made does not meet the expectations of our colleagues who continue to face racism and institutional discrimination within our organisation. We are committed to continuing this work because doing so will make meaningful differences for our colleagues, patients, and the communities we serve.
While we worked on all of the above seven areas, the Core ExCom prioritised tackling issues of abuse and inappropriate behaviour and addressing inequities in our staff rewards and remuneration system.
The update below is, however, not an exhaustive list of all initiatives to tackle discrimination and racism in MSF, but a summary of some of the main movement-wide progress made since the launch of the Action Plan, based on priorities agreed by MSF’s Executive Committee (ExCom). There are many other initiatives being carried out in our projects and headquarter offices that are not covered in this update. For transparency purposes, we have retained the update we provided in February 2022, for the progress made during 2020 and 2021, and the update in mid-2024 for the progress during 2022 and 2023, which can be found underneath this current update.
To provide clarity and aid understanding of MSF’s decision-making and leadership platforms, we have included a short glossary of terms within MSF referred to in this document, at the bottom of this page.
2024 and 2025 updates
1: Management of abuse and inappropriate behaviour
2: Staff reward, including remuneration and benefits
3: Exposure to risk – safety and security
4: People recruitment and development
5: Communications and fundraising
6: Standards of care for the patients and communities with whom we work
7: Executive governance and representation
Conclusion: We’re making steady progress, with more to do
The Core ExCom’s action plan has ultimately aimed to change our culture, governance, and the way we work. We have made significant progress in some areas over the last six years, but we acknowledge that progress in other areas has not been as advanced as we would have liked. But work on addressing the inequities in our organisation nonetheless continues, from the broad, organisation level, through our different headquarter offices, even down to individual initiatives and projects. This is because we are committed to making a real difference to our staff, patients, and communities, and fighting against racism and discrimination. We also continue to hold to our principles of being transparent and accountable.
This update is the last under the structure of the Core ExCom’s action plan to Tackle Institutional Discrimination and Racism, initiated in 2020. Most of this work is being transitioned to a new framework, covering the entire movement. In the years since the plan was started, two initiatives have taken place that are realigning how the movement works. The first initiative was a discussion series MSF undertook, called the MSF We Want to Be (WWTB). Taking place between 2021 and 2024, and drawing on the categories of the Core ExCom’s action plan, it became the most inclusive, representative, and widely attended forum that MSF has organised since our inception.
The aim of this process was to consult MSF staff and association members on the perceived state of key aspects of MSF’s social mission, and the improvements they would like to see in the coming years. The final outputs of this process, alongside the value gained from undertaking the process itself, are movement-wide strategic commitments.
The second one is SPARC, the Strategic Planning, Accountability and Resource Cycle. SPARC is a multi-year strategic and resource allocation framework that guides MSF’s shared objectives from 2026 to 2031. It represents the first collective effort to align movement-wide strategic priorities with resource planning.
The collective commitments made by the MSF WWTB have been translated into joint priorities, and are reflected in SPARC and in individual entity strategic plans. MSF now has some core movement-wide strategic priorities, joint political commitment, and the ability to advance movement accountability on strategic choices. 
SPARC ensures that our commitments to the social mission are adequately resourced, and that we hold ourselves accountable for delivering on these goals. Five of the seven pillars1 of the Core ExCom’s plan are aligned with areas of focus within SPARC, therefore the plan’s outstanding objectives are being integrated into SPARC action plans, to be owned by all at MSF. 
Accountability is a key part of SPARC. Dedicated working groups responsible for Common Strategic Priorities within SPARC are each currently developing specific indicator sets for annual reporting, as is outlined in the overarching SPARC agreement. The first annual report on progress is expected in 2027, and reporting will evolve over the SPARC period; the scope of any public reports is yet to be defined.
As this work moves to a new framework our commitment remains clear: to keep challenging racism and discrimination in all its forms and to keep working towards a more equitable MSF.

OpenAI says it detected malign activity months before Hugging Face attack
