Explainer: What drives Colombia's interest in restoring ties with Israel?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
03:03:54 UTC
12:03:54 KST

Within days of taking office, Colombia's new president has fast-tracked efforts to restore the South American nation's ties with Israel, reversing predecessor Gustavo Petro's strong stance on the genocide in Gaza.
President Abelardo de la Espriella defeated left-wing candidate Ivan Cepeda by less than one percentage point in the runoff vote in June. He took office on August 7.
Within days, de la Espriella fulfilled a campaign pledge, announcing in a video message that Colombia would reopen its embassy in Jerusalem.
He also froze a separate plan, announced by Petro in October 2023, to open a Colombian Embassy in Palestine, saying the office had never become operational.
From Jerusalem embassy to Golan recognition
Under de la Espriella, Colombia formally recognised Israeli sovereignty over the occupied Golan Heights in Syria.
This made Colombia the second country after the US to recognise Israeli sovereignty over the occupied rocky plateau in southwestern Syria overlooking northern Israel.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu welcomed the move in a video statement, thanking de la Espriella.
Furthermore, both nations agreed to implement a mutual visa exemption for their citizens effective September 1.
The two governments also launched the Colombia-Israel Binational Economic Commission.
Additionally, Bogota moved to resume coal exports to Israel that Petro had halted.
De la Espriella's government has also begun withdrawing Colombia's earlier intervention in South Africa's case in the International Court of Justice linked to Israel's genocide in Gaza.
Understanding the shift
Arlene Beth Tickner, a former Colombian UN representative and ambassador-at-large, said the turnaround has little to do with Israel itself.
"I think the main purpose ... is to demonstrate loyalty and proximity to the government of the United States," she told Anadolu Agency.
Glaeldys Gonzalez, a Colombia expert at the International Crisis Group, told Anadolu Agency that framing the shift as a "U-turn" somewhat overstates the change.
Colombia spent two decades before 2024 as one of Israel's closest allies in the region, its second-largest partner in Latin America after Brazil and a longtime buyer of Israeli weapons, before Petro severed ties over Gaza and ended defence contracts, she said.
Gonzalez said the Golan recognition reflects Bogota's broader alignment with Washington's foreign policy.
Gonzalez said Israel "is a central diplomatic priority for Colombia's new government, extending beyond the restoration of bilateral ties."
Mariano Aguirre Ernst, associate fellow at Chatham House, agreed that the pace of the decision signals alignment with the Trump administration while also sending a message to Colombia's conservative political establishment, private sector and military.
What’s in it for Israel?
For Israel, the experts said, the payoff is as much about legitimacy as it is about economics.
Daniel Wajner, an associate professor at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, said being recognised by another country carries practical rather than purely symbolic weight.
He said Colombia was again seeking closeness to Washington, much as it did in the 2000s under former President Alvaro Uribe, with Tel Aviv serving as a "bridge" toward that goal.
Israel, he added, has its own domestic interest in such gestures ahead of elections, using them to show its public that the government is "managing to have good relations with the world" despite facing criticism, boycotts and sanctions over its genocide.
Tickner offered a similar reading of Israel's motives, saying these ties are "important for counteracting the reputational damage that's being caused by its own actions in Gaza and in the occupied territories."
She said she was surprised by how strong Colombian public outrage over the decision had been.
Calling the Golan recognition and the Jerusalem embassy plan an "open disavowal" of international law, UN Security Council resolutions and the UN Charter, she said the move would cause "tremendous damage for Colombia and Colombian interests" rather than the reputational gains de la Espriella may be seeking.

Yayoi Kusama, Japanese artist who turned hallucinations into art, dies at 97
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
03:01:17 UTC
12:01:17 KST

Yayoi Kusama, Japanese artist who turned hallucinations into art, dies at 97
Japanese avant-garde artist Yayoi Kusama, who transformed hallucinations into art and was known for her obsessive dot-covered paintings and pumpkin motifs, has died at the age of 97.
The announcement, made on her official website, said she died on August 14 but did not give a cause of death.
"She continued to paint until her final days, never setting aside her brush, and continued exploration of forever love and eternal soul," the statement, attributed to her studio, read.
"We will carry forward Kusama's wishes and, through art, continue to bring hope and strength for the future to people around the world."
In 2024, the National Gallery of Victoria in Melbourne hosted an immersive retrospective of Kusama's work, including almost 200 works including the greatest number of "infinity rooms" ever included in one exhibition.
These "infinity rooms" — rooms made up of mirrors that would project a pattern or image seemingly endlessly — had been part of Kusama's practice since 1965, and became one of the things she was most known for.
By April 2025, the exhibition, titled simply Yayoi Kusama, had become the most visited in Australian history, with more than 500,000 people attending.
One of those infinity rooms, titled The Spirits of the Pumpkins Descended into the Heavens, is part of the collection of the National Gallery of Australia in Canberra, where it was first exhibited in 2018.
Today, one of Kusama's sculptures, titled Flowers that Bloom in the Cosmos, can be seen outside the Art Gallery of New South Wales in Sydney, in front of the Naala Badu building, which opened in 2022.
A life of obsession
Kusama was born in Matsumoto City, Japan in 1929.
She began drawing and painting when she was just a child, afflicted by visual and auditory hallucinations, anxiety and periods of disassociation, including having flowers speak to her.
Frustrated with the confining nature of Japanese society, and dreaming of becoming a professional artist, Kusama left for New York at 27, where she quickly made a name for herself with her paintings, despite initially speaking very little English.
By 1962, she was exhibiting in group shows alongside the likes of Andy Warhol, James Rosenquist and Claes Oldenburg.
A year later, she unveiled her first room-sized installation, Aggregation: One Thousand Boats Show.
That installation included phallic soft sculptures, which Kusama dubbed Accumulations and had started making in 1961. The sculptures would overtake the room, covering furniture and other objects.
In her 2002 memoir, Infinity Net, Kusama described creating these sculptures as a way of "conquering the fear" of sex she had harboured since she was young.
Kusama also took part in anti-war activities during the 1960s, in so-called "Kusama Happenings". Drawing on anti-war sentiment as well as the hippie movement, she would make experimental movies and stage orgies and public performances, all with her trademark dots.
In 1966, Kusama created an installation at the Venice Biennale, despite not being invited. Titled Narcissus Garden, it featured 1,500 gleaming mirrored balls in front of the Italian Pavilion, with a sign that read: "Your narcissium for sale." Dressed in a gold kimono with a silver sash, she would then sell the balls to passers-by, for $2 each.
Almost 30 years later, she would represent Japan at the biennale in 1993, becoming the first solo woman to do so, with one of her distinctive infinity rooms, titled Mirror Room (Pumpkin).
Around 1977, a few years after returning to Japan, Kusama voluntarily entered a mental hospital and lived there for decades, being driven to her nearby studio each morning.
In Infinity Net, Kusama wrote: "I fight pain, anxiety, and fear every day, and the only method I have found that relieves my illness is to keep creating art."
In 2017, she admitted to still seeing hallucinations.
"Dots come flying everywhere — on my dress, the floor, things I'm carrying, throughout the house, the ceiling. And I paint them."
ABC/Wires

WASHINGTON – US allies are privately warning that the Strait of Hormuz is still likely mined, casting doubt on President Donald Trump’s claim that the US Navy has completely removed and detonated explosives laid by Iran.
The US is likely to have made some progress in removing mines in international waters, according to the people, who asked not to be identified discussing internal assessments.
But they believe that de-mining efforts have not cleared all of the estimated 80 to 150 mines laid by Iran.
That assessment challenges Trump’s repeated statements in recent days that the strait has been cleared.
On Aug 25, he called Hormuz “a very functioning strait” and repeated his claim that no mines remained.
“The mines are gone. You probably saw that – we put it out yesterday – all the mines, we got rid of the mines,” he said on The Glenn Beck Programme.
US Central Command (Centcom) on Aug 26 declined to comment on estimates on mines in Hormuz.
Trump has repeatedly insisted the strait is safe, as part of an administration-wide effort to calm energy markets as he looks to end the six-month war heading into midterm elections in November.
Oil prices have eased from their recent peaks but fuel prices have remained stubbornly high.
Fuel cargoes have been sailing through Hormuz relatively less freely than crude, market participants say, adding to a supply crunch triggered by Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian refiners.
Americans are paying more at the pump for petrol than they ever have for this time of the year.
Allied officials believe the strait-clearing effort also has become more complicated because many mines – even those that have been identified and laid in clusters – are likely to have drifted from their original position due to sea currents.
They caution that giving commercial shippers more confidence to transit the strait requires an international effort that combines the use of sophisticated de-mining equipment with air and naval protection.
Allies want Iran to grant Oman permission to launch such a mission in Omani waters to ensure no vessels are attacked.
“It is highly unlikely that all the mines in the strait have been cleared,” said Becca Wasser, Bloomberg Economics defence lead.
“Even if the mine threat was reduced, Iran could still escalate. Numerous commercial vessels are well in range of Iranian drones and short-range missiles – and many are outside the range of US air defence cover.”
Admiral Brad Cooper, the head of Centcom, told Congress in May that US strikes had destroyed more than 90 per cent of Iran’s estimated inventory of around 8,000 mines in storage.
In April, Centcom said two destroyers transited Hormuz “as part of a broader mission to ensure the strait is fully clear of sea mines previously laid by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps”.
Trump’s assertions have run up against more than just scepticism from security partners.
Traffic through the narrow waterway has picked up but remains far from pre-war levels, while the US has sought to help send wary shippers along the Omani side of the strait.
The International Maritime Organisation on Aug 26 repeated warnings “to exercise maximum caution and to avoid exposing seafarers to unnecessary risk when considering transit through the Strait”.
Tehran continues to threaten attacks on those that attempt passage without its permission.
Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi said again late on Aug 25 that only the Islamic Republic knows where mines in Hormuz are located.
He said on state TV that any US de-mining vessels “would be excellent targets for our armed forces”.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and his Omani counterpart Badr Albusaidi have discussed an initiative to establish a “temporary joint maritime corridor” and project for mine clearance, according to a joint statement carried by the Oman News Agency on Aug 25.
Mine-clearing though remains a painstaking and time-consuming process, particularly as Iran has likely laid harder-to-detect Maham mines.
The US Navy is equipped with drones and other autonomous devices for mine detection, but has long been dependent on European allies that have advanced mine-hunting hardware.
The UK and France have been planning for a broader mission to reassure shippers, including de-mining operations, once a ceasefire is agreed and proves sustainable.
US military chiefs plan to meet their European counterparts once a deal is reached to discuss how to coordinate the so-called reassurance mission, instead of through an international conference that the US originally requested, according to people familiar with the matter. BLOOMBERG

COP17: New global architecture for drought resilience launched at UNCCD meet
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
02:59:15 UTC
11:59:15 KST

(Representative image) DR’s technical monitoring metrics will enable countries to assess their capacity to anticipate, prepare for and adapt to drought (Photo: Reuters).
NEW DELHI: Amid reports that three out of four people worldwide could face drought by 2050, the United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification (UNCCD) during its 17th conference (COP17) on Wednesday took a significant step in advancing new global architecture for drought resilience by showcasing the world's first Drought Resilience Index (DRI) and launching the Drought Resilience Investment Facility (DRIF) to help countries strengthen their drought resilience.DR’s technical monitoring metrics will enable countries to assess their capacity to anticipate, prepare for and adapt to drought while identifying vulnerabilities and informing more effective policies and investments. It’s a new AI-powered features that can help policy-makers, technical experts and the public interpret complex data and turn it into practical insights.On the other hand, DRIF - the first global catalytic financing platform dedicated to drought resilience - will use public capital to reduce investment risks and unlock much larger flows of institutional and private finance for projects that strengthen water security, sustainable agriculture, nature-based solutions and land restoration.“COP17 is about turning commitments into implementation. We now have stronger financing mechanisms, better tools and practical guidance to help countries prepare for drought before it becomes a crisis,” said UNCCD executive secretary Yasmine Fouad.
“The task now is to connect these pieces and put them to work at scale, through governments, development partners, financial institutions and the private sector,” she added.
India, represented by a team led by Union environment minister Bhupende Yadav at COP17, too advocated for strengthening drought resilience. Yadav on Tuesday called for a fundamental shift in the global approach to drought from “reactive relief to proactive technology-enabled resilience”.Underlining India’s core belief that “drought must be managed as a predictable, preventable risk, and not a recurring disaster demanding emergency response”, the minister said, “Preparedness over response, prevention over crisis management, resilience over recovery should be the goal.”
Vishwa Mohan is Senior Editor at The Times of India. He writes on environment, climate change, agriculture, water resources and clean energy, tracking policy issues and climate diplomacy. He has been covering Parliament since 2003 to see how politics shaped up domestic policy and India’s position at global platform. Before switching over to explore sustainable development issues, Vishwa had covered internal security and investigative agencies for more than a decade.

Qatar’s prime minister to visit Tehran, seeking to revive US-Iran talks
Sheikh Mohammed’s visit comes as US-Israel war on Iran nears its sixth month with no diplomatic breakthrough in sight.
Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani is due to visit Tehran on Thursday for talks on de-escalating tensions and reviving dialogue between Iran and the United States.
A spokesman for Qatar’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs announced the visit in a statement on X on Wednesday.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Iran bets economic pain will pressure Trump in game of ‘chicken’
- list 2 of 4Trump threatens Iran’s partners: How do secondary sanctions work?
- list 3 of 4Iran, Oman agree on temporary Hormuz route: What we know
- list 4 of 4Why Hormuz remains high risk for ships despite US claims of mine-clearing
Majed al-Ansari said Sheikh Mohammed, who is also Qatar’s foreign minister, will meet with “a number of Iranian officials” in Tehran to “discuss ways to de-escalate tensions” and “create the conditions conducive to dialogue”.
“The visit comes in line with the State of Qatar’s firm position that the diplomatic path is the best means of resolving differences & promoting security & stability in the region,” he added.
Iran also confirmed the visit, saying the discussions will cover “the continuation of Qatar’s mediation efforts and initiatives, as well as other regional developments”.
Qatar has served as a back-channel negotiator between Washington and Tehran and helped secure a memorandum of understanding in June that briefly paused hostilities. The agreement collapsed in July, and the conflict is now nearing its sixth month, with fighting largely paused but no diplomatic breakthrough in sight.
The US has, meanwhile, promised to increase economic pressure on Tehran by sanctioning its trade partners.
US President Donald Trump told Al Jazeera on Wednesday that he was in “no hurry” to resume talks with Iran, saying that he believed economic and military action against Tehran were both effective.
“I have no time schedule; whatever it takes,” he said.
‘Economic terrorism’
Iran has continued to denounce the economic pressure campaign.
Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi wrote to the United Nations on Wednesday calling the new sanctions an “act of state and economic terrorism” and urging member states not to implement them.
“The sanctions deliberately harm civilians by restricting access to food, medicine, medical equipment, energy and other essentials, violating rights including the rights to life, health, food and an adequate standard of living”, he said.
The two sides also remain at odds over the Strait of Hormuz, the strategic waterway that handled one-fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas shipments before the US-Israel war on Iran began in February.
Iran wants control over the strait, while the US wants it to remain an international waterway that is free for all. That disagreement in part led to the collapse of the memorandum signed in June.
Oil flows through the strait have since fallen to a three-month low, with just 5 million barrels per day (bpd) transiting on Monday. Before the war, the strait carried roughly 20 million bpd of crude oil.
Qatar’s Foreign Ministry said Sheikh Mohammed will also discuss the waterway in his meetings in Tehran on Thursday, focusing on “the need for it to return to the status quo prior to February 28”.
Regional diplomacy
Sheikh Mohammed’s visit comes two days after Omani Foreign Minister Badr Albusaidi met his Iranian counterpart, Araghchi, in Tehran.
Following those talks, Iran’s deputy foreign minister, Kazem Gharibabadi, said the two countries had agreed on a new temporary route for shipping in the strait.
But he insisted that the waterway will not reopen until the US fulfils its commitments under the June deal, including the lifting of sanctions and the release of frozen assets.
Pakistan’s army chief, Asim Munir, also visited Tehran earlier in the week in a bid to “end the stalemate” in the conflict, with Islamabad reporting “significant progress” in those talks.
Mostafa Khoshcheshm, a professor at the University of Applied Sciences in Tehran, said that regional countries were pushing for dialogue because “they believe that the situation is moving towards escalation”.
“They know that if war breaks out, it would be a fully-fledged war and the fire would spill over into the entire region and beyond, leaving a detrimental impact on the global economy,” he said. “So there are hectic diplomatic moves on the part of these countries.”

Israel has decided to hand over the body of a 15-year-old Palestinian boy more than nine months after Israeli forces killed him and withheld his remains, a Palestinian group said Wednesday.
The National Campaign for the Retrieval of Palestinian Martyrs’ Bodies said Jadallah Jihad Jumaa Jadallah from the Al-Fara’a refugee camp in Tubas was killed by Israeli army fire during a raid on the camp on Nov. 16, 2025.
His body has remained in Israeli custody since then.
The campaign said the decision followed a petition filed with the Israeli Supreme Court in March demanding the return of the child’s body.

The campaign said withholding Jadallah’s body for more than nine months had deprived his family of the right to bid him farewell and bury him.
In figures released Wednesday ahead of the annual National Day for the Retrieval of Palestinian Martyrs’ Bodies, the group said Israel is holding the remains of around 1,700 Palestinians, including 799 whose identities are known.
Among the identified bodies are those of 81 children under 18, 99 Palestinians who died in Israeli prisons and 10 women, it said.
The campaign said another 256 bodies are held in so-called “cemeteries of numbers,” where graves are marked with numbers rather than names and Israel retains information on the identities of those buried there.
Israel’s Supreme Court ruled in 2019 that authorities could withhold Palestinian bodies for use as bargaining chips, a policy that was later expanded to cover Palestinians accused by Israel of carrying out attacks.

Hsiao stresses resilience as Taiwan faces climate change challenges
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
02:50:41 UTC
11:50:41 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Vice President Hsiao Bi-khim (蕭美琴) on Wednesday called for stronger infrastructure and greater cooperation between the government and private sector to help Taiwan withstand increasingly frequent extreme weather and natural disasters.
Hsiao made the remarks at the closing ceremony of a climate change forum for civil engineers in Taipei. She said professional and technical forums are important for bringing together experts to work toward a more resilient Taiwan, per a press release.
She added that a “resilient homeland” has been one of President Lai Ching-te’s (賴清德) major initiatives since taking office. Hsiao said both climate change adaptation and Taiwan’s social resilience depend on expertise from across different fields and involve important infrastructure such as water, electricity, and communications that people rely on every day.
As an island with distinctive geographical conditions, Taiwan faces numerous extreme weather challenges worsened by climate change, Hsiao said. Its mountainous terrain and rapid water flows can contribute to flooding, while the country also faces droughts and frequent earthquakes.
She pointed to flooding in eastern and southern Taiwan in the days before the forum as an example of the challenges facing the country. Hsiao said years of work, including the Pearl String Project to improve regional water allocation and flood-control projects implemented by local governments, have already produced results.
However, she said the challenges continue to affect people's lives and require ongoing contributions from professionals across different fields. Resilience does not mean avoiding problems altogether, Hsiao said. Rather, it means having the ability to recover quickly after a setback so that cities and people's daily lives can return to normal as soon as possible.
She said the forum's discussions of water supply, cooling, and power resilience addressed some of Taiwan's most pressing needs. Hsiao said such work cannot rely solely on the government or a single ministry, instead requiring cooperation across sectors and professions, as well as policy and technical teams capable of putting plans into practice, per the press release.
Hsiao said national infrastructure and urban governance must become more resilient as extreme weather becomes increasingly common. Cities cannot afford to be fragile or completely paralyzed by natural disasters, she said, adding that infrastructure must be robust, with backup systems and rapid-repair capabilities. She also praised the private sector for its expertise and willingness to adopt emerging technologies.
Hsiao said she recently visited the Taiwan Provincial Highway 9 widening project in Hualien, where she saw AI being applied to civil engineering and construction safety. She said the technology could make projects safer and more efficient while better meeting public expectations.
Hsiao thanked the forum organizers and engineers for their professional contributions and for creating opportunities to exchange ideas and learn from one another. She added they provide an important foundation to strengthen the country's resilience and advance the goal of sustainable development.

"For the moment, we are not dealing with a terrorist motive, but the investigation is only just beginning," said Bruno Coutanceau, a top security official for Caen.
All of the victims appeared to be men between the ages of 17 and 40, he told AFP.
The suspect, a 26-year-old man born in Russia, was later arrested around 20km (12 miles) away in the port town of Ouistreham.
The mayor of Caen later told local media his car had been tracked by the city's CCTV network.
He was not previously known to intelligence services and police had been aware of him "only for traffic offences", Clavière said.
Social media videos from the scene appeared to show crowds gathering around police cars and ambulances, where a large area was cordoned off.
A spokesperson for the local administration of Calvados told the BBC that some of those injured were receiving treatment in the emergency ward of a nearby hospital.
Police have opened an investigation into the incident, which will be led by detectives from Caen's Specialised Crime Division.

Iraq says international coalition’s withdrawal to be completed by Sept. 30
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
02:35:06 UTC
11:35:06 KST

Mohamed Majed, Mohammad Sio
27 August 2026•Update: 27 August 2026
The withdrawal of international coalition forces from Iraq is gathering pace and is expected to be completed by Sept. 30, Iraqi military spokesman Sabah al-Numan said Wednesday.
The withdrawal is being coordinated directly with the office of Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi, who is also the commander in chief of the armed forces, and is proceeding according to an agreed timetable, al-Numan told Al-Iraqiya TV, according to the Iraqi News Agency (INA).
German forces recently completed their withdrawal from Erbil in northern Iraq after taking part in the US-led international coalition formed in 2014 to fight the ISIS (Daesh) terror group, he said.
German troops had been stationed in Erbil since 2015, focusing on training Iraqi forces and Peshmerga fighters as well as weapons programs and aerial reconnaissance before their withdrawal was completed Wednesday.
The drawdown was coordinated directly with the prime minister’s office, which is overseeing the movement of departing forces and equipment by land and air, al-Numan added.
Facilities previously used by German forces at Erbil airport will be handed over to airport authorities, while other military sites will be transferred to the Peshmerga forces, he said.
The handover follows the transfer of other former coalition bases, including Ain al-Asad and Balad, to Iraq’s Defense Ministry after the coalition ended its missions there, al-Numan stated.
Iraq announced in January that it had completed the first phase of its plan to end the coalition’s mission after US forces withdrew from Ain al-Asad air base in western Anbar province and handed the facility over to Iraqi forces.
The second and final phase, which will continue until Sept. 30, 2026, has begun and includes supporting counter-ISIS operations in Syria from Erbil.
Al-Numan said the prime minister had also ordered the formation of a committee to determine the nature of Iraq’s relationship with coalition countries after Sept. 30.
Future cooperation will focus on continued coordination, particularly intelligence sharing, information exchange and weapons programs, he said.
The plan to end the coalition’s mission stems from an agreement announced by Baghdad and Washington in September 2024. It calls for a gradual transition from the coalition’s military mission to bilateral security ties with member countries, with the process due to conclude in September 2026.
Al-Numan said departing forces are following security procedures and maintaining continuous coordination to secure routes and destinations, with movements subject to official approvals and daily reports submitted to the commander in chief.
The US-led coalition was formed in 2014 to fight ISIS, which at the time controlled large parts of Iraq and Syria. Iraq declared in December 2017 that it had fully retaken its territory from ISIS, though the terror group has continued to carry out sporadic attacks.

Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook denounces Trump’s mortgage fraud claims
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
02:33:08 UTC
11:33:08 KST

Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook denounces Trump’s mortgage fraud claims
The Trump administration has doubled down on its accusations against Cook, despite a Supreme Court ruling in her favour.
Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook has warned the administration of United States President Donald Trump that it has no legal basis to fire her from her leadership position at the central bank.
Her legal team’s latest statement comes as Trump renews his efforts to push her out of her role, a manoeuvre widely viewed as an assault on the bank’s independence.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3US Supreme Court backs Trump’s firings; Fed’s Cook reserved as exception
- list 2 of 3Despite marquee losses, Supreme Court term grows Trump’s presidential power
- list 3 of 3Donald Trump renews effort to fire Federal Reserve governor Lisa Cook
Under US law, Federal Reserve governors can only be removed “for cause”, and not for political reasons.
Trump has levelled accusations of mortgage fraud against Cook, a Democratic appointee, in a bid to meet the legal standard. But Cook’s lawyers, Abbe David Lowell and Norman Eisen, issued a letter on Wednesday offering a detailed rebuttal to the president’s allegations.
“For the second time in a year, we have explained why there is no legal basis for President Trump to remove Governor Cook for cause,” the lawyers said.
“An inadvertent error is not fraud, as the President and a third of his cabinet should know because they reportedly did the same thing. These attacks on Governor Cook are not about real estate paperwork; they are an attempt by President Trump to force the Federal Reserve to bend to his will.”
The letter serves as a response to a threat from the Trump administration this month.
In a message dated August 5, the White House warned that Trump, a Republican, was considering firing Cook “due to there being sufficient reason to believe that you made false statements on one or more mortgage agreements”. It gave her three weeks, until Wednesday, to respond.
This is the second time Trump has sought to use mortgage fraud allegations to remove Cook.
A year ago, in August 2025, he issued similar accusations, telling reporters, “I’ll fire her if she doesn’t resign.” Cook responded with a lawsuit that travelled all the way to the Supreme Court.
She claimed the allegations were a pretext for removing her over policy differences.
In a five-to-four ruling in June, the high court blocked Trump from firing Federal Reserve governors at will.
No president has attempted to oust a Federal Reserve official since the body was founded more than a century ago. The Federal Reserve Act of 1913 enshrined certain protections for the bank to shield it from outside influences that could damage the economy in the name of political gain.
Trump, however, has sought to significantly expand executive power during his second term as president.
The Federal Reserve has been one of his targets. He has sought to increase his influence over the bank, notably by pressuring its members to rapidly slash interest rates, which were elevated to combat inflation.
Experts, however, warn that lowering interest rates too quickly could flood US markets with cash, weakening the value of the dollar.
Interest rates were a point of contention with former Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell, whose tenure as the bank’s head ended in May. He remains a governor on its board.
In January, Powell revealed that the Trump administration opened a criminal probe into his actions related to a renovation effort at the bank’s headquarters.
Powell denounced the investigation as an intimidation tactic. “This is about whether the Fed will be able to continue to set interest rates based on evidence and economic conditions – or whether, instead, monetary policy will be directed by political pressure or intimidation,” he said in a statement at the time.
In March, a federal judge nixed two subpoenas related to the investigation, which he depicted as a barely concealed effort to pressure Powell out of his job.
The investigation was ultimately dropped in April, shortly before Powell’s term as chair expired.

Trump temporarily expands beef import quota to ease prices for US consumers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Diyar Guldogan
27 August 2026•Update: 27 August 2026
President Donald Trump on Wednesday signed a proclamation temporarily increasing the amount of lean beef trimmings that can be imported into the US at lower, in-quota tariff rates, as the administration seeks to ease beef prices amid tight domestic supplies. 
The measure will take effect Sept. 1 and remain in place for 90 days. It will allow up to 100,000 tons of lean beef trimmings per month to enter under the expanded quota, according to fact sheet released by the White House.
The administration said the imported beef will be used to combine with domestic beef in the production of ground beef and is intended to increase supplies and reduce costs for American consumers.
The White House said the measure includes safeguards intended to protect US ranchers. Imports will be encouraged to be sold at a 25% discount from the prevailing import price, while the expanded quota will not apply to countries with country-specific beef quotas or alter existing commitments under US free-trade agreements.
The administration said the temporary measure could increase beef supplies by roughly 10% over current projections while primarily competing with the market for cull cows rather than the fed-cattle market.
The move comes as US beef supplies remain under pressure. The Agriculture Department forecasts US beef production will decline by about 4% from 2025 levels, according to the administration.

NEW DELHI: India on Wednesday issued emergency helpline numbers for its citizens stranded or affected by devastating flash floods in neighbouring Nepal, where intense flooding in the northern region bordering China has claimed more than 150 lives.The Indian Embassy in Kathmandu said Indian nationals seeking assistance or information could contact +977 985 131 6807 or +977 970 910 7500.

Among the foreign nationals reported missing are citizens of Australia, the Netherlands, the United States, Malaysia, the United Kingdom and South Africa.
Nepal was hit by a sudden natural disaster on Wednesday when the Bhote Koshi River, flowing from Tibet in China, triggered massive mudslides and flash floods in the Himalayan nation’s Rasuwa district.The flooding along the Nepal-China border caused widespread destruction, killing at least 160 people and leaving more than 800 others missing.A sudden surge in the Bhote Koshi River struck the Rasuwagadhi-Timure area at around 9 am local time, affecting Rasuwa and parts of the neighbouring Nuwakot and Dhading districts.The floodwaters washed away vehicles, goods, bridges and other infrastructure, while several hydropower projects were also damaged.

Finance Ministry report reveals major salary gaps across Israel's security organizations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
02:24:25 UTC
11:24:25 KST

A new Finance Ministry report has revealed major salary disparities across Israel’s security organizations, with employees in some Defense Ministry auxiliary units earning more than twice the average salary of younger career soldiers.
The report also found that the average state pension of an IDF officer is valued at approximately NIS 9 million.
The figures were published in the Finance Ministry’s Salary and Labor Agreements Division report on defense system employees for 2023-2024. The report examines the impact of the war, salary agreements, and changes in the workforce composition of Israel’s security organizations.
The highest average salary was recorded among Defense Ministry auxiliary units, including the Atomic Energy Commission, where employees earned an average of NIS 34,315 gross per month in 2024.
Employees at Israel’s intelligence agencies, Mossad and Shin Bet (Israeli Security Agency), earned an average of NIS 32,225, while the average salary at the Israel Institute for Biological Research stood at NIS 31,932.
IDF's average salary lowest among branches examined in report
The average salary for civilian employees of the IDF totaled NIS 22,926, while Israel Police employees earned an average of NIS 20,562 and Prison Service employees earned NIS 18,889.
The Finance Ministry noted, however, that significant salary increases granted to police and Prison Service employees from mid 2024 are expected to be fully reflected only in the 2025 report.
Alongside rising salaries, the number of employees across Israel’s security organizations also increased. In 2024, the police employed approximately 26,900 workers, the Prison Service employed about 9,500, and the IDF’s civilian workforce included around 8,500 employees.
Together, the three organizations with publicly available figures employed approximately 44,900 workers, an increase of about 2,500 employees within one year. The number of IDF personnel and employees in the intelligence agencies and Defense Ministry auxiliary units was not disclosed.
The IDF’s overall average salary was the lowest among the organizations examined, standing at NIS 18,756. At the same time, salaries for younger career soldiers continued to rise. The average salary for soldiers in their initial career service period reached NIS 13,845 per month, compared with NIS 11,786 in 2022, an increase of approximately 17.5%.
At the top end of the salary scale, the average monthly salary of an IDF major general reached NIS 73,099. A police commissioner earned an average of NIS 66,084, while the average salary of a Prison Service commissioner stood at NIS 62,946.
The war also contributed to an expansion of the IDF’s civilian workforce. The number of civilian employees increased from approximately 6,600 in 2021 to about 8,000 in 2024, primarily due to recruitment in intelligence, cyber, and technology fields. As a result, the average age of civilian IDF employees declined from 50 to 44.
Average pension higher than 2024 target, report finds
One of the report’s key findings concerns the state pension system for IDF officers. The average cumulative value of an officer’s pension stands at approximately NIS 9 million, with the average retirement age at 45 and the average monthly pension payment reaching NIS 20,019.
The average pension is approximately NIS 4,300 higher than the target set for 2024, which stood at NIS 15,717. The target for 2025 is NIS 15,553, but the report warned that the figures raise concerns that the IDF will not be able to meet that goal.
Under Israeli law, if the average pension of retiring officers remains above the target, the finance minister will be required to establish new regulations governing pension payments.
Women currently make up about one-third of career soldiers in the IDF and 41.2% of employees at the Israel Institute for Biological Research.
However, gender salary gaps widened slightly in 2024, partly due to activity and combat-related bonuses that were primarily awarded to field positions, where the proportion of men is higher.

RIJEKA, Croatia, Aug. 26 (Xinhua) -- China's Yuan Qingcheng and Russia's Miroslav Kiselev, both 14, each claimed a third gold medal at the 2026 World Aquatics Junior Diving Championships here on Wednesday.
Yuan won the girls' Group B 10m platform title as China swept the top two places, while Kiselev triumphed in the boys' Group B 3m springboard.
Scores from five preliminary dives were carried over into the three-round girls' final. China's Jiang Yuehan led after the opening round, with Yuan in second place.
Yuan scored 86.40 points for an armstand back double somersault with 1.5 twists in the second round, cutting the gap to her synchronized partner to less than three points.
Jiang struggled with her entry on her final dive, a forward 2.5 somersault with 1.5 twists, while Yuan finished strongly to secure the title. Jiang took silver and Mexico's Lia Cueva Lobato finished third.
Yuan said the individual platform title was the most difficult of her three golds in Rijeka because she was competing against her strong partner.
"But I thought it would be possible," she added. "The last dive was a little bit bad," Jiang said softly in English. "I don't know what happened. I think I over-rotated."
Yuan and Jiang had earlier teamed up to win the girls' synchronized platform title. Yuan also helped China claim gold in the mixed team event.
In the boys' Group B 3m springboard final, Kiselev won with a total of 492.95 points. Mexico's Ian Caleb Nava Gutierrez finished 16.35 points behind to take silver, while Australia's Hayden Brinckley earned bronze.
Kiselev had previously won the boys' Group B platform title and partnered Kosimov to victory in the boys' synchronized platform, taking his tally in Rijeka to three golds and one bronze.
Russia leads the medal table with four golds, three silvers and two bronzes, followed by China and Mexico.
The girls' Group B 3m springboard and boys' Group A platform events will be contested on Thursday, with the championships concluding on Friday. ■

China sends emergency power supply forces, rescue personnel to mudslide-hit border port in Xizang
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27

11:20:41 KST

BEIJING, Aug. 27 (Xinhua) -- A mudslide in Nepal caused severe casualties at the Gyirong Port in southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region on Wednesday morning, prompting an immediate mobilization of emergency power supply forces, according to the State Grid Corporation of China on Thursday.
Gyirong Port, located in Gyirong Town of Gyirong County, Xigaze City, is a major land port connecting China and Nepal. The mudslide occurred on Wednesday morning in Nepal, resulting in three people dead and 265 missing at Gyirong Port as of 8 p.m., according to initial estimates.
In the wake of the disaster, the State Grid Xizang Electric Power Company Limited has been racing against time to assemble emergency power supply resources in Gyirong Town. As of 4 a.m. Thursday, 85 emergency repair personnel, seven power generating vehicles, two generators and 19 sets of lighting equipment had arrived at the site.
Meanwhile, an additional 30 personnel, five power generating vehicles, 42 generators and 18 sets of lighting equipment have been transported from nearby areas to Gyirong, the company said, vowing to win the battle of ensuring power supply for disaster relief following the Gyirong mudslide.
Going forward, the company will dynamically reinforce its emergency response teams, stockpile and deploy supplies and equipment, and refine power supply plans to advance all emergency power supply work safely and efficiently.
The Ministry of Emergency Management and the National Fire and Rescue Administration have dispatched 111 firefighters and rescue personnel from the China Search and Rescue team to the disaster-hit site.
The first charted plane of the rescue team arrived at an airport in Xigaze city on early morning Thursday. ■

Guterres urges UN peace operations to adapt to new global realities
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
10:20:18 CST
11:20:18 KST

UNITED NATIONS, Aug. 26 (Xinhua) -- UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said on Tuesday that UN peace operations must adapt to new realities amid profound changes in the global security landscape.
"Our approaches to peace operations have evolved over the past eight decades, as conflicts changed and possibilities for collective action fluctuated. Now they must adapt again to dramatic new realities," he told an informal plenary meeting of the General Assembly.
Guterres said geopolitics is shifting, with power becoming more diffuse, new poles of influence emerging and new lines of contestation taking shape. The world is witnessing a resurgence of interstate conflicts and an intensification of internal conflicts that are increasingly internationalized, protracted and difficult to resolve.
Citing frequent conflicts, rapidly-changing nature of warfare and less common comprehensive peace agreements, he called for "a reset in how we think about and use peace operations."
Guterres said UN peace operations should place greater emphasis on preventive diplomacy, peacemaking and the peaceful settlement of disputes, while strengthening the good offices of the secretary-general, envoys and the UN Secretariat.
He also called for more agile and cost-effective operations, stronger accountability, enhanced technological capabilities and closer global-regional partnerships.
"Peace operations are, above all, political instruments," Guterres said, stressing that their success depends on appropriate mandates, will of the parties and support from the Security Council, member states, host countries and international partners.
"We must adapt to a changing world. And together, we must find the will -- and the resources -- to forge pathways to peace," he said. ■

MADRID, Aug. 26 (Xinhua) -- Kylian Mbappe scored a hat-trick as Jose Mourinho celebrated his return to the Santiago Bernabeu Stadium with a 4-1 home win over Real Sociedad on Wednesday night.
Mbappe scored once in the first half and twice in the second as Real Madrid overcame a difficult opening period before taking control after the break.
Real Sociedad did well to keep Real Madrid at bay in the first half, which kicked off after Real Madrid's Marc Cucurella and Real Sociedad captain Mikel Oyarzabal received applause from the Santiago Bernabeu crowd for their roles in Spain's World Cup triumph.

Real Madrid's lead lasted only four minutes before Luka Sucic equalized after the home defense was slow to react when Job Ochieng's shot took a big deflection.
Sucic had time to pick his spot and slide the ball past Thibaut Courtois.
Real Sociedad goalkeeper Alex Remiro reacted well to deny Mbappe a second goal early in the second half and then did well to block a cross from Cucurella, who came on as a substitute at the start of the second half.
Mbappe restored Real Madrid's lead just after the hour following a swift passing move with Jude Bellingham, who turned provider again in the 68th minute when he won the ball from Real Sociedad defender Luken Beitia to set up Vinicius Jr. for his side's third goal of the night.
The World Cup top scorer completed his hat-trick in the 80th minute after an assist from Vinicius to seal a comfortable victory and a winning return to the Bernabeu for Mourinho. ■

Nikita Tszyu and Ben Mahoney's camps exchange verbal barbs after controversial draw
In short:
Nikita Tszyu's promoters have defended the integrity of their company, No Limit Boxing, after a controversial Gold Coast draw against Ben Mahoney.
Mahoney said any rematch with Tszyu would not take place on a No Limit boxing card, saying the result was "a hard pill to swallow".
What's next?
Mick Francis, who is with Mahoney's promoter Tasman Fighters, said he would seek an official review of experienced judge Phillip Holliday's scoring after he awarded the fight to Tszyu 117-111.
Matt Rose has defended the integrity of his company after No Limit Boxing pin-up Nikita Tszyu's controversial draw with Ben Mahoney, who claimed any rematch would not be happening on their card.
Wednesday's IBF super welterweight world-title eliminator was a terrific back-and-forth between two unbeaten Australians that left more questions than answers.
The bout finished in a split draw after three wildly different scorecards.
Experienced judge Phillip Holliday, who beat Jeff Fenech in a distinguished career of his own, awarded the fight to Tszyu 117-111, effectively giving the bookies' favourite nine of the 12 rounds.
But fellow official Sabrina Kerr scored it for Mahoney, 115-113, and the third judge, Carl Zappia, scored the fight a 114-114 draw.
Jeers followed from the pro-Mahoney crowd, who backed their local hope as he defied heavy fire through the middle rounds to finish stronger and leave Tszyu's face battered.
In dramatic post-fight scenes, Tszyu conceded Mahoney had been the better boxer while No Limit boss George Rose took offence to comments from Mahoney's corner, declaring, "I wanna slap the s*** out of someone" before challenging anyone booing "to meet him out front and we'll sort it out".
Tszyu walked back his assessment in the press conference, explaining he was simply disappointed he had not been more clinical.
Tensions flared further when Mahoney's promoter Mick Francis later said he would seek an official review of Holliday's scoring.
Mahoney, who fought to a controversial draw on his last fight on a No Limit card, poured his heart out.
"We're going to have to look at our [rematch] options; I'm open to it but it sure as hell isn't going to be on another No Limit card," Mahoney, who had otherwise shown great respect to Tszyu and his team, said.
"I don't want to throw any officials or judges under the bus. But athletes put their lives on the line for this. I just had a baby and have been in the gym for eight weeks of 14 weeks of her life.
"You come in here, your opponent believes you won and you get a draw. It's a hard pill to swallow."
Francis, a rival to No Limit who also boasts Jai Opetaia and Justis Huni in his stable, said they "hadn't heard the end of it".
"Phil Holliday, I don't know what he was watching … those scores were way wide and I'm going to make an official inquiry about it because that's not right," he said.
Rose did not front the press conference, leaving co-founder brother Matt and manager Glen Jennings to flank Tszyu.
He confirmed there had been a "couple of comments made in the ring" that triggered George and welcomed a review of the scoring in the belief it would favour his man.
"I'd be happy for them to challenge because I don't think the scorecard of 115-113 was right at all," Rose said.
"And that would mean Nikita wins the fight.
"But we'll accept the draw. At the end of the day, I'm not going to complain about the 115-113. That's the decision they made and that's how they saw it."
Rose, whose company holds exclusive broadcast rights with Fox Sports and Main Event to Australian fights, did bite though when told of Mahoney's claim he wouldn't meet Tszyu on a card run by them again.
"What, it's going to be on a Tasman card in front of 200 people?" he fired back.
"Who would stage it then?
"Please don't try to diminish what we do in the sport. The shows we put on are the best in the country.
"If people are going to be critical of judging, it has nothing to do with us whatsoever."

Brazil sues chat platform Discord over failure to protect child users
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
02:11:21 UTC
11:11:21 KST

Brazil sues chat platform Discord over failure to protect child users
The lawsuit is the latest instance of Brazil taking aggressive steps to rein in tech giants over child safety issues online.
The Brazilian government has filed a lawsuit against the chat platform Discord, seeking millions of dollars in damages over alleged failures to protect children and teenage social media users.
The $97m lawsuit, filed on Wednesday, comes after what the Brazilian government describes as failed negotiations with the company.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Brazil fines TikTok $30m for child data privacy violations
- list 2 of 3Meta agrees to settlement, platform changes in youth addiction case
- list 3 of 3TikTok settles with US Justice Department for $400m over child privacy laws
The complaint argues that Discord failed to abide by laws designed to protect young social media users.
“The lawsuit seeks to compel the Discord platform to adopt effective measures to protect children, adolescents, and women in the digital environment,” the government said in a statement, calling for compensation for “collective moral damages”.
The company, however, has pushed back, saying the lawsuit is excessively harsh and does not accurately depict its compliance with the country’s laws.
The lawsuit is the latest instance of a social media company facing scrutiny for allegedly exposing young users to harmful content or eroding their mental health through addictive technology products.
Critics say that tech giants have been slow to implement protective measures, despite evidence linking excessive social media use to mental health issues among young people.
In many cases, plaintiffs have argued that social media companies have prioritised user engagement and profit over health and safety concerns.
Tech companies, however, have countered that they should not be held responsible for all the content published on their platforms, nor for how users interact with the software.
In Brazil, scrutiny fell on Discord in July, after a case in the western state of Mato Grosso do Sul captured the public’s attention.
On July 22, a 13-year-old girl was on a livestream when she killed herself after being goaded to do so by a group of her fellow teenagers.
According to the Brazilian Justice Ministry, the teens first pressured her to kill an animal, but after she failed to do so, they started pushing her to take her own life.
Four teenagers and one adult have been arrested in connection with the case.
In the aftermath, Brazil’s National Data Protection Agency (ANPD) ordered Discord to suspend livestream services on August 12. First Lady Rosangela Lula da Silva also called for the site to be taken down.
The messaging platform, which hosts about 90 million active daily users, said that it would stop streaming services and take steps “to make Discord safer for teens”.
But the Brazilian government said that the company “continues to exhibit flaws in its age verification and user protection mechanisms”.
The ANPD also fined TikTok $30m on Tuesday for child privacy violations, an indicator of the more aggressive approach the Brazilian government has taken on such issues.

China’s Akeso says cancer drug beat AstraZeneca’s Imfinzi in phase 3 trial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

China’s Akeso says cancer drug beat AstraZeneca’s Imfinzi in phase 3 trial
The biliary tract cancer trial is the latest breakthrough for Akeso’s ivonescimab, which has also shown promise in treating some lung cancers
Chinese biopharmaceutical firm Akeso announced on Wednesday that its immunotherapy drug had outperformed AstraZeneca’s Imfinzi in a head-to-head phase three trial for biliary tract cancer.
The result represents another breakthrough for Akeso’s ivonescimab – which has already been licensed by the US firm Summit Therapeutics in a multibillion-dollar deal – as China’s biopharmaceutical industry increasingly looks to compete on the global stage.
The Chinese trial tested ivonescimab and chemotherapy against AstraZeneca’s Imfinzi (durvalumab) plus chemotherapy on a total of 682 patients with advanced biliary tract cancer – a particularly deadly form of cancer with a five-year survival rate of less than 5 per cent, according to a Nature study.
The results showed that patients taking Akeso’s novel drug lived longer than those using the AstraZeneca treatment, the company said in a Hong Kong stock exchange filing released a day ahead of its interim results.
The study marks the first positive phase three study for ivonescimab in gastrointestinal tumours, potentially opening the door for the drug to be used in a “broader range of solid tumours”, said Xia Yu, Akeso’s founder, chairwoman and CEO.
However, Akeso has yet to disclose the exact survival figures from the trial, which the Zhongshan-headquartered company is expected to present at a coming conference.
Ivonescimab has already shown promise as a treatment for non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), receiving initial approval from Chinese regulators. The drug’s licenser, Summit, is also applying for approval to use ivonescimab to treat NSCLC in the United States.

France’s imperiled moderates look weaker than ever ahead of first presidential debate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
02:02:00 UTC
11:02:00 KST

Patrick Martin president of MEDEF at the end of his opening address during the first day of La REF 2026 the Meeting of French Entrepreneurs at Roland Garros Stadium in Paris France on August 26. | Bastien Ohier/Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images
PARIS — France’s first presidential debate on Thursday should have been an opportunity for centrist and conservative candidates to shine.
Taking place at the annual conference of MEDEF, France’s powerful employers’ lobby, on the burnt-orange clay of Roland-Garros, seven presidential contenders will be quizzed about what they’ll do to make France more business-friendly.
Moderates offering a dose of economic realism historically have home-court advantage at Medef events. But this year’s conventional presidential candidates appear rudderless, riven by infighting and ceding ground to the political extremes — who in turn are setting the terms of the public debate on how to fix France’s financial mess.
Advertisement
One of Medef’s most pressing concerns is Paris’ inability to rein in a stubbornly high budget deficit and reduce a massive pile of debt worth more than €3.5 trillion — or 117.5 percent of gross domestic product — even before the recent spike in global borrowing costs.
The solution du jour comes from far-left candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who is calling for the European Central Bank to waive interest payments on its French bond holdings, a move likely to frighten the investors Paris depends on to purchase French sovereign debt. Mélenchon’s proposal is strongly opposed by centrists and the business community, including MEDEF chief Patrick Martin, yet it dominates the discourse on French public debt.
And it’s the latest sign that as France’s economic outlook deteriorates, anti-establishment candidates are successfully pitching themselves as the ones who can fix France’s finances.
French left-wing party La France Insoumise founder and presidential election candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon arrives to deliver a speech in Chateauneuf-sur-Isere on August 23, 2026. | Olivier Chassignole/AFP via Getty Images
“You’d think that it would be a moment … that would profit those who are credible on economic matters,” said lawmaker Erwan Balanant from the centrist Democratic Movement. “But I don’t know who is credible on the economy anymore.”
Surveys continue to show far-right leader Marine Le Pen dominating the field of presidential hopefuls, and a poll released Monday showed Mélenchon on the rise and in a strong position to advance to the second round. The French presidential election goes to a two-candidate runoff if no one clears 50 percent of the vote — and a Le Pen-Mélenchon showdown would be a nightmare scenario for the European Union given their respective antipathy toward some of the bloc’s key pillars.
But Monday’s poll isn’t triggering calls for unity from ideologically similar centrists like former prime ministers Edouard Philippe and Gabriel Attal as well as conservative leader Bruno Retailleau.
Advertisement
It’s instead adding fuel to the vicious internecine battle, and senior centrist figures are increasingly alarmed.
“You’ve seen the polls, let’s name what is happening: It is a collapse of all those who refuse the extremes,” former prime minister and veteran centrist François Bayrou said Tuesday in an interview with BFMTV.
Fighting for match point
In circles close to President Emmanuel Macron, fears are growing that Le Pen and Mélenchon are the only candidates with compelling political narratives.
“Moderate forces need to come up with an innovative and original political offering,” said one of Macron’s close allies who, like others quoted in this piece, was granted anonymity to speak frankly about the state of the presidential race.
General Secretary of French centrist party Renaissance and upcoming presidential election candidate Gabriel Attal speaks to the press in Aulnay-sous-Bois on August 20, 2026. | Kenzo Tribouillard/AFP via Getty Images
Attal and Philippe have promised to eventually unite around whichever one of them is polling better — Philippe said that would happen between November and February — but their rivalry is getting nastier.
Advertisement
An Attal aide on Monday said that the summer was the “collapse of Edouard Philippe,” to which a prominent Philippe supporter countered later that day: “Nothing [Attal does] shows that he wants unity.”
“Lots of people are telling [Attal and Philippe] to reach an agreement, it won’t work,” said the Philippe supporter.
Getting the conservative Retailleau or center-left MEP Raphaël Glucksmann to stand down in favor of a single moderate candidate will prove difficult as well, as they have serious policy and ideological disagreements with the two former prime ministers.
Given those fractures, few expect reconciliation on center court Thursday afternoon in the name of combating the political extremes. Instead, it’s looking more likely that the prospect of an alliance bites the dust.

Push for import ban on 'pervert' smart glasses amid privacy concerns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
02:00:37 UTC
11:00:37 KST

Push for import ban on 'pervert' smart glasses amid privacy concerns
In short:
Smart glasses and other wearable recording devices would be subject to a 12-month import ban under a bill to be introduced to the Senate.
Experts warn Australian laws have not kept up with the privacy risks posed by the flood of cheap camera-enabled devices entering the country.
What's next?
The Greens intend to launch the bill when parliament resumes next month, with several independent crossbenchers also in support.
There is growing support for a ban on the import of so-called "smart glasses" amid an influx of low-cost devices that are being used to film people without their consent.
In recent weeks the devices, dubbed "pervert glasses" by some critics for their capacity to film in secret, have inspired two Australian petitions calling for restrictions on their sale and import which attracted tens of thousands of signatures.
Now the Greens, with support of independents, plan to launch a bill when parliament next sits to halt the import of such glasses as well as other wearable recording devices for at least 12 months, until tougher privacy protections are passed into law.
"If we end up having millions of these devices in the country, there'll be no place that's free for your privacy," Greens senator David Shoebridge said.
"And at the scale that you see these sorts of imports ramping up already, that is what we face".
While first generation smart glasses cost upwards of $500, newer entrants to the market are available for well under $100 from a number of online and shopfront retailers in Australia.
At both ends of the price range, they look like ordinary glasses and yet allow the wearer to record images, video and audio, mostly surreptitiously, with the press of a button.
It is not clear how many pairs of smart glasses are already in circulation domestically, but Senator Shoebridge warned the current crop was just the beginning for wearable cameras.
"Right now it's glasses, but in a month's time it's almost certainly going to be earbuds, maybe it'll be a lapel pin, maybe it'll just be your T-shirt, I don't know".
He said parliament had a narrow window of time to block their large scale importation before such devices "wash through society".
"Maybe we should think ahead for once," Senator Shoebridge said.
"The genie's not yet out of the bottle … let's put a little plug in it until we work out what we want it to do."
Alongside the proposed import ban, which would include carve-outs for legitimate uses, such as aiding people with a vision impairment, the Greens are pushing for new privacy protections.
The bill would amend the Privacy Act to prohibit filming, storing or sharing footage from a "wearable recording device" without a person's express consent.
The change would for the first time extend the Privacy Act from large organisations to individuals.
It also proposes extra powers and funding for the Privacy Commissioner, to enforce those rules.
Ban attracts crossbench support
Independents David Pocock and Kate Chaney are among the crossbenchers in favour of a temporary import ban.
"I do think it's sensible to be pausing the imports … while the parliament actually puts some laws in place," Senator Pocock said.
"I think it would reduce the number of these devices that are on the street."
Ms Chaney described the proposed import ban as an imperfect fix for a lag in Australia's privacy protections.
"An import pause is a temporary solution. We really need to make sure that we can regulate these devices in the long term," she said.
While bills from the crossbench such as this one have a low rate of success historically, the proposal reflects significant public and political pressure on the government to respond to the smart glasses' privacy risk.
Earlier this month Attorney-General Michelle Rowland aired her own concerns about the technology, asking the privacy commissioner to prioritise the issue.
When asked by the ABC, a spokesman for Ms Rowland did not say whether the government was considering an import ban of its own, but acknowledged that smart glasses do "raise privacy concerns".
"These concerns deserve to be met with balanced and holistic policies that protect Australians while preserving legitimate uses of technology," the spokesman said.
"The government is actively considering these issues as part of our second tranche of privacy reforms."
The government committed to a suite of changes to the Privacy Act in September of 2023 and passed an initial wave of amendments it called "tranche one" in December 2024, including anti-doxxing laws and Children's Online Privacy Code, but is yet to act on the majority of the recommendations it agreed to two years ago.
A spokesman for Shadow Attorney-General Michaelia Cash also declined to comment on the specific proposal for an import ban.
Australia already importing 'creepy' social media trends
In countries such as the US and the UK, where the technology is more widespread, it has facilitated doxxing, online shaming and harassment at gyms, beaches and a range of public and semi-public spaces.
One of the biggest concerns is that the incoming tide of cheaper alternatives will bring with it the social media trends which exploit tech like this.
One of the best known examples is "rizzing", where self-described pick-up artists and dating coaches hit on women in public, secretly film the encounter and post the footage online, without the subject's consent or knowledge.
That trend is still in its infancy in Australia, but the ABC was able to easily find local examples of the same practice.
Privacy advocates are worried about the trajectory, and say women and minorities tend to be more heavily targeted by surreptitious recording.
"We see women shamed for being dressed in a certain way, or maybe they're being drunk in public … [recordings are] very rarely used to shame men for the same sorts of behaviour," Tom Sulston from Digital Rights Watch said.
Initially sceptical about the prospect of an import ban, Mr Sulston was ultimately swayed by the growing expectation that Apple will release camera-enabled wireless headphones as soon as September.
"That would be a huge scale point for the amount of covert cameras being used in public in Australia,"
Electronic Frontiers Australia has been calling for a moratorium on the sale of the technology for several weeks, and said privacy violations were already appearing locally.
"I've seen a couple of real-life examples of devices being misused in a gym-type context and also on the beach," EFA chair John Pane said.
He said regardless of what laws were in place, the nature of this technology meant many victims would never find out they had been filmed, let alone have a chance to seek redress.
"It's all the more difficult with smart devices like these because you don't know when they're being used or not."
Mr Sulston said it was a moment for Australians and their government to decide how much surveillance they were willing to accept.
"That sense of being in the panopticon is really bad for us psychologically, and we cannot afford to end up there."

Hong Kong remains most international city in Asia, widening lead over Singapore

02:00:21 UTC
11:00:21 KST

Hong Kong remains most international city in Asia, widening lead over Singapore
City leads in business, connectivity and talent diversity but trails rivals in technology investment, Hong Kong General Chamber of Commerce finds
Hong Kong has widened its lead over Singapore as Asia’s most international city, buoyed by gains in innovation and ideas, but still trails in attracting technology investment, a leading business chamber study has found.
The Hong Kong General Chamber of Commerce’s annual Asian Cities Internationality Index, released on Thursday, ranked Hong Kong first among 11 Asian cities with 74.6 out of 100 points in a measure of seven key areas.
Its lead over Singapore widened to two points, up from 0.2 points last year.
Hong Kong retained first place in business and economy, scoring 78.6 points. It ranked second in quality of life, infrastructure and connectivity, and human capital diversity.
The city rose from fourth to third place in innovation and ideas. It also remained third in government and legal systems for business, and fourth in cultural interaction, for the second consecutive year.
Chamber chairman Jacob Kam Chak-pui said Hong Kong performed well in research and innovation exchanges through its universities and scientific work, and in attracting leading global professionals through talent admission schemes.

Bears and pest control: how Japan is spending its departure tax windfall
Critics say the funds are being channelled into projects with limited direct benefit to travellers and question how the money is being spent
The Japanese government expects to raise 130 billion yen (US$817.7 million) in the 2026 financial year from the International Tourist Tax, after increasing the levy last year on anyone leaving the country through an airport or seaport.
The cost of leaving Japan for foreign tourists and Japanese travellers alike rose from 1,000 yen to 3,000 yen per person on July 1.
During political debate on the increase – when a figure as high as 5,000 yen was discussed – the government emphasised that the additional funds were needed to address problems linked to chronic overtourism in some parts of the country.
The government said additional spending would go towards promoting Japan as an overseas destination and developing large resort facilities.
The industry expressed hope that funds would also be used to hire more tourism staff in rural areas, train guides, improve multilingual signage and information, and upgrade tourism websites.

Deal or no deal: Farage faces polling hit from Restore Britain either way
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

A poster for the Restore Britain political party is pictured in front of a poster for the Reform UK party in Manchester, England on June 16, 2026. | Oli Scarff/AFP via Getty Images
LONDON — Nigel Farage knows he has a Restore Britain problem. Striking a pact with his rival is not a silver bullet.
New polling shared with POLITICO shows a deal between the right-wing Reform UK and a further-right splinter group led by Rupert Lowe would put off some of the former Conservative voters Reform UK is trying to attract.
Farage has made replacing the Conservatives as the main party on the right of British politics his aim — but the Restore outfit Lowe formed after being kicked out of Farage’s team is sapping away support from Reform.
Advertisement
Earlier this month, Lowe offered to put his differences with Farage aside to form a pact with Reform, and Reform officials have been taking Lowe’s public offer of a pact seriously.
“They would like to work with us because he [Lowe] needs us to survive in the long run,” as one Farage adviser, granted anonymity to discuss the rift, put it.
But Lowe’s deal comes with conditions — he advocates mass deportations, including of women and children, a ban on halal and kosher slaughter, a referendum on the death penalty, and the exclusion of Conservative ministers from a future Cabinet.
Luke Tryl, U.K. director of More in Common, which conducted polling on right-wing pacts earlier this month, said a deal with Restore would be “more likely to damage than bolster Reform’s fragile voter coalition.”
“Some Reform voters are open to Lowe’s messages, but they risk deterring the wider pool of voters that Reform would need to win an election.
“It seems that a pact with Restore would cross too many lines for Reform’s wavering voters: this group wants to see Farage condemn racist views, retain a distance with figures on the hard-right like Tommy Robinson, and avoid ethnonationalist positions,” he said.
Advertisement
More damage than good
His think tank’s survey of 2,128 adults conducted between Aug. 7 and Aug. 10 found that a Farage tie-up with Restore would trigger a significant drop off in support from respondents who voted Conservative in 2024 but are now considering voting Reform. That metric drops from 45 percent open to Reform to 39 percent.
Some Reform voters are also put off by the prospect of a Restore pact. The poll suggests 93 percent of voters who backed Farage at the last general election would do so again without a Restore pact, but the figure fell to 83 percent with the prospect of a Lowe team-up.
Leader of Restore Britain Rupert Lowe MP speaks to the media where votes were being counted at The Edge on June 18, 2026 in Wigan. | Ryan Jenkinson/Getty Images
Overall, the polling suggests that a Restore-pact would reduce those willing to consider voting Reform from 32 percent to 30 percent.
Restore is only hovering at around 4 percent in voting intention polling, but the survey found up to 20 percent of Brits would “consider” voting Restore — including half of those who voted Reform at the last general election in 2024.
And Restore draws particular support from non-voters, with some 53 percent of those in the survey definitely considering backing Restore not having voted at all in 2024.
The first-past-the-post system used in British general elections — where only one MP will represent each area — means a fracture on the political spectrum can hand the more united flank of politics the keys to Downing Street.
Advertisement
Yet there are also dangers for Farage in not doing a pact with Restore. Farage himself has conceded that Restore has the potential to do Reform “great harm” by splitting the right-wing vote.
Advisers on both sides of the right-wing divide said the pair haven’t held talks since Lowe published an image of WhatsApp Farage sent him and accused him of “outright lying” over efforts to set up a call.
For Lowe’s part, one Restore official argued the “ball is in their [Reform’s] court” now, pinning hopes on fresh pressure to agree a pact coming if Restore reaches higher polling ground.
Reform UK branding is seen scattered around Clacton on August 13, 2026 in Clacton-on-Sea. | Ben Montgomery/Getty Images
“I suspect if we continue climbing in the polls and scoring well and their decline continues then pressure may increase,” they said.
Restore’s national polling may be fairly low — but the party has been exceeding expectations in recent contests. Restore got 8.7 percent of the first-round vote in the Greater Manchester mayoralty and 6.8 percent in the Makerfield by-election.
Advertisement
Thursday may give another indication for how the right-wing splits can play out in a council by-election in a Conservative stronghold in Dover. Both Restore and Reform are fighting the three-way contest.
Conservative pact
Doing a deal with the center-right Conservatives would also come with its own dangers for Farage — something he and Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch appear cognizant of given they have both dismissed the idea.
Support for Reform fell from 32 percent to 28 percent when the Tory pact scenario was put to respondents.
The 93 percent of Reform voters who backed Farage in 2024 and would support him again dropped to 79 percent if he did a deal with the Conservatives.
That underlines the challenge Farage faces in becoming too closely associated with the long-established center-right party, despite some of its most senior figures defecting from the Conservatives.
Deals or no deals, the mere presence of rival outfits is causing major headaches for those trying to prevent Andy Burnham staying in power.
