US declares Palestine Action a 'terrorist group'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
22:20:20 UTC
07:20:20 KST

Breadcrumb
US declares Palestine Action a 'terrorist group'
The US on Wednesday designated Palestine Action a "global terrorist organisation", following in the footsteps of the British government which last year proscribed the direct action group.
In a notice on its website, the Treasury said it had added the group its sanctions blacklist, accusing it of "supporting numerous acts of terrorism" since July 2020.
The group was one of a number of what the Treasury called "violent far-left terrorist networks" hit by sanctions on Wednesday.
Palestine Action became the first protest group to be proscribed under UK terror legislation in July last year, putting its name alongside the likes of Islamic State and Al-Qaeda. The ban was decried by human rights monitors and resulted in the arrest of thousands of peaceful protesters under the Terrorism Act.
The group is in the process of challenging the proscription and will take its case to the Supreme Court in November.
"Palestine Action’s activities in the US and elsewhere have always been about saving lives by disrupting the Israeli war machine, which is committing a genocide in Gaza with the support of the US government. Trump has been at the centre of the mass murder of Palestinians, enabling the Zionist regime at every turn," Palestine Action co-founder Huda Ammori said.
"The fact that Trump is now taking inspiration from Britain’s repression of the movement for Palestinian freedom exposes just how dangerous this ban is and should be a wake-up call to anyone who cares about free speech and civil liberties. By banning a direct action protest group under terrorism legislation for the first time in British history, Keir Starmer’s government has created a blueprint for authoritarian governments around the world to suppress political dissent, and to criminalise British citizens who travel or live abroad," she continued.
She added: "Trump’s decision to adopt Keir Starmer’s designation of Palestine Action as a ‘terrorist’ group should be the final nail in the coffin of this dangerous, draconian and disproportionate ban."
The US Treasury's actions will freeze its assets in the US and ban American organisations and individuals from dealing with it.
It said that the group had "supported numerous acts of terrorism since July 2020, including acts that have physically injured UK law enforcement personnel, as well as acts intended to intimidate lawful commercial enterprises and coerce the UK government. The group’s actions include multiple high-profile instances of breaking into defense infrastructure and British military installations, and causing millions of dollars’ worth of damage to military equipment."
"Palestine Action has promoted its violent, criminal, and terrorist acts on social media, encouraging the use of similar tactics internationally, including within the United States and along the U.S.-Mexican border," it continued.
Set up six years ago, the group describes itself as a "direct action movement committed to ending global complicity with Israel’s genocidal apartheid regime".
It stepped up its actions after Israel launched its genocidal assault on Gaza in October 2023. It has targeted the UK operations of Israeli arms company Elbit as well as military sites involved in the sale of British arms to Israel.
The US on Wednesday also designated pro-Palestinian group Masar Badil and Italian anarchist movement Autistici/Inventati (also known as A/I Collective) as "terrorist" groups.
"There will be no refuge for violent extremists who wage war on our civilization and plot to undermine law and order, destroy critical infrastructure, assault political opponents, or conspire to conceal their crimes from authorities," Secretary of State Marco Rubio wrote in a post on X.

How Rising Temperatures Likely Contributed to Nepal’s Deadly Flood
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
22:19:44 UTC
07:19:44 KST

Roughly 160 people are dead and hundreds more—including dozens of international tourists—are missing after flash floods hit a region on the mountainous border of Nepal and Tibet on Wednesday. Devastating footage posted to social media shows people fleeing a wall of water that washed away buildings and vehicles.
Initial analysis of satellite imagery and reports from the Nepalese government indicate that the flooding was likely triggered by a landslide caused after a piece of a glacier fell hundreds of feet.
As the region warms, its ice is becoming increasingly unstable, raising the risk of catastrophic flooding.
“The glaciers over there are definitely in retreat,” says Joseph Shea, an associate professor of geography at the University of Northern British Columbia. “There’s a lot of glacier mass up there, but we’re seeing thinning, we’re seeing retreating.”
Since 2000, the world’s glaciers have lost 5 percent of their ice, with much more drastic impacts in certain regions. Nepal’s glaciers lost nearly a quarter of their area between 1970 and 2010. More than 160 smaller glaciers in the country, research has found, have vanished entirely.
A recent study finds that 40 percent of the world’s glacial ice could disappear if the world does not keep warming under 1.5 degrees Celsius.
The impacts of warming on glaciers in Nepal can cause cascading effects. Shea points out that retreating glaciers can help trigger landslides as they get smaller and can no longer hold back sediment. As these glaciers retreat, many are leaving large, dammed lakes at higher elevations. “If you have a landslide suddenly into a lake, you get an overtopping of the dam, and then the whole thing can collapse catastrophically,” Shea says. Known as glacial lake outburst floods, two of these events hit Nepal last year, and research shows millions of people are living in harms way around the world.
Wednesday’s disaster was more likely due to a glacial collapse that fell into the valley below. Daniel Shugar, a geologist at the University of Calgary in Canada, told The New York Times that satellite imagery suggested that a 2,000-foot-wide piece of ice may have fallen almost 4,000 feet, “[pulverizing] the ice into water” with the force of its fall. And while Shugar emphasized that it was still too early to make conclusive statements about the cause of the floods, he noted to Reuters that snow that was present on the glacier earlier in the week may have melted due to warm temperatures.
The collapse and debris flow were so large and forceful that they registered as a magnitude 5.2 seismic event, according to the US Geological Survey.
Glaciers elsewhere have broken apart with destructive results. That includes the collapse of a Swiss glacier last year that buried a town, while on a smaller scale, a glacier collapse in Italy in 2022 killed 11 mountaineers. Both were linked with rising temperatures.
There are a lot of factors in a warming world, Shea says, that can play on each other to destabilize glaciers.
“It’s summertime,” he says. “There’s lots of warming, lots of melt happening, lots of water around. There’s also things like alpine permafrost thaws: The ground temperatures warm up, and big blocks and chunks that would have been frozen in place are now suddenly becoming mobile.”

Fenerbahce beat Olympique Lyonnais 2-1 to return to Champions League
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
22:13:14 UTC
07:13:14 KST

Fenerbahce have defeated Olympique Lyonnais 2-1 away to advance to the UEFA Champions League league phase for the first time since reaching the group stage in the 2008-09 season.
The Turkish side advanced 3-2 on aggregate after the first leg in Istanbul ended 1-1, returning to Europe's elite club competition.
Olympique Lyonnais started brightly, with Malick Fofana forcing Fenerbahce goalkeeper Ederson into a save in the eighth minute with a left-footed effort from outside the box.
Fenerbahce gradually settled into the match and registered their first shot on target in the 13th minute, when Oguz Aydin's effort from the left side of the box was saved by Olympique Lyonnais goalkeeper Dominik Greif following a pass from Talisca.
The visitors grew increasingly dangerous, with Archie Brown seeing his powerful effort from a tight angle saved by Greif in the 19th minute.
Fenerbahce took the lead in the 24th minute.
Oguz Aydin sent a cross into the area, and Vedat Muriqi's initial header was saved by Greif. The Kosovo international reacted quickly to the rebound and fired into the bottom-right corner from close range.
Fenerbahce doubled their advantage four minutes later.
Mason Greenwood delivered a cross from a corner, and Brown rose to head the ball into the top-left corner from close range.
Olympique Lyonnais came close to reducing the deficit in the 35th minute when Vedat Muriqi's attempted clearance from a corner struck his own post.
Slower second half
Fenerbahce went into the break with a 2-0 advantage and a 3-1 aggregate lead.
Olympique Lyonnais began the second half with greater attacking intent, putting Fenerbahce under pressure during the opening 10 minutes.
However, the visitors began to find space on the counterattack, with Oguz Aydin firing high and wide from the left side of the box after being set up by Matteo Guendouzi.
Olympique Lyonnais pulled one back in the 61st minute. Ainsley Maitland-Niles found Fofana on the left side of the box, and the forward sent a left-footed effort into the bottom-right corner to make it 2-1.
The hosts thought they had equalised in the 64th minute when Lois Openda headed Abner Vinicius' cross into the net, but the goal was ruled out for offside following a VAR review.
Olympique Lyonnais were denied again when Kail Boudache scored in the 71st minute, but the referee overturned the goal following a VAR review after ruling that Zachary Athekame had fouled Brown during the buildup.
Fenerbahce looked to restore their two-goal advantage, but Guendouzi's deflected effort from outside the box in the 82nd minute was saved by Greif.
The Turkish side held on for a 2-1 victory, completing a 3-2 aggregate win and securing their place in the Champions League.

Bill Gates warns of AI’s impact, urges the US and China to cooperate
Tech titan argued on Wednesday artificial intelligence needs significant limits or else the harm to humans will outweigh any potential good
2-MIN READ2-MIN
4
 Listen
Vincent Chowin Washington
Cooperation between the United States and China is required to manage the unprecedented societal impacts of rapidly advancing artificial intelligence (AI) technology, Bill Gates wrote in a new essay published on Wednesday.
The call to action comes as the billionaire philanthropist and tech titan warns that AI is ushering in “one of the most turbulent times in human history”, which could either become “the greatest equaliser ever invented, or the worst source of injustice”.
“[The] countries that host the leading AI developers and control critical parts of the supply chain should begin meeting now to set up shared norms, before competitive pressure makes it harder for them to cooperate,” he wrote.
“Building the framework I’m talking about will take years, which is why we need to start now.”
In the 6,000-word essay, the Microsoft co-founder said world leaders are not adequately preparing for the transition to the AI era, which he believes differs from past technological transitions because of the pace of AI progress and the scale of its potential impacts.
“This time really is different,” he wrote.

When is the Champions League draw and who is in each pot?
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher

When is the Champions League draw and who is in each pot?
- Published
The league phase draw for the 2026-27 Champions League campaign takes place on Thursday, 27 August at 17:00 BST in Monaco.
A total of 36 teams will enter that stage of the competition and while 29 teams qualified at the end of last season, the remaining seven places were decided by play-offs.
In the league phase, each team will face eight different teams once, with four home matches and four away matches.
For the draw, the 36 teams will be placed into four pots with one being the highest-ranked and four being the lowest. The pot placements are based on the club's Uefa club coefficient ranking from the five-season period ending at the conclusion of 2025-26.
Each team will face two teams from each of the four pots and cannot face a team from the same country as themselves.
Uefa announced a new rule on Wednesday that sides cannot host the same team in three successive league phases - so Liverpool will not draw Real Madrid at home and Arsenal will not travel to Inter Milan. Those fixtures could be drawn in reverse though.
The teams who finish in the top eight will qualify for the Champions League's round of 16. Those between ninth and 24th will enter the play-off knockout round. The 12 teams ranked between 25th and 36th will exit the competition when the league phase is concluded.

Premier League clubs Liverpool, Manchester City and Arsenal all feature in pot one alongside back-to-back Champions League winners Paris St-Germain, Bayern Munich, Real Madrid, Inter Milan, Barcelona and Atletico Madrid.
Aston Villa and Manchester United both return to the Champions League this season after not featuring last term. They are in pot two with Borussia Dortmund, Roma, Sporting, Porto, Club Brugge, Real Betis and PSV Eindhoven.
Pot three consists of Feyenoord, Lille, Bodo/Glimt, Napoli, RB Leipzig, Villarreal, Shakhtar Donetsk, Galatasaray and Fenerbahce.
Slavia Prague, VfB Stuttgart, Lask, Como, Lens, Sabah, AEK Athens, Slovan Bratislava and Viking make up pot four.

S. Africa sees 12.5 pct rise in tourist arrivals in July
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
06:02:51 CST
07:02:51 KST

JOHANNESBURG, Aug. 26 (Xinhua) -- South Africa received nearly 1 million foreign tourists in July, up 12.5 percent from a year earlier, Statistics South Africa (Stats SA) said Wednesday.
The number of overnight visitors, or tourists, reached 991,696 in July, compared with 881,393 in the same month last year, according to Stats SA's latest International Tourism report.
A total of 3.15 million travelers, including arrivals, departures and transit passengers, passed through South Africa's ports of entry and exit during the month. Of them, about 2.31 million were foreign travelers and 844,503 were South African residents.
Among 1.27 million foreign arrivals, 1.24 million were classified as visitors, including 251,049 same-day visitors and 991,696 overnight tourists.
Tourists from countries in the Southern African Development Community continued to account for the largest share, totaling 785,469 in July. Another 193,637 tourists came from overseas markets, while 11,751 came from other African countries.
Among overseas tourists, Europe remained the largest source region, with 97,461 arrivals, followed by North America with 41,037, according to the report.
The United States was the largest individual overseas source market, with 37,310 tourists, followed by Britain with 25,024 and the Netherlands with 17,066. France recorded the strongest year-on-year increase among the leading overseas markets, with arrivals rising 24.9 percent to 12,496. ■

Unknown Publisher

TEHRAN, Aug. 26 (Xinhua) -- The Islamic Revolution Guard Corps (IRGC) said on Wednesday that the Strait of Hormuz will not be opened if the United States does not accept Iran's conditions, according to the IRGC's official news outlet Sepah News.
IRGC spokesman Hossein Mohebbi told reporters that the strategic waterway remains under Iranian control and no vessel can pass through it without Iran's permission.
"All the enemy warships are at least 400 km away from the Strait of Hormuz, and from the military and territorial perspectives, no vessel is able to pass through this waterway without Iran's permission and management," Mohebbi said, adding that even the route near Oman is fully under Iranian control while underlining that the Strait of Hormuz belongs to Iran and Oman.
He said that Iran and Oman have reached agreements on their respective shares of the strait and its revenues following negotiations.
Mohebbi blamed U.S. "obstructionism" for delaying the negotiation process, noting that if Washington returns to the peace memorandum of understanding (MoU) it signed with Iran in June, "we can open the Strait of Hormuz within the agreed framework."
"Therefore, the United States must accept our conditions. If the United States does not accept our conditions, the Strait of Hormuz will not be opened under any circumstance," he added.
Iran tightened its grip on the Strait of Hormuz on Feb. 28, barring passage of vessels belonging to or affiliated with Israel and the United States following their joint strikes on Iranian territory.
On June 18, the United States and Iran signed the MoU on ending the war in the region on all fronts, including Lebanon. Under the MoU, they were scheduled to hold negotiations within a period of 60 days, which ended on Aug. 17, to reach a final agreement, but the talks' fate remains unclear following the escalation between the two countries last month.
In a joint statement on Tuesday night, Iran and Oman announced that they have discussed a phased framework that includes the establishment of a temporary joint shipping corridor in the Strait of Hormuz and an agreement to implement a joint demining project.
The statement said that technical negotiations will continue towards a permanent shipping corridor and the future administration of the waterway, including information exchange, traffic management, and relevant navigation and security services. ■

Chinese-style designs already enjoy a degree of recognition and appeal among European consumers, said Polish stylist Pawel Marczewski. Having visited China, Marczewski said he had long been drawn to Chinese craftsmanship and patterns, particularly dragon motifs.
He also pointed to the increasing presence of Chinese elements in international fashion, citing Adidas' use of pankou in designs that have attracted extensive attention on social media.
For Marczewski, the key lies in reinterpretation rather than replication. He told Xinhua that traditional details work best when paired with understated and natural designs.

Roundup: Syrians hope removal from U.S. list of state sponsors of terrorism brings tangible gains
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
06:02:10 CST
07:02:10 KST

DAMASCUS, Aug. 26 (Xinhua) -- For Syrians who have endured decades of U.S. sanctions, Washington's decision to remove their country from its list of state sponsors of terrorism has raised hopes of greater foreign investment, new jobs and improved living conditions, though some remain cautious about how quickly they will see real improvements in their daily lives.
The designation, in place since 1979, was formally lifted Monday. While the Syrian authorities have hailed the move as a historic diplomatic achievement, residents interviewed by Xinhua voiced measured expectations, focusing less on its diplomatic significance and more on tangible economic improvements.
"For us, what matters most is the economy, so we can rebuild the country, work, and attract foreign resources," said Osama al-Marji, a man in his 40s from the Damascus countryside. "Today, anyone who wants to start a project says there are sanctions and complications, and we, as citizens, are the first to feel that."
The terrorism listing was just one element of a much broader system of restrictions that accumulated over decades.
Washington imposed additional sanctions and restrictions on Damascus in 2004, which were expanded after the outbreak of the Syrian conflict in 2011, and further intensified in 2020, targeting those supporting the former government.
Since the fall of the Bashar al-Assad government in December 2024, Washington has rapidly rolled back much of its sanctions framework. In May 2025, broad sanctions relief was granted under a general license. A month later, U.S. President Donald Trump terminated the national emergency underpinning the Syria sanctions program and revoked six executive orders that formed its foundation.
Analysts say the decision reflects Washington's changing geopolitical calculations in the Middle East, not least prompted by Syria's strategic position and altered regional alliances following the fall of al-Assad's government.
Yet for ordinary Syrians grappling with shattered infrastructure, shrinking purchasing power and declining living standards, the policy shifts have yet to translate into visible change.
"We have heard this in the media, but we haven't seen anything on the ground. Foreign companies haven't come to the country yet," Khaldoun Qassem, a Damascus resident in his 40s, told Xinhua.
"If foreign companies come and start operating in the country, people will find jobs. But for now, there is still nothing," Qassem added.
Abdul Nafea Hammam, a man in his 60s originally from the central province of Homs and now living in Damascus, echoed that sentiment: "We hope to see something tangible on the ground -- improving living conditions, for example, and a salary sufficient to cover household expenses."
Analysts warned that while the delisting removes a major barrier to financial reintegration, some U.S. restrictions remain in place. International investors also continue to weigh security, banking and regulatory risks beyond sanctions. ■

====================================================================================================

Explainer: How far has the Kurdish-led group's integration into Syrian state gone?
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
06:02:08 CST
07:02:08 KST

Vehicles run at a street in Hasakah, a major city in northeastern Syria, where the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) had maintained a strong presence, Aug. 25, 2026. SDF commander Mazloum Abdi announced Tuesday the dissolution of the force following the completion of its integration into Syrian state institutions, ending a decade-long chapter in which the U.S.-backed group controlled large parts of northern and northeastern Syria. (Str/Xinhua)
by Hummam Sheikh Ali, Lin Jianjie
DAMASCUS, Aug. 26 (Xinhua) -- The dissolution of the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) announced on Tuesday marks a major step toward unifying Syria's military and administrative structures.
However, analysts say translating the political breakthrough into functioning institutions is likely to be a much longer and more complicated process.
WHY NOW?
SDF commander Mazloum Abdi announced Tuesday that the group's mission had ended and that it would cease to exist as an independent military force following agreements to integrate its military and civilian structures into the Syrian state.
The announcement followed months of negotiations over northeastern Syria, where the SDF and its affiliated Autonomous Administration had built separate military, security and governing structures during the country's conflict.
In March 2025, Syrian interim leader Ahmad al-Sharaa and Abdi signed an agreement calling for civilian and military institutions in the region to be incorporated into the state, but implementation stalled amid disagreements over military integration, political representation and the future of Kurdish-run institutions.
A turning point came early this year, when government forces advanced into SDF-held territory and a new agreement in January established a ceasefire and a phased integration process.
Abdullah al-Hamad Arabi, a Syrian political researcher, said the dissolution should be understood as the culmination of a gradual process shaped by the interests of Damascus, Washington and the Kurdish leadership.
He said Damascus sought to extend state authority, while Washington increasingly favored stability and stronger Syrian institutions. The Kurdish leadership, meanwhile, sought guarantees for Kurdish rights and recognition of its role in fighting the Islamic State (IS) group.
Arthur Quesnay, a researcher at Paris 1 Pantheon-Sorbonne University, said Abdi was also under pressure to demonstrate commitment to integration as patience in Damascus appeared to be running thin.
Regional shifts also fostered compromise. Türkiye views the SDF's main Kurdish component, the People's Protection Units (YPG), as closely linked to the outlawed Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK), while Washington relied on the SDF as its key local partner against IS.
Suleiman Elias, director of the Qamishli-based Euphrates Center for Studies, said changing regional circumstances increasingly favored strengthening central state institutions rather than maintaining parallel armed structures.
HOW FAR HAS INTEGRATION GONE?
Assessments about how much integration has actually been achieved diverge sharply. Under agreements, state institutions have expanded their presence in the northeast, while military and security structures have begun to be reorganized.
Elias said major issues, including border crossings, oil resources, weapons, IS detention facilities, and senior administrative appointments, have largely been settled, with remaining work focused mainly on incorporating SDF-affiliated offices and organizations into relevant authorities.
Quesnay, however, said concrete implementation remains limited. "On the ground, things are still controlled by the SDF and salaries are still paid by the Autonomous Administration. So we are really at the beginning, and we will see how it goes," he said.
Two brigades of around 1,300 former SDF fighters each have been formed, he noted, with two more envisaged, while negotiations over security forces and civilian employees continue.
The contrasting assessments illustrate the difficulty of measuring integration: formal authority over strategic facilities can be transferred relatively quickly, while merging chains of command, personnel, payrolls and administrative systems can take considerably longer.
Quesnay said Kurdish-majority areas remain effectively under Kurdish administration, while Autonomous Administration structures, checkpoints and salary systems continue operating in parts of Hasakah province.
Outstanding issues include education and control over oil and agricultural resources. Abdi said Tuesday that he had sought assurances on mother-tongue education rights, while Quesnay said Damascus wants to reassert authority over resources as Kurdish leaders seek to retain some leverage.
More broadly, Quesnay said the core challenge is absorbing not merely fighters and employees but an entire system of governance built during years when Damascus exercised little authority over much of northeastern Syria. "You can integrate individuals, but it's difficult to integrate two systems that are very different," he said.
WHAT DOES IT MEAN FOR SYRIA AND THE REGION?
If successfully implemented, the process could significantly strengthen Damascus' effort to rebuild a unified state after years of territorial and institutional fragmentation, as integrating former SDF forces, border crossings, resources and institutions under national structures would expand central authority and ease friction with Türkiye, analysts say.
Elias said integrating experienced SDF personnel could also strengthen Syria's defense and interior authorities, particularly given their experience combating IS.
For Syria's Kurds, however, the transition presents a different challenge: converting the military and territorial influence accumulated during the conflict into political representation and protected rights within the Syrian state.
Quesnay said the disappearance of the SDF as an independent force would not necessarily mean the disappearance of Kurdish political influence. Former SDF and Autonomous Administration figures could ultimately assume positions within national institutions.
The SDF's dissolution may have settled whether it will survive as an independent military force. The harder question, how its fighters, institutions and political constituency will fit into the Syrian state, is only beginning to be answered, according to the analysts. ■
Vehicles run at a street in Hasakah, a major city in northeastern Syria, where the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) had maintained a strong presence, Aug. 25, 2026. SDF commander Mazloum Abdi announced Tuesday the dissolution of the force following the completion of its integration into Syrian state institutions, ending a decade-long chapter in which the U.S.-backed group controlled large parts of northern and northeastern Syria. (Str/Xinhua)

Chinese solar study inspires Spanish expert to call for better planning
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
06:01:58 CST
07:01:58 KST

BARCELONA, Spain, Aug. 26 (Xinhua) -- A study by Chinese and American scientists on the impact of solar parks on bird biodiversity has prompted a Spanish expert to call for better planning of photovoltaic development to minimize its environmental impact.
Published this month in the journal Science, the study concluded that renewable energy and biodiversity can coexist if greater effort is made to select suitable areas for solar farms.
"This study by my Chinese and American colleagues is useful because it shows that what's been done has had a great environmental impact, and it justifies the need to study the situation beforehand," Francisco Valera, a scientist at the Arid Zones Experimental Station (EEZA) of the Spanish National Research Council (CSIC), told Xinhua in an interview on Wednesday.
"I always say, stopping to light a torch is better than running in the dark," he said.
Researchers compiled data on photovoltaic plants in 2,344 counties across China over the past 10 years and overlaid it with bird diversity maps, revealing widespread impacts with differences among regions and bird groups.
"These studies show which birds are more susceptible, which habitats need protecting more," Valera said. "More of this work could have been done before to avoid some major environmental impacts. But it's never too late."
According to Valera, an adequate environmental impact study should be carried out before a solar park is built, something he said has not always been done in Spain but is becoming more common.
"Zoning studies need to be carried out to see where to place photovoltaic plants, because we need them, but with minimum environmental impact," he said.
Building solar parks requires clearing vegetation that provides nesting areas for steppe birds and the invertebrates and seeds they feed on. The study's authors also found impacts on migratory and predatory birds and on both protected and unprotected species.
Valera said research groups are increasingly producing zoning maps, including in cooperation with authorities, to identify where photovoltaic plants can be placed without major impacts on biodiversity.
"The only pity is that this should have been done before," he said. ■

LONDON, Aug. 26 (Xinhua) -- British household energy price cap will rise 4 percent in the fourth quarter of 2026, the country's energy regulator Ofgem said on Wednesday.
From Oct. 1 to Dec. 31, the price cap will rise by 60 pounds (about 82 U.S. dollars) per year to 1,723 pounds (about 2,343 dollars) for the average household using both electricity and gas, according to Ofgem.
The energy price cap protects around 22 million households on default tariffs by limiting the maximum rates and standing charges that energy suppliers can charge. It is updated every three months to reflect changes in the underlying costs of supplying energy.
The rise from October is pushing household bills to their highest per-unit level in three years, and the price cap will further rise in January next year, according to energy consultancy Cornwall Insight.
Mixed signals over the next stages of the Middle East conflict have seen gas prices spike over recent weeks, it said, adding that this combined with a summer heatwave across Europe, supply disruption in Norway and strong demand from Asia have led to low winter gas stock levels.
Rising bills in the first three months of winter, with forecasts of a further increase in January will put pressure on the government to lay out how it plans to support vulnerable households, both through this winter and further ahead, it noted. ■

During searches of the suspect, investigators seized a smartphone containing evidence of his work for Russia. They also found a virtual wallet that he had created in anticipation of receiving cryptocurrency transfers from the Russians.
SSU investigators charged the agent under Part 2 of Article 111 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine – high treason committed under martial law.
The suspect is being held in custody without the possibility of bail. He faces life imprisonment with confiscation of property.
As reported by Ukrinform, SSU counterintelligence officers recently detained in Lviv a Russian agent who was coordinating strikes against Ukrzaliznytsia facilities, government institutions and military installations.

Dolly Parton Hated Working Out. But She Loved 'Rejoicing Exercises'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
21:42:44 UTC
06:42:44 KST

Dolly Parton knew a thing or two about working 9 to 5. Working out was another matter.
“If you tell me I’ve got to do an exercise routine…I dread it so bad,” she told Allure in 2021. Her workaround was “rejoicing exercises”: a freewheeling combination of gospel music, singing, stretching, shouting, and praising. “I do more ‘rejoicing’ than I do ‘working out,’” she said. She occasionally added a few floor exercises and squats—especially, as she put it, “diddly-squats.”
In doing so, she stumbled upon an important truth: Movement doesn’t have to feel like punishment to count.
“Dolly honored herself through movement,” says Michelle Segar, a lifestyle-change sustainability scientist at the University of Michigan and author of The Joy Choice: How to Finally Achieve Lasting Changes in Eating and Exercise. Parton tossed out the rules about what exercise was supposed to look like and designed something that reflected what she needed. “She knew this was for her,” Segar says. “And because it was for her, she had to design it for herself.”
That instinct—to stop chasing the supposedly perfect workout and start with movement that feels good, meaningful, or restorative—could make it easier to keep moving over time. Here’s what we all can learn from Parton’s views on exercise and movement.
“Rejoicing exercises” were quintessentially Dolly
Parton’s routine combined the forces that shaped so much of her life: faith, music, and creative self-expression. She began singing in her maternal grandfather Jake Owens’ church at age 6, and later described feeling divinely inspired as a songwriter, says Leigh H. Edwards, a professor of English at Florida State University and author of Dolly Parton, Gender, and Country Music.
“She often approached her expression on her own terms,” Edwards says, “just as she did when she created her own Dolly image and charted her own trailblazing path for her career.” Exercise was no exception.
Judy Eaton, a professor of psychology at Wilfrid Laurier University in Ontario, teaches positive psychology—the study of how people flourish, rather than only how they struggle. She calls Parton “the poster child for positive psychology.”
Many of Eaton’s students arrive knowing Parton only from Hannah Montana. Eaton introduces them to her as an example of gratitude, optimism, and authenticity; after Parton passed away, former students emailed to say they were grateful her class had helped them understand who she was as a person.
Stop looking for the “right” way to exercise
Many people have absorbed the idea that there’s one correct way to exercise. “We as a society have been taught you’re supposed to exercise in this way for this long, and your body has to feel this way,” Segar says. “You have to breathe hard.” If you can’t—or simply don’t like it—“you don’t do it.”
Public-health guidelines are useful for describing how much activity is associated with certain health benefits. But they don’t necessarily tell people how to fit movement into hectic, unpredictable lives. Fitness marketing has strengthened the idea that a workout only counts when it meets a particular standard, Segar says, creating an all-or-nothing trap: Do the “right” workout, or do nothing.
Parton built her routine around what she would actually do. Instead of deciding exercise wasn’t for her, she decided the gym-and-sweat version wasn’t for her. “We don’t start with the right way,” Segar says. “We start with our way.”
Dr. George Hennawi, physician executive director of geriatrics and senior services at MedStar Health, sees particular value in that approach as people age. When he asks his patients what it means to age successfully, their answers usually involve continuing to do what they already love—whether that’s traveling, gardening, singing, or spending time with their grandchildren.
“She flipped the equation,” Hennawi says of Parton. “What makes me happy? How do I define living successfully, living happily, aging well?” Her answer, as he sees it: “I don’t love exercise—let me bring exercise to the stuff that I love to do.”
That also means reconsidering why you’re moving. Goals like losing weight or preventing a disease years from now can be “abstract, future, often even shame-producing reasons for exercise,” Segar says. Parton’s reason was immediate and personal: She wanted to rejoice. “She’s using movement to fuel herself and live her life,” Segar says, “not to comply with doctor’s orders or to meet some standard of beauty.”
Ask how you want movement to make you feel
“Joyful movement” is a useful phrase, but Segar encourages people to expand their vocabulary. Not every worthwhile walk will make you giddy. It might instead make you feel grounded, energized, connected, or less stressed. It could help you shift out of work mode before walking through your front door—or give you five quiet minutes before the rest of the day begins.
Start by asking: “What do you want to feel while you’re moving?” Segar suggests. Then choose an activity likely to deliver that feeling.
The answer will look different for everyone. “For one person, it could be, ‘I’m going to close my door and put on headphones and dance for five minutes,’” Segar says. Someone else might grab a colleague and walk the stairs at lunch, or chase their kids around the backyard. A walk might serve an entirely different purpose: “I want to transition from my work brain to my family brain,” someone might decide, and head around the block before going home.
Think of movement as a menu rather than a prescription. “You choose what you want based on what you feel like,” Segar says—and that might change daily. “When we toss out the rules, physical movement can be the mechanism for achieving those things.”
Connecting movement to something personally meaningful can also make it more motivating. “Doing things because we have to is never the right way to get us to engage in them more,” Eaton says. “If tying it to something that’s really meaningful to you gets you doing it, then all the better.” For Parton, that meant singing gospel songs and praising—a routine she traced to her Pentecostal upbringing.
Positive emotions can create momentum, too. Eaton points to psychologist Barbara Fredrickson’s broaden-and-build theory: “If you can make yourself experience positive emotions, it makes you more willing to try new things,” she says. A favorite song might put you in the mood to start moving; movement can lift your mood further, making it easier to come back for more.
Rejoicing exercises could engage the mind along with the body, Hennawi adds. “When you’re dancing and singing, you’re stimulating your brain,” he says. “You’re stimulating your body, and you’re connecting all those dots.”
Create your own rejoicing exercises
There’s no official choreography—and prescribing one would miss the point. Choose music you love, if that helps. Dance, stretch, sway, walk, garden, or wave your arms around your living room. Try it for five minutes instead of waiting until you have time for 30. The goal is to finish feeling better than when you started.
Here’s one very Baltimore example from Hennawi: Suppose an older adult’s idea of joy is watching the Ravens and eating ice cream. Without missing a play, they could add arm raises or gentle knee and hip movements while watching on the couch. “Can you add a tiny little bit of exercise?” he asks. “We can do it incrementally, step by step.”
Eaton suspects Parton wouldn’t have issued instructions for copying her routine. The point isn’t to move exactly like Dolly. It’s to move more like yourself. “I think she’d just say, ‘Do what feels good to you,’” she says.

Colombia’s president proposes prison ships and mega-jails to fight crime
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
21:40:02 UTC
06:40:02 KST

Laura Gamba
27 August 2026•Update: 27 August 2026
Colombian President Abelardo De La Espriella reaffirmed his commitment to an overhaul of Colombia’s penitentiary system Wednesday, pledging to build maximum-security mega-prisons and deploy converted naval vessels as offshore jails to isolate the country's most dangerous criminal leaders.
Speaking during a ceremony recognizing the country’s new military leadership, De La Espriella emphasized that his administration is actively advancing plans to develop high-security infrastructure to dismantle organized crime networks operating from behind bars.
“My commitment to building maximum-security mega-prisons to incarcerate the country’s most dangerous terrorists remains unchanged,” he declared, noting that the new facilities will be developed “in partnership with the private sector.”
In a move aimed at disrupting extortion and terror operations directed from inside correctional institutions, the administration is preparing to isolate major cartel leaders at sea.
The Ministries of Defense and Justice, alongside the National Penitentiary and Prison Institute (INPEC), are advancing a project to convert a Colombian Navy vessel into a floating prison.
The strategy mirrors a similar proposal announced in Ecuador by President Daniel Noboa to station prison ships off the Pacific coast. It also builds on a historical precedent in Colombia. In 2007, under former President Alvaro Uribe, prominent criminal leaders including Central Bolivar Bloc warlord Carlos Mario Jimenez, alias “Macaco,” and Norte del Valle Cartel boss Diego Fernando Montoya, alias “Don Diego,” were temporarily held aboard naval ships to enforce absolute isolation.
De La Espriella recently celebrated the high-security transfer of 20 incarcerated gang members from Barranquilla to Bogota.
“I’m coming for all of them,” the president stated. “I put an end to their privileges, their criminal control from behind bars, and the crime operations from which they sought to extort, threaten and sow fear among working people.”
The government’s broader plan aims to reverse a longstanding trend of correctional facilities acting as operational hubs for crime.
De La Espriella issued a direct ultimatum to INPEC Director Col. Daniel Gutierrez, demanding immediate results in retaking control of the nation’s jails and warning that officials who fail to meet strict security objectives will face immediate dismissal.
“It is regrettable that Colombia’s prisons have ceased to be places of incarceration and have instead become dens of crime --universities of crime -- from which extortion and threats are carried out, murders are ordered, and terrorist organizations are directed,” De La Espriella said.

OpenAI calls Hugging Face cyber breach ‘warning shot’ over autonomous AI agents
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
21:38:54 UTC
06:38:54 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
27 August 2026•Update: 27 August 2026
OpenAI described a cybersecurity breach involving Hugging Face, a widely used artificial intelligence (AI) platform, as a “warning shot,” saying it demonstrated that highly capable AI agents could autonomously bypass safeguards and carry out dangerous actions.
The US AI company released a technical report Wednesday detailing the incident, which occurred during internal tests designed to measure the cybersecurity capabilities of several OpenAI models.
The models, operating with reduced safeguards, circumvented controls intended to isolate them from the internet, exploited vulnerabilities in OpenAI’s research infrastructure and accessed third-party systems.
OpenAI said the activity was primarily driven by an internal-only research model comparable in scale to GPT-5.6 Sol.
GPT-5.6 Sol was also involved in parts of the incident.
The agents turned an internally hosted package-management system into an unauthorized message board, allowing them to share technical information and coordinate without human direction.
After gaining internet access, they found publicly exposed Hugging Face credentials and combined them with vulnerabilities in the company’s infrastructure.
Between July 11 and 13, the agents executed code on 41 Hugging Face production dataset workers, gained root access to at least one production node and downloaded four private code repositories, according to the report.
OpenAI detected suspicious activity on July 19, informed Hugging Face the following day, and publicly disclosed the incident on July 21.
The company said no OpenAI customer data, products or services were affected, stressing that the testing conditions did not reflect its normal production environment.
OpenAI said it would introduce stricter network restrictions, more isolated testing environments, stronger access controls and enhanced monitoring to prevent similar incidents.

Mark Carney on Sept. 16 will also attend European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen’s annual State of the Union address to the European Parliament in Strasbourg, according to local media reports.
European Parliament President Roberta Metsola said the visit would be an opportunity to “deepen EU-Canada ties and strengthen our bond.”
The visit comes as relations between Canada and the US deteriorated following the collapse of trade negotiations and Washington’s imposition of new tariffs on Canadian goods, with Ottawa quickly retaliating.

Carney has increasingly sought to diversify Canada’s economic and diplomatic partnerships and strengthen ties with countries beyond the US.
Conversely, Canada and the EU have also moved to strengthen their strategic partnership in recent years, with cooperation spanning trade, technology, energy, security, and defense.
In June, Canada became the first non-European country whose companies were allowed to participate in the EU’s Security Action for Europe (SAFE) defense initiative, which is backed by up to €150 billion ($175 billion) in financing for joint defense procurement.
A European Commission spokesperson told CBC News that Carney’s visit is a “strong sign of the close relationship between Canada and the EU” and is intended to “clearly signal the intention and ambition on both sides to upgrade our partnership.”

Carney also became the first leader of a non-European country to participate in a European Political Community summit when he attended the gathering this May in Yerevan, Armenia.

Halis Sunnetci
27 August 2026•Update: 27 August 2026
Fenerbahce defeated Lyon 2-1 away on Wednesday to advance to the UEFA Champions League league phase for the first time since reaching the group stage in the 2008-09 season.
The Turkish side advanced 3-2 on aggregate after the first leg in Istanbul ended 1-1, returning to Europe's elite club competition.
Fenerbahce were barred by UEFA from the Champions League for two seasons following the 2011 match-fixing investigation, which prevented the Turkish club from competing in Europe's elite competition despite winning the 2010-11 Super Lig title.
The club and former president Aziz Yildirim were later acquitted in a retrial, while a 2016 prosecution indictment described the match-fixing case as a plot by members of the Fetullah Terrorist Organization (FETO) who had infiltrated in Türkiye’s judiciary and police.
Lyon started brightly, with Malick Fofana forcing Fenerbahce goalkeeper Ederson into a save in the eighth minute with a left-footed effort from outside the box.
Fenerbahce gradually settled into the match and registered their first shot on target in the 13th minute, when Oguz Aydin's effort from the left side of the box was saved by Lyon goalkeeper Dominik Greif following a pass from Talisca.
The visitors grew increasingly dangerous, with Archie Brown seeing his powerful effort from a tight angle saved by Greif in the 19th minute.
A minute later, Oguz Aydin came close to opening the scoring when his deep corner struck the crossbar.
Fenerbahce took the lead in the 24th minute.
Oguz Aydin sent a cross into the area and Vedat Muriqi's initial header was saved by Greif. The Kosovo international reacted quickly to the rebound and fired into the bottom-right corner from close range.
Fenerbahce doubled their advantage four minutes later.
Mason Greenwood delivered a cross from a corner, and Brown rose to head the ball into the top-left corner from close range.
Lyon came close to reducing the deficit in the 35th minute when Vedat Muriqi's attempted clearance from a corner struck his own post.
Ederson then denied Tyler Morton in the 41st minute, pushing away the midfielder's powerful effort from outside the box.
Fenerbahce went into the break with a 2-0 advantage and a 3-1 aggregate lead.
Lyon began the second half with greater attacking intent, putting Fenerbahce under pressure during the opening 10 minutes.
However, the visitors began to find space on the counterattack, with Oguz Aydin firing high and wide from the left side of the box after being set up by Matteo Guendouzi.
Lyon pulled one back in the 61st minute. Ainsley Maitland-Niles found Fofana on the left side of the box, and the forward sent a left-footed effort into the bottom-right corner to make it 2-1.
The hosts thought they had equalized in the 64th minute when Lois Openda headed Abner Vinicius' cross into the net, but the goal was ruled out for offside following a VAR review.
Lyon were denied again when Kail Boudache scored in the 71st minute, but the referee overturned the goal following a VAR review after ruling that Zachary Athekame had fouled Brown during the buildup.
Fenerbahce looked to restore their two-goal advantage, but Guendouzi's deflected effort from outside the box in the 82nd minute was saved by Greif.
The Turkish side held on for a 2-1 victory, completing a 3-2 aggregate win and securing their place in the Champions League.

Germany reportedly considers helping fund UK nukes
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
22:30:13 BST
06:30:13 KST

Germany is reportedly considering helping to fund Britain’s nuclear deterrent as Berlin examines closer integration with existing UK and French nuclear forces rather than developing an independent German arsenal.
Germany is reportedly considering financial support for Britain’s nuclear deterrent as part of discussions over how European states could rely more heavily on existing British and French nuclear capabilities, the Telegraph reports.
According to an exclusive report by The Telegraph, officials in Berlin are examining whether German funding could contribute towards the UK’s nuclear programme as part of a wider attempt to strengthen Europe’s nuclear deterrence and reduce dependence on the United States.
The newspaper reports that Germany’s preference is to integrate more closely with the nuclear forces already maintained by Britain and France rather than pursue its own atomic weapons programme, with one source saying Berlin has a strong interest in seeing Europe’s existing nuclear powers increase their capabilities.
A source quoted by The Telegraph said: “We have a very strong interest that the existing nuclear powers in Europe extend their capabilities.”
The reported discussions involve London, Berlin and Paris and are said to have gathered pace as European governments consider the implications of a reduced American military commitment to the continent. Germany is reportedly looking at several forms of support, ranging from financial contributions towards the British deterrent to conventional military assistance intended to protect the infrastructure that supports it.
Among the more concrete options reported by The Telegraph is the possible deployment of German-operated Patriot air defence systems to important British nuclear sites, including HMNB Clyde at Faslane in Scotland, where the Royal Navy’s ballistic missile submarine force is based.
A British defence source cited by the newspaper reportedly regarded that type of conventional contribution as more credible than a substantial German role in building Britain’s nuclear submarines, saying: “The ability to contribute to the defence of Faslane is more credible, likely and appropriate.”
German officials are nevertheless also reported to have considered whether the country’s industrial base could contribute to future British programmes involving submarines, missiles or uranium enrichment. The same report notes doubts on the British side over whether German industry has the specialist experience necessary to play a major role in the construction and maintenance of the UK’s nuclear-powered submarine fleet.
Britain is currently replacing its four Vanguard-class ballistic missile submarines with four Dreadnought-class boats, which will carry the Trident II D5 ballistic missile and maintain the UK’s Continuous At-Sea Deterrent. London is also developing the Astraea nuclear warhead alongside the American W93 programme.
The UK’s deterrent remains sovereign in terms of decisions over nuclear use, but important parts of the programme depend upon cooperation with the United States. Trident missiles are manufactured in America and supported through facilities at Kings Bay in Georgia, while British and American warhead development also remains closely connected.
That dependence is reportedly one of the issues under discussion in Berlin. A security source quoted in The Telegraph’s report said: “There is thinking and talking about how the existing nuclear capabilities [such as Trident] may play a bigger role for the defence of Europe, and of deeper cooperation among European countries.”
The discussions would not give Germany control over British nuclear weapons, nor does the reporting suggest that Berlin would participate in decisions over their use. The proposals instead concern Germany contributing financially, industrially or with conventional military forces to the wider infrastructure supporting Britain’s deterrent.
Germany is reportedly holding similar discussions with France, whose nuclear forces remain entirely under French national control and include both submarine-launched and air-launched weapons. Paris has already opened a broader debate with European partners over the possible role of French nuclear forces in continental deterrence.

As the US and China compete over AI, Asean must secure strategic autonomy

Opinion
As the US and China compete over AI, Asean must secure strategic autonomy
Asean’s choice is not between technological dominance and isolation but between dependence and agency
3-MIN READ3-MIN
3
 Listen
Dr AbdulWahed Jalal Nori is an assistant professor at  International Islamic University Malaysia (IIUM) and coordinator of the Centre for Foresight Studies. 
International relations has long measured power through familiar instruments: military capability, territory, energy, capital and control of trade. The digital revolution added information to that equation. Artificial intelligence (AI) is taking the transformation further by turning information into a strategic capability that can shape economies, governments and societies.
For the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean), the central question is no longer whether Southeast Asia will participate in the AI revolution. The more consequential question is whether Asean will possess enough control over the infrastructure, knowledge and systems behind AI to shape its own future or whether it will have to rent intelligence from others.
Southeast Asia is rapidly becoming an important physical centre of the AI economy. Data centres are expanding and investment is flowing into digital infrastructure. The International Energy Agency expects electricity demand from data centres in Southeast Asia to more than double by 2030.
Malaysia and Singapore are emerging as major regional hubs, while Indonesia and Thailand seek to capture a larger share of the digital infrastructure boom. However, beneath this expansion lies a strategic paradox: Asean might provide the land, electricity, connectivity, markets and physical infrastructure for the AI economy while depending on external powers for advanced chips, foundational models, cloud platforms and technological standards.
This marks a subtler dependency: states retain sovereignty while increasingly relying on foreign AI systems to run critical functions. This matters because Asean’s traditional concept of strategic autonomy was developed in a world where states could diversify their economic and diplomatic relationships without necessarily having to choose their technological architecture.
That assumption is becoming less secure. The United States and China are developing competing technology ecosystems. Reuters reported earlier this month that Washington was preparing to encourage countries taking part in its Pax Silica initiative to choose between competing US and Chinese AI frameworks. Meanwhile, China is expanding AI engagement with Southeast Asia through training, infrastructure, research and industrial applications.

UK launches mini solar scheme … into a thicket of red tape
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
21:30:00 UTC
06:30:00 KST

LONDON — Andy Burnham’s government desperately wants to find ways to help Brits save money on soaring energy bills.
The latest idea: Getting them to put mini solar panels on their balconies so they can generate their own power.
From Thursday, the tech — already a success story in countries like Germany — will be available to buy in high street stores and install in U.K. properties for the first time. Plug-in solar panels are “a simple, affordable way for households to take control of their energy bills and start saving straight away,” Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh said.
But to get there, ministers face a clutch of problems, including uncooperative landlords, safety fears, and hundreds of pounds in upfront costs.
Advertisement
Regulation, regulation, regulation
The technology was badged as a simpler solution for renters or other people without space at home for traditional rooftop panels.
People who want to install the kit may need permission from landlords, freeholders or councils, therefore. And some are already not playing ball.
One housing association, Sovereign Network Group — which manages 86,000 homes across London and the south of England — said it has a blanket ban on letting residents install plug-in solar in the buildings it manages.
“While solar panels may be installed through our planned retrofit programme, we do not permit plug-in or ‘plug and play’ solar panels in SNG properties,” said Carol Bailey, SNG’s building and occupational safety director, citing potential “electrical safety risks.”
Claire Hibbit, corporate affairs director at another housing association in England, Notting Hill Genesis, which manages over 60,000 properties, said they wanted to help tenants use cleaner power — before listing all the hurdles tenants would need to clear before plugging in solar panels: ensuring they were bought from a reputable outlet, holding an electricity safety certificate, safe installation, no extra fire risk, the right weight for a balcony, and not breaking any rules governing conservation areas.
A third, L&Q, which manages over 105,000 properties, said it welcomed the potential of plug-in panels to help cut bills. But its Director of Health and Building Safety Steve Pettitt added: “As this technology is new, we're still considering the detail, including how it can be used safely in residents’ homes.”
Advertisement
“Plug-in solar panels send electricity in the opposite direction in your property’s wiring,” said Luke Osborne, technical director of the charity Electrical Safety First. His organization has “concerns plug-in solar panels may damage older devices in people's homes which protect people from electric shock,” he warned.
Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh, who talked up the benefits of plug-in solar panels, arrives at 10 Downing Street for a cabinet meeting on July 21, 2026. | Dan Kitwood/Getty Images
Another trade association, the Electrical Contractors Association, warned ahead of the government's roll out that plug-in solar could “overload circuits — creating a risk of fire and electrical shocks — without careful checks by qualified electricians.”
‘Robust’
The government insisted plug-in solar is not intended for every home, and has been made legal only after “rigorous, independent safety testing,” using panels “safe and compatible with U.K. wiring.”
“As a government, we are quite confident that the safety case is robust, and the additional work that we've done to assure ourselves of that is giving us the confidence to be able to legalize these in the U.K. and assure ourselves that they will be safe for people in their homes,” added Energy Minister Martin McCluskey.
He said he had written to landlords to make the case for plug-in solar and hoped “that would be looked on favorably” by them. The government has flagged a detailed safety checklist as part of the roll-out.
The government reckons that each piece of kit could produce enough power to cover 20 percent of average household energy use, according to an announcement from the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero Wednesday.
Advertisement
Ministers said the “easy-to-install” panels could save homes up to £110 per year in energy bills, part of Andy Burnham’s effort to give people some “breathing space” on the cost of living. The promise came on the same day the regulator announced household energy bills are set to rise once again from October, driven up by the war between the U.S., Israel and Iran.
Saving money (slowly)
Plug-in solar panels also come with a hefty upfront price, even as the government promotes them as a way — over time — to save money.
As of Wednesday, one U.K. online retailer, flagged by McCluskey as a potential provider of plug-in solar, had set the price for a piece of kit at £699. The government believes the price of a single panel will settle, thanks to market competition, between £400 and £600, the minister said.
This means, as the U.K. heads into higher energy prices this fall, the £110 annual savings proposed off the back of plug-in solar would not help voters start recouping the costs until the end of the decade.
McCluskey ruled out government support to cover the upfront costs of the tech, such as schemes that already exist for other clean power like heat pumps and larger-scale rooftop solar panels. Ministers could revisit the issue in the future, he added.
Even at a higher price of between £500 and £700, the so-called “payback period” is “still lower than you would get from rooftop solar,” McCluskey later insisted.
Advertisement
The push comes as worries grow about the impact of rising household energy bills.
Data released this week by consumer group Citizens Advice showed more than 10 million British households are worried about how they'll afford their bills in the colder months ahead. The government must find a way to help people “trapped in cold, dark homes this winter,” urged Citizens Advice boss Claire Moriarty.

The USD as global reserve currency
I've often wondered why central banks around the world consider the US Dollar as a "Safe Haven". The USA has been responsible for multiple financial disasters, and if it was a company would have been declared bankrupt long ago.Without Kissinger's dodgy deal in 1974 with Saudi Arabia, the dollar would be worthless.
- Stan
Hi Stan,
Part of that has to do with the fact that the US economy has been sitting at the centre of the global economy, and the US dollar has been the global reserve currency, since the end of WWII.
That's why, during the GFC, we still saw a massive "flight to safety" into the US dollar, even though the US was ground zero for the financial crisis, because the USD was considered the ultimate "safe haven" asset (which is an annoying tautology, because a haven is safe by definition) and source of liquidity.
But interestingly, you may have seen an opinion that JD Vance (the US vice president) shared on this topic in 2023, which has resurfaced in recent weeks.
He made the argument that he doesn't think the US has derived a net benefit from the USD being the global reserve currency:
"This is like maybe super heterodox," he said.
"I'm not sure that I think the reserve currency has actually been good for the United States.
"I think there is a good argument that reserve currency status is akin to coal in Appalachia - it's a resource curse, right?
"It allows your consumers to consume very cheaply. That's been the story of the American economy for the last 15 or so years, even before that, is we can just borrow, basically in an unlimited way, because we have the reserve currency, so that's a massive subsidy to incurring debt and the debt is cheaper even in a raised interest rate environment."

The RBA is right to be diplomatic about how it discusses a reduction in the share of US dollars in its portfolio and if this occurred during the H1 2025 US-led turmoil then it appeared to be in good company among global central banks in trimming its dollar holdings, though many emerging market central banks chose gold instead of the euro.

'RBA must remain vigilant' as household spending grows, analyst says
Household spending is growing at its fastest pace in three years, according to an APAC economist at global job site Indeed.

Key Event
RBA 'quietly' sold US dollar reserves
It has been revealed that the Reserve Bank reduced its target share of US dollars in its foreign reserves portfolio by 10% in 2025.
The RBA lowered its allocation from 55% to 45%, taking it back to 2012 levels.
"During 2024/25, the portfolio allocation to the US dollar was adjusted to 45 per cent from 55 per cent while the allocation to euro was adjusted from 20 per cent to 30 per cent," the 2025 RBA Annual Report noted.
"Our largest allocation remains the US dollar, reflecting the significant depth in US dollar currency and asset markets."
In a research note today, Deutsche Bank described the move as a "quiet reduction" in reserves.
By the reduction in the RBA's exposure to US dollars happened over 12 months ago now, so why is Deutsche Bank raising it now?
Here's what Deutsche's Macro Strategist Lachlan Dynan said:
We bring it to light now as fresh questions are asked on whether US dollar reserves and Treasuries have lost some of their previously exceptional appeal, and especially more recently as a strained US fiscal position has led to some concerning signals on the usability of US dollar reserves for intervention purposes.
The reduction in the US dollar allocation takes the share back to levels seen in 2012, when the Eurozone debt crisis may have been important in seeing the RBA reduce their EUR share of reserves given the impact on the liquidity and replicability of the portfolio back then.
Indeed, the EUR share of global reserves declined by ~7ppts from 2011-2015. So it is interesting that 2025 saw the RBA effectively reverse that change (in terms of the USD share) at the same time as US-centric fiscal and policy concerns lifted.
Mr Dynan highlighted the extraordinary nature of the disclosure in the annual report.
As far as we are aware this is the first G10 central bank to have effectively confirmed some reduction in its target USD allocation in recent years, even if the allocation remains within the range of historical allocations.
The RBA Assistant Governor Christopher Kent was recently quizzed on the moved and played it down.
"The change ... just reflected that from time to time we look at our benchmarks and we review those, and we thought we were a little bit long on the US dollar at the time, so there was just a small change in our allocation. But I’m one of the first people to say you can’t really predict exchange rates and where they’re going. So it wasn’t really based on some deep insight because I don’t have any deep insights on exchange rates, other than: don’t predict where they’re going"
But here's a key point. Could it be that the RBA's exposure to the US dollar was too great considering the risks?
As Deutsche Bank points out in its research note, those risks have only increased.
1. Treasury liquidity loosing some of its shine, especially after liberation day
2. Risks of more US-centric shocks given strained US external and fiscal positions: "Indeed, in the event of a major US-centric fiscal episode, its plausible that the broader Australian Dollar would be volatile at the same time as the US Dollar and Treasuries were coming under downward pressure, and market liquidity notably impaired."
3. Emergence of a tail risk around accessibility: "A less liquid Treasury market is one thing, but not being able to sell or access reserves is a risk that was implausible until recently, especially for allies, but may be a tail risk that is at least worth considering more recently," Lachlan Dynan noted.
Deutsche Bank has raised the idea that a major US fiscal "episode" led the RBA to make a noteworthy shift in its foreign currency reserves, to avoid too much exposure to the US dollar.
Absolutely watch this space.

The latest pressure campaign comes nearly six months after the US and Israel launched the war against Iran in late February. Large-scale fighting has subsided following a series of temporary agreements, but efforts to reach a lasting settlement have stalled, while Washington has stepped up economic pressure on Tehran.
Iran has denounced the expanded sanctions as a violation of international law and argued that Washington’s attempt to force other countries to sever economic relations with Tehran amounts to interference in their sovereignty.

U.S. diesel fuel inventories fell to a record seasonal low

U.S. diesel fuel inventories fell to a record seasonal low
Kyiv • UNN
U.S. diesel fuel inventories fell to 103.4 million barrels—the lowest level for August since records began. Prices exceeded $5.60 per gallon.
U.S. diesel fuel inventories ahead of the fall demand season have fallen to the lowest seasonal level ever recorded. As of August 21, inventories of distillate fuel, which predominantly includes diesel, stood at 103.4 million barrels, Bloomberg reports, according to UNN.
Details
According to the U.S. Energy Information Administration, inventories had not reached such a low level during this period since record-keeping began in the early 1980s.
Global demand for diesel typically rises around October due to the start of the heating season and increased agricultural activity. Low inventories amid growing demand could lead to further increases in fuel prices and intensify inflationary pressure.
The global market is losing part of its supplies
The situation is being affected by disruptions in the international petroleum products market. Due to the war with Iran, exports of refined fuel through the Strait of Hormuz have nearly ceased, while russia has reduced diesel exports following Ukrainian drone attacks on its oil refineries.
Russia to extend ban on diesel fuel exports until September - Reuters25.08.26, 23:37 • 3692 views
Retail diesel fuel prices in the United States have already exceeded $5.60 per gallon. This is close to the highest level since the start of the war between the United States and Iran and less than 20 cents below the record set in 2022.
At the same time, margins at U.S. refineries producing diesel have reached record levels in recent weeks. U.S. fuel exports have also risen to a very high level, but their volume does not offset the decline in global supplies.

Iran says US owes full compensation for damages caused by unilateral sanctions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
21:26:22 UTC
06:26:22 KST

Mohammad Sio
27 August 2026•Update: 27 August 2026
Iran said Wednesday that the US bears international responsibility for damages caused by its unilateral sanctions and must provide full compensation, including restitution and reparations.
In a message to the UN and Security Council, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi described the US measures as an “economic terrorism campaign” carried out through unilateral coercive measures, which he said are unlawful under international law.
“The Islamic Republic of Iran reserves its right to resort to all available means to pursue accountability, compensation and redress, and to hold the perpetrators of these inhumane and unlawful acts accountable,” Araghchi said, according to Iran’s state broadcaster IRIB.
He said the US campaign “entails international responsibility, including an obligation to provide full compensation for all material and moral damages, including restitution and reparations, in accordance with international law.”
Araghchi also said the US bears “full international responsibility” and can face individual criminal responsibility, if the relevant legal elements are established, for the consequences of “unlawful and criminal acts and the harm caused to the Iranian people.”
He urged the UN Security Council and member states to condemn and reject Washington’s use of “unilateral coercive measures and secondary sanctions” to pressure sovereign states into changing their legitimate economic interests and trade relations.
Iran also called on countries not to recognize, approve or implement such measures that seek to link their sovereign rights to policies unilaterally determined by Washington.
Araghchi urged the US “to immediately halt threats and coercive actions aimed at forcing third countries and their nationals to alter legitimate economic relations and interests.”
He also called on the UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres to assess and report on the humanitarian and human rights consequences of such measures, including their impact on civilians’ access to food, medicine, health care, energy, transportation and humanitarian assistance.
Araghchi said relevant evidence should be independently assessed, documented and preserved to ensure future accountability.
On Monday, the Trump administration launched “Operation Economic Outcast,” a sweeping sanctions campaign aimed at further isolating Iran from the global financial system.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the measures target key Iranian economic sectors, including aviation, shipping, gold, technology and digital assets, with more than 60 entities, individuals and vessels blacklisted.
Bessent said Washington’s objective was to sever Iran’s economic lifelines, describing the campaign as the “economic asphyxiation” of the Iranian government.
Last week, US President Donald Trump announced his intention to launch what he called “the most crushing economic operation ever taken against any country,” describing his maximum-pressure campaign against Iran as “economic warfare and isolation on an unprecedented scale.”
He also said countries that provide Tehran with an economic “lifeline” – through their financial institutions, businesses, airports, or government entities – would face severe economic consequences.
The US and Israel launched attacks on Iran in late February, prompting Tehran to retaliate against Israel and US military assets across the region before a ceasefire agreement was reached in April.
In mid-June, Washington and Tehran signed a memorandum of understanding calling for freedom of navigation in the Hormuz Strait, but the deal’s implementation later stalled amid persistent differences.
Last month, the US resumed its attacks on Iran, while Tehran responded by targeting US military facilities and equipment in a number of Arab countries.

In Iceland, 51% of citizens support resuming negotiations on joining the EU
Kyiv • UNN
Ahead of the referendum, 51.3% of Icelanders support resuming negotiations on joining the EU. The vote will take place on August 29.
The majority of Iceland’s residents support resuming negotiations on the country’s accession to the European Union ahead of the referendum to be held on August 29. According to Yle, 51.3% of those surveyed support the negotiations, while 48.7% oppose them, writes UNN.
Details
The poll was conducted by the Maskina Research Institute on August 21–25, surveying 1,019 people. The gap between supporters and opponents of the negotiations has narrowed compared with the previous poll, in which 52.2% supported resuming them and 47.8% opposed it.
Iceland applied to join the EU in 2009, and negotiations began in June 2010. In 2013, the country completed the negotiations, but the accession process was not finalized.
The war waged by Russia against Ukraine, statements by US President Donald Trump regarding the possible annexation of Greenland by the United States, and the rising cost of living have influenced the debate on membership.
Iceland is already part of the single European market, the Schengen Area, and the European Free Trade Association, but it has no formal voting rights in EU decision-making.
If the referendum produces a positive result, accession negotiations could begin by the end of 2026 and last several years. Membership would entail, among other things, Iceland’s participation in EU decision-making, joining the customs union, and potentially adopting the euro.
