Hamas and other armed factions in Gaza have agreed -- for the first time -- to surrender their weapons and transfer full civilian and security authority to a UN-recognized transitional administration, Nikolay Mladenov, the Gaza Peace Board’s high representative, said Wednesday.
Mladenov made the remarks at a UN Security Council briefing on implementation of the US-backed Gaza peace plan, according to statements made by the board on US social-media company X.
“For the first time, Hamas and the armed factions in Gaza have agreed to hand over their weapons and to transfer full governing authority -- civilian and security -- to a transitional administration recognized by the United Nations,” Mladenov said.
He claimed the move could “dramatically improve life in a sustainable way for Palestinians in Gaza; to provide durable security for Israelis.”
The Board of Peace unveiled a 15-point roadmap in late July calling for the disarmament of Hamas and other armed factions, the transfer of Gaza’s administration to a National Committee, and a phased Israeli withdrawal.
Earlier this month, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu rejected the plan, saying Hamas must be fully disarmed before any Israeli withdrawal.
Hamas responded by calling for international pressure on Israel to implement the roadmap, saying it remained committed to understandings reached with mediators and the Board of Peace.
All types of weapons
Mladenov said that the roadmap calls for the removal of “every category of weapon in Gaza. There is no grey zone and no category left out.”
The process applies to heavy weapons and their production facilities, arms depots, tunnels, personal firearms and weapons held by armed factions.
Under the plan, the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG) will become the only body authorized to possess, store or control weapons.
“Withdrawal follows verified decommissioning and proceeds in phases. It is sequenced and reciprocal. Each step rests on the successful completion of the one before it,” Mladenov said, adding that “progress is performance-based, not calendar-based.”
He said implementation would follow the principle of “trust nothing and verify everything.”
Mladenov identified three conditions for advancing the process: “The International Stabilization Force must deploy; Israel’s undertakings under the Sharm al-Sheikh Protocol must be implemented; and Hamas must adhere to its commitments.”
He added that “every use of force that does not answer an imminent threat costs this process something very hard to buy back.”
“In the opposite direction, every weapon still carried, every tunnel still worked and every convoy still obstructed sets the process back,” Mladenov said.
Israel: Disarmament first
Netanyahu, meanwhile, continues to insist that Hamas must be fully disarmed before any Israeli withdrawal from Gaza or the start of reconstruction.
On Aug. 17, Netanyahu discussed implementation of the plan with Mladenov and US envoy Jared Kushner amid ongoing differences over the sequencing of the steps.
Hamas insists on a phased and reciprocal process, while Israel demands that disarmament be carried out first.
Netanyahu’s hardline position comes ahead of an Israeli election on Oct. 27 and amid mounting pressure from far-right coalition partners opposed to making concessions on Gaza.
Far-right Israeli ministers attacked the roadmap after its announcement, including Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, who called for Hamas to be fully disarmed before any Israeli withdrawal.
Mladenov’s comments come amid daily Israeli attacks on Gaza, in which Palestinians are killed and homes destroyed -- along with tents for the displaced -- despite a ceasefire that ostensibly went into effect last October.
On Sunday, Netanyahu and Defense Minister Israel Katz threatened to step up attacks -- and displace residents from parts of Gaza -- after kites flown by Palestinian children reached Israeli areas near the embattled enclave.
Hamas accused Israel of using the incident as a pretext for escalation.
Transitional administration
On governance, Mladenov said that “Gaza’s crisis has never been only a security or humanitarian problem. It has always been a political and governance problem.”
He said the National Committee was composed of “independent Palestinian professionals. Its purpose is to govern during the transition and restore effective administration.”
The success of the transition “will ultimately be judged not by the structures we establish, but by whether Palestinians experience greater security, more reliable services, and a measurable improvement in daily life,” Mladenov said.
The NCAG was established in January under Palestinian Authority official Ali Shaath to oversee civil and security affairs during the transition.
Last November, the UN Security Council adopted Resolution 2803 endorsing the US-backed framework for Gaza’s transition, including a technocratic Palestinian administration and an interim international stabilization force.
Since Israel launched its genocidal war on the Gaza Strip in October of 2023, more than 73,000 Palestinians have been killed and over 174,000 injured, according to Palestinian figures.

Credible defence media and the fight against online misinformation
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
17:56:50 BST
01:56:50 KST

Earlier this year a claim began spreading online that a British warship had been struck by a Hezbollah missile in the eastern Mediterranean, initially appearing as speculation around an attack Hezbollah said it had carried out against an Israeli vessel, before changing fairly quickly into a much more specific story that the missile had actually hit a British ship.
HMS Dragon was the name that appeared most often online relating to this supposed incident. The Type 45 destroyer had been sent to the eastern Mediterranean as part of the British military presence protecting UK bases and interests around Cyprus, so to somebody seeing the claim without much other context it probably sounded plausible enough, and once screenshots began circulating the story started to acquire extra details as it went.
RFA Lyme Bay was mentioned too in some of the material being passed around. Within a fairl short period of time we were getting messages about it from readers and other people asking the obvious question: had a British warship actually just been hit by a missile?
We didn’t know immediately, and there was a period during which the only responsible answer was that we could not verify what was being claimed. Saying “we don’t know” isn’t a bad thing. So that is what we said publicly while we started checking it.
There is always pressure with stories like these moving at that speed to get something out quickly because everybody else is talking about it, particularly when screenshots are appearing from accounts which themselves appear to be quoting other sources, though at that point all we really had was a claim which had been repeated a lot, and repetition does not make something more reliable.
What we were doing behind the scenes
Several things were being checked at roughly the same time.
We were looking at the available open-source information to get a picture of where ships were, checking AIS information and other vessel tracking where it was available, and trying to work out whether anything we could see actually supported the claimed location of the incident.
A colleague was also watching aircraft movements around Cyprus and the eastern Mediterranean, because if a Royal Navy ship had genuinely suffered a serious missile strike then there was a reasonable chance that something else would start happening around it, perhaps helicopter movements, search and rescue activity, casualty evacuation or some other unusual pattern which might be visible through open-source tracking.
Military activity is not all visible on public tracking systems and warships quite routinely disappear from AIS, so the tracking could only ever form one part of the wider picture and we kept checking elsewhere.
We contacted the Ministry of Defence, UK Maritime Trade Operations and other sources as well, while continuing to look at what was circulating and, importantly, where some of the claims were actually coming from because by then people were quoting screenshots of screenshots and it was becoming difficult to tell which details belonged to the original allegation and which had simply been added afterwards.
That happens remarkably quickly with stories like this on social media.
One account says a British vessel may have been involved, another names HMS Dragon, somebody else adds that the ship has been damaged and within a few rounds of reposting the final version can look much more detailed and much more certain than the information it originally came from. People repeated it as fact because someone else repeated it.
Our checks weren’t producing anything that supported it, thankfully.
We couldn’t find evidence of the reported strike on a British vessel, we were seeing no activity that looked like the aftermath of a serious attack and the people we were speaking to weren’t corroborating the story either.
Then the MOD came back and confirmed that the claims were false. That answer came quickly, and in this particular case the speed mattered because the story was still moving online. We could go from saying that we had seen the reports and couldn’t verify them to telling people that the British government had directly denied that a Royal Navy vessel had been struck. We could shut the story down and answer the people reaching out to us.
The correction was therefore now travelling while the original story was still being shared, rather than arriving the following morning when thousands of accounts had already accepted the thing as established fact.
Why saying “we don’t know yet” matters
There is a wider lesson here about defence reporting, there is an extraordinary amount of defence information online now. Some of it is excellent, some of it comes from people with genuine expertise and some of it is anonymous material being repeated by accounts which have no obvious way of knowing whether the thing they have just posted is true.
For an outlet operating under normal editorial standards, there is a responsibility attached to putting something out under your own name. UK Defence Journal is regulated by IPSO, our journalists are named and we work under the Editors’ Code, and if we publish something significant which turns out to be wrong then we have to account for it.
At one stage the most useful thing we could tell people was that we knew about the story and were checking it, but we could not verify it. It is a fairly limited update, though it gives readers something solid to work with while the rumour is moving around them.
People were already sending the claim to us because they wanted somebody to check it. Once the MOD responded we could put an authoritative answer into the same information space, through an audience which was already paying attention to the story, and that meant the denial had a chance of catching up with the rumour before the rumour became accepted simply because everybody had seen it.
The MOD deserves some credit for the speed of the response here as well, that was really helpful here. Press offices quite reasonably cannot chase down every strange thing somebody posts online, and there are plenty of occasions where the government will either have no immediate answer or will be unable to provide one for operational reasons, but a claim that a deployed British destroyer has just been struck by a Hezbollah missile is obviously significant and in this case the answer came while it could still make a difference.
If it had taken until the next day, we’d still have done the same checking and we could still have reported that none of the available evidence supported the claim, though there would have been a much longer period where the information vacuum remained. That is the main thing myself and our team took from the whole episode.
The relationship between journalists and defence press offices gets built through loads of much less exciting exchanges, questions about deployments, equipment, exercises, timings, things which sometimes result in a story and sometimes don’t, and most of that work is fairly mundane. Then something like this happens and having people who know who to call, and somebody at the other end who understands why an answer is needed quickly, suddenly becomes much more important.
The Dragon claim was false.
For a few hours, though, the episode became a useful example of how this sort of thing now develops. A dramatic claim appeared, it was repeated internationally and picked up extra details, readers wanted to know whether it was true and we had to work through several different ways of checking it before we could give them a firm answer.
Open-source checks gave us part of the picture, sources filled in more of it and the MOD’s quick response allowed us to publish a firm denial while the claim was still circulating.
That is why the everyday relationship between defence organisations and the journalists covering them still matters.

Tim Curry, actor famed for 'Rocky Horror Picture Show,' dead at 80
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
16:55:23 UTC
01:55:23 KST

Tim Curry, the baritone-voiced British actor who pranced to movie fame as a singing, lingerie-clad "sweet transvestite" in the 1975 cult classic "The Rocky Horror Picture Show," has died at the age of 80, Variety and other outlets reported.
A cause of death was not immediately given, but Curry had been in ill health for some time.
Curry appeared in numerous movies, often as a hammy villain, was nominated three times for a Tony Award for Broadway roles, and performed voice work in many animated films and TV shows.
But his best-known role was Dr. Frank N. Furter, which came in his debut film, the outrageous, crowd-pleasing horror-comedy-musical "The Rocky Horror Picture Show," co-starring Susan Sarandon and Barry Bostwick.
"I'm not much of a man by the light of day. But by night I'm one hell of a lover. I'm just a sweet transvestite from transsexual Transylvania," Curry sang in one scene as he strutted around with garish eye shadow and lipstick, in a skimpy black outfit complete with black stockings and garter belt.
In a 1975 television interview, Curry noted the risk of having his career defined by such an outlandish role - a prescient worry, as it turned out. "When I read it, I just thought it was very, very witty and funny," Curry said, although he confessed to some initial reluctance.
"I mean, I was hesitant in that, if it worked, it might be a difficult thing to shake off. But, really, I've always thought that it (a part) wasn't worth doing unless you took a risk," Curry said.
Among his other films were "Charlie's Angels" (2000), "Muppet Treasure Island" (1996), "The Shadow" (1994), "The Three Musketeers" (1993), "Home Alone 2: Lost in New York" (1992), "Clue" (1985), "Legend" (1985) and "Annie" (1982).
Some of Curry's best work was on Broadway
Curry did much of his best work on stage. He was nominated for a Tony, Broadway's top honor, in 1981 for his role as Mozart in "Amadeus," a tale of the great composer's interaction with jealous rival Salieri. Curry was also nominated for a Tony in 1993 for "My Favorite Year" and in 2005 for his role as King Arthur in the zany "Monty Python's Spamalot."
Possessing a rich baritone voice, he was in demand as a voice actor for animated films and TV shows. He won a Daytime Emmy Award in 1991 for his voice work on the animated "Peter Pan & the Pirates."
With his sinister grin and menacing laugh, Curry was frequently cast in Hollywood films as a villain - sometimes with comic overtones, which let him deliver the type of over-the-top performances for which he was famed.
"I do love those roles – they're always the best written," Curry told interviewer Andrew Kay in 2011.
He conceded that some of his movies were mediocre, singling out 1995's "Congo," a tale of diamond mines and killer gorillas.
"I was really very bad in it," Curry said. "I won a Razzy award for one of the worst performances of the year – and I richly deserved it, too."
From Cheshire to Birmingham to New York to LA
Curry was born in the English village of Grappenhall, Cheshire, on April 19, 1946. His father, a Royal Navy chaplain, died when he was 12. His mother was a school secretary.
Curry studied drama at Birmingham University.
In 1973, he landed the part of Dr. Frank N. Furter in the original London stage version of "The Rocky Horror Show." He performed the play in New York and Los Angeles before it was made into a film, renamed as "The Rocky Horror Picture Show."
The movie was not an instant hit but won a cult following in midnight screenings in New York City and elsewhere, with audience members often dressing up as "Rocky Horror" characters.
Curry withdrew from a British stage production in 2011 due to ill health. In 2013, his agent said that he had suffered a stroke but was recovering "in great humor." From then on he used a wheelchair and reduced his workload. In 2024, he did, however, return to the big screen, appearing in the horror film "Stream."
Curry, who lived in Los Angeles, never married and had no children. A composer and a singer, Curry also performed with his own rock band and released a handful of albums.

US removing Syria as sponsor of terror is 'blow' to victims, impacts on sectarian violence unknown
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
16:55:19 UTC
01:55:19 KST

Washington’s decision on Monday to remove Syria from its list of state sponsors of terrorism has dealt US victims of Syrian-sponsored terrorism “a heavy blow,” attorney Aryeh Portnoy from Crowell & Moring told The Jerusalem Post on Wednesday. He represents American victims against state sponsors of terrorism.
The delisting, posted on the US Treasury’s website, took effect after a 45-day congressional review period triggered when US President Donald Trump formally notified Congress on July 8 of his intention to rescind the designation.
“These actions were all taken in recognition of the positive actions taken and further commitments by the Syrian government under President Ahmed al-Sharaa to fully distance Syria from acts of international terrorism,” US Secretary of State Marco Rubio noted in a statement.
American victims of Syrian terror feel move diminishes their experience
Though some have argued that the move will allow Damascus the financial recovery needed to bring stability to a country that has suffered more than a decade of civil war, as well as a dictatorship responsible for multiple crimes against its own people, Portnoy said that declaring Syria “open for business without accounting for the Americans whose lives were destroyed by Syrian state-sponsored terrorism” was devastating to its victims.
Though victims and their families who have obtained a final judgment in a US district court against a designated state sponsor of terrorism are meant to be compensated through the US Victims of State Sponsored Terrorism Fund (USVSST Fund), using seized and forfeited assets and settlements from companies that have violated US sanctions, it remains unclear whether Syria will be required to pay any amount toward outstanding judgments or future lawsuits.
Notably, the Anti-Defamation League (ADL) is still in the process of suing Syria on behalf of 130 US citizens who were killed or injured on October 7 and family members of American victims.
Launched in July 2024, less than half a year before Sharaa’s HTS forces seized control from former president Bashar al-Assad, the lawsuit alleges that Syria, along with North Korea and Iran, “provided material support to Hamas that enabled it to commit atrocities in Israel on October 7, 2023.”
For example, in Colvin v. Syrian Arab Republic, a US court ruled that the Syrian regime must pay $302.5 million in damages to the family of Marie Colvin, a war correspondent killed in a targeted attack in Homs in 2012.
Other countries who were removed from list had to compensate US victims
Though now under a different leadership, other countries have been expected to pay out millions to victims as part of an agreement to be taken off the list of state sponsors of terrorism.
In 2008, for example, Libya compensated families of US victims of Libyan terror attacks, including the bombing of Pan Am flight 103 over Lockerbie, Scotland, in 1988, two years after Libya was removed from the list as part of a $1.8 billion deal.
“[American] victims now can only hope their government will not forget them and that it intends to address the claims and judgments Congress allowed them to pursue in US courts and not render that commitment to help them seek justice an empty promise,” Portnoy said, adding, “It also is unclear how Syria and its new business partners will be protected from the claims of hundreds, if not thousands, of judgment creditors who will need to identify other ways to enforce their judgments if left unaddressed.”
Dr. Tamim Khromachou, the Syrian-Alawite president of the Levant Council of the United States and the Americans for Levant Foundation, told the Post that delisting Syria does not address the sectarian violence in Syria and could inadvertently strengthen actors responsible for abuses seen in recent years, though it would undoubtedly be beneficial for Syria’s economy and diplomatic efforts.
“It is also important to remember that Syria moved from the political dictatorship of the Assad regime into a period of civil and sectarian violence while Syria was under the same terrorism-related designations. So, ultimately, the designation itself does not determine which direction Syria takes,” Khromachou said.
“The will of the new authorities, the nature of the institutions they build, and the commitment of those supporting Syria’s transition will be far more consequential,” he explained.
“Removing the designation could provide an important opportunity for Syria, but that opportunity needs to be accompanied by meaningful safeguards, accountability, and guarantees that the emerging state will protect all Syrians regardless of their sect or identity,” he said.
Israeli expert sees move as positive to tackle Syrian sectarian violence
Though minorities in Syria may waver in how they view this latest move, Ely Karmon, a senior researcher at the International Institute for Counter-Terrorism at Reichman University, told the Post that Washington’s decision could only help tackle the bad actors involved in the sectarian attacks.
Explaining that the Islamist groups operating in Syria hadn’t taken as quickly to the “charismatic” Sharaa as had European and American leaders, Karmon made clear that he didn’t believe Sharaa’s government had been responsible for the sectarian violence. But, he said, Washington’s decision to delist Syria would likely encourage him to act more strongly against it.
“The Syrian army was not yet really under control and still is not completely under control,” he said.
Sharaa will need to prove he can provide a stable future for Syria in order to see the country freed from financial restraints, notably by the European Union, he explained. With the removal of US sanctions, though, Damascus will have more breathing room to create that stability, he argued.

The United States designated Palestine Action on Wednesday as a terrorist group, as US President Donald Trump's administration seeks to crack down on left-wing groups in its counterterrorism efforts.

Trump singled out the anti-fascist antifa movement on the campaign trail in 2024, and vowed to take action against left-wing groups he accuses of fomenting violence after the killing of conservative activist and Trump ally Charlie Kirk last year.
"Far-left extremists, their fronts, and their enablers should be on notice: We will bring the full weight of our economic tools to bear," Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent said in a statement on Wednesday.
"Political terrorism has no place in our society, and we will continue to cut the financial lifelines of these groups until they are eliminated."
Italy-based entity sanctioned for supplying antifa, other far-left groups
The US Treasury Department on Wednesday also imposed sanctions on an Italy-based entity it accused of supplying digital architecture, tools and services for antifa and other far-left groups.
Britain has also previously banned Palestine Action as a terrorist organization. Palestine Action had increasingly targeted Israel‑linked defense companies in Britain, especially Israel's largest defense firm Elbit Systems.
Responding to the US move on Wednesday, Huda Ammori, co-founder of Palestine Action, said the group's activities "have always been about saving lives by disrupting the Israeli war machine."
"The fact that Trump is now taking inspiration from Britain’s repression of the movement for Palestinian freedom exposes just how dangerous this ban is and should be a wake-up call to anyone who cares about free speech and civil liberties," Ammori said in a statement to Reuters.
UK Supreme Court to hear appeal against Palestine Action ban
The United Kingdom's Supreme Court has said it will hear an appeal against a lower court ruling that Britain's decision to ban campaign group Palestine Action as a terrorist organization was lawful.
The US. Treasury Department also imposed sanctions on Wednesday on the transnational group Masar Badil, saying it operates as a front for the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine. The latter group had already been designated by the US. as a Foreign Terrorist Organization.

Revolution Medicines gets FDA approval for targeted pancreatic cancer drug
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
16:54:25 UTC
01:54:25 KST

The US FDA has approved Revolution Medicines' groundbreaking pancreatic cancer drug after it was shown to double the survival rate of patients with advanced disease in a large trial, offering new hope to those with the deadly cancer.
The once-daily pill, to be called Rasonque, was approved for metastatic pancreatic cancer in patients who have received prior treatment or cannot receive combination chemotherapy. The drug is designed to block several forms of the RAS protein, which helps drive tumor growth in many pancreatic cancers.
Revolution said the drug is now available in the United States at $39,800 for a 30-day supply. The company added that it would make assistance available as well.
When Revolution announced the trial results in April for the drug, it set off a firestorm of demand. The FDA quickly granted early access to it under its compassionate use program, which allows patients with serious or life-threatening conditions to get experimental treatments outside clinical trials prior to authorization by the regulator.
The treatment has already offered some patients with early access to the drug a reprieve from the toll of chemotherapy.
New treatment a 'godsend,' patient says after drug approved
Barbara Andes, 88, of Fullerton, California, who began taking it in July after a year of chemotherapy, said the pill allowed her to resume regular activities and caused far less nausea and fatigue.
"It's going to open this door now commercially for so many, many more people who are suffering," Andes said. "It's a godsend."
The drug was part of the Food and Drug Administration's new expedited review process, designed to shrink timelines to as little as one to two months from the usual 10 to 12.
"This approval validates more than a decade of work aimed at pancreatic cancer, primarily RAS-driven disease, and one of the most difficult challenges in medicine, cancer biology, and drug discovery," Revolution CEO Mark Goldsmith said.
Investors have flocked to Revolution on expectations that Rasonque could become a major new treatment option, driving the company's stock up 166% this year. Its approval was widely expected and Revolution shares were relatively flat at $211.70.
RBC Capital Markets analysts said the rapid approval, along with more than 2,000 patients already enrolled in the Expanded Access Program, could help drive an estimated $28 million in US pancreatic cancer revenue in the third quarter. Fourth-quarter sales could reach $148 million.
Longer term, the analysts estimated the drug could generate $11.5 billion in annual global sales. The American Cancer Society estimates about 67,350 patients to be diagnosed with pancreatic cancer this year.
Doctors expect Rasonque to transform how they tackle a disease that has been very difficult to treat.
"This is just the tip of the iceberg in terms of what we're going to see in terms of targeting the RAS pathway for pancreas cancer," said Rachna Shroff, chief of hematology and oncology at the University of Arizona Cancer Center.
"Not only did people live longer, but their quality of life improved," Shroff said, noting that patients stayed on the drug longer than they did on chemotherapy.
Peter Hosein, associate director for clinical research at the Pancreatic Cancer Research Institute at Sylvester Comprehensive Cancer Center, described it as a paradigm shift.
"Researchers have been trying to make a breakthrough in RAS inhibition for decades and, due to unrelenting persistence, this breakthrough is finally here," he said.

'Open dialogue, inclusive to all': RSS reacts to row over Mohan Bhagwat's New York event

RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat will address the 'Universal Oneness Celebration' at Madison Square Garden on August 29.
A major RSS outreach event is being planned in New York, with Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) chief Mohan Bhagwat scheduled to address the "Universal Oneness Celebration" at Madison Square Garden on August 29.The event is being organised by American Hindus for Engagement and Dialogue and is expected to bring together Hindu-American organisations and members of the Indian diaspora around the themes of shared heritage, interfaith dialogue and unity.
The programme, however, has triggered a political controversy even before it takes place, with New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani publicly opposing Bhagwat’s appearance.Mamdani, New York’s first Muslim and Indian-American mayor, said he did not support the planned rally, describing the RSS’s vision as exclusionary and contrasting it with his own understanding of India as a pluralistic country. At the same time, he acknowledged that the event is privately organised and said he was unsure whether the city had the legal authority to cancel it.The controversy is particularly significant because of Mamdani’s own Indian heritage and his position as mayor of one of the world's most diverse cities.
His criticism has also drawn support from groups opposed to the RSS, while critics of the mayor have questioned whether his position amounts to singling out a Hindu organisation.The RSS, meanwhile, has pushed back strongly against the criticism.
RSS communications chief Sunil Ambekar said the New York gathering represents an interfaith forum where Bhagwat will engage with a “diverse, multicultural, and multi-faith audience”.He said the event reflects what the RSS describes as the inclusive and welcoming nature of the Bharatiya ethos, and invited anyone interested in understanding the organisation’s philosophy to participate in open dialogue.The timing of Bhagwat’s visit is also important. The RSS is marking its centenary in 2025-26, and the New York programme forms part of a broader international outreach by Bhagwat covering the United States, Canada and the United Kingdom. The stated objective is to engage Indian-origin communities abroad and present the RSS’s views on India, Hindu society and its own philosophy.

Iran emphasises self-sufficiency in battle against US economic war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
16:53:20 UTC
01:53:20 KST

Iran emphasises self-sufficiency in battle against US economic war
Iranian authorities believe they can withstand US sanctions, but warn of a tough year ahead.
Tehran, Iran – Iranian authorities are adamant that their country’s domestic capacities will be able to keep the country’s economy afloat, despite new economic sanctions targeting Iran unveiled by the United States this week.
The US aims to use the sanctions to force Iran into submission in the six month-long war between the two countries. But Iran’s government says it is prepared, with Economy Minister Ali Madanizadeh referring to a two-year plan on state television on Monday night.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Trump tells Al Jazeera ‘not in a hurry’ for Iran to return to talks
- list 2 of 3Iran, Oman agree on temporary Hormuz route: What we know
- list 3 of 3Why India is sharing missile secrets with its private sector
“We have our own tools and we also know the game,” Madanizadeh said, in reference to Iran’s years of experience in trying to circumvent sanctions. He added that Tehran could potentially “go on the offensive” in a world where the US was no longer the only dominant force, and was confidant that many countries would effectively reject US President Donald Trump’s threats to cut off all links with Iran.
Stockpiling essential goods, foreign currencies and gold has become a main tactic for Tehran. The government has also been forced to resort to rationing energy in one of the most resource-rich countries in the world.
Central Bank Governor Abdolnasser Hemmati told senior business representatives during a meeting earlier this week that oil exports, Iran’s main foreign currency income source, have almost totally stopped. But Hemmati reassured the business leaders there was no shortage of foreign currency for essential goods as the central bank had cash stockpiles “in places [the US] cannot access”.
Hemmati acknowledged “serious issues” like runaway inflation and constantly declining purchasing power for the people, but said, “enduring hardship is very different from collapse and what the US is after”.
Iranians must not expect conditions to get any better over the next year, government spokesman Fatemeh Mohajerani told state-linked media on Tuesday. She also said Iran’s Supreme National Security Council would have to grant authorisation for the government to reveal data on poverty levels in the country.
Iran’s national currency fell to a new all-time low of 2.05 million rials against the US dollar on the open market on Tuesday, before slightly recovering on Wednesday.
Make it at home
Despite the turmoil, Iran’s newly-appointed security chief Mohsen Rezaei urged younger Iranians during a state TV interview earlier this week to “enter the economy” and begin manufacturing goods needed by their households and communities at home.
That mentality has permeated the Islamic Republic’s strategic thinking for decades, with national development plans repeatedly emphasising “self-sufficiency” and setting targets to achieve it at great cost.
To reduce its reliance on food imports for a population of around 90 million, the government claims that Iran can produce 85 percent of its agricultural products domestically, even as concerns remain over what the increase in domestic agricultural production means for Iran’s dire water scarcity problems.
Agriculture Minister Gholam-Reza Nouri said on state television on Tuesday that Tehran aimed to increase domestic food self-sufficiency to 90 percent in the short-term, ahead of ultimately producing all of the country’s essential food domestically.
Nouri said that Iran imports about $16bn and exports $8bn in agricultural products – although exports of some products were suspended in March shortly after the start of the war.
Iran relies on imports for essential foods and feed commodities, including wheat, maize, rice and vegetable oils. The United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia are among Iran’s top suppliers of refined sugar and wheat flour through re-export hubs. Russia and Central Asia can also provide some grain through the Caspian Sea into northern Iran.
The United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization said in March that rising import costs, logistics disruptions and policy responses aimed at protecting domestic supply are accelerating food inflation and reducing household purchasing power in Iran. It also warned that overland trade routes do not have the capacity to replace the much larger volumes of goods normally transported by sea.
Food prices in Iran were more than 128 percent higher in July than they were a year earlier, according to the latest report by the Statistical Center of Iran. The same amount of money now buys far less food in Tehran and across the country than it did six months ago.
Iran’s government also says the country produces some 97 percent of its medicine, although imported medicines account for a much larger share of total pharmaceutical spending.
Salman Eshaghi, spokesman of the parliament’s health committee, said in May that Iran faced some levels of shortages for nearly 1,000 medicines. Medicine prices have also surged over recent months, including this week, after the government confirmed that it was gradually cutting off cheap currency allocation to some imports.
Hard war-time choices
Iran’s authorities have said they are working quickly to repair some of the damage dealt to Iran’s infrastructure during the war, including to oil, gas and utility facilities extensively bombed by the US and Israel.
The was has compounded Iran’s existing energy shortages and infrastructure problems.
Daily power blackouts continue to plague households and industrial units in Tehran and cities across the country, while natural gas shortages are expected to hit within a few months when the weather gets colder and demand rises.
On Tuesday and Wednesday, a considerable number of petrol stations in Tehran, Mashhad, Karaj and several other cities also ran out of fuel allocated to them by the government, leading to lengthy queues.
Government spokesperson Mohajerani on Wednesday promised that existing fuel prices and quota levels would remain unchanged through the end of the current Iranian calendar month on September 22. But the government has already cut fuel quotas for private vehicles.
The National Iranian Oil Refining and Distribution Company promised on Wednesday that the inauguration of two new refineries in southern Iran by the end of the current year in late March would add about 12 million litres per day to Iran’s production capacity, helping offset some of the shortage.
Iran’s government has no choice but to engage in “painful reforms” by increasing fuel prices in order to avoid another “bloodshed” during social unrest, Iranian economist Sadegh Alhosseini warned in a speech on Tuesday.
“If Iran heads toward large-scale chaos – kilometres-long petrol queues and becoming like Venezuela – something much worse will happen that will be much more difficult to handle,” he said.
But another fuel cost hike will further increase inflation by ramping up transport costs, and many people are already struggling to get by. Iran may continue to withstand historic levels of pressure, but it is becoming increasingly vulnerable to a cycle in which its resources and capacity are steadily depleted.

Notes from Central Taiwan: Taiwan needs more than a missile shield
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
16:48:11 UTC
01:48:11 KST

Bloomberg reported earlier this week that the People’s Republic of China (PRC) “has developed hypersonic glide vehicles that can launch air-to-air weapons, an advancement meant to threaten high-value targets such as command-and-control aircraft thousands of miles away.”
Military Watch magazine reported in 2024 on one of the designs: “the vehicle is designed with payload options that include electronic warfare and reconnaissance suites, as well as bombs and both supersonic and subsonic drones that detach from the vehicle during flight,” while noting that the PRC is a world leader in such technologies.
The threat from the PRC is not only increasing, but expanding and evolving.
Photo courtesy of the Presidential Office
Meanwhile the Chinese-language Liberty Times (the sister paper of the Taipei Times) reported this week that draft-eligible men is expected to fall below 80,000 by next year, thanks to collapsing birth rates. Inevitably, the military is short of personnel. One solution would be a “foreign legion” approach offering citizenship to those who serve, especially to foreign soldiers with small children. But that requires the kind of imagination our leaders sorely lack.
National Chungshan Institute of Science and Technology last week released the technical specifications for the Chiang Kung (強弓) missile (also known as the Tien Kung IV, 天弓四型), seemingly hoping to influence the legislative “debate” on the defense budget. Funding for the advanced high altitude interceptor is not included in the defense budget recently passed by the legislature. Hence, it has to be funded through a supplementary budget.
The budget problems have disrupted the military’s planning for a the “T-Dome” missile defense program. The legislature, controlled by the pro-China Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) and Taiwan People’s Party (TPP), is well aware of the effects of its funding decisions on weapons development and acquisition programs.
TT file photo
There’s entirely too much focus in the pundit world on the possibility of a pro-China politician taking the presidency in 2028 and delivering Taiwan to the PRC. In fact that appears to be quietly unfolding in the legislature (weirdly that argument appears to apply only to a pro-China president). Once again I quote Taiwanese historian Lee Hsiao-Feng (李筱峰) who observed in the Independence Evening Post (自立晚報) in 2001 that if one day Beijing wants to take Taiwan, the first place they attack will be the Legislative Yuan.
Last week the Economist reported on the dismal state of the US defense industrial base, made obvious by the idiotic war on Iran.
“Taiwan worries that 102 [Patriot missiles] ordered years ago will not arrive this year as scheduled,” it said, adding: “Lockheed Martin, which makes the most advanced version, the PAC-3 MSE, says it cannot guarantee delivery times to any foreign client, given the Pentagon’s power to divert them.”
An Aug. 4 Heritage Foundation study, cited by the Economist, estimated that, under its baseline assumptions for a major Indo-Pacific conflict with China, US forces could require roughly 19,400 PAC-3 MSE and 5,500 THAAD interceptors, in addition to thousands of ship-based SM-3 and SM-6 interceptors. Even the report’s more optimistic scenario required about 7,100 PAC-3 MSEs and 1,400 THAAD interceptors, plus substantial naval inventories — far more than the US currently possesses or can quickly produce.
“At current inventory levels,” the report states, “the PLA could render key US bases… unable to sustain adequate operational tempo or render them inoperable within the opening days of a conflict.” Iranian attacks on US bases in the Gulf have caused damage, casualties and operational disruption.
Ballistic missiles fired by aggressors are much cheaper than the missiles necessary to intercept them, while drones are peanuts by comparison. Worse, typically the defender fires two or more missiles to raise the probability of an intercept. Hence, many nations have moved to attacking missile launchers and to strikes elsewhere in the enemy nation to make the aggressor stop, as Ukraine is currently attempting. However, attacking launchers and bases was the US approach to Iran, with mixed results.
Consciously or not, our deterrence focuses on rendering a PRC attack on Taiwan pointless by improving our defenses so that the cost is too great for the results achieved. What the US debacle in the Strait of Hormuz shows is that modern ballistic and drone technologies are so good that even destroying large numbers of launchers is unlikely to defeat them. Nor can they easily be intercepted.
Moreover, let’s assume total optimism. We give the US-Taiwan missile defense 100 percent effectiveness. All incoming missiles and drones are knocked down. The PRC attack is defeated. Taiwan’s missile defenses will then be expended. Does anyone think the PRC will never try again? Who will rebuild their missile packages more rapidly, Taiwan-US-Japan or the PRC?
Perhaps it is not our deterrence that is failing, but our conception of it. Those who argue that we should throw in the towel and opt for some form of surrender (“make a deal”) because we probably can’t stop the PRC’s missiles are carefully avoiding mentioning another form of deterrence that makes more sense: deterrence by punishment. The appeal of “make a deal” lies in the misconception of deterrence as a program of knocking back an attack. It should be a program of degrading an attack while applying massive, unacceptable damage to the aggressor.
Deterrence by punishment offers both a powerful deterrent effect, and in the case of war, the ability to degrade or eliminate manufacturing and logistics facilities that will be used for the PRC to recover its missile forces. It can even be escalated in a fine-grain, tit-for-tat way, if desired. They hit our ports, we hit theirs, and so on.
It is now easier to see why the PRC hates Taiwan’s drone development program: it equips Taiwan with the ability to strike not only landing craft and ships in an invasion, not only launchers and bases, but also manufacturing and logistics sites (as Ukraine is doing). I suspect that this capability is what the PRC truly objects to, and that this possibility is a major deterrent to attacks. That alone is argument for a shift in the way deterrence is thought about.
What should Taiwan do? To a certain extent it is already committed to strikes on the PRC, but that must be vastly expanded. Among other things, it should rapidly expand its current Hsiung Feng III (“Brave Wind”) missile production, and build out a stockpile of strike drones, including a core of long-range strike drones that can reach factories deep inside the PRC. Once again, it should turn its currently useless high school and college military education courses into courses in drone flying, civil defense and first aid.
The South China Morning Post reported this week that PRC intimidation ship patrols hit a record high for the third month in a row last month.
How much longer do we have?
Notes from Central Taiwan is a column written by long-term resident Michael Turton, who provides incisive commentary informed by three decades of living in and writing about his adoptive country. The views expressed here are his own.
When we recall the 1990s, we usually identify them as the time of great transitions, from authoritarianism to democracy, and the public’s shift to acknowledging a Taiwanese identity. But another transition occurred, one that we take for granted and hardly notice anymore. The 1980s opened with the massacre of members of the family of democracy activist Lin I-hsiung (林義雄). While Lin was in detention, on Feb. 28, 1980, persons still unknown broke into the Lin family home despite round-the-clock police surveillance. Lin’s mother and two of his three daughters were slain. His eldest daughter survived multiple stab wounds. The following year

The case remains unsolved today. Despite an extensive two-month search, the three men’s bodies were never found. The incident came just a year after five National Tsing Hua University students died on the mountain on July 25, 1971, after being unexpectedly caught in a typhoon, prompting serious concerns about hiking safety. Tunghai University graduate Chiu Kao (邱高) and Fu Jen Catholic
The Taiwan People’s Party (TPP) is facing some difficulties, and there are some tensions in their alliance with the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT). However, though these problems are real, the local press is blowing them out of proportion and hyping too much out of context. Take, for example, a poll released by Z.media on Wednesday of 1,070 adults with a sampling error of ±3 percentage points. Museum to open comic exhibition inspired by Taiwanese folk culture
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
16:48:10 UTC
01:48:10 KST

The National Taiwan Museum of Comics (NTMC) in Taichung is today launching an exhibition titled “Taiwanese Lives of Ghosts in Comics,” which showcases Taiwan’s folk culture through nine contemporary Taiwanese comics during Ghost Month.
Ghost Month, the seventh month of the lunar calendar, reflects people’s awe and fear of ghosts and their understanding of life, emotions and memories, NTMC Preparatory Office director Chen Ching-kuan (陳靜寬) said at a promotional event yesterday.
It has also served as an important source of inspiration for literary and comic works, she said.
Photo: CNA
The exhibition draws on familiar Taiwanese night-market imagery, incorporating food such as fish-ball soup and steak, as well as ring-toss games, to create an immersive setting.
The nine selected works feature Taiwanese folk elements such as the Zhongyuan Pudu ritual, ghost marriages and the Earth Deity (Tudigong, 土地公), but ultimately tell stories about human experiences and connections, curator Jean Chen (陳怡靜) said.
Zhongyuan Pudu is a traditional Ghost Festival ritual held to honor spirits believed to be released from the underworld during Ghost Month. This year’s Ghost Festival is today, while Ghost Month runs from Aug. 13 to Sept. 10.
The exhibition runs from today until March 1 next year.

Trump’s Kim gambit deepens doubts over US reliability
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
16:48:09 UTC
01:48:09 KST

US President Donald Trump’s olive branch to North Korean leader Kim Jong-un at the expense of a long-standing ally comes at a pivotal moment for US security ties in Asia, as partners from Japan to India reassess how much they can rely on Washington.
The US president’s abrupt decision to cut back military drills with South Korea last week, which he described as hostile to Pyongyang, has reinforced fears that Trump’s unpredictability could strain alliances that have long maintained peace in the region, government officials and security experts said.
Japan worries it too could find itself in Trump’s cross-hairs as it embarks on thorny security negotiations; Taiwan is warily watching an upcoming summit between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平); and India is growing less certain of its place in Washington’s strategic calculus.
Illustration: Mountain People
“The decision will certainly fuel growing doubts in the region about US security commitments,” said Jeremy Chan, a senior analyst with political risk consultancy Eurasia Group and former US diplomat in Japan and China.
Adding to the anxiety, the US cancelled another military exercise with South Korea scheduled for next month, Seoul said on Monday, after Washington cited constraints on US forces due to the Iran war.
Trump has been frustrated by the failure of US allies to support the war and made it clear that many of them must spend more on their own defense, a White House official said. He is eager to restart talks with North Korea and secure a win on the international stage to counter his unpopular conflict with Iran, a person briefed on discussions between US and South Korean officials said.
Trump’s push to meet Kim — which has so far drawn a frosty response from Pyongyang — could backfire and embolden nuclear-armed North Korea, former Japanese minister of defense Itsunori Onodera said. Such a prospect is “extremely troubling” for Tokyo, he said on Thursday last week. Despite Trump’s overtures, Pyongyang fired a volley of ballistic missiles off its east coast earlier that day, triggering alerts in South Korea and Japan.
What worries Japanese officials more is Trump’s approach as Tokyo embarks on talks with Washington over how much it should pay toward the cost of hosting US forces, the US’ largest overseas deployment.
Japan is bracing for the possibility that Trump could, with little warning, demand a sharp hike that would be politically difficult to swallow, a senior Japanese government official said, requesting anonymity due to the sensitivity of the matter.
Trump could also wield upcoming US military exercises with Japan in October as leverage, analysts say. Officials in Washington and Tokyo said they did not expect the exercises to be curtailed, although Trump could change his mind at any point, they added.
The drills, known as Keen Sword, might already be smaller than their 2024 iteration because of the diversion of US assets and personnel to the conflict with Iran. That shift — which saw the US’ only forward-deployed aircraft carrier in Asia, the USS George Washington, depart for the Middle East to relieve the beleaguered USS Abraham Lincoln — has stirred concern that US deterrence against China is being eroded.
During a visit to Asia this month, Pentagon policy chief Elbridge Colby said that working with allies to ensure combat readiness along the First Island Chain that runs from Japan through the Philippines is a priority for Washington.
Nowhere are concerns about China’s growing military pressure more acute than in Taiwan.
Trump has held up approval of a US$14 billion package of arms sales to Taipei in order to maintain warm relations and a fragile trade truce with Xi.
As Trump prepares for his latest round of summitry with Xi in Washington next month, officials in Taipei say that they expect Washington would at the very least carve up the arms sales into smaller chunks to try and avoid upsetting Beijing too much.
Domingo I-Kwei Yang (楊一逵), assistant reseatch fellow at the Taiwanese defense ministry’s Institute for National Defense and Security Research, said that there is a distinction between Trump’s rhetoric and actual US behavior, adding that US intelligence sharing, training and patrols with Taiwan remain substantial. A US Navy aircraft transited the Taiwan Strait on Friday in a move the US described as demonstrating its “commitment to a free and open Indo-Pacific.”
Trump’s latest actions have also rocked confidence in India, where the US risks squandering years of efforts to draw New Delhi closer as a counterweight to Russia and China, security analysts say.
It also comes after the Pentagon’s decision in June to rename its Asia military headquarters to Pacific Command from Indo-Pacific Command, a move some analysts say is a sign India is no longer as strategically important to Washington.
The Pentagon denied any such shift. However, Trump’s steep tariffs on Indian exports and repeated claims that he had mediated an India-Pakistan ceasefire had already exasperated New Delhi. Officials there are “very, very cautious” about committing to long-term defense deals with Washington, two Indian sources with knowledge of the matter said.
“The latest decision only reinforces President Trump’s transactional view of foreign affairs and serves as a reminder that differences over specific policies, even among allies, can carry costs for the broader bilateral relationship,” said Pearl Pandya, senior analyst at Armed Conflict Location and Event Data, a conflict monitoring group.
The Iran and Ukraine wars are rewriting modern military strategy. These conflicts are demonstrating that a less conventionally powerful state, by leveraging asymmetric capabilities, can impose major costs on an aggressor and fundamentally reshape the outcome of conflict. Taiwan is not only drawing lessons from those conflicts, but also translating them into practice. Far from seeking to match China ship for ship, missile for missile or aircraft for aircraft, Taiwan needs to make Chinese aggression so costly, problematic and uncertain that Beijing is deterred from launching an attack. Kinmen stops pork shipments amid ASF
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
16:48:07 UTC
01:48:07 KST

The Kinmen County Government has since Tuesday suspended shipments of pork and processed pork products to Taiwan proper and other outlying islands after African swine fever (ASF) was detected in a pig carcass that drifted ashore.
Regulations ban live pigs from being shipped to Taiwan proper and other outlying islands, but the announcement expands that ban to pork and processed products until Monday next week.
The Coast Guard Administration’s Kinmen-Matsu-Penghu Branch found the dead pig on the shore of Wushajiao (烏沙角) in Jinning Township (金寧) on Saturday, the Kinmen County Department of Economic Development said.
Photo courtesy of the Kinmen County Government
County animal health officials collected tissue samples from the pig, disinfected the site, and incinerated and buried the carcass before disinfecting the surrounding area, it said.
The Ministry of Agriculture’s Veterinary Research Institute on Monday confirmed that the sample tested positive for ASF viral nucleic acid.
Local veterinarians inspected a total of 5,886 pigs from 22 pig farms within a 10km radius of the site, and all pigs were found to be healthy, the county government said.
The Central Emergency Operation Center for ASF said it was the latest case of ASF-positive pig drifting ashore this year, bringing the number of such cases to 23 since 2018.
The case underscored the risk of ASF-infected pig carcasses drifting ashore via ocean currents and the importance of maintaining coastal patrols, prompt reporting and strict border quarantine measures, the center said.
The Ministry of Agriculture on Tuesday also issued a notice suspending shipments of Kinmen pork and processed pork products to Taiwan proper and other offshore islands.
The restrictions are to remain in place until there have been no new ASF cases in Kinmen for at least one consecutive week, the ministry said.
Meanwhile, the ASF response center warned that the Mid-Autumn Festival late next month, a peak time for gift-giving and online purchases of meat products, poses a high risk for ASF prevention efforts.
The center urged people not to bring or mail mooncakes containing pork, meat jerky, sausages, cured meats or other pork products into Taiwan from ASF-affected areas such as China, or import such products through overseas online shopping platforms.
Violators face a fine of NT$200,000 (US$6,285.75) for a first offense and NT$1 million for repeat offenses, the center said.

Opposition drone bill leaves major holes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
16:48:06 UTC
01:48:06 KST

Vice President Hsiao Bi-khim (蕭美琴) has questioned major parts of military drone procurement bills sponsored by opposition lawmakers, saying that the omissions would hurt the industry and Taiwan’s preparedness.
Fourteen variations of the bill are expected to be put to a vote in the opposition-controlled legislature by the end of this month after cross-caucus talks broke down last week.
At the center of the debate are two questions: how the procurement of drones should be funded and which agency should be in charge of the project.
Photo: CNA
Among the highest-profile proposals awaiting a vote, the Cabinet has earmarked NT$210 billion (US$6.6 billion) in a special budget running from this month through the end of 2031, while the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) has earmarked NT$240 billion, to be drawn from the general budget over six years, with an annual spending cap of NT$40 billion.
In an interview with the Central News Agency on Friday last week, Hsiao said the NT$40 billion annual spending cap could leave the Ministry of National Defense’s (MND) drone procurement plans underfunded, as payments vary over the course of a contract and are bound to balloon during peak delivery periods.
The NT$40 billion cap could restrict payments, she said.
“On this point, we should respect the MND’s force-building schedule and requirements,” Hsiao said.
The KMT has highlighted the larger overall amount proposed in its bill, arguing that the annual spending cap would require expenditure to be reviewed each year, strengthening oversight and reducing the risk of misuse.
Another point of contention between the Cabinet and opposition parties is which agency should be the bill’s competent authority.
The MND is the overseeing ministry in the Cabinet proposal.
The KMT and the smaller opposition Taiwan People’s Party designated the Ministry of Economic Affairs as the competent authority in their proposals.
The opposition parties have said that supporting drone manufacturers, importing key technologies, conducting cybersecurity reviews and planning drone testing sites fall within the economic ministry’s remit.
However, Hsiao said the MND should oversee the bill’s implementation, with their focus on using the drones for the actual purpose, defending Taiwan.
“Only the MND can determine what it needs: types, models, specifications and functions of the drones required,” she said.
Beyond filling a critical defense need, how the bills are handled has strategic significance, Hsiao said, adding that other countries are watching to see whether Taiwan is determined to defend itself when faced with threats, pressure and harassment from China.
“I have received many foreign guests in this room,” Hsiao said. “Many of them asked: ‘Are the Taiwanese people committed to defending themselves?’”
Hsiao said Russian President Vladimir Putin might have miscalculated when he decided to invade Ukraine, because he was overconfident and believed he could quickly capture Ukraine.
“We cannot allow the regime in Beijing to miscalculate Taiwan’s determination to defend itself,” she said.
Under the Cabinet’s proposal, the bill would fund 1,446 coastal reconnaissance drones, 208,200 coastal attack drones and 1,320 uncrewed suicide surface vessels, in line with the MND’s request.
Asked why the MND identified those drones for local production rather than source them from abroad, Hsiao said they fit Taiwan’s “island defense” and “multidomain denial” strategies.
In addition, she said their “high demand” would help develop the local drone industry, equipping it with the capabilities needed for high-volume production, such as automation, which can help bring down unit costs and make Taiwan’s drones more competitive internationally.
“The industry needs to be able to see a future,” she said. “When the government makes large-scale purchases and helps build these capabilities, international orders and competitiveness will naturally follow.”
Legislators from the ruling and opposition parties yesterday debated their proposals in a cross-party caucuses’ meeting, but failed to reach agreement. They collectively agreed to have Legislative Speaker Han Kuo-yu (韓國瑜) reschedule the plenary session for voting on the bills slated for tomorrow to today.

Millions of Indonesians risk health complications from exposure to thick haze covering several cities and towns, officials said yesterday, as El Nino-fueled wildfires wreak havoc on Borneo and Sumatra islands.
Indonesia, a vast archipelago, has for weeks battled wildfires that have led to school closures and thousands of people requiring medical treatment, with smoke also reaching neighboring Malaysia and Singapore.
The Indonesian Ministry of Health said 3.4 million people living in seven provinces on Borneo and Sumatra were at risk of respiratory infections due to exposure.
Photo: Reuters
In Pekanbaru, the capital of Sumatra’s Riau Province, thick smog forced the government to shutter dozens of schools as it urged residents to stay indoors.
“The smog gets thicker at night, making Pekanbaru almost like a dead city. A lot of people don’t dare go out, and if they do, they wear masks,” Abdullah, a 38-year-old entrepreneur, said.
“My eyes sting so badly. When I go outside, it really feels like breathing in the smoke from freshly burned trash,” added the Pekanbaru resident who, like many Indonesians, has one name.
In Jambi, also on Sumatra, 31-year-old homemaker Farida said the haze had already affected her family’s health.
“My four-year-old child and I have begun coughing so much, especially when we stay outdoors too long,” she said. “I have trouble breathing.”
The Jambi government has ordered home schooling for children in kindergarten and elementary school for the remainder of the week.
The health ministry said it had distributed more than 260,000 masks to residents of the hardest-hit areas.
Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto on Tuesday said the government had deployed dozens of helicopters, aircraft, water pumps and thousands of personnel to battle the blazes.
“Now I think it has begun to be brought under control, mitigated. In several places, I believe, and I hope that within the next one to two weeks everything can be resolved,” Prabowo said.
Most wildfires are blamed on slash-and-burn practices to clear land for farming.
Police said that over the weekend they had arrested 72 people on suspicion of starting fires.
Fires between January and last month burned more than 200,000 hectares of land — an area three times the size of the capital Jakarta, the government said last week.
That is already larger than during previous El Nino seasons in 2019 and 2023.
Muslims in Indonesia, celebrating the birth of Prophet Mohammed on Tuesday, prayed for rain.
Malaysia said it stood ready to help put out fires.
Poor air quality in Malaysia’s Sarawak state, on Borneo island which it shares with Indonesia and Brunei, led to the closure of nearly 600 schools last week.
At one point yesterday morning, tracker IQ Air ranked the Malaysian capital, Kuala Lumpur, the second-most polluted city globally.

Ukrainian commander recounts trek through the ‘kill zone’ to save troops
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
16:48:01 UTC
01:48:01 KST

Seeing two wounded fighters stranded on the battlefield — one of them still strapped to a land drone immobilized by a Russian strike — Ukrainian commander Vladyslav Polskyi knew he had to do something.
The 29-year-old — a former science teacher who joined the army in 2023 — was watching the soldiers on a screen in his command post about 15km away.
Between them stretched the “kill zone,” riddled with mines and swarmed by aerial drones ready to attack anything that moved.
Photo: Ukrainian Presidential Press Service via Reuters
Polskyi, whose military call sign is “Teacher,” hopped into his gray pick-up truck and raced past scorched fields and the charred husks of other vehicles left on the battlefield of northern Ukraine. He had no helmet or body armor.
“If it had happened to me, I would’ve wanted them to come take me away, and not just leave me there,” the junior lieutenant said, recalling his Aug. 15 mission to save both men, who were members of another battalion.
His feat captured the country’s attention and, days later, earned him its highest military honor, Hero of Ukraine. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy presented him with the award at Independence Day celebrations in Kyiv on Monday.
Photo: Ukrainian Armed Forces via Reuters
“People must be taken care of. Thank you, Vladyslav,” Zelenskiy said, announcing the award.
Speaking less than a week after the operation, Polskyi described speeding toward the men while planning how he would load them onto the flatbed of the truck.
The two Ukrainian soldiers had been wounded during a combat mission in the Kharkiv region and were being evacuated atop an uncrewed ground vehicle when it was struck by one of Russia’s small, agile helicopter drones loaded with explosives.
Kyiv’s forces have been using remote-controlled uncrewed vehicles to help limit human involvement in dangerous tasks like evacuations inside the “kill zone,” seeking an edge against Moscow’s bigger army.
Russia’s attack cast light on the limits of the relatively slow and rudimentary vehicles. The Russian drone knocked out the land drone’s Starlink terminal, severing the link with its pilot and leaving it immobilized.
One of the wounded soldiers had crawled into a ditch off the road and hid in the vegetation; the other lay helpless on the four-wheeled vehicle under an open sky, his right foot dangling from the bone.
Ukraine has also made widespread use of attack drones on the battlefield, and says it is killing or wounding about 30,000 Russian soldiers a month — a figure Moscow dismisses as exaggerated.
Both sides frequently post videos of drones hunting down each other’s soldiers in the “kill zone.”
Surveillance drone footage, obtained from Polskyi’s unit, the 475th Assault Regiment, shows his truck hurtling down a gravel road before turning and rapidly reversing toward the damaged drone.
Reuters verified the exact location of the rescue using the full-length footage. However, the regiment asked not to disclose where it took place for security reasons.
At another nearby command post, drone-platoon leader “Malyi” watched as the rescue played out on screens in real time.
“Everyone in the command center was shocked,” said the 22-year-old, who asked to be identified by his call sign.
Just a single Russian drone or land mine could have killed all three men, he added.
Polskyi — dressed in a T-shirt and shorts — hoisted both men onto his truck and raced home, evading the flying Russian drones that had been detected heading toward their new target.
Looking back, he remembered the fear in the men’s eyes. He was afraid, too.
“But you need to know how to control it,” he said.

EDITORIAL: Success as life expectancy rises
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
16:47:59 UTC
01:47:59 KST

Life expectancy in Taiwan last year was 81.27 years, up from 80.77 years in 2024, with the number of deaths falling for a third consecutive year following the COVID-19 pandemic, Ministry of the Interior data showed. Last year’s figure was just below the 2020 peak of 81.32 years. Life expectancy rose to 84.75 years for women and 77.93 years for men, higher than the global averages of 76.2 and 70.9 years respectively.
Longer lives are a social success, but they are a policy challenge when combined with low birthrates and a shrinking working-age population. The problem is not that Taiwanese are living longer, but that the country must adapt its economy, pension system and healthcare infrastructure to a society in which fewer workers support more retirees.
Taiwan became a “super-aged” society last year, with people aged 65 or older accounting for more than 20 percent of the population. The demographic shift is putting pressure on healthcare and long-term care as the workforce shrinks. Taiwan’s Long-Term Care 3.0 policy, launched this year, seeks to integrate home, community, institutional and medical care while expanding services as demand grows.
The aging population is also changing the meaning of retirement. The number of employed people aged 65 or older surpassed 500,000 in March, a record, up from about 250,000 in 2015. For some, continuing to work might be a choice; for others, rising living costs and inadequate retirement savings make it a necessity.
Meanwhile, the pension system faces growing pressure as the number of retirees rises while the working-age population shrinks.
A growing elderly population also means more people living alone. The number of households consisting of a single person aged 65 or older surpassed 713,000 in March, another record. At the end of 2024, such households accounted for about 76 percent of Taiwan’s more than 800,000 elderly households. Traditional family structures that once provided much of the care for elderly people are fracturing, leaving more vulnerable to illness, injury and isolation.
The government is responding. In March, the Executive Yuan earmarked NT$6.25 billion (US$196.43 million) for this year and next year to expand services for elderly people living alone, including home visits, emergency-response systems, meal deliveries, telephone check-ins and assistance with medical appointments. The Ministry of Health and Welfare has also begun a nationwide survey of elderly people living alone to identify those at risk and connect them with support.
There is no single solution to an aging population. Taiwan can make its pension and healthcare systems more sustainable by encouraging delayed retirement, allowing flexible transitions into retirement, improving preventive healthcare and expanding long-term care. Pension reforms might require some combination of higher contributions, slower growth in benefits, greater individual retirement savings and later retirement. Such changes should be gradual and fair, giving people time to adjust while protecting those who cannot continue working.
Taiwan should also be more open to immigration from countries with younger and more stable populations. Foreign workers already play an important role in caring for elderly people in Taiwan, and expanding opportunities for qualified caregivers and other workers to settle permanently could ease labor shortages while adding taxpayers and pension contributors.
Immigration would not eliminate the demographic imbalance, but it could help offset some of its effects. Taiwan has already expanded pension and employment-insurance coverage for some foreign professionals, showing that immigrants could play a larger role in its long-term economic future.
Technology can help as well. Taiwan is pursuing greater use of artificial intelligence (AI) and digital technology in healthcare and long-term care, while the Long-Term Care 3.0 policy calls for closer integration of medical and social-care systems. AI could reduce administrative burdens on nurses and caregivers, improve scheduling and monitoring, and allow health professionals to devote more time to patients. It cannot replace the human contact that elderly people need, but it could help a shrinking workforce care for more patients efficiently.
However, there is a limit to what the government can do. People are living longer, and societies will inevitably have to devote more resources to the later stages of life.
Taiwan should not regard longer life expectancy as a problem to be solved, but as a success that requires preparation. The goal should be not merely to add years to life, but to add healthy and productive years while ensuring that those who need care can live their final years with security and dignity.
A society that succeeds in doing that will have turned one of its greatest demographic challenges into one of its greatest achievements.
The Iran and Ukraine wars are rewriting modern military strategy. These conflicts are demonstrating that a less conventionally powerful state, by leveraging asymmetric capabilities, can impose major costs on an aggressor and fundamentally reshape the outcome of conflict. Taiwan is not only drawing lessons from those conflicts, but also translating them into practice. Far from seeking to match China ship for ship, missile for missile or aircraft for aircraft, Taiwan needs to make Chinese aggression so costly, problematic and uncertain that Beijing is deterred from launching an attack. Taiwan cannot become a bigger wolf than China, but it can ensure that

China-born Li Zhenxiu (李貞秀), a former Taiwan People’s Party (TPP) legislator who lost her seat earlier this year over her nationality status, yesterday announced that she would run for mayor of Jhubei City (竹北), although her eligibility is yet to be determined by election authorities.
Li, the first China-born spouse of a Taiwanese national to serve as a legislator, said that she would run for mayor of the city in Hsinchu County, adding the bid was “a commitment to the city after enduring rigorous political challenges.”
Her campaign team released a white paper outlining five areas of focus: transportation, education, recreation, environment and governance.
Photo: Chen Yi-kuan, Taipei Times
Li said that she had prepared for the race and it was not a sudden decision.
“Others see Jhubei through politics. I see it through everyday life,” Li said, describing herself as a “Jhubei mom” and asking residents to entrust her with the job.
If approved, Li would be running as an independent against former TPP legislator Andy Chiu (邱臣遠), Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) candidate Wu Hsu-chih (吳旭智) and Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) candidate Tseng Sheng-kai (曾聖凱).
Jhubei is led by Cheng Chao-fang (鄭朝方) of the DPP, who plans to run for Hsinchu County commissioner.
The mayor of the neighboring Hsinchu City is Ann Kao (高虹安), a former TPP member who withdrew from the party in 2024 after she was charged with corruption and suspended as mayor. She was acquitted in a second trial in December last year and reinstated as mayor.
Li, who has lived in Taiwan for more than three decades, was sworn in as a TPP legislator-at-large on Feb. 3.
She faced scrutiny over allegations that she was not eligible for the role under the Nationality Act (國籍法) and the Act Governing Relations Between the People of the Taiwan Area and the Mainland Area (臺灣地區與大陸地區人民關係條例), as she holds Chinese citizenship.
She was expelled from the TPP in April and lost her legislative seat. She later filed an administrative lawsuit against the Central Election Commission (CEC) and Legislative Yuan to try and revoke the decision.
The Taipei High Administrative Court rejected her request, ruling that she had not first gone through the required appeal process.
Asked about Li’s eligibility, CEC Chairman Michael You (游盈隆) yesterday said that the Hsinchu County Election Commission is responsible for reviewing mayoral candidacies for Jhubei.
The CEC would only intervene if there is a dispute or special circumstances, he said, adding that the agency respects rulings by the Mainland Affairs Council (MAC), which enforces the cross-strait act.
The CEC last month said that if someone from China applies to register as a candidate, their local election commission would ask the appropriate household registration office whether the applicant has submitted proof of relinquishing their Chinese household registration.
Candidates must have submitted proof of giving up their Chinese household registration and waited 10 years before becoming eligible to run for public office, the CEC said.
Li in March last year submitted a certificate to the National Immigration Agency, which she said proved that her Chinese household registration had been canceled on April 26, 1993.
The MAC said that the format and content of the certificate were “unusual” and the council had never seen such wording before.
