US Ambassador Barrack has a unique position, balancing work in Syria, Turkey, Iraq - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
15:24:15 UTC
00:24:15 KST

In recent weeks a crisis between Turkey and Israel over Syria policy has turned a spotlight onto US Ambassador Tom Barrack. As both ambassador to Turkey and envoy to Iraq and Syria, he is in a unique position vis-à-vis US policy in the Middle East. Considered close to US President Donald Trump, Barrack’s position is part of the personal diplomacy belonging to the wider global Trump doctrine. This White House does not do policy conventionally; rather, it leans into personal diplomacy and a willingness to think outside the box.
The Trump administration has been thinking outside the box on Syria policy. It was quick to follow advice from Saudi Arabia, and also likely from Turkey, regarding embracing the new Syrian government after the fall of the Assad regime.
Trump met with the new Syrian President Ahmad al-al-Sharaa and took a liking to him.
In Jerusalem, the new government in Damascus was met with intensive skepticism and eventual hostility. When the Assad regime fell, Jerusalem appears to have been taken by surprise, and some believed that a new government headed by the former leader of Islamist group Hayat Tahrir al-Sham (HTS) would not be able to unify the country.
Though the Trump administration believed Sharaa would succeed, Israeli officials called him a “terrorist in a suit,” and some even threatened to target him.
Israel embarked on a policy backing the Druze in Syria, and some floated the idea of backing the Kurds and Alawites. Israel also seized areas near the Syrian border and grabbed the summit of Mount Hermon.
While Damascus's new ruler believed he could reach an agreement with Jerusalem, initial contacts didn’t turn into a deal. Syria policy percolated through several crises in 2025, until the Trump administration was able to arrange a trilateral meeting in January 2026. However, this hadn’t ended Israel-Syria tensions or Israel-Turkey tensions over Syria.
Barrack has been vocal following Israeli airstrikes in Syria
This month those tensions exploded into view with Israeli airstrikes in northern Syria.
Barrack, who has been playing an important role in Syria for the last year, is now front and center. In the past, he has preferred to work a bit more behind the scenes. He has praised energy deals in Syria. He has helped pave the way for the US-backed Syrian Democratic Forces to integrate into the new government’s security forces. He has likely helped guide US policy on Iraq regarding disarming the Iranian-backed militias and supporting the new prime minister Ali al-Zaidi.
However, Barrack is careful not to make these incredibly complex policies too personal.
Dealing with Iraq and Syria is a thankless job. Both countries are going through transitions, and both sit at the crossroads of the Levant. They have been centers of terrorist threats, the war on ISIS, and competition between Iran, the US, Russia, Turkey, and other countries. Even China is involved.
Other policymakers in Washington who played a role here, such as Brett McGurk and United States Special Representative for Syria Engagement James Jeffrey saw how difficult this was.
In addition, Joel Rayburn, the former special envoy for Syria, and former US ambassador to Bahrain William Roebuck, who served as deputy special envoy for the Global Coalition Against ISIS, also saw this up close.
As such, Barrack took over his role in the footsteps of others who had seen the Gordian knot of US policy in Syria and Iraq up close.
Dealing with the new minefield of Israel-Turkey tensions is a difficult task. In part, this is because US policy on Israel tends to be separate from some other broader, regional policies.
Other US officials who played a key role in 2025 on Trump’s policy regarding Israel have already seen themselves critiqued in the media. Steve Witkoff, who played a key role in bringing the hostages home and in other US policies regarding Iran, Russia, and other places, is one example.
What are media accounts saying about Barrack now?
What are media accounts saying about Barrack now? “US working on deconfliction mechanism among Turkey, Israel, and Syria, US envoy says,” Al-Monitor reported.
Israel Hayom asked: “Is Tom Barrack’s job on the line because of Golan Heights comments?”
“A US envoy clarifies his comments on Golan Heights that contradicted Trump’s position,” the Associated Press noted.
Turkiye Today wrote, “Trump envoy says Barrack’s Türkiye role part of ‘larger policy’ amid Israel tensions.”
At The Jerusalem Post we recently had an analysis noting “US envoy Tom Barrack’s Israel criticism tests his credibility as a mediator.”
Israel’s Ynet went even further: “How US envoy Tom Barrack nearly ignited an Israel-Turkey war.”
After several days of a war of words regarding Barrack, there appears to be some climbdown on the rhetoric.
Ben Caspit wrote in Al-Monitor’s Israel Pulse: “Israel is rethinking its hard-line Syria policy and seeking to repair ties with US envoy and Donald Trump’s confidant Tom Barrack.”
Ynet also reported that Azerbaijan is seeking to mediate Israel-Turkey tensions. Baku is a close friend of both Ankara and Jerusalem. It doesn’t usually play a major role in Middle East issues, preferring to remain out of the spotlight and out of controversy. However, it wants to see Syria stable and has made this clear. North Press in Syria has also reported on how Israel and Turkey are trying to reduce tensions.
Barrack's role in US's Syrian policy
Barrack has played a key role in US policy. Combining the Iraq and Syria roles in the shape of the US ambassador to Ankara might seem like putting a lot of work into the hands of a single person. However, concentrating policy in the hands of one type of American proconsul may streamline policy. In the past, the US has run into problems when its policies were not aligned.
In the days of the Obama administration, the US played a Janus-faced role in Syria. One part of the US government was backing Syrian rebel groups. This largely dovetailed with what Turkey, a NATO ally, wanted. Jordan, another US friend, was happy to support the rebels alongside the United States and other Western powers. At the State Department and the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA), this seemed like a logical choice.
However, the Pentagon was tasked in the fall of 2014 with fighting ISIS as part of Joint Task Force Operation Inherent Resolve.
US Central Command (CENTCOM) had to go out and find partners in Syria. They began working with the YPG. In Ankara, this was greeted with surprise because it views the YPG as basically the Syrian version of the Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK) and thus a terrorist group. The YPG helped form the basis for the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) in 2015.
Turkey now wonders how its NATO ally was working with “terrorists” to fight ISIS.
Outside observers might think that the US could streamline this. Get the State Department, CENTCOM, the CIA, and others in the same room at the White House and figure out what to do on Syria.
Instead, the SDF crossed the Euphrates River to liberate Manbij from ISIS in 2016. Turkey then invaded Syria during Operation Euphrates Shield to basically put a stop to the SDF advance. For a moment, it looked as if US-backed forces might run into other US-backed forces. How this would help defeat ISIS or topple the Assad regime was unclear.
Thus, putting American policy on Syria in the hands of one person, rather than having everyone doing their own thing, is probably best. Having a diplomat who has the trust of Ankara, as well as Damascus, and can speak clearly with the White House makes sense from a policy point of view.
Whether this can reduce tensions with Israel and Turkey remains to be seen.

Institutional responses across the three countries combine hydrometeorological monitoring with preparedness and social protection measures.
El Salvador plans temporary cash transfers for the most vulnerable families, while Honduras has an anticipatory action mechanism backed by the UN. Panama is preparing sector-specific programs covering water, housing, health, food and humanitarian assistance.

Breadcrumb
UK Green members prepare 'Zionism is racism' motion ahead of party conference
Ahead of the UK Green Party conference in October, pro-Palestine members are preparing a motion to be heard that could officially declare the party as anti-Zionist.
The "Zionism is racism" motion seeks to define Zionism as a racist, settler‑colonial ideology and declare the party as against it.
Its key demands include supporting the Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions (BDS) movement and enforcing embargoes like those used against South Africa during apartheid, releasing Palestinian prisoners, acknowledging the right to resistance under international law, and supporting a single democratic Palestinian state with equal rights and the right of return.
"This is a historic motion that could change the face of British politics," Lubna Speitan, Palestinian activist and author of the motion, told The New Arab.
"We're not asking for something new, to acknowledge Palestinian rights to not just self-determination but to resistance by all available means, as per international law."
"This is something that's based on law, the Equality Act, international law, the Geneva Convention."
Despite facing accusations of antisemitism and being reported to anti-terrorism police, the motion received a record-breaking number of 745 co-proposers, double that of the last motion, which garnered 333.
It has also been endorsed by over fifty organisations and individuals, including Greta Thunberg and Mohammed El Kurd.
The motion is currently on the prioritisation ballot, where members can decide the order they want to see motions come forward in October.
While the motion was scheduled to be debated at the Spring Conference in March, it never reached the floor, but supporters hope it will not only be heard but also passed.
"I think that should this motion pass, it will have ripple effects in sort of British and international politics," Tariq Khawaja, member of the Green Party and one of the backers of the motion, told The New Arab. "[The motion] already has achieved what we set out to achieve."
"It has changed the conversation. There are people now who are talking and questioning about Zionism in a way that they weren't doing a year ago; there are signs that we're seeing on protests that weren't there a year ago."
Speitan and Khawaja highlight that the Green Party is the first UK political party to acknowledge that Israel is an apartheid state committing genocide.
"This is basic stuff. For a UK political party to be the first political party to call for equality amongst Palestinians in Palestine, and also to call for liberation of Palestinians, but also to call for justice and reparations," Khawaja said.
"We have a responsibility as the arbiters of empire and imperialism to be a voice for those that don't have one."
Khawaja also noted that they are in discussions with supporters worldwide in other political parties, hoping the motion will pass internationally as well.
Following the appointment of Zack Polanski as leader of the Greens, the party has seen a surge in support from voters concerned about Palestine, reflected in recent elections and polling.

Reported by
A court in Yerevan ordered the eldest son of former Armenian President Robert Kocharyan held in pretrial detention on Wednesday, expanding a sweeping corruption investigation that has ensnared the former leader and several high-ranking ex-officials.
The decision to hold Sedrak Kocharyan for two months followed his detention on Tuesday alongside his father. Investigators carried out coordinated raids on family-linked real estate and commercial holdings, escalating a long-running political battle between Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan and the country's former ruling elite.
Lawyers for the younger Kocharyan said they would appeal the ruling, with defense attorney Alexander Kochubayev describing the case as an "extralegal prosecution" driven by political motives.
Armenia’s Anti-Corruption Committee stated that the elder Kocharyan, who served as president from 1998 to 2008, used his office to acquire state property at artificially low prices and accept substantial bribes. Officials said several prime parcels of land were improperly funneled to the family and later developed into commercial ventures.
Investigators are scrutinizing financial wire transfers to Sedrak Kocharyan between 2001 and 2019 totaling approximately 144 billion drams (about $392 million), $309 million, 77 million euros, and 18 million rubles.
Authorities detained six people in connection with the probe. Tax officials simultaneously sealed the offices of Toyota Yerevan and Orange Fitness, two businesses linked to the family, as part of a parallel tax-evasion inquiry.
The Prosecutor General’s Office said criminal proceedings were initiated on Aug. 24 against the former president for abuse of power, bribery, and large-scale money laundering. Nine others were also named, including former President Serzh Sargsyan—who also previously served as defense minister—a former prime minister, a former mayor of Yerevan, and a prominent businessman.
Following his arrest, the former president’s office reported that his health had deteriorated at the Anti-Corruption Committee’s headquarters, requiring emergency medical attention following a recent medical procedure. His office characterized the arrests as "another assault by the authorities."
The legal actions came shortly after a fiery clash in parliament between Prime Minister Pashinyan and the former president’s younger son, Levon Kocharyan, an opposition lawmaker whose home was also searched.
In parliament, Levon Kocharyan accused the prime minister of exerting improper political pressure on the judiciary. Pashinyan countered by questioning the origins of the family's wealth, promising that assets acquired at public expense would be returned to the state "piece by piece."
Ex-President Kocharyan previously faced charges of "overthrowing the constitutional order" linked to a deadly crackdown on post-election protests in Yerevan in 2008. Armenia’s Constitutional Court ruled in 2021 that the legal provision used in that case could not be applied retroactively, leading to the dismissal of those charges.
Former President Serzh Sargsyan, who succeeded Kocharyan in 2008 and is also facing criminal prosecution in the same case, was summoned to the Anti-Corruption Committee headquarters in Yerevan on Tuesday.
Speaking to reporters outside the building, Sargsyan said he did not yet know the specific reason for the summons.
“When we receive the case materials, we will talk. I don’t understand anything,” he said.
Sargsyan was placed under a travel ban on Wednesday.

Surge in families renting puts more children at risk of housing insecurity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
15:15:43 UTC
00:15:43 KST

More children are growing up in rental housing and moving every couple of years
In short:
A new report by researchers at Adelaide University shows children who grow up in rental housing move every 2.3 years, on average.
Around one-in-eight children who grow up in rentals have moved at least 10 times by age 14.
The proportion of Australian children growing up in private rental housing jumped by 20 per cent between 2001 and 2023.
More children are growing up in private rentals and facing housing insecurity, a new report finds, warning that it could have long-term implications for their development, physical health and mental wellbeing.
The study by four researchers at Adelaide University — Amy Clair, Emma Baker, Lynne Giles and Claire Morey — has been released by the Australian Housing and Urban Research Institute today.
By analysing a range of comprehensive and long-term datasets, such as the Household Income and Labour Dynamics in Australia (HILDA) survey and the Longitudinal Study of Australian Children, the authors attempted to determine the effects of Australia's multi-decade housing affordability crisis on children.
The report found that as housing prices surged between 2001 and 2023, the proportion of households with children living in homes owned outright plunged 52 per cent.
Those in social rentals fell 46 per cent as the public housing sector stagnated, those who owned with a mortgage increased 27 per cent and those in private rentals rose 20 per cent.
Research lead and associate professor Amy Clair said the latter statistic was particularly concerning as children growing up in private rental properties moved every 2.3 years on average.
"By age 14, a child in a private rental had moved an average of six times. By comparison, those in households that owned their home had moved a little over twice on average, and children in social housing had moved just over four times," she said.
The data shows children growing up in households with a mortgage tend to have moved about three times by age 14, which is half as often as those in a family renting.
However, those averages also mask more extreme housing instability in many cases.
Around one in eight children growing up in private rentals had lived in 10 or more homes by age 14, compared to approximately one in 40 children living in a home owned with a mortgage, the research found.
"Results were concerning, as housing impacts mattered most during developmental transitions, such as starting school, when disruption can compound other disadvantages,"
It may not surprise you to learn that few households with children were renting by choice, with only 7 per cent reporting they did so because they preferred it and 8 per cent saying they appreciated its flexibility, while more than half said they did not have a housing deposit saved and around half said they could not afford to buy.
'Housing a critical determinant of physical and mental health'
The research also showed that children growing up in rental housing were more likely to live in a household suffering financial stress or poor living conditions.
Roughly 18 per cent of households with children in private rentals were late on a housing payment, compared to about 7 per cent of households with a mortgage, while around 10 per cent of children in private rentals experienced overcrowding, which was more than twice the rate of children living in owner-occupied homes.
Dr Clair said children's experiences were often ignored in the public discussion of housing affordability, partly through a lack of data about their housing status, and better information could help foster the housing conditions that allowed children to thrive.
"There is a growing evidence base positioning housing as a critical determinant of children's physical and mental health, behavioural outcomes, developmental vulnerability and educational attainment,"
"However, Australia's data is fragmented, creating blind spots that hinder early intervention, response targeting and accountable policy."
The report suggests that maternal and child health services, early childhood education, schools and primary care services could routinely collect indicators of affordability stress, overcrowding and dwelling problems, while population surveys could include indicators of thermal comfort, damp, mould, crowding, safety and amenity.
"Children's lives are being shaped by housing, but we need the data to see how this is happening, and for policymakers to use the insights to craft policy that will improve housing outcomes for children," Dr Clair said.
She said the resulting insights could support early warning systems, local service planning and targeted intervention.

Hundreds Feared Dead, Including Foreign Tourists, After Flash Floods in Nepal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
15:14:01 UTC
00:14:01 KST

More than 300 people have been killed and at least 900 are missing after devastating flash floods swept through the Himalayan region along the Nepal-Tibet border, local officials confirmed Thursday.
Severe flooding was reported across the districts of Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading, and Gorkha, north of the Nepalese capital Kathmandu early Wednesday. Much of the flooding occurred along the Trishuli and Bhotekoshi rivers in the north of the country.
The Nepali tourism board said that, based on records from travel and trekking firms, 644 travelers are still out of contact. More than a hundred of those are Indian nationals who were on pilgrimage to Mount Kailash in Tibet, a Nepali tourism official is quoted as telling the Associated Press.
Thursday’s count from the tourism board shows 65 missing travelers are from the U.S., and the State Department said it was aware of the Americans impacted by the floods. Among the others still unaccounted for are foreign nationals from Canada, the United Kingdom, Malaysia, Australia, Japan, and Singapore.
The U.S. embassy in Nepal issued a warning to U.S. citizens in Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading, Gorkha, Chitwan, and Tanahun, urging them to “stay away from riverbanks and low-lying areas, seek higher ground, and follow local instructions.” The embassy added that it was working to account for Americans affected by the flooding.
Nepali Prime Minister Balendra Shah met with local Members of Parliament (MPs) on Wednesday to discuss issues including flood damage, condition of settlements in local areas, rescue and relief work, his office said.
“The government has intensified the search and rescue operations by deploying security forces in the flood-affected areas,” Shah’s office added.
What do we know about the floods?
It remains unclear what caused the floods, but Nepal is highly vulnerable to the climate crisis.
The U.S. Geological Survey reported initial shaking as an earthquake, though it later determined that the tremors were caused by “a glacial collapse and debris flow that caused subsequent catastrophic impacts downstream.” That event generated seismic energy equivalent to a 5.2-magnitude quake.
The Kathmandu Post reported, citing the country’s national disaster authority, that an initial analysis of satellite imagery from Planet Labs indicated that an avalanche of ice and rock triggered the flood in the Lhende River, about 20 km (12 mi) north-east of the Rasuwagadhi border crossing between China and Nepal.
Nepal has thousands of glaciers, but with the Himalayan region warming, many of them are melting.
How Nepal is responding to the crisis
Data from the disaster risk reduction agency also showed that of the more than 900 missing, 28 are Nepali police, 44 are from the Nepali Army, and 13 are from its specialized paramilitary Armed Police Force.
Nepali Police published details of 66 people hospitalized due to injuries from the flooding, most of whom are from the Nuwakot and Rasuwa regions.
Video shared by police showed catastrophic flooding, with entire buildings swept away in the powerful currents. Other footage shared shows a bridge and multiple buildings on the banks of the Trishuli River destroyed in the flooding. Officials have since confirmed that 32 bridges and nearly 40 km of road were swept away.
Police also issued a warning that they expect the flooding to continue down the Bhotekoshi River into the regions of Dhading and Muglin in the center of the country.
The Prithvi Highway, one of Nepal's busiest roads that connects Kathmandu to the second-largest city, Pokhara, passes through these regions along the Trishuli River. Police confirmed Wednesday this section of the highway would be closed.
The flooding has also resulted in widespread casualties at the border between Nepal and China’s Tibet region. A mudslide occurred near the Gyirong checkpoint on the border, resulting in at least three deaths and more than 550 people missing in Gyirong County, according to Chinese state media.
Chinese President Xi Jinping ordered “all-out efforts” for search and rescue operations in response to the mudslide, as well as calling for the strengthening of “monitoring and early warning, ensure scientific rescue operations and guard against secondary disasters,” Chinese media reported.
Footage from the checkpoint shows water engulfing buildings as people flee the oncoming currents. TIME has been unable to independently verify the footage.

US says Chinese hackers broke into Justice Department, NASA, Federal Reserve, Senate and more

- The hacking was linked to Nanjing Xinjiuwei Network Technology Company, connected to China's Ministry of State Security, military, and civilian intelligence.

AI generated
WASHINGTON - The United States said on Aug 26 that it had disrupted a Chinese hacking operation responsible for break-ins at the US Justice Department, NASA, the Federal Reserve, the US Senate, and other sensitive government agencies.
In a statement, the Justice Department said that it had seized domains used by two hacking platforms, dubbed “QScan” and “QTRouter,” which it said had been used as part of the campaign.
An affidavit identified the US Department of Energy, the Department of Health and Human Services, the National Institutes of Health, and four unnamed companies in the United States and South Korea as being among the hackers’ victims.
The Chinese Embassy in Washington did not immediately return a message seeking comment.
Beijing routinely denies responsibility for hacking activity.
The Justice Department said that the platforms were run by a China-based firm, the Nanjing Xinjiuwei Network Technology Company, whose clients it said included China’s civilian intelligence agency, the Ministry of State Security and its military, the People’s Liberation Army.
Nanjing Xinjiuwei did not immediately respond to a request for comment outside normal business hours.
The affidavit said the group’s computer infrastructure had been used to compromise critical infrastructure and other sensitive networks in the US and worldwide since at least 2018.
The level of access they gained ranged, according to the affidavit.
The hackers unsuccessfully attempted to gain access to NASA networks in August 2019 by targeting a virtual private network vulnerability.
In September 2024, the hackers carried out intrusions at three unnamed Energy Department laboratories, the NIH, an unnamed HHS agency, and a US security device manufacturer, according to the affidavit.
Representatives for the agencies and government organisations that the Justice Department identified as targets did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Chinese-linked hacking campaigns have compromised a string of sensitive US government and private networks in recent years.
In March, the FBI notified Congress that hackers had penetrated certain agency networks related to people under FBI investigation, with public reporting later attributing the compromise to China.
Chinese-linked hackers have also been tied to a compromise of certain US House of Representatives committee networks, as well as multiple major telecommunications companies in recent years.
Experts who follow Chinese cyber activity say that private contractors routinely carry out high-profile intrusions on behalf of various Chinese government agencies.
“Over the last decade, the number of companies offering niche offensive services has exploded,” said Dakota Cary, a China analyst with cybersecurity company SentinelOne. REUTERS

As of the end of August, the defense line under the army corps' responsibility extended up to 171 kilometers—about 12% of the total length of the front. Overall, the corps' warriors eliminated almost 23,000 occupiers and wounded more than 16,500 others, captured 362 Russians, destroyed more than 126,000 drones of various types, over 220 electronic warfare systems, 55 multiple-launch rocket systems, about 40 tanks, and more than 310 artillery systems.
Commander of the 79th Separate Tavriia Air Assault Brigade, Colonel Eduard Kolodii. From January to August 10 of this year, the brigade's units under Colonel Kolodii's command carried out a range of defensive, offensive, assault, and search-and-strike actions in the Pokrovsk, Myrnohrad, Oleksandrivka, and adjacent areas. During this period, they inflicted more than 1,000 personnel casualties on Russia, captured seven Russian occupiers, and destroyed equipment, communications systems, and ammunition depots. In the difficult conditions of intense combat, Eduard Kolodii ensured stable command of the brigade and the timely deployment of reserves, making it possible to disrupt a number of the enemy's offensive and counteroffensive actions and hold important defensive lines.
The President awarded 31 service members the Orders of Bohdan Khmelnytskyi, 1st–3rd Class, and \"For Courage,\" 1st–3rd Class, as well as the medals \"For Military Service to Ukraine.\" The Head of State conferred the military rank of brigadier general on Colonels Oleh Honcharuk, Valerii Skreda, and Oleksii Khalabuda.
As a result of the Oleksandrivka operation, which has been ongoing since January of this year, it was possible to liberate 745 square kilometers of territory and return 26 villages in the Dnipro, Donetsk, and Zaporizhzhia regions to Ukrainian control. Russian losses amount to at least 9,550 killed and more than 6,600 wounded. It was also possible to replenish Ukraine's prisoner-exchange fund.

The Siberian Ring Photon Source: Inside Russia’s latest megascience site (VIDEO)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
15:03:08 UTC
00:03:08 KST

The Siberian Ring Photon Source: Inside Russia’s latest megascience site (VIDEO)
Russia’s latest megascience undertaking lies not far from the river Ob, south of Novosibirsk in Siberia, some 3,000 km east of Moscow. The Siberian Ring Photon Source (SKIF) synchrotron complex is effectively an ultra-powerful X-ray microscope for research ranging from medicine and chemistry to metallurgy and geology.
RT has been granted access to SKIF, a state-of-the-art megascience project built to let scientists examine matter at the atomic scale.
SKIF was officially unveiled by Russian President Vladimir Putin earlier this month. At the time, he said that the opening was postponed from 2024 because foreign suppliers failed to deliver certain equipment due to Western sanctions, forcing Russian teams to reproduce key components domestically. Now, the first research stations are expected to enter operation before year-end.
The construction of the nearly $600 million facility began in 2021, becoming one of Russia’s most expensive scientific projects. As for its principles, the device accelerates electrons to almost the speed of light and sends them around a 476-meter storage ring, where magnets bend their path and make them give off extremely bright radiation. Scientists can then select the part of that radiation they need, from infrared through hard X-rays, and aim it at a sample.
The scientists can then watch a chemical reaction as it happens, studying how metals behave under shock waves, examining proteins and medicines, or looking inside archaeological objects without cutting them open. The method is also expected to drastically reduce the development time for new materials, pharmaceuticals, and cancer drugs.
“The emission that the source creates is well suited to studying the atomic or molecular structure of a compound… It’s viruses, medicine, bone fractures, aircraft engine, turbines, chemical reactions, high-speed processes. Indeed, it’s useful to everyone,” SKIF Director Evgeny Levichev told RT.
One of the upcoming experiments will examine titanium-based catalysts used to produce ultra-high-molecular-weight polyethylene, while other planned work includes studying difficult-to-extract gold and searching lake sediments near the site of the 1908 Tunguska event for possible extraterrestrial particles.

Cambridge Pixel will show its software for uncrewed and autonomous surface vessels at SMM 2026, a maritime trade fair running September 1-4 in Hamburg, Germany.
The UK-based company will set up at Hall B1, Stand 321, where it plans to demonstrate radar, camera and sensor processing modules used for tracking, data fusion, display, control, recording and simulation on USVs and ASVs.
Cambridge Pixel has supplied software components to USV and ASV developers for more than a decade, working with manufacturers across the United States, Europe and Asia. The company says its software is integrated with more than 80 different radar systems, providing tracking, navigation and situational awareness without requiring additional hardware.
The company’s core product for this market is SPx Server V2, which handles radar video processing, proximity detection and tracking for collision avoidance and autonomous navigation. A Detection Server configuration within that software provides plot extraction and proximity detection, while a Tracking Server configuration adds multi-hypothesis target tracking. Cambridge Pixel says the software can output obstacle and target data to external autonomy or vessel-control systems using formats including ASTERIX, NMEA-0183, TAK and SAPIENT.
The company says its technology also supports navigation in GPS-denied environments, along with camera control and unlocking maritime radar systems for use with custom software.
Cambridge Pixel lists customers in 65 countries, including BAE Systems, the British Royal Navy, Echodyne, Furuno, Hanwha, Hensoldt, L3Harris, Lockheed Martin, OSI Maritime, QinetiQ, Raytheon, Saab, Thales and the U.S. Navy.
SMM 2026 is expected to draw more than 2,200 exhibitors and nearly 50,000 visitors from over 100 countries, according to the event organizers. This year’s edition will include a new Maritime Security and Defence Expo section, featuring exhibitors focused on unmanned systems, cyber solutions, maritime surveillance and critical infrastructure protection.

AI Is Lowering the Barriers to China’s Information Warfare Against Japan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
15:03:00 UTC
00:03:00 KST

Japan’s Ministry of Defense recently released its 2026 Defense of Japan white paper, once again drawing attention to China’s rapid advances in artificial intelligence and their implications for the regional security environment. Yet the most immediate danger to Japan may not come from AI’s application to conventional military systems. Generative AI is also lowering the barriers for Chinese information operations targeting Japanese society.
In late 2025, Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae made comments in the Diet linking a Taiwan contingency to Japan’s own security. Since then, disinformation targeting Japanese political figures and domestic issues has grown – not only in volume but also in sophistication. Research by organizations including the Sasakawa Peace Foundation and OpenAI suggests that China-linked influence operators are increasingly using AI to adapt their activities to Japan’s online environment and improve the efficiency of their operations.
AI is beginning to erode what was once one of the most obvious weaknesses of Chinese information operations against Japan: the linguistic and cultural barrier. Content that once featured grammatical mistakes, awkward translations and unnatural expressions is becoming harder for ordinary users to identify at a glance.
If these capabilities are deployed to interfere with elections, discredit politicians or amplify social divisions, their effects could extend far beyond any single piece of false information.
A special report by Nikkei in February found that more than 400 China-linked social media accounts spread negative content about Takaichi during Japan’s House of Representatives election. Separately, the Yomiuri Shimbun, citing research by Japan Nexus Intelligence, reported that under a different set of criteria, thousands of coordinated accounts on X were involved in sharing and amplifying related content.
The narratives did not focus solely on attacking Takaichi personally. They also linked Japan’s efforts to strengthen its defense capabilities with concerns over social welfare, seeking to promote the argument that military expansion was coming at the expense of ordinary people.
In the past, such accounts often left obvious clues. Some had been created only recently. Their Japanese reflected Chinese word order and linguistic habits, while others mixed simplified Chinese characters with Japanese usage. AI-generated images also frequently contained visual errors that made them relatively easy to identify.
Those weaknesses, however, are becoming less pronounced.
The Sankei Shimbun has continued to track PAPERWALL, a China-linked information network that includes 15 websites masquerading as Japanese news outlets. The continued operation of these sites, and the broader ecosystem surrounding them, points toward an increasingly localized approach to influence operations. Improvements in language, imagery, and the appearance of fake news sites are making it more difficult for ordinary readers to distinguish legitimate sources from fabricated ones.
A report released by OpenAI in February offered another important clue. The company found that China-linked actors had used ChatGPT to assist in planning an online influence campaign targeting Takaichi. Influence actors appear willing to incorporate different AI systems into their existing workflows whenever those tools make their operations more effective.
What matters is not the nationality of the model. What matters is that generative AI is reducing the cost of cross-language information operations. In the past, producing large volumes of content tailored to a Japanese audience required translators, graphic designers, social media operators and people familiar with Japanese political and cultural contexts.
Large language models can now help operators correct grammar, adjust tone, generate images, and produce multiple versions of the same narrative for different audiences within minutes. In other words, AI is making China’s information warfare more scalable, faster and more localized.
How, then, should Japan respond? Taiwan offers one useful point of reference.
Taiwan has faced Chinese information operations for years and shares a Chinese-language environment with the mainland. Beijing therefore does not face the same linguistic barrier when targeting Taiwanese society that it encounters in Japan. Precisely for that reason, Taiwan was forced to develop social mechanisms for dealing with large-scale disinformation campaigns and networks of suspicious accounts.
Taiwan’s experience does not rely solely on government agencies or third-party fact-checkers. Individual users also identify, report, and block suspicious accounts, while civil society organizations and researchers continuously monitor information networks and patterns of coordinated behavior.
Language and culture themselves can also serve as tools for identifying manipulation. Although Taiwan and China both use Chinese, there are clear differences in vocabulary, grammar, social experience, and political context. Chinese influence operators can use AI to reduce these differences, but they cannot easily reproduce the cultural background and lived experience accumulated within another society.
Japan retains the same kind of advantage. Japanese language and social culture are highly contextual. Even if Chinese operators use AI to improve translation and content generation, that does not mean they can fully understand the linguistic and political differences between generations, regions, and social groups in Japan.
Japan should therefore move beyond a defensive model that waits for false information to appear and then fact-checks it. The more important task is to strengthen society’s ability to recognize coordinated influence operations before they gain traction.
This is also why information-security cooperation between Japan and Taiwan should become more institutionalized. The two sides could deepen exchanges on identifying coordinated accounts, detecting deepfakes, analyzing foreign influence networks and monitoring information environments during major disasters, elections, or political crises.
AI is making Chinese information operations cheaper, faster and easier to deploy across language barriers. But it still cannot fully replicate the cultural knowledge and lived experience embedded in a society.
Japan therefore does not need to build a wall capable of blocking every piece of false information. It needs to build an information environment in which foreign influence operations are less likely to succeed. As Japan and Taiwan confront increasingly similar information-security threats, sharing their experience in identifying and countering Chinese influence operations could become an increasingly important part of regional security cooperation.

Genetic vulnerability appears to have amplified the pandemic’s toll on teen mental health
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
15:00:54 UTC
00:00:54 KST

A recent study provides evidence that adolescent mental health declined markedly during the COVID-19 pandemic, with youth who carry a genetic predisposition for psychiatric conditions experiencing an even greater overall burden of symptoms. The findings indicate that the environmental stressors of the pandemic caused lasting emotional and behavioral difficulties, particularly for adolescent girls. The research was published in Translational Psychiatry.
The COVID-19 pandemic introduced widespread disruptions, including school closures, social isolation, and shifted daily routines. These rapid lifestyle changes took a heavy toll on young people worldwide. For example, a 2021 meta-analysis found that rates of clinically elevated depression and anxiety symptoms among children and teenagers roughly doubled across the globe during the first year of the pandemic. Researchers have been trying to understand why some adolescents adapted to these changes over time while others experienced worsening psychological health.
Psychiatric conditions are known to have a strong hereditary component, meaning genetic differences play a role in how adolescents handle environmental stress. A study covered by PsyPost in 2024 found that a higher shared genetic risk across various psychiatric conditions was strongly associated with a persistent pattern of high depressive symptoms throughout adolescence. To measure this inherited risk, scientists often use polygenic risk scores. These scores combine the small effects of thousands of genetic variations into a single number to estimate an individual’s broad biological susceptibility to mental health conditions.
“We are particularly interested in the impact of social isolation on adolescents’ health,” said Chun Chieh Fan of the Center for Population Neuroscience and Genetics at the Laureate Institute for Brain Research. “While there were many studies reporting the crisis among youth, there was limited discussion on who is most susceptible.”
To identify these at-risk groups, Fan and co-lead author Lucy Shao of the University of California San Diego analyzed data from 10,374 adolescents. The participants were drawn from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development Study, a large ongoing project tracking child development in the United States. The youth were between 10 and 14 years old in 2020.
The researchers tracked 20 different measures of mental health over five assessment waves. These visits covered the period before the pandemic, the early pandemic in 2020, and the late pandemic extending into early 2022.
The team calculated four distinct polygenic risk scores for each participant based on past genetic research in adults. These scores estimated the genetic likelihood of compulsive disorders, psychotic disorders, neurodevelopmental disorders, and internalizing conditions like depression and anxiety. By comparing these scores with parent-reported and self-reported mental health surveys, the scientists could track how symptom levels changed over time in relation to each participant’s genetic profile.
The findings indicate that the pandemic was associated with broad increases in psychological distress. During the early pandemic, symptom scores across various mental health measures increased by 4% to 14% compared to pre-pandemic levels. Symptoms tended to remain elevated during the late pandemic period, ranging from 6% to 24% above early pandemic levels. Specifically, parent-reported withdrawn behavior, depression, and rule-breaking increased, as did self-reported internalizing problems.
Genetic predispositions also played a distinct role in symptom severity. For every one-unit increase in a participant’s neurodevelopmental or internalizing polygenic risk score, they experienced between a 3% and 21% increase in symptoms across most mental health categories.
“The COVID pandemic imposed a long-term impact on youth, especially when the disruptions lingered over years,” Fan told PsyPost. “The cumulative stress compounded upon those who are particularly vulnerable, emerging a wide range of behavioral issues among youth.”
The researchers noticed marked differences when separating the data by sex. Female adolescents exhibited a greater increase in mental health challenges during the early pandemic, including a 25% increase in parent-reported affective problems. In contrast, male adolescents showed a smaller initial bump in symptoms that tended to stabilize or even decrease during the later pandemic stages. Female participants with a high genetic risk for neurodevelopmental conditions also experienced a larger increase in conduct problems and aggressive behavior during the early pandemic.
These results are in line with research covered by PsyPost earlier this year, which found that the global population-level burden of mental disorders surged among children and teens during the pandemic. That earlier study, which modeled broad disorder prevalence rather than tracking specific symptom scores in a cohort, similarly noted that female youth experienced the largest increases in anxiety and depression.
The study has some limitations to consider. The polygenic risk scores used by the researchers are broad statistical tools designed to measure traits across a large population. They are not diagnostic tests and cannot predict individual behavior or clinical outcomes for a specific child. The genetic data primarily relied on models derived from adults, which might not perfectly capture how mental health conditions develop during early adolescence.
The calendar-based periods used to define the pandemic phases do not isolate the specific causes of adolescent distress. Increased symptoms could be tied to school closures, financial strain at home, fear of infection, or physical health changes, but the data cannot separate these intertwined factors. The researchers also adjusted for age, but because adolescence is a period of rapid emotional change, normal developmental shifts might still overlap with pandemic-related trends.
Future studies could focus on identifying which specific pandemic disruptions had the strongest impact on adolescent well-being. Researchers might also examine protective factors in the home or community that help mitigate mental health risks. Expanding genetic research to include more diverse ancestral populations would help ensure that these scientific models accurately reflect the experiences of all youth.
The study, “Contributions of Genetic Liability and the COVID-19 Pandemic to Rising Psychopathology Among Youth in the United States,” was authored by Lucy Shao, Jonathan Ahern, Robert Loughnan, Bohan Xu, Holly E. Baker, Susan F. Tapert, Fiona C. Baker, Wesley K. Thompson, Orsolya Kiss, Eva M. Müller-Oehring, Marie Gombert-Labedens, and Chun Chieh Fan.

US Air Force rescues five Navy crew after hard landing
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
16:00:17 BST
00:00:17 KST

Two HH-60W Jolly Green II helicopters were launched from Nellis Air Force Base to recover five US Navy personnel after an MH-60S Seahawk made a hard landing in mountainous terrain near China Lake.
US Air Force rescue crews have recovered five Navy personnel after their MH-60S Seahawk made a hard landing during a high-altitude training flight in mountainous terrain near Naval Air Weapons Station China Lake, California, the UK Defence Journal understands.
The incident occurred on 10 August, prompting the Air Force Rescue Coordination Center to notify the 88th Test and Evaluation Squadron at approximately 11:30am. According to a US Air Force account of the rescue, the squadron immediately recalled personnel and coordinated with the Navy unit involved while the 355th Aircraft Maintenance Squadron prepared two HH-60W Jolly Green II combat rescue helicopters for the mission.
Despite the alert arriving on what had been scheduled as a training day, maintenance personnel generated both HH-60Ws in less than 30 minutes. The rapid preparation included troubleshooting an electrical problem on one of the helicopters after a circuit breaker issue threatened to prevent it from launching and no replacement component was immediately available.
Staff Sergeant Lucas Seney, an aerospace propulsion craftsman with the 355th Aircraft Maintenance Squadron, said, as quoted in the news update: “When production gave us the word for a real-world mission, I gathered the Airmen I had on the line and started directing traffic. The crew worked well together, and I was proud to see just how efficiently everyone was able to get the job done.”
Staff Sergeant Cody Adams, an avionics craftsman, helped identify the fault affecting one of the aircraft. He said: “We diagnosed the master caution warning press-to-reset button as what was causing the circuit breaker to pop and provided aircrew with a workaround to keep the system operational and allow on-time takeoff.”
The two HH-60Ws departed Nellis Air Force Base at 1pm. By 3pm, their crews had established two-way radio communications with the stranded Navy personnel and visually identified their position. Captain John Howe, a combat rescue officer with the 88th Test and Evaluation Squadron, then led the pararescue element into the landing zone to assess the five survivors.
The team confirmed that none of the Navy personnel had been injured. After evaluating the terrain and the condition of the survivors, the rescuers elected to move the helicopters to a closer landing area rather than requiring the group to make a more demanding movement through mountainous terrain.
Lieutenant Colonel Kenneth “Buddy” Wilkins, commander of the 88th Test and Evaluation Squadron and flight lead for the mission, said the crews had to carefully consider aircraft performance in the high-altitude environment. He said: “It was a good call by the team getting on the ground, making a good patient assessment, and then solid planning on the aircrew side of the house to determine what our ragged-edge power margins were that we needed to get into the zone and get out.”
The HH-60W is the US Air Force’s current-generation combat rescue helicopter and is designed for personnel recovery in demanding environments. High-altitude operations can be particularly challenging for helicopters because thinner air reduces rotor and engine performance, making aircraft weight, temperature and available power important considerations when selecting landing sites and extraction profiles.
All five sailors were aboard the rescue helicopters by 3:50pm. They were subsequently returned to their unit’s ramp at Naval Air Weapons Station China Lake before the Air Force helicopters flew back to Nellis.
Howe said preparation before an emergency was central to the speed of the response: “The preparation is what makes the execution smooth. It’s the combination of preestablished operating procedures, keeping equipment staged and ready for use, and hasty mission planning prior to departure, that makes this process effective, and expeditious.”
The Air Force said the operation drew directly on repeated training between the 88th Test and Evaluation Squadron and the 355th Aircraft Maintenance Squadron. Wilkins said: “This mission was a really good example of us taking the lessons learned from those previous events and executing as quickly and efficiently as possible. Within five minutes, I knew we had tails. Within 30 minutes, they were ready for us to go out.”

How valid are U.S. commitments under Trump?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
15:00:09 UTC
00:00:09 KST

How valid are U.S. commitments under Trump?
TEHRAN - Under Trump, America’s agreements increasingly appear conditional, reversible, and vulnerable to sudden policy shifts, raising fundamental questions about the credibility of U.S. commitments.
Chas Freeman, former U.S. ambassador to Saudi Arabia and former assistant secretary of defense, said: “We’ve convinced the entire world that we don’t know what we’re doing, and we can’t be trusted, and we don’t keep our word, and we don’t even stay consistent from one day to the next. So how can you deal with us? That’s the question everybody has out there.”
American duplicity and betrayal intensified following the conclusion of the U.S.-Iran memorandum of understanding, signed on June 17, 2026, by Trump at the Palace of Versailles.
Pakistan, with the assistance of several regional countries, mediated the agreement. It was described as an initial accord intended to pave the way toward a broader, final agreement. The memorandum contained 14 provisions setting out the terms for an immediate ceasefire and mechanisms for negotiating a lasting peace.
Trump quickly reneged on his commitment to the memorandum. John Mearsheimer, professor of political science at the University of Chicago, said in July 2026 that, from Iran’s perspective, the United States had failed to honor its commitments under the agreement.
“When we look at what is happening from the Iranian perspective… the Iranians [rightly] believe that the United States has failed to honor its commitments under the agreement,” he pointed out.
The Strait of Hormuz and oil-export waivers
Iran had several reasonable grounds for accusing Trump of failing to comply with the agreement. Provision 5 addressed what had replaced enriched uranium as a central focus of the illegal war: Iran’s position on shipping through the economically vital Strait of Hormuz.
The provision was understood to mean that Iran would lift its blockade while continuing to oversee and direct maritime traffic. When Iran took control of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz in March 2026, it replaced the pre-war shipping route, which ran through the middle of the strait, with another route directing vessels along its own coastline.
After the memorandum was signed, however, the Trump administration began directing ships onto a different route through Omani territorial waters. Following the ceasefire, there were three routes: one along the Omani coast, the central route used before the war, and one along the Iranian coast.
“We violated [the memorandum] by creating a southern corridor,” said retired U.S. Army Colonel Daniel Davis, host of the Deep Dive podcast, which focuses on geopolitical issues.
“There is nothing in the memorandum we signed that authorizes the creation of a southern corridor, or allows the United States to enter it and unilaterally determine how it should operate. It simply is not there in the memorandum.”
Davis, who returned from Afghanistan and exposed in 2012 how civilian and military officials had misled the public about the course of the war there, said the U.S. move in the Hormuz Strait was a deliberate provocation.
According to American writer Brian McGlinchey, author of the Stark Realities blog, whether intentional or not, it was indeed a provocation by the United States.
After issuing radio warnings to vessels attempting to use the southern route, Iran fired disabling projectiles at them. Trump then resumed his bombing campaign against Iran, prompting Tehran to retaliate against U.S. forces and the countries hosting them. The Iranian armed forces subsequently began a prolonged cycle of retaliatory strikes.
Then there is Provision 10 of the memorandum, under which the Trump administration promised to issue sanctions waivers allowing Iranian oil and petroleum products to be exported without restrictions. Trump revoked the waivers on July 7, citing Iranian attacks on vessels that had failed to comply with its control over the Strait of Hormuz, a control that the United States had implicitly accepted under Provision 5.
Legitimizing Israeli occupation of Lebanon
Given its enormous importance to Iran, Provision 1 of the memorandum called for “the immediate and permanent cessation of hostilities on all fronts, including Lebanon.” The provision did not specifically focus on Iran and the United States, but rather on their allies: Hezbollah, aligned with Iran, and Israel, America's staunchest ally in the world.
Nevertheless, the Zionist regime continued its aggression and the wholesale destruction of civilian infrastructure in southern Lebanon, on a scale comparable to what the regime's occupation forces had done in Gaza.
Some might argue that the United States was not in a position to impose the memorandum’s provisions on Israel. Even if that were true, Trump should not have signed a memorandum implicitly committing him to do so.
The Trump administration went a step further, taking measures to legitimize the Israeli regime's occupation of Lebanon.
“The memorandum stipulated that the Israelis had to leave Lebanon. We made no effort to achieve that. On the contrary, Marco Rubio mediated an agreement between the Lebanese government and Israel to jointly attack Hezbollah. What is that, then? At the very least, it was an unwise course of action,” Freeman pointed out.
More importantly, Trump’s conduct strengthens the credibility of the Iranian government and armed forces, who have long argued that Washington cannot be trusted and that negotiations should be backed up by military readiness.
The Saudi-U.S. nuclear deal
Trump’s repudiation of agreements has not been limited to adversaries of the United States who have been hit by his sudden reversals of terms he himself had accepted. Take Saudi Arabia for example.
On July 22, U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright and his Saudi counterpart, Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman, signed an agreement allowing the kingdom to build nuclear reactors and enrich uranium using American technology.
Both governments issued official statements, and the agreement was hailed as a victory for Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman.
The very next morning, Trump stunned, indeed, blindsided, the Saudis and his own officials with a social-media post adding a major condition retroactively: there would be no nuclear agreement unless Saudi Arabia joined the “Abraham Accords,” which entail recognizing the occupying regime's legitimacy and establishing formal diplomatic relations.
Trump’s demand that Saudi Arabia move closer to Israel comes at a time when Muslims in the kingdom and throughout the Islamic world are outraged by the regime's destruction of Gaza and southern Lebanon, making such a demand politically risky for the Saudi royal family.
Contrary to the agreement signed by his own energy secretary, Trump also suddenly announced that there would be no enrichment of nuclear material inside Saudi Arabia.
“Trump makes a deal, signs it, announces it, boasts about it, and within 24 hours radically changes its terms,” observed Trita Parsi, executive vice president of the Quincy Institute, on the Deep Dive podcast. “If this is what he will do to Saudi Arabia, a country with which the United States has extremely close relations… and with which the Trump family also has very close business ties, what will he do to Iran? How long is any U.S. commitment to Iran under Trump actually valid under any agreement?”
More recently, Ambassador Freeman told Colonel Davis: “We have convinced the entire world that we do not know what we are doing, that we cannot be trusted, that we do not keep our promises, and that we do not even maintain a consistent position from one day to the next. So how can anyone deal with us? That is the question everyone is asking.”
Alastair Crooke, a former British intelligence officer and diplomat, believes that American diplomacy may never return to what it was.
Summarizing the impact of Trump’s multi-front assault on confidence in the United States, Crooke said on Norwegian academic Glenn Diesen’s podcast: "I think the U.S. capacity to negotiate in the traditional diplomatic sense is over. I mean, we are in a new era!"

Once upon a time, insects had 24 legs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
15:00:00 UTC
00:00:00 KST

Once upon a time, insects had 24 legs
This ancient oddball fills a major gap in the fossil record
Insects are famous for their six-legged body plan, but that wasn’t always the rule. A 324-million-year-old fossil dug up from a shale bed in West Texas had a markedly different setup, sporting a whopping 18 extra legs along its belly — a body plan unlike that of any living insect.
It is one of the oddest insects ever found, and possibly the most consequential, researchers report August 26 in Nature.
The discovery “straddles a big gap in the fossil record,” says paleoentomologist Erik Tihelka of the University of Cambridge. It offers a glimpse of the transition from many-legged, shrimplike ancestors to the six-legged insects of today. “It shows that there were these transitional forms along the way,” he says, before insects shed their extra legs and settled on six.
Tihelka and his team named the fossil Chosha praecursor. It is inspired by the Navajo creation myth, in which a primordial world was inhabited by insectlike people whose descendants went on to populate Earth, combining the Navajo word for “insect” (ch’osh) with the Latin for “predecessor.”
For decades, however, the fossil bore a different name. Collected from a rocky outcrop north of Big Bend National Park in 1985, the specimen was initially mistaken for a juvenile of a crustacean called Tesnusocaris goldichi, found in the same dark shale. Researchers saw little significance in the find, and it languished in a museum drawer in San Diego for years.
Then Tihelka spotted a line drawing of the fossil in a Russian paleontology textbook he had bought secondhand. He tracked down the original papers, but the specimen’s supposed identity as a crustacean didn’t sit right with him. He traveled to the San Diego Museum of Natural History to see it for himself.
At first glance, the unassuming fossil resembled little more than a “black smudge,” Tihelka recalls. But by peering at it through polarized light filters, which cut the glare and sharpened contrast, he could make out a series of anatomical details that all pointed toward insects: a three-segmented thorax; an extended abdomen with 11 sections; whiplike antennae; a long central tail flanked by two shorter ones; a stiff tube for laying eggs; and, of course, three pairs of walking legs.
There was just one, tiny hangup. The Chosha fossil had nine extra pairs of short, stubby legs on its abdomen, the rear ones ending in flattened, grooved paddles. These paddles may have helped the insects swim or scuttle through muddy shallow seas.
What struck Tihelka was that he had seen other fossils like it, including a 405-million-year-old specimen from Scotland and an undescribed pair of multi-legged, insectlike fossils from the Mazon Creek beds of Illinois.
Comparing the bodies of these ancient oddballs with known insects and crustaceans, both living and extinct, more closely, Tihelka could see that Chosha and the other fossils all landed same place. They all sat just outside the group containing every insect alive today, with crustaceans a distant branch away.
The picture that emerges, then, is of Chosha and its many-legged kin, with their extra limbs and paddlelike appendages, living semi-aquatic lifestyles. Somewhere along the way, one such protoinsect presumably made the leap onto land full-time, shedding the surplus legs until only six remained. That terrestrial ancestor then gave rise to the millions of insect species on Earth today.
“It’s a funny thing,” Tihelka says. “We call insects ‘hexapods,’ meaning six legs. But it turns out that the original ones had many more.”
For all its strangeness, though, Chosha may offer a surprisingly straightforward explanation for how insects made the leap from water to land. “This fossil is a major milestone in a puzzling period when everything was changing from mostly aquatic to terrestrial, and we had almost no fossil evidence from that time,” says Dany Azar, a paleoentomologist at Lebanese University in Fanar and the Nanjing Institute of Geology and Palaeontology in China.
“It opens a lot of doors to the study of insect evolution,” says William Shear, a retired paleobiologist from Hampden-Sydney College in Virginia. “And one can only hope that more fossils of this particular organism will turn up upon further searching.”

Early trial of "common cold" vaccine candidate shows encouraging signs
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
22:59:50 CST
23:59:50 KST

LONDON, Aug. 26 (Xinhua) -- A vaccine candidate designed to protect against rhinoviruses, which cause the great majority of common colds and exacerbate chronic respiratory illnesses, has shown encouraging early results in a Phase 1 clinical trial, Imperial College London said Wednesday.
Initial findings suggested that the candidate, known as APL-10456, was well tolerated in healthy volunteers and that a single dose generated immune responses against all three major rhinovirus species.
The vaccine was developed through a collaboration between Imperial and biopharmaceutical company Apollo Therapeutics, building on years of research led by Sebastian Johnston, a professor of respiratory medicine and allergy at Imperial's National Heart and Lung Institute.
Since 2017, Imperial researchers and Apollo have evaluated and refined different vaccine approaches. More than 20 preclinical studies conducted with contract research organization VirTus Respiratory Research Ltd helped identify the candidate and produced evidence supporting its progression to human testing.
Enrollment and dosing have been completed in the randomized, placebo-controlled Phase 1 trial involving 144 healthy participants, according to the university.
The first stage assessed the safety, tolerability and immune response of APL-10456 in healthy participants and evaluated three single-dose levels in adults aged between 18 and 54. The second stage is evaluating a two-dose regimen in adults aged 55 and above, with further data expected in the fourth quarter of 2026.
There are around 180 rhinovirus strains across three species -- A, B and C -- making them a difficult target for vaccine development. Although most infections cause a mild common cold, the viruses are a major cause of flare-ups in people with asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, or COPD. No targeted antiviral treatment or vaccine for rhinovirus infection has yet been approved.
"It is very encouraging to see this progress into clinical results, which follow years of research and development," Johnston said.
However, further clinical research is needed to determine whether APL-10456 can prevent rhinovirus infections or reduce illness in people with asthma, COPD and other respiratory conditions. A study involving COPD patients is anticipated to begin in the first half of 2027. ■

Why a Christian group is suing the Dutch government for West Bank trade ban
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
14:59:22 UTC
23:59:22 KST

Why a Christian group is suing the Dutch government for West Bank trade ban
The Israeli Product Centre says it has not been given enough time to sell off its stock of wine from illegal Israeli settlements.
Dutch group Christians for Israel is taking the government to court in the Netherlands over its plans to introduce a ban on importing goods from illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank and Golan Heights.
The ban, which was announced in July, is due to take effect on September 22 and will run for three years. It bars importing, buying and selling goods produced in Israeli settlements, as well as intermediary services and any attempt to circumvent the rules.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Israeli forces raid UNRWA training centre in occupied East Jerusalem
- list 2 of 3How Israel’s Netanyahu weaponises religion in his war rhetoric
- list 3 of 3US lawmakers urge Trump team to free American student held by Israel
But the Israel Product Centre (IPC), part of Christians for Israel (CvI), a Dutch evangelical organisation which a recent study found has donated about $300,000 to illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank, has responded by filing summary proceedings against the state, with the hearing due today.
Here’s what we know about this case.
What is the case about?
The IPC has issued summary proceedings against the Dutch state, seeking to block the July decree.
The IPC argues the measure is “one-sided” and that the window it now has to clear its existing stock – some 20,000 bottles of wine – is too short.
It is also arguing that a national ban conflicts with the European Union’s principle of free movement of goods.
A verdict is not expected for about two weeks.
How has this case come about?
EU rules have long required goods from illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank to be labelled by their origin – Palestine – rather than as “product of Israel”, but the bloc has not placed an outright ban on trading with Israeli settlements. That remains up to individual countries.
In February 2020, the Dutch advocacy group DocP urged consumers to file complaints with the Dutch food safety authority, NVWA, if they found wine and Dead Sea cosmetics had been mislabelled.
Following complaints, the IPC changed its labelling to “product uit een Israelisch dorp in Judea & Samaria [product from an Israeli village in Judea and Samaria],” which it argued accurately reflected the exact geographical and administrative reality of the origins of the products without deceiving the buyer. Judea and Samaria is the biblical name used by the Israeli government to refer to the West Bank. DocP argued this fell short of the requirement to label products correctly, and continued its campaign.
In 2021, the NVWA agreed and fined the IPC 2,100 euros (about $2,500) for mislabelling goods.
Then, in July 2024, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) issued an advisory opinion that Israel’s presence in the occupied Palestinian territory is unlawful and must end “as rapidly as possible”.
This shifted the legal argument beyond mere consumer labelling, with the court saying countries should take steps to prevent trade or investment relations which help to maintain the unlawful presence of Israeli settlers in the Palestinian territories.
The lower house of the Dutch parliament acted on that in September 2025, proposing an import ban.
The national decree against importing goods from Israeli settlements was made in July this year.
Does Christians for Israel describe the West Bank as ‘Israel’?
CvI describes the West Bank as a “disputed territory” rather than accepting the international legal description of it as “occupied Palestinian territory”.
It says it believes that Israel has strong claims to sovereignty there and that Jews have a right to live there.
The vocabulary matters in a legal sense, as “disputed territory” is not the same as “annexed territory”, therefore, the legal apparatus which would make settlement trade unlawful doesn’t straightforwardly apply.
The group’s stated reasons for funding projects there, it says on its website, are rooted in the Bible; it cites Ezekiel 47:21-23: “Peace for the Jewish people and resident foreigners inheriting alongside the tribes of Israel.”
However, the ICJ’s July 2024 advisory opinion is clear that the Fourth Geneva Convention’s Article 49(6) and successive Security Council resolutions treat the territories as occupied and the settlements as unlawful.
How have other Christian organisations in the West responded to trade with settlements?
Western churches are split on the issue, with CvI sitting at one end of the spectrum.
Mainline Protestants, including the Presbyterian Church in the United States, have divested shareholdings in Caterpillar, HP and Motorola Solutions as early as 2014, and from Israeli bonds in 2024. The United Methodist Church has opposed Israeli settlements since 1996 and sold its Israeli bond holdings last August.
The World Council of Churches called for sanctions against illegal Israeli settlements in 2025, divestment and an arms embargo.
The Vatican calls settlements an obstacle to peace but has avoided divestment so far.
Christian Zionist bodies, however, including Christians United for Israel (CUFI) and the International Christian Embassy Jerusalem, send funding for settlements and fight against boycotts.
How significant is this ban?
It is significant considering that the Netherlands is one of only four EU countries currently imposing a ban on trade with illegal Israeli settlements.
Trade from illegal settlements to the EU is estimated to be worth up to $400m per year.
The Netherlands is also a big market for the illegal settlements; a recent investigation by legal advocacy group Global Echo, which analysed thousands of shipments from Israeli settlements between 2017 and 2026, shows that within the EU, the Dutch market is the largest importer of goods from illegal settlements, with about 30 percent destined for or passing through the country.
Which European countries have banned products from West Bank settlements?
Spain has banned all imports of products from illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied Palestinian territory, including the West Bank, East Jerusalem and the Golan Heights, since September 2025. The decree also enforces an embargo on defence exports and dual-use technology to Israel, bans ships carrying military fuel for Israel from Spanish ports, and restricts advertising for services or goods linked to Israeli settlements.
Ireland’s parliament approved the text of its Israeli Settlements (Prohibition of Importation of Goods) Bill in May and the bill was signed into law in July. It covers all goods produced in Israeli settlements, but excludes services.
Belgium’s federal government approved a draft royal decree in July introducing a specific regime for goods from Israeli settlements in the West Bank and East Jerusalem. The precise details of the new law will be determined by the government in due course.
Slovenia imposed restrictions on imports from Israeli settlements under its previous government, but the new conservative government reversed them in June 2026.
The EU as a bloc remains deadlocked over whether a ban counts as foreign policy requiring unanimity or trade policy needing only a qualified majority, with ministers not meeting again in a decision-making format until October.
Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar last year described the push by some European governments to implement the ICJ advisory opinion as “shameful”.
Which European countries still allow trade with West Bank settlements?
Nearly all of them.
Outside the three European Union states which still have bans in place, settlement goods can be sold legally everywhere, including in most of the EU.
At a July 2026 meeting of EU foreign ministers in Brussels, which addressed trade from Israeli settlements in Palestinian territories, Germany, Austria, Czechia and Hungary were opposed to an EU-wide ban.
Beyond the EU, the United Kingdom does not forbid trade with illegal Israeli settlements, although new Prime Minister Andy Burnham is reportedly considering a ban. In a recent parliamentary briefing, Amnesty International called on the UK government to implement a ban.
It said: “The argument for a UK ban on trade with settlements is clear. The UK government itself accepts it should take stronger action in response to settlement expansion and annexation. The International Court of Justice has directed states not to trade with Israel in relation to the Occupied Palestinian Territory; and there is precedent in UK law and policy to not trade with illegally occupied lands, ie Crimea and other illegally occupied parts of Ukraine.”

Bahrain re-arrests human rights defender Naji Fateel two years after royal pardon
